This paper explores an approach to addressing convergence issues that arise from the discretization of certain stochastic control problems, specifically those involving rough paths and slow paths. By establishing a link between these problems and their continuous equivalents, we demonstrate the importance of analyzing convergence in a modified context that accounts for varying levels of regularity. Key components of our findings include: (1) an investigation of the convergence of adapted rough path rough controls, accompanied by a key convergence result for these controls; (2) a definition of extended Young integrals, enabling the extension of classical Young's inequality to settings involving different levels of regularity; (3) application of our methods to a specific optimal control problem on the real line. Ultimately, our research enables the validation of schemes for approximating critical points in related stochastic control problems. An analysis of cosmic ray anisotropy at energies exceeding 4 EeV has revealed a previously undetected dipole amplitude in the Northern Hemisphere. The under-explored sky map around the direction of Ursa Major in the sidereal system now requires further investigation in the energy range between 4 to 40 EeV. The study presented here extends that work by incorporating six years of data from the TAHD array and compares the results before and after removing local contamination from the data. The findings before removal show a significant anisotropy at a 4.8 sigma confidence level with a dipole amplitude of about 0.16%; this anisotropy is oriented at 125 degrees inclination and 21 degrees east-longitude. The location of the anisotropy remains substantial but its amplitude drops to a 2.5 sigma confidence level and a dipole amplitude of about 0.058% after removing local contamination. However, the orientation of the anisotropy undergoes a notable shift to 175 degrees inclination and 47 degrees east-longitude. It is also observed that the anisotropy around the Ursa Major direction in the Northern Hemisphere exhibits an energy dependence on cosmic ray energies between 4 to 40 EeV. The anisotropy at lower energies displays an energy dependence similar to that of cosmic rays at intermediate energies, as opposed to the little dependence seen in very high energy cosmic rays. The anisotropy itself however disappears above 29 EeV in the energy range studied here. It is also discovered that the anisotropy around the Ursa Major direction in the Northern Hemisphere exhibits an annual modulation in the energy range between 4 to 40 EeV, with a maximum anisotropy amplitude occurring in October-November and minimum in May-June. The location of the anisotropy also exhibits an annual modulation in both longitude and latitude, with the anisotropy shifting towards the east and decreasing in latitude from October-November to May-June. It is hypothesized that the local interference may be responsible for the annual modulation observed in the anisotropy around the Ursa Major direction in the Northern Hemisphere, with the shift in the anisotropy's direction and latitude occurring in sync with the change in the Earth's right ascension and the direction of the Ursa Major anisotropy corresponding to that of the Earth's direction towards the anisotropy's source in the sky. Our study examines how the centrality of lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV and lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV influence the variation of the nuclear modification factor, with a focus on low-momentum charged particles. Initially, we find an increase in the variation of $NSD/\pi$ among different centrality ranges in both sets of collisions, with the variation sensitive to the centrality of collisions. In mid-central collisions, this increase is linked to diverse initial conditions resulting from varying neutron loss at different research centers, which is corroborated by comparisons between different research centers and averaged data. Notably, this variation is more pronounced at 2.76 TeV and is largely eliminated when comparing research center data at the same neutrals loss at 5.02 TeV. Additionally, we observe an enhancement in the variation of $NSD/\pi$ when comparing research center data at the same neutrals loss at both collision energies, which is attributed to distinct initial condition evolution in mid-central collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. In more central and peripheral collisions, additional factors such as flow influence the variation of $NSD/\pi$. Our analysis suggests that research center dependencies in heavy ion physics can provide valuable insights into the interplay between diverse initial conditions and medium response in heavy ion collisions.

We've reexamined noncommutative quantum mechanics with position and momentum coordinates expressed as differential operators that commute with each other. Our analysis shows that this system is equivalent to standard commutative quantum mechanics and we derive the relationship between these operators in terms of functions of a commuting momentum space, with corresponding potentials defined in a way that maintains mathematical consistency. Furthermore, we've established the general form of Hermitian operators within this context and applied this understanding to solve a specific scattering problem involving harmonic potentials. Our approach also facilitates the direct computation of wave function normalization constants and time-dependent positions within this noncommutative setup. Notably, we've discovered that the deformed coordinates can be expressed in terms of ordinary differential operator exponentials, and we relate our work to other proposals existing in the scientific literature. Our methods offer a direct new approach for tackling general quantum mechanical problems in this noncommutative setting.

Accurate cancer characterization through histopathology relies on human technicians who manually inspect and interpret tissue samples. Their judgments are based on visual assessments which can be subjective and only capture a snapshot of the tumor environment. To fully understand cancer, it is essential to comprehensively analyze tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, which involve complex processes such as tissue digitization, feature extraction, and statistical analysis. This paper focuses on the latter two processes, particularly evaluating various digitization methods and extracting features from images using different techniques. It reviews common approaches to digitization, including grid-based and hierarchical methods, and evaluates their accuracy in detecting lymphocyte cells by conducting experiments on actual tissue samples. It also examines different extraction methods, including mathematical and biological features, and assesses their effectiveness using statistical analysis on actual lymphocyte cells, further exploring hierarchical analysis through multidimensional scaling. This research is an initial step towards a comprehensive cancer characterization, which will ultimately pave the way for better cancer monitoring and treatment through more effective visualization and reporting of clinical findings to medical professionals. It also includes a cancer characterization system to illustrate its concepts and demonstrate the overall process from tissue sampling to analysis and reporting. This system is designed to be adaptable to various cancer types by incorporating expert judgments and medical knowledge. It is available online at https://github.com/alexliao1/Cancer-Characterization-System. This work is part of the author's PhD research at the University of British Columbia under the supervision of Dr. Edwin K. Lee. It has been publicly accessible on arXiv since 2020. To provide a clear overview, the paper has undergone significant revisions incorporating valuable feedback from three anonymous reviewers. It is now published in the IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging after a thorough review process. Despite its comprehensive nature, this paper is intended to serve as a foundational guide for cancer characterization, which remains an ongoing research area in the community. It is essential to continue developing and refining the proposed methods, especially expert judgment and data analysis, to provide a more precise and comprehensive cancer characterization, ultimately contributing to cancer monitoring and better treatment through effective visualization and reporting of clinical findings to medical professionals. It is also necessary to adapt the cancer characterization system to various cancer types, incorporating expert judgments and medical knowledge, and making it publicly available for the community's benefit. To enhance the performance of optical communication systems prone to burst errors, we integrated the joint Weak Signal Detection Filtered Equalizer and Maximum Likelihood Sequence Estimator (WDFE-MLSE) method into a coherent optical direct detection system. The WDFE-MLSE system used a new trellis structure and scoring function to compensate for signal phase and amplitude distortions caused by the receiver's nonlinear response. When comparing the WDFE-MLSE system to the conventional WDFE system, simulations showed that the WDFE-MLSE system can correct up to 17 gusts of errors, whereas the WDFE system can only correct single-bit errors. Furthermore, the WDFE-MLSE system had a 2.5 dB advantage in signal-to-bit-error ratio over the WDFE system when receiving weak signals with moderate channel attenuation. Additionally, the WDFE-MLSE system outperformed the maximum-likelihood sequence estimator using the Viterbi algorithm by 9 dB in signal-to-bit-error ratio when receiving weak signals with high channel attenuation. The WDFE-MLSE system's ability to correct burst errors makes it an effective method for improving the weak signal performance in optical communication systems. The system's weak signal performance can be further enhanced by using a higher-quality photodetector, but this would increase system cost. However, using a higher-quality photodetector can provide up to 11 dB gain in signal-to-bit-error ratio when receiving strong signals with high channel attenuation, making it a worthwhile investment despite the higher cost. The WDFE-MLSE system's ability to correct burst errors and its weak and strong signal performance make it an attractive solution for optical communication systems prone to errors caused by signal phase and amplitude distortions, burst errors, and varying signal intensities. Time-Convolutional Networks (TCNs) have made significant progress in various sequence understanding tasks, however most current approaches still rely on TCNs with fixed dilation factors and network depths. This typically requires extensive experimentation and tuning to achieve optimal performance. In this research, we introduce an Automatic Dilation Optimizer (ADO) for TCNs, enabling autonomous dilation pattern design during training. ADO succeeds in enhancing the efficiency of TCNs in both model size and inference latency, without compromising accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that ADO outperforms manual optimization across multiple benchmark datasets, and its efficiency gains are substantial, resulting in model size reductions of up to 13.8 and inference latency decreases of up to 38.6. Our evaluations also show that ADO's efficient designs generalize well across tasks, leading to average performance improvements of 1.1% across 0.1 to 5% compression ratios. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/NJUAS-TCN-AO for reproducibility purposes. Our ADO approach redefines the optimization of TCNs, establishing a new benchmark for the community to build upon. It is only compatible with PyTorch at this time. Our ADO-based models have been successfully deployed in real-world applications at Alimama, a leading e-commerce company.

We establish that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra in a universal enveloping algebra of a simple Lie algebra is solvable and nilpotent. This achievement expands on previous findings regarding the dimensionality of these algebras. Furthermore, we prove that certain 3-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, initially discovered by Shen and Wang, constitute all possible finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras when these algebras are defined over an algebraically closed field and have a specific simple Jordan triple product. Shen and Wang had previously unknown motivations for their discovery of those algebras. Our research reveals that they were, in fact, inspired by the free Zinbiel algebras and their relationship with free Lie algebras. Lastly, our theory includes an explicit computation of the first Cohom group of the free Zinbiel algebra on one generator. This result arises from a particular extension of the first Cohom group of the free Lie algebra on one generator and demonstrates that the Zinbiel algebras that extend the free Zinbiel algebra on one generator are in a direct relationship with the elements of one weight of the first Cohom group of the free Lie algebra on one generator. This research expands our understanding of the relationship between Lie algebras and Zinbiel algebras, specifically free and finite-dimensional algebras. This concept is particularly useful in databases managed by multiple users with different access permissions. A new approach has been proposed, utilizing four values to represent more accurate and consistent query results. This method ensures that queries return values indicating the basis for their validity, such as consistency with all provided data or with data that has been implicitly inferred. However, existing four-valued logic methods rely on advanced algebraic operations for databases that use relational structures. In contrast, this study develops the first four-valued logic query language for databases with tuple structure, building upon established three-valued logic principles by adding a undefined-can-be-defined value. Furthermore, this new value enables queries to differentiate between tuples that are known to be false (represented by the f value) and those whose falsity is derivable, allowing for additional expression of queries regarding the implicit definition of tuples as false. A formal analysis demonstrates that the proposed language is computationally equivalent to first-order logic with equality when considering databases that contain no null values, further illustrating its capability to express complex queries. We introduce the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel extension of the Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (PARX) model. TV-PARX effectively addresses complex issues like nonlinear dynamics and sudden changes in rates by allowing its parameters to change over time. A TV-PARX estimation method is proposed, which leverages B-splines to impose smoothness constraints on the variables and adapt them to locate structural breaks. The proposed method is evaluated through simulations and real-world applications, including a case study of an insurance company with changing loss rates and a medical study examining the effectiveness of interventions on disease rates. Additionally, TV-PARX provides a suitable framework for modeling time-varying intensities in point process data. The implementation of TV-PARX is made possible by the R software environment and the Shiny web framework, with the tvparx R package allowing for flexible point estimation methods and graphical diagnostics. Inspired by human manipulation, researchers have been attempting to automate tasks like object rearrangement and assembly using robotic hands. While advances in machine learning have simplified this process by limiting the requirement for extensive task training, there's still a significant gap to bridge when it comes to learning from very few demonstrations. Current methods typically assume a high degree of doability for demonstrated actions and overlook the ability to generalise to new starting states or objects, which is a crucial aspect of human skill transfer. This research introduces Neural Descriptor Fields, a novel framework that represents tasks as dynamic relationships between objects and allows the learning of complex manipulation tasks from only a small number of demonstrations. By linking object features to a task-specific graph and using graph convolutions, the field can capture the dynamic aspects of tasks. It uses a decoder network to produce a structured loss function, enabling the learning of actionable predictions from only a small number of demonstrations. Experimentation shows that Neural Descriptor Fields can generalise easily to new starting configurations and objects, surpassing the performance of baseline policies that have been trained on the same tasks. Additionally, it demonstrates the ability to learn from just a single demonstration when the task involves interacting with multiple objects. This work also introduces a new dataset called TIO (Task-Independent Object manipulation) that consists of 12 distinct manipulation tasks, with multiple starting configurations and objects, and is available for download at this link https://sites.google.com/view/neural-descriptor-fields. The code for this research can be found at this link https://github.com Facebook/Neural-Descriptor-Fields. All data, experiments, and models have been carefully stored in this repository, along with a fully functional example notebook that shows the full workflow of this work. A detailed analysis of the metal-rich globular cluster Tononzintla 2, located in the Virgo cluster, has yielded interesting findings. Based on the study of 704 red giant members, researchers discovered a higher degree of elemental dispersion within the cluster, exceeding the average spread seen in other richly metalized Galactic clusters like Omega Centauri. Furthermore, Tononzintla 2 exhibits a composition that is equally as enriched as Omega Centauri, with an overall metal content of [Fe/H] equaling -0.62. Notably, the cluster's metallicity distribution exhibits a broad range, extending from -0.09 to -0.94, with multiple distinct peaks. In contrast to Omega Centauri's primarily bimodal metal distribution, researchers found a more pronounced multi-modal structure within Tononzintla 2's metallicity framework. In addition, the cluster's chemical composition reveals a complex pattern, featuring multiple overlapping features that include enhanced levels of magnesium, aluminum, and scandium, as well as a spread in carbon levels, and a metal distribution that mirrors a condition seen in the cluster's central regions. Based on its unique metal composition and the overlap with Omega Centauri's metal envelope, researchers suggest that Tononzintla 2 may have originated from the same parent system that gave rise to the Southern Large Magellanic Cloud's metal-rich globular clusters, specifically those found in the Magellanic Clouds' metal-rich population, which is thought to have originated from the cluster's interaction with the SMC during a gravitational encounter. Additionally, researchers propose that Tononzintla 2 may have originated from a stellar group that interacted with the SMC's dense core, potentially leading to the cluster's unique metal composition. In conclusion, Tononzintla 2 offers an extraordinary opportunity to examine the development of multiple generations of stars within a richly metalized cluster setting. This study analyzes the underlying structure of the dependency graph in the Formal Archive of Fundamental Theories (FAFT) by calculating key network characteristics and comparing them to those of scale-free distributions commonly found in scientific publications, including the dependency graphs of topologists and field theorists. As the FAFT continues to grow, its dependency graphs will provide valuable insights into the development of formal proof libraries and the effectiveness of reasoning tools in mathematics. Additionally, considering the increasing importance of assessing the evolution of knowledge, this research offers a framework for exploring other large datasets in the future. This finding is unique to the AMP algorithm among approximate message passing methods. Recent advancements in the design of metasurfaces have been significant, with their potential to create compact, adaptive, and multifunctional devices. A key factor behind their success lies in the generalized sheet transition conditions, which provide a link between the surface and its interacting fields, thus enabling robust parametric modeling of metasurfaces. However, the availability and accuracy of backward wave data are major constraints in the design process. This paper proposes an efficient framework for designing metasurfaces from scratch, leveraging their parametric form and incorporating uncertainty into numerical data to minimize trial and error in finding suitable designs. The framework is applied to the design of two holographic antennas and achieves local optimizations with minimal expertise. Notably, it is shown that often, optimal designs can be found among the initial guesses, and the proposed uncertainty-based approach can lead to even better performances. Moreover, the complexity of forward problems makes it more feasible to use approximate closed-form expressions for GSTCs in numerical simulations. The proposed framework is now available online as an interactive design tool at https://www.gpmetasurface.com. This website enables users to upload their own surface data and interactively design metasurfaces, ultimately accelerating the development of cutting-edge holographic antenna technologies. As such, it provides the community with a valuable resource for further exploring the capabilities and limitations of metasurfaces. 

This paper differs from the previously cited paper [1] in that it presents an even more streamlined approach to modeling metasurfaces, focuses on their design rather than analysis, and introduces uncertainty into numerical data to avoid overreliance on specialized software. Consequently, it offers a more general framework that is both more accessible to the community and more suitable for high-level design iterations.

As a result, this model eliminates the finite basis set size as a source of error and achieves more accurate electron densities and energies than its angular central potential neural network counterpart. Our investigation of two-electron systems demonstrated that the equalized central polar neural network can determine the ground state and its associated energy with very high precision, performing essentially identically to the full Hartree-Fock reference standard. This method doesn't depend on the absolute calibration of photometric data and instead utilizes relative measurements from various satellites and the Earth's shadow technique. An initial estimation of the aerosol optical density in the vertical direction was developed using the Radiative Transfer Vector Element Discrimination method. We propose an approach called projection grouping, which identifies and links projected points across different poses, enabling more accurate pose estimation in complex scenarios. By incorporating super-parsing and super-retrieval techniques, our method successfully handles instances with limited training data. This efficiency enables us to handle multiple poses with ease. Experimental evaluations on the AMPs dataset demonstrate substantial performance gains, with an overall success rate of 84.2% compared to the baseline algorithm of 26.8%. Moreover, our approach outperforms existing methods dealing with occlusions and shadows. The traditional theory of elasticity is enhanced by peridynamics, a novel approach that focuses on materials with micro-cracks. This method involves introducing a non-local bonding force between material points that are at a distance less than a given threshold, known as the bond-slip distance. Researchers have explored various structures for the peridynamic kernel, and in this study, we investigate two specific forms: a constant traction bond-slip kernel and a linear bond-slip kernel. By analyzing these kernels, we demonstrate that the linear bond-slip kernel can be represented as an integral of the constant traction bond-slip kernel over multiple layers. This discovery enables us to apply the linear bond-slip kernel to model cracks within materials by dividing the domain into thin layers and defining a constant traction bond-slip force within each layer. This approach results in a system of integral equations that can be solved for the crack surface within each layer, and subsequently, the total crack surface throughout the entire domain can be determined. Finally, we validate our linearization method against the original linear bond-slip kernel in the limit of infinitesimally small layer thickness. This analysis provides insight into the linear bond-slip kernel's behavior and facilitates the solution of crack problems by simplifying the complex linear bond-slip kernel to a constant traction bond-slip kernel for each individual layer. This approach can also be applied to other crack problems that involve different force laws within each layer. Moreover, our method offers an alternative way to solve crack problems by dividing the domain into thin layers, and it is an essential companion to our earlier work, where we linearized the linear bond-slip kernel to demonstrate that its behavior is similar to that of the Michaelis-Menten kernel. This comparison enables us to apply the results from our earlier work to the current crack problems. Lastly, we conclude this study by exploring its broader implications for nonlinear mechanics, particularly in relation to the Michaelis-Menten kernel's applicability to biological systems. This analysis includes a discussion of potential applications to enzyme kinetics and non-local damage theories within materials science. Our new model includes a series of nested sparse graphs, and through careful analysis, we established the consistency of its estimators and provided updated Bayesian information criteria for model selection. Furthermore, GLSC outperformed the standard Graphical Lasso approach as well as a model that assumes latent variables are observed, as demonstrated by our simulations and real-world applications. Specifically, our results showed that GLSC yields higher accuracy and better precision in network estimation, as evaluated through the area under the ROC curve and mean absolute error, respectively. Additionally, GLSC proved particularly effective in scenarios with a limited number of observations and small sample sizes. We have also established the feasibility of estimating GLSC models using an iterative Lasso approach and made our software freely available for public use. Ultimately, our work offers an enhanced Graphical Lasso framework that facilitates the identification of multiple, nested sparse graph architectures. This, in turn, may help to further develop the field of network estimation itself. In our accompanying technical report, we outline the rationale and key aspects of our research in greater detail. This paper examines the challenge of corruption in reinforcement learning, specifically when an intelligent adversary has control over certain episodes. We introduce the Filtered Policy Gradient algorithm, which is resistant to this type of sabotage and provide a learning guarantee showing that it achieves a reliable optimal policy. Notably, our method is efficient, requiring only a single value function estimator per action under optimal conditions. We demonstrate the feasibility of the algorithm by applying it to a range of scenarios, including games against an adversary manipulating state transitions and when there are multiple adverse agents. Interestingly, we found that a key underlying dynamic, presence of a unique optimal action under optimal conditions, is a crucial factor in learning efficiency. Interestingly, this presence of a unique optimal action under optimal conditions is not always guaranteed in complex games like poker. Consequently, we investigated methods to relax this assumption, demonstrating that the algorithm performance degenerates to the baseline when the assumption is violated. Moreover, we explored an alternative approach using an adversary model, which facilitates the use of corrupted transitions in online learning. We evaluated our algorithm in multi-ADP scenarios and found that the Filtered Policy Gradient algorithm outperforms baseline methods, including the standard policy gradient algorithm, PPG, and FPG without filtering. Additionally, we observed significant improvements in complex game settings, achieving a notable return gain of over 500 in a critical game. The source code for our algorithm is openly available online.

This study proposes a cutting-edge algorithm named Dilated Dense Attention Unet for automatically segmenting esophageal tumors from MRI images. The baseline model, Unet, has been widely applied in medical image processing but is limited in handling complex tumor cases by itself. To enhance tumor detection accuracy, the Dilated Dense Attention Unet was developed to focus attention on difficult image regions by incorporating dense attention layers. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of Dilated Dense Attention Unet in comparison to the baseline model, Unet, by conducting experiments on a newly collected dataset of esophageal cancer cases and assessing the generalizability of the algorithms across different imaging modalities and pre-processing techniques. The comparison showed that Dilated Dense Attention Unet significantly improved tumor segmentation accuracy by reducing the mean surface distance from 5.08 to 3.76 when compared to Unet. The findings also demonstrated the robustness of the algorithm in detecting tumors on cases with varying degrees of difficulty and imaging modalities with different resolutions. Furthermore, the code for the algorithm is now publicly accessible on GitHub, along with the data and experiments described in this study. However, due to the large file size, the esophageal cancer dataset cannot be shared as a single file. The dataset comprises over 150 MRI cases (axial, coronal, and sagittal images) acquired at two different resolution levels (isotropic 0.7mm, and 0.35mm respectively) and can be obtained individually in 10GB chunks due to size constraints. The code for the algorithm in Python, along with the code for the Deep Learning framework Pytorch, is also available in 10GB chunks and therefore cannot be shared as a single file either. Therefore, the code for the algorithm is being made openly accessible and is available for use in the community at GitHub. However, due to size constraints, the dataset itself cannot be openly shared as a single file, but it can be obtained in 10GB chunks along with the code for the algorithm. Therefore, anyone interested is requested to contact the corresponding author directly to obtain the dataset in 10GB chunks along with the code for the algorithm. It is worth mentioning that the algorithm's code has been successfully run on an NVIDIA V100 16GB GPU but it cannot be guarantees that it will run on lower-end GPUs due to the algorithm's complexity. It is also important to note that the algorithm has been successfully tested on over 150 esophageal cancer cases but its performance on other medical image datasets has not been evaluated

Real-time formation evaluation is crucial in oil and gas well operations and is typically performed using a method called dynamic radial systems modeling (DRS). However, this approach has limitations when dealing with complex reservoir geometries and transverse variability. An alternative method, based on linearized models (LM), addresses these challenges but requires significant computational time to match observed pressures during well testing. To balance speed and accuracy, we present a new limited-memory extension of the nonlinear least-squares method (EnRML) that splits the reservoir into small zones and applies LM on each one. This approach preserves the accuracy of nonlinear models while reducing computational time. Numerical tests using actual well data and a synthetic case demonstrate that the new method matches the accuracy of nonlinear models while minimizing computational time. The limited-memory variation further enhances efficiency by limiting the number of past iterations, making it suitable for real-time applications and capable of handling complex reservoir scenarios. The new method's efficiency and efficacy make it an attractive option for real-time formation evaluation systems. Furthermore, this approach may be an appropriate starting point for future nonlinear methods seeking to tackle fully coupled reservoir models. Additionally, we believe that this method has value in other applications involving small-scale nonlinear systems and time-series data. To facilitate adoption, an open-source implementation of the method is also available online. Nevertheless, to fully realize the method's potential, there is a need for more efficient and adaptable nonlinear solvers that can handle large crosswell reservoir models in the energy industry. This study undertakes a theoretical examination of the named entity recognition task from a machine learning perspective, with a focus on the impact of corpus-level knowledge on model performance. It develops a series of theoretical NER systems, each incorporating varying levels of corpus information, ranging from none to all available data, and evaluates their effectiveness through both human annotation and large-scale corpus data. The findings indicate that the ideal approach depends on available data, with an NER system leveraging domain-specific knowledge achieving the highest accuracy. However, this research is currently presented in a form that is not easily reproducible due to limitations in accessibility. Consequently, the work is being re-examined with a focus on practical applications, particularly using the SpaCy NER tool, with initial results showing a 5.3% improvement in F-score on the CONLL 2002 dataset after fine-tuning on additional corpus data. These improvements can be generalized across other NER datasets, with an example showing a similar improvement of 5.8% on the iTASS 2019 dataset after corpus-level fine-tuning. Moreover, the work is contributing to the development of a named entity annotation toolkit that is both more annotated and has the potential to be more accurate than existing approaches. We consider a tropical quartic K3 surface in the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(2,4)$ and analyze how its bitangents evolve under a change of coordinates. These bitangents may become rational in some cases and irrational in others, with the degree of irrationality depending on a specific tropical divisor. A key finding shows that there exists a vast array of irrational bitangents with a particular topology, forming an infinite number of distinct subsets within the set of all tropical quartic K3 surfaces. Furthermore, this conclusion yields a long-sought example of a non-rational, topologically rational curve in positive characteristic. This new example takes the form of a quartic hypersurface defined over a finite field and is constructed through a process involving Desargues' theorem. Finally, we establish that the rationality of these high-genus curves is closely linked to that of their tropical counterparts. This research is a key step in a broader program aiming to employ tropical geometry to better comprehend and construct more instances of non-rational varieties in positive characteristic. Ultimately, this program seeks to achieve a deeper understanding of the relationships between tropical rationality, geometric rationality, and the rationality of corresponding varieties in positive characteristic. This research is complemented by an exhaustive list of all possible ways in which edges can twist in a tropical quartic curve within the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(2,4)$. This analysis, conducted through a systematic application of tropical normalization, reveals a diverse array of distinct edge configurations, encompassing both rational and irrational cases, along with various intermediate scenarios. Notably, this study identifies an essential distinction between two fundamental types of twisting scenarios in tropical quartic curves: a more intricate type, prevalent within the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(2,4)$, and a simpler type, evident in the tropical K3 surface. This distinction highlights a fundamental geometric principle, where the more complex type of twisting is inherently linked to the presence of a specific geometric attribute and can be comprehensively captured through an appropriately defined tropical divisor. In contrast, all cases of twisting outside of $\mathrm{Gr}(2,4)$ can be comprehensively analyzed through a much more rudimentary framework. Located at the center of the Earth, the anti-podal point with respect to a observer on the surface is difficult to determine precisely without elaborate calculations, however it is intriguing to consider if this task is feasible with the help of neural networks. In this work, we develop a method to approximate the anti-podal point by training a neural decoder that maps coordinates to their antipodes. Although the proposed approach achieves impressive results when tested with artificially generated data, it also effectively localizes points in real-world scenarios, surprisingly even when trained with data from the Earth's surface. Our findings show that when trained with ideal simulation data, the algorithm performs remarkably well with a localization error of just 0.2 degrees. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that neural antipodalization works across various scales and shapes, including spheres of different sizes and irregularly shaped polyhedra. Interestingly, when trained with real-world data without any reference to antipodality, the algorithm still successfully identifies the anti-podal point with a slightly higher error of about 1.5 degrees. This implies that neural networks can somehow intuitively recognize the anti-podal point, and that our method might be applicable to other complex geometric tasks. To contribute positively to these societies, NLP should be a tool that enhances life across multiple languages and promotes cultural inclusivity.  Many proficient non-English speakers face employment and social opportunities being limited due to their language background. The growing popularity of computer vision has been coupled with increasingly accessible image descriptions, mainly through the development of automatic image captioning tools. Yet, visual impairment remains a significant barrier for many individuals, emphasizing the importance of clear and concise image descriptions. Presently, generated captions mostly mirror the technical capabilities of image captioning models, rather than catering to the needs of visually impaired users. There is a lack of comprehensive stylistic guidelines tailored to this audience, probably because creating and evaluating such guidelines is a complex task. This paper introduces a multifaceted set of guidelines for image descriptions, rooted in theories of perception and language use, and also develops various evaluation metrics to assess their practical effectiveness. We examine the impact of adhering to these guidelines on the quality of image descriptions, both through crowdsourced feedback and professional reviewers' assessments. Our findings suggest that following these guidelines leads to more accessible and easier-to-read descriptions, and that users with visual impairments prefer and benefit from these descriptions. Furthermore, even though the technical image captioning model performs well, it does not naturally produce these preferred descriptions. Therefore, we propose a simple yet adaptable framework that combines the technical model with style-based constraints, resulting in more suitable image descriptions for visually impaired users, as validated by user surveys. Our results show that our simple framework yields better outcomes than a fully-fledged generative model, and that the generated captions are preferred by visually impaired users who participated in our study. Additionally, we observed a notable improvement in performance when using the technically superior image captioning model, and that there is considerable room for enhancement in this area. Consequently, we are sharing this research, including the style guidelines and associated datasets, in the hope that it will contribute to the development of more accessible image descriptions that can benefit visually impaired individuals. To accurately calculate energy loss functions for Tantalum oxide layers, particularly near the surface, it is essential to consider both short-range interactions among the electrons and the influence of spin-orbit coupling.  This requirement holds true even in situations where these effects appear minor.  A study employing the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the local density approximation together with the energy loss function formalism has been performed to evaluate energy loss functions of Tantalum oxide in both bulk and surface forms.  Results for both forms are presented in real and momentum space, offering insights into how energy loss evolve with energy from 0 to 800 eV, and how they vary based on the location within the crystal or on the surface.  A comparison with experimental data in the form of electron energy loss spectra is also undertaken to assess the accuracy of the theoretical calculations.  To facilitate replication of these results, the quantities calculated will be made freely available for scientific use.  Moreover, a comparison with data from electron energy loss spectroscopy helps evaluate the validity of these calculations.  To facilitate independent verification, calculated data will be openly accessible for further research.  A noticable feature where our calculated results differ significantly from both experimental data and other theoretical studies is Ta oxide in the bulk form.  Another aspect where our approach proves useful is a scheme for dividing the electron density into localized atomic components, which can be quite beneficial for creating visual representations of the electron cloud at the atomic level.  In our study, this technique has been particularly useful for illustrating how the electron cloud reorganizes itself to accommodate vacancies in the Ta oxide system.  Two particular methods, one based on the Fermi surface topology and the other on charge flow between atoms, have also been employed to identify the orbital types most responsible for contributing to such vacancies.  Interestingly, the outcomes of these two approaches are the same, showing that in both the bulk and surface forms of Ta oxide, the most relevant orbitals are of the d$_{3/2}$ variety.  Additionally, our study has also explored how a Ta oxide layer interacts with nearby Ta oxide molecules through the electron cloud.  This investigation has particularly focused on how energy loss functions are affected when a Ta oxide layer is placed near a Ta metal surface or within a Ta oxide layer on a metal substrate, such as Al or Ta, and how these interactions might be more accurately modeled using a supercell method over alternative approaches. The inherent challenges of machine learning, including resource-intensive computation and costly annotation, have sparked interest in minimalistic approaches that achieve exceptional performance with limited means. Our work focuses on developing a simple, efficient method for small-scale dataset utilization in high-dimensional feature spaces. Unlike conventional transfer learning, our approach doesn't rely on domain matching. Instead, we leverage an unsupervised technique to extract a low-dimensional, representative subset of features with maximum variance from a small, annotated dataset. This feature reduction enables successful deployment of an efficient neural network on a modest computing device, yielding significant improvements over existing methods. Our experiments demonstrate superior performance on unsupervised low-dimensional projection and feature extraction tasks, utilizing extremely small datasets in high-dimensional spaces. Furthermore, our method achieves successful classification on a small dataset within the retina layer of a biological system, using only 10 annotated images per class out of over 1 million possible inputs. A notable computational challenge in quantum field theory is resolving the instanton equation, which is a highly nontrivial diffusion equation with a built-in oblique intersection property. Researchers have made significant progress in solving this equation, specifically in its manifold-based form, which is referred to as the Euler-Arnold equation. A recent study has established that this equation can be solved efficiently by re-expressing it as an optimization problem within the context of Hamiltonian mechanics. This research is an extension of that study, which investigates the Euler-Arnold equation in its full capacity and confirms that it can be solved by converting it into an optimal transport problem. Consequently, this leads to the development of an efficient and straightforward Monte Carlo algorithm for solving the instanton equation. Notably, this novel approach yields an exceptionally high rate of convergence, with an optimal $O(N^2)$ computational complexity for evaluating the instanton equation, where $N$ represents the degree of the manifold. Additionally, Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate the efficacy of this algorithm in determining accurate instanton solutions. It is worth noting that while this algorithm may appear computationally demanding due to its underlying optimal transport framework, it can actually be implemented using a simple and efficient gradient descent method, which is directly applicable to numerous other diffusion equations with similar properties. Lastly, this research may have broader implications for the study of quantum field theories in curved spacetime.

While automated testing for conversational interfaces has made significant progress, there is still a pressing need to refine existing evaluation metrics to assess the performance of these systems. Current automated testing frameworks often prioritize system-wide correctness over user-centered experience and natural language nuances, usually at the expense of triggering system failures. To address this, we introduce a novel approach to automated testing, centered on generating natural-sounding user inputs that simulate real-user interactions. Our method leverages a generative model to create unlimited diverse inputs, allowing for the detection of grammatically or semantically flawed system responses. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by improving the performance of two conversational system components: a named entity recognizer in dialog systems and a conversational recommender system. Our results show that our method yields substantial improvements over baseline approaches in both applications. Furthermore, we highlight issues arising from the limited scope of existing evaluation protocols and pose several thought-provoking questions about the future of automated testing for conversational systems. Our approach and associated code are publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/yonghongwang/convost.

Researchers used the Microlensing Observation Experiment telescope in Haleakala, Hawaii, to examine the gravitational influence of an unidentified body in the Milky Way galaxy. Between 2011 and 2020, they collected and analyzed data on gravitational microlensing events affecting two degrees of the sky, discovering an unobscured area surrounding the position of an Earth-mass object at a distance of approximately 5800 parsecs, or about 19 thousand light-years, from the Galactic Center. This object would produce detectable gravitational effects over 90% of the sky and is likely to have already passed close to several stars in the Andromeda galaxy's disk during its journey to the Galactic Center. It is possible that this object has originated from the Andromeda galaxy and is one of many similar objects produced by massive star formation events. As a result, it may have a companion with a mass thousands of times more massive, consisting of two objects separated by several astronomical units. In the future, this object may pass near the Earth, potentially causing a microlensing event with a maximum magnification of about 1.02, but only for a brief period of about 15 minutes. Furthermore, it may produce detectable effects during close approaches to stars in the Milky Way galaxy's globular clusters, offering opportunities to constrain its orbit and potentially determine the cluster containing its massive companion. In the years to come, this object is likely to produce significant microlensing events affecting distant stars in the Milky Way galaxy's bulge and globular clusters. As a result, it is crucial that existing and future microlensing surveys in the Southern Hemisphere remain vigilant for signs of this object's presence. Ultimately, discovering this object highlights the importance of combining optical and infrared data to distinguish between different mass objects and identify those with a major mass component, such as small black holes or massive white dwarfs, which could also produce close approaches with significant effects in the future. In addition, it underscores the value of examining high-magnification microlensing events from multiple telescopes to better comprehend the underlying mass distribution of the galaxy. In this research, the authors estimate that about 8000 such objects exist in the Andromeda galaxy, producing close approaches with stars in the Milky Way galaxy about once every two weeks. Consequently, it is essential for existing and future microlensing surveys in the Southern Hemisphere to remain vigilant for signs of these objects, which could significantly impact the field in the years to come. This paper proposes a cross-lingual memory retriever to leverage monolingual data during parallel corpora learning. By incorporating a simple memory retriever into the encoder of the parallel corpora model, the cross-lingual memory retriever allows the model to directly access relevant parallel and monolingual data during training and inference. Our experiments show that the cross-lingual memory retriever enhances traditional bilingual translation memory methods and outperforms them by improving precision and overall performance. It also proves effective in tandem with other methods such as parallel corpora learning and cross-lingual pre-training methods, yielding notable gains in all evaluated metrics. Notably, the cross-lingual memory retriever enables successful low-resource domain adaptation from a high-resource source domain to a low-resource target domain, yielding gains of 2.8 BLEU in English-Spanish and 6.1 BLEU in Chinese-Arabic. Recent analyses indicate that certain anomalous patterns found in the Cosmic Microwave Background can be attributed to a combination of Hawking points and low-variance circles produced by branes in the early universe. However, these features are only visible at a scale of around $10^3$ times the Planck scale, which is more elusive than the cosmic string produced by the same scenario. In order to make the case for the existence of these features more compelling, it's essential to understand both the production mechanisms of these brane manifestations and their detection limits. By examining the likelihood of finding them in various scenarios, we aim to explore the sensitivity of future experiments in this context. Specifically, we assess how well the BICEP/KECK telescope will be able to detect signals from both Hawking points and low-variance circles, including those with a comb-like pattern, caused by the motion of D3-branes in an anti-de Sitter space. We also investigate the ability of these experiments to distinguish between these cosmic brane signatures and the background signal, considering both the sky coverage and polarization modes, with a focus on the impact of foreground contaminants. Our findings indicate that even with foreground removal, the KECK telescope should be capable of detecting signs from large-scale Hawking points, of around $10^2$ times the Planck scale, up to $10^{2.5}$ times the Planck scale for a comprehensive search with full sky coverage. However, detecting low-variance circles, including those with a comb-like pattern, produced at a scale of around $10^3$ times the Planck scale will be more challenging. We also establish that the likelihood of finding these cosmic brane signatures is significantly influenced by the total available parameter space for the extra dimensions, as well as the volume of the extra dimensions, which affects the scale at which they appear. In addition, we identify that the production of both Hawking points and low-variance circles, including those with a comb-like pattern, is significantly constrained by the Einstein gravity limit, resulting in a minimum detectable scale of around $10^3$ times the Planck scale. Our study anticipates that future experiments will be able to distinguish between the cosmic string produced by the same scenario and these brane manifestations, as well as differentiate between the comb-like pattern caused by the motion of D3-branes in an anti-de Sitter space and the background signal. We expect that a comprehensive analysis of these cosmic brane signatures will contribute significantly to the understanding of the fundamental principles of these theories

The primary obstacle in few-shot learning for the K-nearest neighbor (KNN) classifier is outlier examples within new categories. The reason is that novel classes often contain samples that are far from the mean of the support set and, as a result, influence the prediction decision. To overcome this challenge, we present a modified KNN model that reduces the impact of outlier samples. The proposed method involves calculating the distance from each sample to the mean of the support set and the standard deviation in the feature space. Based on these values, we determine an adjusted distance that considers both the mean and standard deviation. By using the adjusted distance instead of the standard Euclidean distance in the KNN algorithm, we are able to mitigate the impact of outlier samples. The performance of the proposed method is compared to a traditional KNN model through a series of few-shot learning experiments on the CIFAR-100 and miniImageNet datasets. The results show that the proposed method achieves better performance than the baseline KNN model. Additionally, we investigated the effects of different parameters on the proposed method and found that it is robust to various parameters. This concept is further solidified through an example involving the stable set problem from graph theory, where an exotic formulation with half the number of variables compared to the extended formulation is discovered. A general framework is established to transform exotic formulations into their equivalent forms with fewer variables, addressing previous issues of scale and computational complexity. These advancements open up possibilities for the application of exotic formulations to other problems, where their variables may be more efficiently interpreted and understood, even if their direct form is difficult to compute. Most existing research has focused on cross-domain adaptations, such as transferring between MRI and CT or adapting between different imaging modalities. In contrast, this study explores domain adaptation within the same source domain, specifically between head and neck MRI scans obtained with different protocol combinations. We investigate how different source domain data influences model performance when evaluating on unseen data and propose a self-adaptive protocol-free approach using a disentangled domain invariant neural network. This method allows us to extract a domain-invariant representation from data with different protocol combinations in mind, thereby improving the generalizability to new protocol combinations. Experimental results demonstrate that our self-adaptive approach achieves superior output quality compared to protocols-specific models and generalizes more effectively to new protocol combinations. Moreover, mixed-source domain adaptation leads to more robust model performance and outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods at various protocol combinations. To address storage challenges posed by in-memory computing and scalable persistence, researchers have proposed using solid-state memory as a persistent memory medium. Despite existing solutions, several issues remain with current approaches, hindering their potential for optimal system performance. This work introduces NOVA-relaxed, a novel file system designed to optimize the NVM persistent memory map (NVMM) for Optane Data Center Persistent Memory Modules (DC PMMs). NOVA-relaxed focuses on minimizing the performance impact of small, persistent writes by applications. To evaluate its effectiveness, we conducted an experiment using various Linux system applications with different memory access patterns. The results showed that, without any optimization, small persistent writes can significantly slow system performance, even causing it to resemble best-case scenario performance. Moreover, our study found that many Linux system applications do not require system calls for persistent memory updates and can instead use direct mapping of NVM persistent memory. Furthermore, we discovered that some applications, including some runtime systems and system applications, can benefit from relaxed persistence, allowing them to execute persistent memory operations more efficiently. Ultimately, our experiments revealed that NOVA-relaxed can boost the overall system performance by 10-30% for some applications and up to 50% for others in specific scenarios. Additionally, we found that our approach has minimal overhead on system performance without relaxed persistence and that it does not compromise data integrity. To facilitate replication, our evaluation was conducted using a variety of Linux system applications with different memory access patterns and sizes of persistent memory mappings. Lastly, our research demonstrates that there is a performance advantage to be gained from optimized storage of persistent memory applications and that this advantage can be realized with minimal additional cost when using Optane DC PMMs. This work is part of a larger research effort to explore ways to optimize storage for in-memory computing and scalable persistence. As part of this effort, we also investigated other storage approaches, including log-structured storage, disk-based persistence, and persistent memory compression, among others. However, our analysis indicated that these methods either fail to deliver additional performance benefits or introduce performance-degrading overheads. In contrast, our NOVA-relaxed file system can enhance system performance by 10-30% for some applications and as much as 50% for others in specific scenarios, without compromising data integrity, and with minimal additional overhead when system calls are not optimized. For the classical finite Coxeter group Bn, we derive the modified exchange laws that result from generalizing its standard generating set to those elements with a specific number of descents. Additionally, we explore how the modified laws interconnect and establish a connection to the Coxeter length and descent set of the group's elements. This analysis enables us to distinguish between the different versions of the exchange laws associated with distinct numbers of descents. We also identify the simplest case related to Bn's fundamental representation. Lastly, we discuss potential applications of our findings to the study of root systems. Our techniques involve manipulating the laws in a computationally efficient manner and leveraging the graph representation of the Coxeter system to verify the exchange laws' validity. We conclude by highlighting the broader implications of our approach for exploring other Coxeter systems. This includes examining whether analogous methods can be applied to other finite Coxeter systems, particularly those derived from the Artin group of the dihedral series D4. We display the exchange laws for this system in their generalized form and suggest that our approach may be useful in analyzing the Artin group's defining relations. We end by posing several questions related to these laws and their connection to the group's presentation. This research is part of the candidate's PhD thesis.

To explore the properties of galactic halos, we utilize the SDSS-GALAH and APOGEE surveys to analyze 426,434 stars across the Milky Way's halo. The formation of massive star clusters would have accounted for about half of the galaxy's mass creation rate across its early life span. The features of the galaxy's halo, including the scattering of stars and clusters, velocity dispersion, and mass distribution, are all consistent with the predictions of the EAGLE simulation. This study proposes an automated method to identify tumors in high-resolution CT images obtained from lung cancer patients, utilizing a unique combination of morphological analysis and region-growing algorithms. The proposed framework initially employs a set of pre-defined characteristics to filter CT images and eliminate noise. It then applies a morphological analysis to divide the cleaned images into distinct regions based on defined shapes, and identifies the area with irregular boundaries as a tumor. The proposed method is tested using CT images from lung cancer patients, and compared with a conventional region-growing technique. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework is as effective as the conventional technique, but offers a more efficient way of growing regions and less prone to noise. A significant advantage of this method is its ability to provide a precise measurement of tumor irregularity, enabling effective guidance for surgeons during a lung cancer tumor resection procedure, such as an anatomical lung resection. The method has also been implemented using MATLAB, and is available for download at no cost. Further development of this method is planned to accommodate various types of cancer and image modalities. The technique is also expected to be of value to medical practitioners and surgeons, and could be optimized for cloud computing platforms for more scalable performance. However, this is yet to be experimented with experimentally.

Our research also analyzes the relationship between these numbers and an equation involving Artin-Lerch series, and confirms that when the complex number $\beta$ is non-residue, the corresponding modified degenerate Bernoulli number is indeed zero. Lastly, our work delves into the relationship between these numbers and the roots of a polynomial constructible from an integer $n$ that indicates whether a particular complex number $\beta$ is irreducible or not. Researchers using radial velocity surveys face a challenge in maintaining optimal telescope performance, specifically low RV jitter.  A previous study introduced a novel approach to selecting lines from a line list, which demonstrates RV stability similar to that of spectra from parametric searches. However, the authors argue that a critical component of this method has been misrepresented, leading to confusion. The proposed method's key feature relies on a randomized algorithm, which guarantees the same level of RV jitter performance as desired. In contrast, the authors claim that the distinction between using a randomized or parametric model for line selection is merely a distinction without a difference, as both methods produce identical results in terms of RV jitter. The authors further contend that the randomized approach offers an alternative to the more complex parametric model, which can lead to lines being over-structured. The randomized algorithm can produce lines that are more robust against small-scale variations, which the authors believe are necessary for low RV jitter. The study includes an illustration of this concept, along with a demonstration of the efficacy of the randomized algorithm for line selection. The authors also suggest applying this approach to existing line lists to achieve similar RV performance. The study's findings are particularly relevant to the APOGEE-2D dark fibre survey, which will employ this method of line selection. The authors anticipate a modest increase in the number of target fields as a result, along with a greater scientific return for the same number of observations. The new approach to line selection is anticipated to yield improved results for several research areas, including stellar dynamics, the detection of RV variations in faint active galaxies, and the study of the cool disc. The study also introduces a graphical user interface called LineChooser for selecting lines, which is available online. The authors' results with this new approach have implications for other high-resolution spectroscopic surveys, which could incorporate similar strategies to line selection. The authors' approach to line selection is open to feedback and suggestions from the community. The "hidden terminal problem" poses a significant challenge to efficient data transfer in sensor networks that employ ad-hoc routing protocols. As sensor networks continue to grow in size and complexity, the impact of this issue worsens, limiting the capacity for in-band communication and ultimately constraining the effectiveness of data communication. Existing solutions to the hidden terminal problem have been primarily focused on localized techniques, which operate within the confines of individual nodes. In contrast, our investigation proposes a new hierarchical routing framework for sensor networks, which incorporates a segmented routing system that divides areas into overlapping regions to mitigate the hidden terminal problem. Through simulation-based analysis, our results indicate a substantial reduction in packet loss and increased network capacity for data transfer. Furthermore, our approach offers improved energy efficiency and prolonged network lifespan. Additionally, we found that the optimal configuration for our proposed system exists at a power level two orders of magnitude lower than current standards, and this optimal setting is achieved when the network is divided into sectors with a specific optimal size. Our methodology is applicable to any slotted-CDMA based sensor network, and we provide specific guidelines for parameter optimization. Our approach also facilitates the assignment of optimal power levels for individual nodes, and we present a new algorithm for dynamic adaptation of power levels in response to changing network conditions. Through simulation-based analysis, our results confirm that our approach results in a significant improvement in network performance. Deep object detectors like Single Shot Detectors (SSDs) have achieved prominent success in various tasks and have become a fundamental component in many applications, also influencing the development of other techniques like track-by-detect methods. However, most existing studies focused on general-purpose object detection within a single context, leaving gaps in situations that involve multiple contexts or when context information is limited or absent. To address these challenges, we propose a context-aware object detector called Context-Aware Detector (CAD) that incorporates contextual information from object proposals without relying on additional context-specific object proposals. CAD is particularly useful for tasks such as vehicle detection in raw images, where the target vehicles may not be directly visible but contextual information from detected off-road vehicles can be utilized to improve the detection of raw images. We also introduce a simple approach called Multi-Context Aware Detector (MCAD) that generalizes CAD across multiple contexts. Our experimental evaluations on the Baidu Vehicle Dataset and the MS COCO dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of CAD and MCAD, with code available on GitHub. The code can be found at the following link: https://github.com/hanghangda/CAD. The benchmark model for the Baidu Vehicle Dataset has been uploaded to the model archive at the following link: https://github.com/hanghangda/CAD/blob/main/model_archive.txt.

This study examines the existence of solutions for a given elliptic system of equations under specific conditions, where the nonlinear terms of the equations satisfy particular growth restrictions. Certain assumptions regarding the behavior of the function f_i, particularly as its absolute value increases, are a key focus of the investigation. It is demonstrated that when the function f_i exhibits a certain type of growth, solution existence can be guaranteed. Furthermore, the relationship between this growth and the dimension of the underlying space is clarified. Additionally, the study establishes an inequality that provides a more precise definition of the weak solution class than the standard Morrey--Sobolev space, which in turn enables better control of the norm of the solution. Finally, it is shown that when the nonlinear term belongs to a specific class, it can be bounded by a multiple of the norm of the solution. This boundary estimate is achieved through an application of an iterative technique accompanied by an estimate of the whole solution on a given set. The most significant consequence of this investigation is the proof that when the dimension of the space is greater than four, solution existence can be guaranteed for the given elliptic system of equations, provided that the nonlinear terms satisfy particular growth restrictions. It is worth noting that this investigation is an extension of prior research offered in [J. Huang, J. Liu, S. Zhou, A note on an elliptic system of equations, Math. Research Letters 19 (9), 2021]. No analog of this investigation holds in the case of lower dimensional spaces; for example, in the case of 3-dimensional space, solution existence cannot be guaranteed even under very mild growth constraints of the nonlinear terms, which is clear from the counterexample offered in [J. Notable cases where such conditions hold are seen in binary perceptrons, submodular functions, and polynomial functions of a certain degree. This paper obtains new concentration inequalities for two key scenarios: 1) When the function $f$ is convex, we derive a relevant inequality by leveraging the large deviation probability of the largest variable. 2) For polynomial functions of any degree, we establish a concentration inequality by conditioning on the maximum variable. A key tool in this case is a new deviation probability estimate for the sum of a random variable and an independent copy of another variable. This new estimate generalizes a previous result by Bakhta et al. Our findings provide a stronger concentration inequality for the sum of Bernoulli variables, with an improved deviation probability expression. This improvement generalizes earlier results by Dubhashi and Panconesi, and also improves upon the previous state-of-the-art techniques by Buser and by Frieze and Kan. Our method for the polynomial case introduces an alternative to earlier methods by Kohler and by Weller. To facilitate precise measurements of the W boson forward scattering off a nucleus at the LHC, it's crucial to accurately understand the dihadron fragmentation function, especially the asymmetry in the cosine of the rapidity difference between the two hadrons. This work delves into the theoretical aspects of the asymmetry in the rapidity difference distribution in hadron pairs produced in W boson scattering off a heavy nucleus, specifically focusing on the contributions of quark and antiquark targets and developing a framework to relate the asymmetry to the dihadron fragmentation function. As the LHC is well-suited to study the dihadron fragmentation function, this work also explores the potential of the LHC to study the dihadron fragmentation function through W boson scattering, even in the presence of significant systematic uncertainties. To illustrate this, this work presents several feasibility studies for the LHC at various energy and luminosity settings, including the LHCb acceptance cut effects. Ultimately, this work highlights the theoretical and experimental aspects of the asymmetry in the rapidity difference distribution in hadron pairs produced in W boson scattering off a heavy nucleus, positioning it as a promising probe of the dihadron fragmentation function. In the context of general relativity, we've determined how the concept of invariant length is redefined on a de Sitter spacetime. This leads to a specific volume element that becomes a well-defined 4-dimensional invariant area. A set of new coordinates is also established to represent this spacetime in a simplified manner. Within this framework, we've identified a relationship between the concept of invariant length and the Fock transformation. Our analysis confirms that the latter effectively changes the spacetime metric from its hyperbolic form to a Euclidean metric, with the variation of the invariant length playing a key role in this transformation. A discussion on the implications of our findings in relation to the Fock transformation is also presented. Moreover, our approach results in a scaling symmetry becoming apparent in the simplified coordinates. This symmetry can be viewed as a manifestation of the self-similarity inherent in the de Sitter spacetime. A key aspect of our analysis is the restriction that our study is confined to a finite region of the de Sitter spacetime, making it free from singularities caused by closure. An interesting consequence of our framework is the presence of a universal length scale in the spacetime, effectively representing an "effective Planck length" when considered in the context of an Einstein gravity theory with a non-zero cosmological constant. This analysis also lays the groundwork for the exploration of fundamental theories on the spacetime of a de Sitter universe. As an illustration of the utility of our approach, we consider a thought experiment involving the study of an isolated system on the spacetime of a de Sitter universe. As expected, such a system should remain closed in regards to its total quantum field theory dynamics. This expectation is realized when the concept of the invariant length is accounted for, resulting in the effective redefinition of the spacetime as a fundamental unit rather than allowing for the decay of a fundamental system into particles. This outcome is achieved through the effective imposition of a non-permeable boundary at a specific finite distance on the spacetime, effectively preventing the emergence of an "anti-particle" on the opposite side of the spherical system. As a result, the total system can be viewed as being comprised of a single fundamental "particle" with an opposite charge. This fundamental "particle" is found to have an inherent mass dimension of five, with its effective action being non-renormalizable. Consequently, this fundamental "particle" can be viewed as an effective description of fundamental closed spacetime loops in Einstein gravity theory with a non-zero cosmological constant. In modern recommender systems, entities with rich underlying structures like graphs play a key role. User interests towards these entities are influenced by both the entities' attributes and their connection to other entities in the graph. To enhance entity representations, we propose a novel approach called Combined Entity Representation Learning (CERL). This approach establishes a dual AR model that efficiently leverages both the entity's feature vector and its underlying graph structure. By combining the topology and content in the dual space, CERL is able to learn entity representations that not only fit the user's interaction history but also maintain a consistent structure. We compare CERL to the latest recommender systems at the 25th ACM International Conference on Research and Advanced Techniques in Information Systems. Datasets used include Amazon and CiteSeer. Our results show that CERL outperforms the competition in all metrics, delivering a 9.5% improvement on average. Moreover, to handle large-scale datasets, we've incorporated a parallel computing technique called oneAllReduce. This efficient implementation allows us to process 10 billion parameters in under 20 seconds on a 512-node cluster. To facilitate further research, the code for CERL is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/aliakhmadi/CERL. It includes the source code for CERL as well as oneAllReduce, and we've included example use cases to make it easier for others to build upon our work. To provide a foundation for future work, we've also released oneAllReduce as a standalone Python library at https://github.com/aliakhmadi/OneAllReduce.
