By integrating incompatibility as a state variable in an MDP, our innovative method is capable of evaluating decisions regarding the acceptance of donated kidneys. In this setting, making an acceptance decision results in a new state, rather than a terminal state. By incorporating incompatibility as a state variable, our approach enables us to analyze the implications of accepting or rejecting an incompatible kidney donation. Unfortunately, conventional value iteration methods are incapable of handling this type of state transition, where an action transitions into a non-terminal state with the same name. To overcome this limitation, we propose an alternative approach utilizing a graph-based algorithm to compute the optimal expected future value for each state. In theory, our proposed method achieves the maximum expected reward compared to any other algorithm for compatible MDPs. Through practical applications to kidney transplantation, our method demonstrates potential to increase the number of transplants by accepting incompatible kidneys. In certain instances, it is also capable of finding an optimal policy that accepts more than half of incompatible kidneys. In cases where the kidneys are highly incompatible, our method may prioritize the acceptance of donations with a lower level of incompatibility, even if this means accepting fewer kidneys overall. In situations where multiple kidneys with low levels of incompatibility become available at the same time, our method may prioritize the acceptance of these kidneys over single incompatible kidneys. In theory, our approach can handle an infinite number of available transplants, but in practice, this is not a limitation. In the special case of multi-armed MDPs, our method provides the maximum expected reward compared to any other algorithm. Our method is an important step towards creating practical MDPs that account for the implications of actions in real-world scenarios. Additionally, our method offers a solution to the long-standing problem of computing optimal policies for MDPs with functionally dependent states. In our analysis of kidney transplantation, we employed an MDP model that assumes the player always has the option to delay their next action. This led us to develop an alternative approach to computing value functions and identifying optimal policies. Our method is particularly relevant to any scenario that involves deciding whether to accept an incompatible offer, such as the allocation of bone marrow donations. To facilitate the computation of our proposed method, we have created a suite of efficient graph-based algorithms that can handle a wide range of complex MDPs. These algorithms are capable of computing optimal expected future values for individual states, prioritizing the acceptance of compatible kidneys over single incompatible kidneys, prioritizing the acceptance of multiple incompatible kidneys over single compatible kidneys, and computing optimal policies

This paper presents a novel Bayesian method for estimating parameters in a specific type of copula, known as the hierarchical Archimedean copula, which has recently seen increased adoption in discrete data analysis. Currently, there is a significant gap in statistical research regarding the hierarchical Archimedean copula, particularly for categorical variables, as most existing research focuses on continuous data. Our proposed approach addresses this gap and offers a comprehensive solution for both unsupervised and supervised parameter estimation. In the absence of a known density function for the hierarchical Archimedean copula, we utilized the exchange algorithm in conjunction with a Bayesian method to overcome computational challenges. Our results demonstrate that the proposed methods yield accurate estimates and can be applied to real-world discrete data sets. One such application involves modeling election outcomes in multi-candidate elections with distinct voting systems. The associated R package, called $RCA$, is publicly available and enables users to employ our proposed methods directly within R. The package can be acquired through the following repository address: https://github.com/AbdullahAlShohat/RCA. A detailed guide to utilizing the package is included in the supplementary materials section of this paper. In addition, multiple data sets utilized in our research are accessible via the following data repository address: https://data.duke.edu/elections/. The hierarchical Archimedean copula offers a versatile framework; however, its major limitation remains the challenging computation involved in parameter estimation. Despite these difficulties, our research demonstrates that Bayesian methods in conjunction with Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques can efficiently address these computational issues and yield accurate estimates. The additional benefits of our results include the ability to derive posterior correlations between the parameters and the stretching function, as well as obtaining point estimates and interval estimates for the proposed method. The challenges computation involved in the hierarchical Archimedean copula is extensively examined across multiple data sets, showing that our proposed Bayesian approach achieves the desired level of convergence and provides point estimates that are remarkably close to the findings of alternative methods. The distinctive features of our results also include the ability to efficiently handle large data sets, as demonstrated by our analysis of election outcomes in US House elections from 1900 to 2012. The associated paper is currently available on arXiv at the following link: arXiv preprint arXiv_2109.13866v2 and has been previously presented at the 28th Conference on Applied Inferential Statistics in 2021. This study presents an innovative approach to creating tailored word embeddings for the financial domain. Existing embedding techniques like Word2Vec and GloVe systematically confuse opposites like 'buy' and'sell' as semantically similar, which is detrimental for financial applications. To address this, we developed a novel loss function, named Hyperplane Mixture Loss (HML), that effectively distinguishes antonyms in the financial context. However, we observed HML-enabled embeddings struggled with capturing the complex relationships among highly synonimous words like 'add/subtract', 'buy/sell', and 'long/short'. Therefore, we introduced a Multi-Axis Hyperplane Loss (MAHL) that successfully handled both frequent and infrequent opposites, and demonstrated superior performance over state-of-the-art methods in six key financial tasks. Our models achieved exceptional results on both real and synthetic data across three evaluation metrics, and we found MAHL to be particularly effective at handling the peculiar antonymy patterns unique to the financial domain. Furthermore, we found MAHL to be highly versatile and compatible with both BERT-based pre-trained models and the recently introduced SimpleELMO. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/hfawaz/mahl-financial-embeddings. Our pre-trained models have also been successfully integrated into Hugging Face's Transformers repository under the name 'hfawaz/mahlfina-embeddings'.

In multi-band signal transmission, the waveforming process plays a crucial role in optimizing end-to-end throughput and fairness. This study classifies a wideband transmission system into two categories and proposes two optimization goals: fair-throughput and sum-throughput. We establish mathematically equivalent forms for these objectives and develop flat-fading based waveforming strategies using an algebraic approach, achieving maximum or fair throughput with no increase in computational complexity. We further investigate an inclined-fading scenario and employ the big-M method for optimization. Notably, this method does not escalate the computational complexity but may lead to suboptimal solutions. We numerically validate the effectiveness of our proposed methods across various scenarios, including flat-fading, inclined-fading, and real-world environments, and find our flat-fading based solutions sufficiently competent in such cases. This approach offers a valuable reference for the research of waveforming strategies in more complex scenarios, such as dynamic environments and non-cooperative systems. What's more, most of our proposed flat-fading based waveforming strategies can be implemented with no additional computational complexity than traditional methods, which is of great value to the community given the computational constraints of many practical large-scale array systems. What's more, our results open up new avenues for the study of waveforming, enabling the community to explore other optimization targets, such as weighted sum-throughput and secure-throughput, with minimal computational increase. A new approach is introduced that utilizes a neural network to model the unknown functions in a partial differential equation (PDE) description of the Rayleigh--B\'enard instability, allowing for a stochastic constraint to be imposed and resulting in a numerically tractable problem. Although the method's global optimality cannot be guaranteed due to the use of a neural network, it has been successfully applied to accurately predict the onset of instabilities in both horizontal-plate and spherical geometries, matching previously validated numerical results obtained through traditional methods. Notably, the proposed approach requires significantly less computational time ($O(10^4)$ times faster) than the finite-element method for similar numerical accuracy. Additionally, the neural network model exhibits robustness when subjected to variations in the type of random noise used to train it. A key aspect of the method is its ability to incorporate a stability criterion derived from the Hamiltonian operator into the neural network framework. It has been demonstrated that this stability criterion is an overestimation of the actual stability boundary; however, it remains a topic for further investigation how the method could be modified to yield a more conservative estimate. The code used in this research has been made publicly accessible. Advancements in computing power may hold potential for the method to be applied to larger-scale problems in the future. The proposed approach presents a promising direction for the use of neural networks in addressing fundamental challenges in fluid dynamics. To tackle the challenge of language ambiguity, a proposed approach suggests using a new interpretation of tree transformations called the least fixpoint interpretation. However, implementing this interpretation method for the regular tree grammar system results in a right-linear grammar, which lacks the ability to handle true ambiguities. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a type of tree that incorporates null children, allowing us to handle ambiguous situations. Building upon this new tree structure, we redefine the least fixpoint interpretation and prove that it leads to a valid parsing method. Consequently, we demonstrate that any context-free grammar can be converted into a tree grammar that uses the novel node structure and left-linear production rules. This conversion maintains the same level of generative capacity as the original context-free grammar. Moreover, the resulting tree grammar can be optimized for better efficiency in terms of the number of nodes. To showcase the practical applicability of our approach, we successfully apply it to a real-world machine learning model, specifically a part-of-speech tagger. Our study provides a feasible path to achieving a feasible and efficient parsing method for context-free languages while addressing the issue of linguistic ambiguity. Furthermore, we converted the CKY algorithm into a tree grammar and interpreted this as a model for first-order logic. This interpretation led to a feasible but less efficient method, indicating that further optimization is necessary for practical use. Nonetheless, our work offers a theoretical framework for exploring the relationship between context-free languages, tree grammars, and first-order logic. This research is an extension of my previous studies on language-based data analysis and machine learning, and it paves the way for investigating more advanced topics in computational linguistics and montonic logic. We introduce a variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework to enhance policy gradient estimation in reinforcement learning. By allocating new sampling weights to past experiences, VRER reduces the variance of a gradient estimate and helps the agent break out of local minima. We show that our proposed method achieves a theoretical variance reduction factor of $\frac{1}{1-h\beta}$ in a finite horizon setting, where $h$ is the sampling period and $\beta$ is the eligibility trace decay factor. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method learns from experiences sampled from a policy entirely distinct from its current policy, leading to an asymptotic convergence to an optimal solution. We also derive a practical sampling ratio-independent method using importance sampling, resulting in a simplified but less efficient variance-reducing estimator. Our algorithm's effectiveness is validated through grid world, robot manipulation, and video game examples. Source code is available at https://github.com/strawman0808/vrer. Our paper's key contribution is publishing a general variance reduction based experience replay framework, along with a specific practical variance-reducing policy gradient estimator. Notably, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art policy gradient method in several tasks. Moreover, we achieve comparable performance to other advanced reinforcement learning algorithms while utilizing a relatively simple method. Ultimately, we believe our paper's results provide significant value to the reinforcement learning community, offering a publicly accessible code repository and a theoretically grounded, general framework for further exploration. Using the $d$ vector and orbital composition from theoretical band-structure calculations, we classify the superconducting gap in BaFe$_2$As$_2$ using laser-based ARPES. The analysis reveals a two-fold classification: one with a dominant $ab$-plane orientation and the other with a dominant $c$-axis orientation. The gap size around the zone corner in BaFe$_2$As$_2$ is significantly larger than in other iron-based superconductors, requiring a critical temperature of at least 20 K to be compatible with the isotropic $s$+-wave scenario. Our results also indicate that the superconducting gap is maximized along the (001) direction near the zone corner, with a value of 13.5 meV, thus providing a clear distinction from other iron-based superconductors that are $ab$-plane dominated. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the superconducting gap in BaFe$_2$As$_2$ can be accurately reproduced using the matrix formation of $d$-vector and its coupling to an s-wave, in contrast to other iron-based superconductors which can be explained by $d$-wave pairing. Additional analysis using the $d$-vector coupling to an s-wave in BaFe$_2$As$_2$ yields a critical temperature of at least 30 K for the $A$4 symmetry and 20 K for the $A$2u symmetry, with corresponding orbital compositions of $d_{xz}$-dominated and $d_{xy}$-dominated, respectively. Notably, our results also indicate that the superconducting gap in BaFe$_2$As$_2$ exhibits an anisotropic distribution across the Brillouin zone, with a notable variation of approximately 4 meV compared to the 8 meV variation observed in other iron-based superconductors, thus highlighting the critical need for high-resolution ARPES in the thorough investigation of the superconducting gap in iron-based superconductors. Our study sets a precedent for the integrated application of ARPES and band-structure calculations in the precise classification of the superconducting gap in complex systems. Ultimately, our results underscore the inadequacy of the isospin $s$+-wave model for the superconducting gap in BaFe$_2$As$_2$ at low doping and the corresponding necessity for a more comprehensive theoretical framework that can accommodate multiple pairing symmetries across different iron-based superconductors.

The ability to generate dialogue through the process of reasoning about another's mental state, or Theory of Mind (ToM), is a crucial component of Conversational Artificial Intelligence (CAI). While previous studies have explored the relationship between ToM and CAI by analyzing online data, this study instead examines offline data to investigate the correlation between ToM and dialog generation tasks. Our large-scale survey of 1,086 participants from diverse occupations and educational backgrounds reveals significant correlations between ToM and various measures of creative writing, with effects mediated by cognitive factors such as motivation, self-efficacy, and writing style. These findings suggest that ToM plays a key role in the generation of fictional texts and even more realistic dialogues, and imply that CAI systems may benefit from incorporating mechanisms that simulate ToM, in addition to cognitive architectures that mimic human writing processes. Our study also raises important methodological considerations for conducting offline data analyses and exploring the underlying psychological mechanisms of human behavior in CAI. In the long run, a deeper understanding of these mechanisms may lead to more effective CAI systems capable of generating natural and engaging human dialogue. In the short term, our study can inform the design of scoring rubrics for dialog generation tasks, a crucial step in the offline evaluation process. Ultimately, our research paves the way for a more comprehensive CAI theory that incorporates psychological factors and is grounded in empirical data from offline studies. In the context of dialog generation, this theory posits that the ability to generate acceptable dialogue is a function of ToM, influenced by factors such as motivation, cognition, and writing style, and is distinct from other abilities like semantic knowledge and grammar. ToM is thought to exert its effects on dialog generation through the process of writing, with possible pathways mediated by cognitive factors such as attention, memory, and executive functions. This study sets the stage for further offline data analysis and subsequent experimentation with CAI systems, with potential applications in the creation of engaging and realistic dialogue for various purposes, including entertainment, education, customer service, and more. In addition, our theory may be applicable to other language generation tasks, such as text summarization and creative writing, and could be extended to include additional psychological factors and domain-specific knowledge. In the long run, a comprehensive CAI theory will provide a unifying framework for the myriad techniques and models developed for conversational AI, informing the design of future systems and empirical research, and ultimately contributing to the creation of human-like CAI systems that can adapt to various contexts and purposes. The surface's reflection characteristics are represented by two linked variables: a fading factor and a phase shift. As these variables change in a correlated manner, the capacity of the system also varies. The research focuses initially on understanding the average value of the capacity with multiple realizations of the surface's behavior, and then moves on to analyzing the probability of the capacity exceeding a certain threshold as the surface's behavior is experienced over time. We develop a new evolution framework, chordal Schramm–Loewener evolution (CSLE), by generalizing the chordal Loewener equation to allow for rotation. This leads to a corresponding domain growth model, similar to Schramm–Loewener evolution (SLE), which enables us to establish a mapping between CSLE and the domain growth process. Our study also reveals that a specific CSLE trace, SLE$_6$, behaves like a random surface in the upper half-plane, diverging in $3$ dimensions. Furthermore, we show that CSLE can be viewed as the evolution of "imaginary surfaces" constructed from the conformal auto-maps of the unit disk, which expands conformally. This surface evolution model (SEModel) provides an alternative to SLE, which evolves from the conformal auto-maps of the upper half-plane. Notably, we derive an explicit formula for the growth rate of the area of a surface under SEModel, which corresponds to a gamma distribution with a $3/2$ shape parameter. Ultimately, we found that the one-dimensional front dynamics model performs similarly to the original $\kappa$-$f$ model for the tested conditions, but with significantly reduced computational overhead. This new model retains the efficiency of the front thickness model while providing more accurate dynamics, making it suitable for use in efficient front methods. It is also compatible with the $\mathregular{E}$-$\mathregular{f}$ closure and may be an effective alternative to other dynamic front thickness models. To facilitate further development, we have made the new model's source code publicly available.

A fascinating area of study involves ultralight dark matter, which may be linked to neutrinos through a common interaction with an ultra-light boson. Developing applications that require strong consistency across replicated data has grown in relevance, especially with the rise of distributed systems. Though research into Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) has been prolific, building large-scale systems using existing CRDT designs is complicated due to limited documentation and understanding of the underlying theories. To address this issue, we propose a design framework that categorizes existing and future CRDTs into six fundamental patterns, effectively providing a blueprint for designing new consistent data types. By identifying common themes across twenty-one established CRDTs and leveraging this framework, developers can create novel data types with consistency guarantees by combining the basic patterns and tailoring them to specific use cases. Moreover, we demonstrate the practical utility of this framework by designing two novel CRDTs – a consistent set of maps with user identifiers and a consistent multi-graph – and successfully implemented and tested these designs. Finally, the framework can facilitate better comparison and classification of existing and future CRDTs, contributing valuable insights for researchers. Using vast computational resources, our study employs the entire human protein sequence space to predict the effects of protein sequences on genotype-phenotype relationships. Our approach identifies significant correlations between protein properties and the likelihood of associated SNPs, their effect sizes, and the underlying molecular mechanisms responsible for phenotypic variations. Our results indicate that protein primary structure plays a more substantial role in determining effect sizes, with post-translational modifications also influencing phenotypes significantly. Furthermore, we find that the influence of protein sequence on phenotypes is highly variable and depends on the specific trait in question. Our analysis highlights the complex interplay between genomics and phenomics, shedding light on the fundamental principles that govern the relationships between protein sequences, structures, biophysical properties, and their functional roles in the cell. Ultimately, this comprehension can facilitate the development of precision medicine approaches by targeting specific protein sequences and their associated phenotypes. The LHCb experiment allows for the study of proton-proton collisions at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV, and for the examination of strange particle production in various multiplicity contexts. This research features an extensive dataset of around 100 million minimum bias and optimized trigger events, accompanied by precise strangeness measurements in various secondary particles, including $\phi$, $\Lambda$, $\Xi$, $\Omega$, $\Lambda_{c}^{+}$, and $\Xi_{c}^{+}$. The findings reveal notable enhancements of strange particle yields in high-momentum ranges, along with significant deviations from perturbative QCD predictions. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the enhancement of strange hadrons in proton-proton collisions is remarkably consistent with that observed in heavy ion collisions, and that it persists in all center-of-mass energies examined. Additionally, the results show that the ratios of strange baryons to nonstrange particles exhibit notable dependencies on both transverse momentum and energy, and that $\phi$ meson production exhibits an anomalous rise in high-momentum ranges at 7 TeV. The research also identifies unique patterns of strange particle creation, with variations that depend on the production mechanism, isospin, and number of quarks, all of which provide new insights into the nature of strange particle enhancement. These findings are expected to serve as a crucial basis for comparisons with theoretical models, ala EPOS, PYTHIA, and EPOS LHC, which seek to explain the underlying physics of strange particle production in proton-proton collisions. The full dataset at 7 and 8 TeV will be utilized to investigate strange particle transverse polarization, and the research is anticipated to contribute significantly to the understanding of strange quark behavior within hadronic collisions. The study of $\phi$ meson production, characterized by its s s-bar quark composition, is of particular interest, as it offers new insights into strange particle enhancement and may provide a more direct view of the strange quark behavior. The research is further expanded to include the analysis of $\Lambda_{c}^{+}$ and $\Xi_{c}^{+}$ baryons, which represents the first-ever strangeness measurement in this context. The study reveals that the ratios of heavy-flavor baryons to nonstrange particles exhibit significant dependencies on transverse momentum, energy, and multiplicity, and that $\Lambda_{c}^{+}$ production exhibits an anomalous rise in high-momentum ranges at 7 TeV. The number of known neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries in our Galaxy remains limited, which makes the exact population size difficult to determine. By examining the spatial and luminosity distribution of these binaries, we calculated the population size to be around 24+14/-8. We discovered a population ratio of 0.76+0.15/-0.13 for low-mass X-ray binaries containing neutron stars, compared to those containing black holes, based on a volume-corrected analysis. This ratio suggests that the birthrate of low-mass X-ray binaries is similar for neutron stars and black holes. By comparing this ratio to the population of millisecond radio pulsars, we estimated that around 45% of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries have low luminosities. If so, there could be as many as 70 Galactic millisecond radio pulsars awaiting discovery. We also found that low-mass X-ray binaries containing neutron stars are more likely to enter the low-luminosity phase over time. If this is the case, neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries with low luminosities have an average time span of around 10 billion years. We speculate that binary mergers could be influenced by the neutron star's initial spin rate. Finally, we anticipate that future radio pulsar surveys will enhance the known population by at least 10 and as much as 50%.

The first approach involves eliminating outliers in line width distributions, while the second method considers multiple line widths from spectroscopic data. We applied these techniques to three open clusters with wide binary members spanning a large velocity dispersion, and found the second method yielded the most reliable results. By analyzing 189103 signal-theta-polarization matrices from URSAT-2S at 430 MHz and examining 1351 instances where the measurement error was less than 5% (accounting for 0.16% of the total samples), a significant correlation between the curvature of the radio spectrum's polarization and the polarization of the sources was found. Furthermore, the results indicated that the curvature of the polarization spectrum is negatively correlated with the median fractional polarization of the sources, and the relationship varies depending on the source polarization. The findings also revealed that the Rayleigh distribution effectively models the curvature of the polarization spectrum's distribution. Additionally, the model developed in this research enables the removal of magnetic field pitch-angle distributions from the curvature of the polarization spectrum. The tendency of weak shocks to become strong in certain high-speed flows has been observed in one-dimensional and two-dimensional simulations of the Euler equations. A new analysis explains this phenomenon by examining the interaction between weak shocks and large-scale flow structures, classifying it as a boundary-passage problem. A mathematical model is developed to study the underlying physics and estimate the effects of shock transition on global behavior. Numerical simulations demonstrate how shock instability at a boundary can lead to the formation of large vortices in subsonic flows, and how this affects flow structure and transition patterns. In supersonic flows, however, the primary impact is the creation of small-scale turbulence at the boundary. Shock transition patterns are highly influenced by flow conditions, especially in the vicinity of the boundary, but are relatively stable elsewhere. In contrast, flow structures at the boundary are largely steered by initial conditions, even after shocks have fully transitioned. As a result, the distribution of transition patterns around a sphere can be quite non-uniform, with hotspots forming over boundaries with specific flow conditions, even after shocks have fully transitioned. This finding is consistent with experimental data from laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy. The influence of flow structures on shock transition is validated by direct numerical simulations of highly resolved two-dimensional and three-dimensional cases, involving large clusters on the surface of a sphere. The resulting distribution of strong shocks is shown to closely mirror that of large flow structures, with hotspots forming over areas with significant cluster sizes. This has significant implications for re-entry missions, where shocks can have a profound impact on surface heating patterns, with potential consequences for spacecraft durability. To mitigate this, future missions may need to prioritize understanding the physics of shock transition, including the role of flow structures, boundary conditions, and cluster formation. This knowledge could ultimately inform more effective thermal management strategies, reducing the need for excessive heat shielding. This research is an initial step in this scientific pursuit, with numerous opportunities for further exploration along this multifaceted scientific path. This library provides a suite of high-performance, parallel solvers for the Euler equations, with highly optimized multi-domain techniques for efficient solutioning of complex flow problems. To speed up human response time in large-scale scaling experiments for dialog research, a common approach is to utilize automatic completion of sentences. Nonetheless, this method solely assesses accuracy and neglects the importance of semantic variety in the generated text. Moreover, the evaluation protocols for these experiments usually focus on single-metric optimization, neglecting the intricate means of combining multiple objectives in real human conversations. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel objective function that simultaneously optimizes both accuracy and the diversity of sentences in a dataset. We have successfully applied this approach to enhance the performance of three widely used datasets in dialog completion. The results show that our method not only raises the bar for various evaluation metrics but also leads to more lifelike conversations combining multiple objectives. Moreover, an unprecedented study compares different types of sentence generators with both pre-trained and pre-trained-and-finetuned models, revealing that our method proves resistant to these variations. Ultimately, our results are shareable with the community to facilitate further research and improvement in dialog completion models. The code and models employed in this research are now available for public access at https://github.com/strml/Scoring-Dialog-eval. Nonetheless, we invite dialog researchers to collaborate with us in evaluating both the methodology and the results. Moreover, we look forward to deriving advantages from their successful experiments, which we hope will lead to increased capability and better performance in dialog completion beyond this study. Lastly, we intend to expand this study to additional datasets and testing environments with more sophisticated settings in the future. Until then, we welcome all feedback and suggestions from the community in this area.

To enable safe and reliable driver assistance systems, online action recognition is a crucial component. This application demands a high level of robustness in order to proceed with safe actions even in the presence of noisy sensor data. We propose a novel deep learning framework for real-time action recognition that generates bounding box-based activity predictions. These predictions can serve as input for subsequent tasks such as activity-driven object manipulation and the detection of critical events like impending collisions. Our framework incorporates spatial and temporal attention mechanisms to minimize noise sensitivity. It showcases improved performance when compared to a baseline model in online action recognition and robustness in the presence of common perturbations. The code is available at: https://github.com/kuangchi/AttentionActionNet. Our paper's key contributions are as follows: (1) We propose a online action recognition framework that combines spatial and temporal attention for reducing noise sensitivity. (2) This attention mechanism is integrated into a robust predictor, enhancing performance when compared to a baseline model. (3) The benefits of robust predictions are demonstrated through activity-driven object manipulation and critical event detection. (4) The framework's capability to handle real-world scenarios is validated through online action recognition and robustness testing. (5) The code is openly shared for the benefit of the computer vision community. Overall, our goal is to contribute to more reliable and safe driver assistance systems through real-time action recognition. A novel method has been developed for reconstructing hadrons from decay products using artificial neural networks in combination with probability density functions. This approach was specifically designed for the LHCb experiment at the CERN, where identifying decays of certain hadrons relies heavily on measuring the properties of particles produced from the hadron's decay. For example, identifying $B_s$ mesons requires analyzing the characteristics of hadrons produced from the $B_s$ meson's decay, such as stopping times for specific particles like $K^-$. By training an artificial neural network on a large dataset of decay products from various hadrons, it becomes possible to estimate the probability of a given decay product set originating from a specific hadron. This in turn enables the derivation of likelihood functions for different hadrons, which can be used to obtain the best hypothesis for the parent hadron. To validate this new method, several analyses were performed on simulated data for the LHCb experiment. The results show that the artificial neural network approach is as effective as the traditional method based on particle properties, and possibly even more so in some cases. Notably, this new method allows for the discovery of new hadrons with specific properties, such as an unusual decay rate. One such example is the $B_s$ decay into a hadron $\kern 0.5em \overline{} \kern -0.5em B}^{0}_{s}$, which has a very short stopping time and could indicate the existence of a new meson. Although this result needs further verification, it highlights the potential of the artificial neural network method to uncover new hadronic decays, especially those involving a golden decay mode like the $\Lambda_c^+$ meson decaying into a hadron $\kern 0.5em \overline{} \kern -0.5em B}^{0}_{s}$. Additionally, the new method demonstrates improved performance in certain cases, such as the identification of charm hadrons decaying into a hadron $\kern 0.5em \overline{} \kern -0.5em B}^{0}_{s}$. To facilitate a direct comparison with the traditional method, several analyses were conducted on actual LHCb data, resulting in a confirmation of the artificial neural network approach's validity. However, it was discovered that one of these comparisons involved an extrinsic bias, which was an artifact of how the hadron decay products were generated, rather than an inherent property of the artificial neural network.

However, evaluating the impact of closed-loop feedback on bipedal robots involves examining the divergence of trajectories under open-loop conditions and comparing it to their behavior with closed-loop feedback in a finite-time gait cycle. In this study, we introduce a method to analyze the effect of closed-loop feedback by calculating the distance between trajectories in phase space. Our findings indicate that closed-loop feedback reduces the rate of divergence in both scenarios, with a notable reduction in the case of the VICKI robot. This study examines the complexity of algorithmic problems within power series fields over finite fields through the development of an computationally verifiable version of the Dickson Lemma. Initially, we investigate the computability of elements within power series fields using a total residue map when the underlying field has infinite characteristics, leading to the discovery that having an infinite field enables the decidability of this computability question. Furthermore, we establish that over finite fields, the computability of an element depends on the field's degree. Building upon this finding, we prove that adding a total residue map to the computable structure of a power series field results in an $2$-decidable but not $\omega$-decidable theory when the underlying field has infinite characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this addition yields a theory with an undecidable set of valid formulas when the underlying field is finite. Finally, we establish that over finite fields, the added relation significantly enhances the complexity of the theory, leading to a $2$-decidable but not $\omega$-decidable or $3$-decidable theory. This research is grounded in the work of R. Rumsewski and J. R. Shutt in 'Computable Properties of Power Series Fields' presented at the 9th International Conference on Computability Theory.

Recent studies have demonstrated the viability of Flush+Reload attacks in detecting and mitigating various side-channel leaks, including Spectre, NetDown, and PageHole. However, these attacks are hampered by the relatively long time frames and large number of memory blocks they require to identify and fix all vulnerable functions. We introduce HyperDegrade, an enhanced Flush+Reload technique that not only reduces the required time frames and number of memory blocks from $2^\lambda$ (where $\lambda$ is the security parameter) to a few dozen, but also determines all affected functions in a single experiment with high probability. We showcase the effectiveness of HyperDegrade by applying it to a set of real-world examples, including an optimized version of the Libreswan IPsec implementation and a variety of benchmarking tests with MySQL and PostgreSQL. Furthermore, we compare HyperDegrade to existing Flush+Reload approaches and demonstrate its superior performance. Additionally, we have publicly released our HyperDegrade framework on GitHub for the community to utilize. Whether attackers are motivated by curiosity or intend to launch malicious HyperDegrade-based attacks, we provide guidance on how to employ and customize this technique to suit their needs. Lastly, we have made all our research data fully accessible on our public GitHub repository.

Utilizing an iterative three-loop scheme for the renormalized self-energies of neutrinos within the Standard Model, we calculate thermal effects on the stability of compact stars. Our results indicate that when neutrinos are massively, the standard scheme yields the expected stability of compact stars with no additional restrictions. However, when neutrinos are massless, except for one very small mass state, we find the standard scheme fails to account for instability in these stars. Conversely, the renormalized two-loop standard scheme does not exhibit neutrino mass-induced instability in compact stars. We also found that if the sum of the squared mass states of neutrinos exceeds the scalar meson mass of the Standard Model, compact stars become unstable. Moreover, we found that in the limit of heavy neutrinos, their mass can be constrained to be above $100\,{\rm GeV}$ in order for compact stars to remain stable. We further conclude that in the limit of heavy quarks, the standard scheme demonstrates stability of compact stars, with their mass dependent on the flavor of the quarks. Conditions derived from our calculations can be applied to constraints on the properties of neutrinos and other fundamental particles, contributing to a deeper comprehension of the Standard Model. Our study highlights the significance of incorporating thermal effects from renormalization group equations into the study of compact stars, particularly in relation to strong QCD and the properties of neutrinos. We anticipate that our findings will guide further research in the field. This study conducts an in-depth examination of privacy vulnerabilities in the context of vertical federated learning (VFLE). We first establish the limitations of existing privacy-enhanced VFLE approaches and then undertake a comprehensive review of privacy breaches against learning protocols, encompassing inference and membership attacks in addition to data recovery. We also outline the intricacies of computing attack success rates in vertical settings. To address these challenges, we develop metrics that account for client data variability and establish secure knowledge baselines for comparison in robustness assessments. Through numerical computations and realistic scenario simulations, we demonstrate the imperative need for enhancing privacy in VFLE. We further investigate the interplay between privacy and efficiency, revealing the complex relationships between attack success rates, protocol efficiency, and data recovery in vertical settings. Finally, our proposed robustness frameworks offer actionable insights for researchers and practitioners alike, facilitating the design of more secure and efficient VFLE protocols.

This paper examines the method of Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF) as a means to diminish the requirements of Gaussian Random Features (GRF) in various applications of kernel methods, particularly in Support Vector Machines (SVM). We first present an analysis of how PRFF surpasses RFF in both dimensionality reduction and predictive accuracy, and subsequently investigate the PRFF variant optimized for SVM. Through simulated data analysis, we find that the optimized PRFF method generally outperforms the other alternatives, albeit with the caveat that the difference may be insignificant in certain datasets. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the optimized PRFF method exhibits lower computational demands compared to the conventional SVM technique, while also facilitating improved interpretability of feature coefficients. We also explore applying PRFF to a real-world dataset, with a real-valued attribute, and observe consistent performance across multiple randomizations of the feature mapping. Our study's key contribution lies in enhancing the previously proposed method for Gaussian kernel using PRFF, and exploring its efficacy across diverse scenarios. We have publicly disseminated the Python code associated with our experiments via an open-access repository.

This paper delves into analyzing how to refine base networks in Feature Pyramid Networks-based object detection frameworks to enhance accuracy across different scale objects. Initially, we explore various ways to optimize base network loss functions without exchanging information between scales. Later, we investigate methods to incorporate loss functions for objects at various scales into the base network training process. Moreover, with careful optimization, incorporating object-distinguishing losses into the training process results in a 2.2% improvement in mAP. Our proposed approach is compatible with popular base networks and can be applied to the DetectoR framework. Additionally, we examine strategies to enhance precision by refining the base network with additional data and incorporating boundary-aware loss functions in the base network. Understanding complex language involves navigating various difficulties, including both subtle contextual elements and intricate word forms. While neural language models have excelled in context-based tasks, they often fall short when confronted with morphologically complex words and languages. This study introduces a set of written expressions that combine both significant contextual and lexical challenges. A series of experiments with these examples revealed that certain neural architectures can accurately predict context-dependent word meanings but struggle with words whose form implies a different meaning. Notably, this struggle is particularly pronounced when using BERT. A key finding shows that when words with context-dependent meanings are incorporated into training datasets, the performance of all tested models improves, especially in domains they have not been trained in. Furthermore, both semantic and syntactic analysis show that the primary issue with these words is their polysemy, with their meanings tied to both contextual context and inherent properties, rather than being solely governed by context or form. Moreover, when words with polysemy are included in training datasets, both BERT and the other tested models perform better in domains they have not been trained in, which suggests a level of robustness. Additionally, when words with multiple related meanings are included in training datasets, both BERT and the other tested models perform better in context where these words appear, which indicates some level of generalization. In summary, this study reveals that neural language models perform better when trained with words whose meanings are influenced by both context and form, and that these models are robust enough to perform well in domains they have not been trained in, which has significant implications for the further development of these models. Additionally, this study provides a tool that can produce the desired types of challenging examples, allowing for the creation of custom datasets that can be used to test the limits of neural language models. This study's findings can be viewed as an initial step towards a broader investigation of how neural language models handle the various degrees of semantic and syntactic complexity within language. Consequently, this study hopes to spark a greater interest in this area and pave the way for more comprehensive research. Current advanced models excel in following complex instructions on their own, but they struggle with combining multiple free-form instructions from different sources, a common challenge in many applications, including video editing and cooking. To understand how well algorithms compare to humans in this scenario, we developed a new task called Sequential Instruction following, which involves using unordered lists of instructions with no specified order to complete a task. To standardize evaluation, we created a dataset called SInCk, which contains instructions for creating a collage by following specific rules and using specific images, and includes a way to measure both human and machine performance. Our results show that even the best current models perform significantly worse than humans in this scenario, and that there are some models that perform better than others, which suggests that machine learning can be improved with more sophisticated architectures and better methods of processing natural language. Forming planets in our solar system and likely other solar systems requires understanding how small particles coalesce into massive objects in a surrounding environment. A critical step in this process involves the formation of solid chunks, or planetesimals, which can then come together to form full-fledged planets. Despite its significance, the exact mechanism for planetesimal formation remains unknown and is the subject of a longstanding debate in the planetary science community. 

Some researchers believe that planetesimals could emerge when the gravitational pull of dense regions within protoplanetary disks overwhelms their surrounding environments, potentially forming solid chunks as they collapse under their own weight. Others propose that planetesimals form as a result of collisions between smaller objects in a protoplanetary disk, suggesting that their formation is more of a gradual process.

Our study utilizes high-resolution simulations of developing planetary systems to gain insights into planetesimal formation. We started by assuming that protoplanetary disks are devoid of pre-existing planetesimals and instead focused on how small particles behave under the influence of gravitational forces and their own collisions. Our simulations, which were capable of resolving down to 1 km in diameter, showed that even in areas of high density within protoplanetary disks, objects not significantly larger than 1 km in diameter were destroyed through collisions rather than surviving as distinct entities.

On the other hand, smaller objects in these environments tend to stick together, gradually forming larger objects over time as they move at relative speeds of less than a meter per second in a protoplanetary disk. Our research offers a detailed picture of the size distribution of objects in developing planetary systems and confirms the theoretical framework that governs the behavior of colliding objects in a given velocity environment. Ultimately, our study reveals that objects in the 0.1-10 km range in protoplanetary disks are in a state of continuous flux as they collapse, merge with fellow objects, or are destroyed through collisions. 

However, our simulations also indicate that over time, objects within this size range have a tendency to gravitate towards specific stable orbits, which are characterized by slow object movement and reduced collision frequencies. Our research identifies these orbits as "planetesimal reservoirs" and suggests that the objects formed within these regions have a higher likelihood of eventually coming together to form full-fledged planets. 

Finally, our analysis indicates that the location of these planetesimal formation pathways can shift based on factors such as the flow of matter within a protoplanetary disk as well as the presence of forming stars, and that the resulting planetary systems can exhibit distinctive patterns of organization,

Future experiments such as CLIC and CEPC will offer improved sensitivity, potentially reaching detection limits below $10^{-20}$ for specific decay channels by 2025. However, these experiments have limitations when dealing with heavy neutral leptons with masses above the $Z$ boson mass threshold or those that decay to active neutrinos. In this study, we investigate how production and decay processes of heavy neutral leptons can lead to photon signatures in the context of CLIC. We find that, with the help of shower parton approaches and detector simulations, we can set more stringent limits on the effective mixing parameter $\rho$ until at least $4.4 \times 10^{-20}$, offering a more than one order of magnitude improvement over current sensitivity limits. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, in regions of parameter space that are difficult to constrain for CEPC and future LHC searches, the production of heavy neutral leptons can lead to distinctive signals in photon spectra. In particular, we show that, with an integrated luminosity of three inverse femtobarns at $\sqrt{s} = 3.0$ TeV, CLIC can discover a 4.5 TeV mass threshold for a specific decay channel by 2025. Additionally, we find that, although direct production of heavy neutral leptons at CLIC lacks sufficient sensitivity to influence $Z$ precision data, we can still constrain their parameters with a precision of $\Delta \rho \simeq 2 \times 10^{-18}$, a value that can be further refined with complementarity from precision data at CEPC and future LHC searches. In conclusion, this study highlights the capabilities of CLIC to enhance the understanding of heavy neutral leptons, particularly in regions of parameter space that are challenging to constrain with other experiments. A specific example is provided in the form of a Michelson-like Sagnac interferometer, where the generation of counter-propagating beams with optical path length differences of 10 cm and 40 cm enables the direct detection of frequency differences of 10^(-16) and 10^(-18) respectively. Reconstructing a three-dimensional face from multiple two-dimensional views poses a challenging algebraic problem. Researchers have made significant progress on this issue by relying on face models on specific poses. In contrast, no existing method has successfully derived a comprehensive face model from both pose-dependent and pose-independent factors. Most current approaches typically focus on analyzing factors with a fixed basis, which limits their applicability and generality. To overcome these constraints and limitations, we propose the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), an end-to-end network that can produce an all-encompassing face model from any given number of two-dimensional views. SADRNet successfully decomposes both pose-dependent and pose-independent factors and successfully regenerates a face from any number of input images, provided that the head is visible in the images. Moreover, our network is capable of generating a face even if some views are missing, which we achieve by developing a novel dual pathway. This innovative design successfully separates over-complete and noise factors and effectively produces a comprehensive face model. Notably, our network does not need any face model as input and can still successfully produce a detailed and realistic face model, as evidenced by our high-quality results and overall effectiveness. Our method ultimately outperforms all current competitors, including those that rely on face models, as validated by both qualitative and quantitative assessments. Moreover, our non-rigid algebraic formulation makes SADRNet highly versatile and capable of handling any number of input views. This versatility is further highlighted by our ability to successfully regenerate faces even when some views are missing or under-complete, which we demonstrate through our missing view analysis. Our code is available for public review at our Code Repository: https://github.com/zhkspace/SADRNet. Our results can be found in the Supplemental Materials available at our Project Website: https://zhkspace.github.io/SADRNet/. Our paper is registered and will be presented at CVPR 2020.

As governments invest heavily in low-carbon energy and storage technologies, optimizing the performance of these resources across different risk-management approaches becomes increasingly vital. Our study develops a stochastic model that accounts for risk-averse storage operations and integrates carbon emissions standards in multi-energy systems. We employ a robust optimization algorithm to compute equilibrium strategies for storage resources and other generators under various risk preferences, defined by their ability to tolerate probability thresholds. Our algorithm enables us to efficiently obtain solutions by leveraging the flat rate method and graphical analysis for a two-settled case. Our results show that when the number of time periods increases, our robust optimization model can still compute optimal solutions in a timely manner. Furthermore, our findings indicate that when the number of settlements exceeds the number of time periods, our robust optimization model can be computationally demanding. We demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm by applying it to an actual case study of a multi-energy system in an Australian region. Our results provide valuable insights into the behavior of risk-aware storage resources and highlight the importance of considering storage specific risks in future low-carbon energy systems. Finally, our study's findings can inform policy decisions that affect storage assets, such as pricing mechanisms and carbon emissions standards, ultimately maximizing the full potential of these assets. Our study offers new insights into the behavior of Mars' baroclinic storms and the planet's global circulation patterns. By utilizing the Bottenhausen-Busse multiple scale method to simplify a model of the Martian atmosphere, we obtained a quasi-linear equation that replicates the behavior of baroclinic waves similar to those observed on Mars. Our analysis reveals that the storms exhibit an irregular shape, influenced by the Martian atmosphere's rotation and the gradient of the CO2 gas and temperature distributions. Notably, the circulation patterns on Mars display striking similarities to those found in Earth-like atmospheres. Furthermore, our study indicates that the Martian storms can transition from a baroclinic to a barotropic state, with potential implications for the transport of heat and chemical constituents between the poles and the equator. Our research also suggests that the Martian atmosphere's baroclinic instability can occur at mid-latitudes, and that the storms may be responsible for the residual heat transport and polar warming observed on Mars. Lastly, our findings suggest that the Martian storms could play a crucial role in the planet's atmospheric evolution. However, validating these conclusions will require additional observations and modeling efforts in the future. Our analysis provides a foundation for exploring the interactions between the Martian surface and atmosphere through the study of baroclinic waves. It sets the stage for examining the impacts of atmospheric chemistry, solar radiation, and geothermal heat on Mars' circulation patterns and storm behavior. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of these processes will be essential in preparing for future human missions to Mars, which may rely on the resources of the Martian atmosphere. Those missions will need to be capable of adapting to the harsh, unpredictable environment of the Martian surface, and perhaps even leveraging the planet's atmosphere to reduce reliance on landed cargo. In that context, our study highlights the importance of continuing to explore and understand the complex and fascinating atmosphere of Mars. It also emphasizes the value of using simplified models in atmospheric science, which can provide new insights and lay the groundwork for further numerical simulations and empirical validation. Ultimately, a collaborative effort between theoretical modeling and empirical research holds the key to a deeper understanding of the Martian atmosphere and its many mysteries. It remains to be seen whether future missions to Mars will be capable of answering even half of the many questions still surrounding the planet's atmosphere. It is clear, however, that future missions to Mars will face significant challenges in adapting to the harsh conditions they will encounter. It is our hope that this study will contribute meaningfully to the ongoing effort to understand and overcome those challenges.

Current active learning methodologies suffer from an issue where they select nearly the same samples for multiple algorithms, masking the inherent variability of $f$ on large datasets like ImageNet. This leads to misleading performance predictions, as seen in Section \ref{sec:variable-batching}. A more significant problem arises when these methods are applied to smaller benchmark datasets, where variations in sampling can significantly affect the performance of the model. To address this limitation, we assess the performance of various active learning techniques on smaller datasets following an unusual protocol: after randomly selecting a small group of labeled samples from a benchmark dataset (e.g., CIFAR-100), we add the remaining unsampled data to the pool. Notably, almost all active learning algorithms perform exceptionally well on this smaller pool of data. However, when we add the entire dataset to the pool, the performance of these methods drops substantially. This phenomenon highlights the importance of evaluating active learning algorithms on smaller subsets of large datasets rather than on the full dataset itself. Building upon this observation, we investigate the active learning methods that perform best on smaller datasets (CIFAR-100 in our case) and find that they underperform when confronted with the entire dataset. To address this issue, we propose a new protocol for benchmarking active learning algorithms on smaller subsets of large datasets. Furthermore, we introduce the Deblurring Active Learning (DAL) approach, which enhances the effectiveness of active learning algorithms when applied to smaller datasets. The proposed DAL framework addresses issues such as unsampled data confounding active learning and targets the challenging case of large datasets. We validate our approach by evaluating it on smaller subsets of the large ImageNet dataset, comparing it to conventional active learning algorithms. The proposed study introduces an innovative concept of relative algebraic multiplicity (RAM) for a given point in the spectrum of a linear operator. This concept is then applied to develop a novel algebraic expression for the index of a linear operator in its definitive form. Specifically, the index $\idx(T)$ of an operator $T$ is equivalent to the RAM of the identity operator $I$ when considered within the algebraic closure $\overline{\mathcal{A}}(T)$. Notably, this relationship allows us to bypass the usual requirement for antitonicity in defining the index. Moreover, it yields a geometric interpretation of the index through the use of a Schur operator and its properties. Ultimately, this framework is utilized to establish a connection between the index and the multiplicity of an operator's eigenvalues, yielding both theoretical and practical methods for computing the index. These methods are then demonstrated via computations of the index for various operators, including a notable example involving a matrix whose index cannot be determined via traditional methods. Conversely, our approach makes it possible to determine the index directly. Additionally, our discussion includes a discussion of volume growth rates related to Schur operators and their relationship to the study of Schr\"{o}dinger operators. Our work builds upon previous results from both Klein and Simon as well as from Simon. Our approach offers a more general framework that is applicable across a broader range of operator algebras and their respective spectral properties. Our work is additionally relevant to ongoing research related to Schr\"{o}dinger operators and their spectral properties, particularly as it relates to volume growth rates and its potential connection to Weyl law estimates. Our study also introduces a new concept of relative multiplicity that may be of independent interest within the context of algebraic geometry and the study of polynomial invariants. Our approach and results are equally relevant to both compact and non-compact manifolds. Our work is further accompanied by an Annotated Bibliography that is both comprehensive and critically informative. Our Annotated Bibliography is a valuable resource that is both a necessary companion to our main results and a vital contribution in its own right. Our investigation demonstrates how two-mode squeezing can be utilized from a non-classical channel to enhance optical phase sensing, essentially applying quantum homodyne measurement to channel-based resource development. When the channel contains two-mode squeezing, our findings show that phase sensing becomes nearly optimal with just one unit of two-mode squeezing per unit of loss, achieving this optimal performance when using homodyne measurement without any loss. Notably, this two-mode squeezing-based enhancement outperforms single-mode squeezing-based improvement in phase sensing when the number of photons per mode is low. We also examine how this two-mode squeezing-based improvement translates to enhanced interferometer visibility in multi-path phase sensing, finding that it can improve over single-mode squeezing-based improvement under certain conditions of photon loss in individual channels. To illustrate the practical applicability of these findings, we propose a quantum-enhanced phase sensing protocol utilizing two-mode squeezing based on entangled photons generated from bi-photic luminescence of a single molecule. This protocol demonstrates how two-mode squeezing can compensate for multi-path photon loss in interferometer-based phase sensing. However, we also identify a fundamental limitation imposed by the non-zero minimum loss per mode in actual entanglement generation processes. In consequence, two-mode squeezing-based improvement may not fully leverage its potential in practical applications due to this imposed limitation of minimum loss per mode. In our case, using entangled photons from bi-photic luminescence of a single molecule, this minimum loss per mode is approximately 10^-8, making this protocol unsuitable for sensing small phase changes due to this extremely small loss threshold. Nevertheless, this protocol remains superior to single-mode squeezing-based improvement in multi-path phase sensing with controllable photon loss in individual channels, notably when the entanglement generation process itself incurs substantial loss in at least one mode, such as when entangled photons are generated from bi-photic luminescence of different dye molecule-filled containers with significant spectral overlap, in which case multi-path photon loss becomes unavoidable. In such cases, our investigation shows that two-mode squeezing-based improvement outperforms single-mode squeezing-based improvement by several orders of magnitude. Our investigation advances the development of multi-path phase sensing, a crucial application of quantum sensing, and could catalyze the improvement of interferometer visibility in actual quantum-homodyne measurements through the optimal utilization of non-classical channels. This, in turn, may spur the creation of novel, efficient entanglement generation methods with minimum loss per mode. Researchers utilize nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond to implement quantum computation and communication by developing spin-based protocols. However, finding efficient methods to efficiently implement two-qubit logic operations like the TOG gate without relying on sensitive optical readout remains a significant challenge. A study demonstrates that combining silicon and diamond in a single device can efficiently achieve the necessary two-qubit operations by utilizing the unique properties of nitrogen-donor ensembles in silicon. By carefully placing and tuning the donor atoms, it's possible to perform accurate two-qubit logic gates, even when the donor and vacancy centers are spatially separated. In this approach, the donor electrons are used to perform the two-qubit operations, eliminating the need for precise control over the optical readout of the nitrogen-vacancy centers. Consequently, this method enables robust execution of the TOG gate using a nitrogen-donor pair in silicon and a nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond, with only minimal adjustment needed to achieve optimal results. In gallium arsenide quantum wells with a small effective mass, we've observed unusual oscillations in electrical resistance near the zero Landau level when subjected to high magnetic field strengths.  This behavior appears in large samples but not in nanoscale ones, and is linked to scattering at the edge of mini-bands within the energy spectrum.  A simple theoretical model reveals that these oscillations result from the interplay between the scattering between the zero Landau level and adjacent levels, and the inequality of these levels' chemical potentials, which is a hallmark of small effective mass systems.  In our setup, this inequality is sufficiently large that the chemical potentials remain relatively constant across multiple Landau levels, thus rendering the oscillations around the zero level uniquely pronounced.  This research is further validated by comparing experimental findings with more sophisticated simulations that account for the full spin and valley spectrum of the material, and is relevant to the interpretation of experimental data in low-mass systems where the zero Landau level may be difficult to access.  In such cases, the oscillations we've identified may be misinterpreted as being associated with the zero level rather than the nearby levels.  This distinction holds significant implications for our current understanding of the behavior of high-field electrical resistance in low-mass systems, particularly in the context of superconductivity in the magnetic field.  In these systems, the zero level is often the limiting factor in determining the maximum field strength before electrical resistance disappears, and thus appears to set the boundary for the onset of superconductivity itself.  However, our research shows that this level is not a fundamental limit, and that the actual constraint is imposed by the nearby levels whose chemical potentials are equivalent to that of the zero level, and which may not occur until much higher magnetic field strengths.  This distinction has far-reaching implications for the broader field of high-field superconductivity research, and highlights the importance of accurately identifying the zero Landau level when interpreting experimental data. Substantial research has been devoted to developing private machine learning algorithms that meet differential privacy standards, but little attention has been given to analyzing the impact of dataset connectivity in graph structures on privacy loss computation. We investigate this issue in the context of two popular graph-based private learning methods: node classification using K-Nearest Neighbors and graph classification using the Small-World network. We demonstrate that interconnecting data points forms a high-risk network that facilitates significant privacy loss computation, making it essential to incorporate graph structure into the analysis to avoid overestimating privacy losses. Our results demonstrate various configurations of graph structures, including small-world networks and random connections, that demonstrate substantially lower privacy loss computation compared to fully connected and disconnected graphs. Current automated lane keeping systems rely on machine learning algorithms and have primarily been evaluated using real-world data with minimal artificial inputs. Nevertheless, validating their capability to handle complex scenarios relies on simulated environments. Nonetheless, even high-end simulation platforms are prone to limitations, such as incomplete or inaccurately represented road data, vehicle malfunctions, and insufficient training of sensor modules. Consequently, there is a pressing need to create challenging road networks that can test the robustness and reliability of automated lane keeping systems in a scalable and modular simulation framework. To address this issue, we developed a novel approach to generating artificially complex road scenarios that can be integrated with existing sensor modules and vehicle models. This approach enables the creation of demanding scenarios in a scalable and modular fashion, allowing for greater control over the level of difficulty and specific challenges incorporated into the environment. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability of this approach by constructing two particular challenge scenarios and conducting experiments to assess their effectiveness in robustness testing of automated lane keeping systems. The findings from these experiments were validated against systems employing real-world data and machine learning algorithms. Ultimately, we found that artificially generated environments can provide a reliable and efficient means of conducting robustness testing of automated lane keeping systems in a simulation environment. This approach can be viewed as a publicly accessible module on GitHub, alongside two illustrative use cases, and is compatible with the iTASC simulation framework. Overall, our research offers a previously unseen perspective on the development of challenging road networks and contributes a pioneering approach to generating artificially complex scenarios that can be applied to a broader range of autonomous driving scenarios. Consequently, we believe this innovative approach has the capacity to motivate further investigation into the creation of robust automated lane keeping systems. Lattice Model, allowing the simulation of quantum effects like non-equilibrium
quantum correlations and interactions within condensed matter systems. This new
approach overcomes limitations of older methods when dealing with these scenarios.
As a test case, it was applied to a Kubo linear response calculation for the
insulating phase of Cuprate, yielding accurate simulations of quantum effects,
outperforming traditional methods. This was confirmed by comparisons against
experimental data from ARPES. The new hydrodynamic scheme also demonstrates
improved convergence under large system sizes, outperforming alternative methods
by several orders of magnitude. In contrast to equilibrium situations, where
hydrodynamic theory aligns with simulation results, the non-equilibrium regime
remains a subject of investigation. The developed linearized hydrodynamic
scheme can be leveraged to study other Lattice Models, such as Superconductors
and Semiconductors, providing a more precise understanding of quantum effects
towards developing novel device concepts. The implemented method is also
available through the KuboLinearResponse package on Zenodo. The Python-based
GUI, named ElectronsLab, offers users an intuitive user interface to define
and run simulations. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/fzijl/ElectronsLab GUI. Recent advances in feature learning for actions have primarily focused on utilizing single-source data, despite the wealth of information contained in dual-source data comprising both video and audio components. Many current approaches simply concatenate the extracted features without exploring more effective ways of fusing them. To fully leverage the dual-source information, we propose the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN), a framework that employs dual context aggregation blocks to seamlessly combine video and audio features. By consistently increasing the number of combined contexts, DCAN progressively refines action proposals by considering multiple moments in videos and audio signals. Experimental evaluations show that DCAN outperforms state-of-the-art methods for action proposal generation on ActivityNet, achieving a proposal quality score (A-P) of 0.755 and average recall at 50 (R@50) of 0.734 for diverse proposal thresholds. Moreover, DCAN exhibits improved performance when compared to the baseline method for action classification on ActivityNet, yielding a mean class accuracy (MCA) of 42.5%. The code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/zx0750750/DCAN. The advantages of DCAN over conventional methods primarily result from its ability to effectively fuse dual-source information using a context aggregation strategy. This technique demonstrates potential applications in other vision-and-audio-based tasks, such as activity recognition and multi-modal learning. This study focuses on the PTM phenomena observed during the JET ELMy free scenarios. To understand the frequency link between edge localized modes and magnetic island Bradley arrays, a new mode formation location was proposed, based on the $m=5$ $\alpha$-mode and island Bradley arrays from a previous case. The proposed mode formation area around the Bradley coalescence site is called the "palm tree mode". Edge localized modes can cause the activation of PTMs when magnetic flux accumulates in the edge region, breaking symmetry and triggering the mode at the Bradley coalescence site. A mode with a similar frequency but different nomenclature was previously reported in an MHD seismology study on JET. The proposed palm tree mode theory is supported by a quasi-singular value decomposition wall mode recovery technique. The edge magnetic field spectra obtained from this method show a mode with a similar frequency to the PTMs, and the mode location and direction can be inferred from the eigenfunction. Notably, this method is able to reproduce the observed frequency shift in an MHD scenario without a significant change in the mode frequency on the magnetic flux surface, despite edge magnetic field changes. The proposed palm tree mode theory provides a new framework for understanding the edge magnetic field dynamics in the edge localized modes and magnetic island Bradley coalescence region. It is suggested that this mode is an ideal candidate for an MHD seismology probe in future JET and ASAS tokamaks with edge localized mode-free or highly reduced ELMy scenarios. To optimize the PTM frequency downshift experiment on JET in the next campaign, it is proposed that (i) the wall mode recovery is performed immediately after the wall only low field side (LFS) plasma refilling in a wall only low field side (WOLFS) discharge, and (ii) the ELMy free scenario is achieved through a slow plasma start-up without plasma prefilling in the wall case, to maximize the edge localized mode-free duration. It is also suggested that the PTM downshift experiment is conducted on ASAS, with a focus on understanding the PTM physics and exploring the potential of PTMs as an MHD seismology tool. Finally, this study proposes that the PTM could be controlled by applying a magnetic field on the magnetic island Bradley coalescence site, and this concept should be investigated both experimentally and theoretically. Then, the feasibility of the suggested approach is demonstrated through hands-on experiments with a mobile robot navigating past a stationary obstacle in both circular and triangular forms.
