Current methods of evaluating and comparing fuzzers are limited by a lack of a unified framework for measuring their effectiveness, which is further hindered by the absence of a standard metric for assessing their quality. While some studies have attempted to assess fuzzers using mutation analysis, their findings are hindered by the limited understanding of how to accurately apply these techniques to evaluate fuzzers. To address this issue, this paper introduces a comprehensive approach for comparing fuzzers that leverages modern mutation analysis techniques and incorporates relevant factors such as coverage, reachability, and test case diversity. To support this approach, the paper also includes an evaluation of different mutation analysis tools and techniques, an analysis of the costs and benefits of applying these techniques to evaluate fuzzers, and an exploration of the implications of using them for comparison purposes. Additionally, the paper presents an empirical study that compares the effectiveness of seven popular fuzzers, including Huffman, a leading binary fuzzer, and outlines an improvement to Huffman that demonstrates substantial gains in efficiency and effectiveness. The empirical study and experimental results are made possible by an open-source evaluation framework, named Arches, which is also an important contribution of this paper. This framework is an extension of the popular fuzzbench benchmark and evaluation framework and can be found at https://arches.dev. The empirical study and experimental results that make the paper's findings possible also rely heavily on an advanced mutation analysis technique, named RelaQ, which is an enhanced version of the Q2C technique. This technique can be found at https://github.com/relaq-project/relaQ. The empirical study that compares the effectiveness of seven popular fuzzers is conducted on the Linux kernel and includes the results of over 1,500 distinct mutation analysis experiments. The empirical study demonstrates that current evaluation methodologies are insufficient and fail to do justice to the differences they observe between fuzzers, often failing to account for various confounding factors such as coverage, reachability, and test case diversity. The study also reveals that the best-performing fuzzer on a given set of targets is not necessarily the most effective in other cases and highlights the need for a more comprehensive comparison of fuzzers that takes into account various factors beyond coverage alone. To address this requirement, the paper proposes an empirical study that compares the effectiveness of fuzzers based on mutation analysis results from a diverse set of targets. However, due to space constraints, this empirical study is only briefly outlined in the paper and will be extensively discussed in future work. In addition, the paper also includes an evaluation of four different mutation analysis techniques

This study investigates the application of nearest mean classifiers in continual learning for natural language classification, using pre-trained models like BERT.  By analyzing various settings and evaluation metrics, our research reveals that the simple NMC approach achieves impressive results, outperforming advanced continual learning methods in many cases and consistently providing stable performance across multiple tasks.  Our findings also demonstrate that NMC's effectiveness can be attributed to its ability to effectively exploit the overlap between tasks, a crucial aspect in multi-task learning.  While the NMC approach sometimes falls short with very small datasets or highly distinct classes, its overall performance makes it a valuable reference point for the evaluation of more complex continual learning models.  Our code is openly accessible on GitHub, enabling replication of our experiments and further research into NMC's properties.  This research includes a thorough analysis of NMC's performance across 17 tasks, utilizing the GLUE benchmark and the SuperGLUE benchmark, in addition to the Sogou Chinese Corpus.  Our results provide valuable insights into the NMC method's behavior in various contextual scenarios, offering a useful baseline for other continual learning models to compare against.  We also explore methods to enhance NMC's capacity to adapt across multiple tasks, outlining potential pathways for further research in this area. We make the first investigation into a broader framework of Lipschitz games, where each player has their own individual Lipschitz constant. This more general version of the game involves analyzing mixed strategy profiles and paying attention to the specific Lipschitz constants of the payoff functions for each player. A key aspect of our study is presenting an upper bound for an equilibrium payoff profile that takes into account the effects of player-specific Lipschitz constants. Additionally, we explore an algorithm to find an $\epsilon$-approximate mixed strategy profile that is consistent with the player-specific Lipschitz constants, and this method is grounded in the application of projected gradient descent. A widely accepted method for assessing performance and preventing overfitting is cross-validation. Despite its widespread adoption, many models still struggle with unreliable estimates due to overfitting, particularly when working with large datasets. To address this issue, we introduce J-K-fold cross-validation, a more stable performance estimator that incorporates a wider range of subsamples. J-K-fold cross-validation involves selecting the best-performing K out of J different K-fold cross-validation settings, which significantly enhances the model's performance stability. Notably, our algorithm is highly versatile and can be applied to various performance metrics as well as model selection. Furthermore, we have analytically proven that J-K-fold cross-validation yields the most stable performance estimates by minimizing the variance of model performance. Additionally, we have determined that J-K-fold cross-validation can be viewed as a specific instance of a random sample performance estimator that incorporates a maximum performance threshold. To facilitate seamless integration into existing workflows, we have developed a Python implementation of J-K-fold cross-validation that can be used with scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and PyTorch APIs. Our experiments have demonstrated substantial improvements in model stability and reliability across diverse datasets and scenarios. As such, we highly recommend incorporating J-K-fold cross-validation into machine learning workflows, particularly when working with large datasets. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/samuelc899/JK-Fold-XVal. The Python package is openly accessible on PyPI at https://pypi.org/project/jkfoldxval/.

Recent advances in computer vision have primarily focused on designing complex networks with high computational demands. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of Teacher-Student architectures to achieve exceptional performance from lightweight student networks while reducing energy consumption. Typically, the teacher network is optimized for high accuracy, while the student network is trained to mimic its performance under training constraints, often with a compression factor. Unlike conventional methods that fix the compression factor, our proposed framework dynamically adjusts it during a two-stage training process. Initially, the student and teacher networks are identical, with the student network gradually being compressed in the second stage. To facilitate this process, our method refines the compression factor based on the validation loss of both the teacher and student networks. As a result, our approach outperforms existing methods with reduced compression factors, delivering even better accuracy from the student network. The benefits of this method are confirmed through experiments on semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and image classification. Compared to the method where the compression factor is set before training, our approach achieves similar accuracy with a student network that is 2.3 times smaller in parameters. Our method also achieves 97.6% higher mIoU than the standard sub-network (4 times smaller) on the Cityscapes validation set, outperforming existing methods that achieve around 40.6% mIoU. The code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/TSAF.git. Our approach, known as Tuning Student Architecture Factor, is now the best method for adapting Teacher-Student architectures according to our comprehensive evaluation on three popular datasets (Cityscapes, MS COCO, and Stanford Indoor) and three popular benchmark tasks (semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and image classification). Notably, our method delivers the current state-of-the-art accuracy from lightweight networks on Cityscapes validation set with small evaluation loss, outperforming existing methods with compression factors that are often achieved at the expense of significant increases in parameters. In instance segmentation, our approach achieved the third highest accuracy from lightweight networks on MS COCO validation set with a compression factor of 1.2, delivering the best evaluation performance with a compression factor of 1.5, outperforming existing methods with compression factors of 1 and 2. Similarly, our method delivers the best accuracy from lightweight networks on Stanford Indoor validation set with an average compression factor of 1.2, outperforming existing methods with compression factors of 1, 1.5, and 2. Bucket Elimination (BE) is an influential algorithm for inferring and optimizing graphical models that leverages a variable ordering to achieve efficiency. However, determining an optimal BE ordering remains computationally intensive and is often addressed by simplistically ordering variables randomly. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel BE ordering framework, BucketOrdering, which identifies an optimal ordering by solving a nested subset inclusion problem through the application of recent breakthroughs in the theory of graphs. Specifically, this includes the use of recent results on the recognition of certain graph classes and the properties of order-equivalence in graphs. We demonstrate that BucketOrdering outperforms existing BE ordering methods in accuracy and exhibits near-optimal performance in terms of encoding size. Moreover, we demonstrate the benefits of BucketOrdering in conjunction with BE compared to other model selection algorithms. We have re-examined the concepts of jamming in isotropic and shear deformations for both frictionless and frictional systems, with particular attention to three-dimensional glassy mechanics. Our re-evaluation yields the relationship between isotropic and shear jamming, and we've confirmed that the exponents at both types of jamming transitions do, in fact, differ. As a result, the distinction between frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming cannot be eliminated, and we've re-interpretated existing data through this new framework, gaining new insights into the underlying mechanisms driving these transitions. Furthermore, our model suggests that the exponents at frictional shear jamming transition may be described by $h_{SI} = 2/3$, $k_{SI} = 1/2$, $T_{sh} = 0$, $h_{sh} = 1$, and $k_{sh} = 1/2$. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of jamming transitions and may provide a framework for interpreting future data. Additionally, our model predicts the existence of distinct mechanical states at both frictionless isotropic and frictional shear jamming transitions, and we propose that these states lie on separate universality classes of phase transitions. We've also obtained theoretical predictions for the exponents at both jamming transitions, and these predictions differ from existing experimental measurements, which could be worth re-examining. Our work on this topic is now complete, and we hope that it will spark renewed interest in the underlying mechanisms driving jamming transitions, particularly in three-dimensional glassy mechanics systems. Nevertheless, more extensive research is still needed to fully comprehend the mechanisms governing these transitions and to resolve any existing discrepancies in the data. In this sense, our work on this topic is largely exploratory in nature, and our primary objective was to introduce a new framework for analyzing jamming transitions, even if this framework may require further refinement in the future. Ultimately, we believe that this research lays the groundwork for a more in-depth investigation of the mechanisms governing jamming transitions, particularly in three-dimensional glassy mechanics systems, and we're willing to engage in this research, either independently or in collaboration with others, as needed. In this context, we invite the scientific community to contribute their perspectives, share their expertise, and collaborate with us in the pursuit of a deeper understanding of these transitions and the associated mechanical states. In this sense, our work on this topic is now available for public review, and we're open to any feedback

By comparing one-dimensional cross-section data to total cross-section data, the velocity distribution of incident halo WIMPs is contrasted with its one-dimensional counterpart, revealing an imbalance between the two. Furthermore, this discrepancy is illustrated through a hypothetical experiment involving a moving Earth and WIMP source. Existing research that utilizes the one-dimensional velocity distribution model is cautioned, as it may inaccurately represent the true incident WIMP distribution. An alternative approach is proposed to accurately determine one-dimensional cross-sections from total cross-section data, taking into consideration the true WIMP velocity distribution. Finally, the differences in one-dimensional and total cross-sections are analyzed in relation to the heavy WIMP target scenario. Public sector employees who are not tech-savvy may not be aware that search engines utilize personalized ranking systems which can produce biased results, leading to misdirection in their professional searches. This study examines the effect of inferred biases in search engine rankings on public sector professionals' information-seeking behavior, with a focus on how they respond to health promotion initiatives. A survey among adults in one region served as the basis for our experiment, which aimed to gauge the impact of biased search results on public sector professionals' information-seeking patterns. The findings of our study suggest that algorithmic bias can lead to professoionals being misdirected from their original search goals, with potential consequences for their actions. Consequently, it is essential for public sector professionals to be informed about the potential for biased search engine results and for search engines to prioritize clear disclosure practices. Furthermore, our study identified several factors which influence how much users are directed from their original search goals, including user characteristics and contextual factors, with women and younger adults appearing to be directed less from their original search goals in our study. Our study's results also indicate that users who are directed from their original search goals are less likely to visit relevant websites and may be less likely to engage in healthy behaviors, with potential consequences for their physical health. Consequently, it is crucial for search engines to prioritize transparency and accountability in their personalized ranking systems to avoid unintended consequences on users' lives. Our study's findings can serve as a foundation for further research aimed at comprehending the intricate relationships between algorithmic bias, information-seeking patterns, and individual behavior in various contexts. Ultimately, our study stresses the necessity for a multidisciplinary approach to examine the societal implications of personalized ranking systems and develop humane design principles for algorithmic systems that promote transparency, accountability, and user-centered practices. Our study's results are relevant to any setting or community where personalized Web search may have a significant impact on users' lives and their search engine-based information-seeking patterns. A TeV-scale muon collider, which would enable studies of high-energy processes involving top quarks, Higgs bosons, and supersymmetric particles, is currently the most advanced concept for a next-generation particle collider. To assess the sensitivity of such a detector to these phenomena, researchers are developing theoretical models that can guide the design of the detector and reconstruction algorithms. In this context, we examine the potential of a 1.6-TeV, 2-TeV muon collider to discover or rule out various extensions of the standard model, assuming a detector with the performance characteristics expected for the Future Circular Collider, muon collider-style detectors, or a simplified detector model. Our findings indicate that with 3 ab$^{-1}$ of data at each energy, a 1.6-TeV, 2-TeV muon collider can achieve a 5 sigma discovery power of 2.2, 1.3, and 0.7 for a top-squark mass of 600, 1000, 1500 GeV, respectively. For the Higgs boson, the expected sensitivity is 0.8, 0.2 sigma for 1.6, 2 TeV, respectively. In the supersymmetric scenario with compressed spectra, with a neutralino mass of 150, 300 GeV and a 1.6, 2 TeV muon collider can achieve a 5 sigma discovery power of 1.1, 0.7, respectively. These findings highlight the advantages of a muon collider over a hadron collider for discovering top-squarks and compressed supersymmetry spectra at the highest energy scales. To facilitate further optimization of the detector design, we have incorporated our analysis into the HOLISH code, which is publicly available for a wide range of new physics scenarios.

A new way to collect data, known as rCASPR sampling, is proposed to counteract the limitations of traditional linear sampling in microscopic imaging. The rCASPR approach is designed to enhance the point-spread function and image contrast by collecting additional data points at varied sample positions. A computer model simulated the proposed sampling method and compared it to linear sampling for in-flight particle detection and optical sectioning. The results showed that rCASPR outperforms linear sampling in both scenarios. Specifically, rCASPR was found to increase the detection yield by a factor of two, while also improving the resolution in optical sectioning from 2-fold to 4-fold over linear sampling. Furthermore, rCASPR was found to offer better contrast due to its ability to collect data at different propellant angles. The study demonstrates the potential of rCASPR to enhance the sensitivity and resolution of in-flight imaging systems. However, it also highlights the need for more advanced data analysis methods to fully utilize its capabilities. In-flight particle detection and optical sectioning are key technologies for various applications, including in-flight biohazard detection, planetary science, and spacecraft navigation. While rCASPR's benefits are most pronounced in the context of in-flight imaging, the approach could potentially be adapted for other microscopic imaging scenarios. Nevertheless, implementing rCASPR would require modifying existing in-flight imaging systems to accommodate additional data collection at different sample positions. Consequently, a middle-ground approach is also explored in the study, involving a simplified variant of the algorithm that maintains some of rCASPR's advantages while minimizing system modifications. This alternative approach, referred to as CASPR-S, collects data at a limited range of sample positions and compares favorably to linear sampling in terms of point-spread function and image contrast. Ultimately, the investigation paves the way for further research into rCASPR, including simulations of the approach with complex samples, in-flight biohazard detection, and other applications. Moreover, potential modifications to in-flight imaging systems that could facilitate rCASPR are also identified and warrant exploration. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the potential of rCASPR to counteract the point-spread function limitations of in-flight imaging systems through additional data collection at varying sample positions. While its full potential remains to be realized, the investigation also indicates that rCASPR could be adapted for other microscopic imaging contexts, albeit with possible system modifications. Consequently, the study raises both practical and theoretical implications for in-flight imaging systems and other applicable contexts, and and further research is and necessary to explore these possibilities further. Unlike previous methods that relied on Monte Carlo simulations, our exact approach determines the correct p-value by directly calculating the number of favorable permutation outcomes. The development of an efficient algorithm allows us to perform the test on large datasets that would otherwise be computationally inaccessible. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to a real-world dataset of nanosecond precision voice recognition data, showing improved accuracy compared to the Monte Carlo approximation. Furthermore, our exact method provides a ground truth for evaluating the performance of machine learning models in this domain. Additionally, we identify and address several issues with the current practice of publishing results from paired-permutation tests in the field of computer speech and audio processing. This includes the limited scope of the ISOTURE dataset and the absence of a publicly available implementation for conducting the test. This study examines how the collapse of shipping cartels affected freight rates and shipping volume through a theoretical and empirical analysis. A non-cooperative game theory model is employed to illustrate the negative consequences of cartels dissolving, which is then empirically validated using historical data from the shipping industry from 1970 to 2006. Our empirical findings suggest that the breakdown of shipping cartels led to increased freight rates and decreased shipping volume in the short term, but eventually, both freight rates and shipping volume returned to their previous levels. This is consistent with our theoretical model's prediction that shipping cartels have an adverse effect on welfare. Notably, our results differ from previous studies on cartels, which typically find that their dissolution results in higher production and lower prices in the short term. Our research offers a new perspective on the topic and is particularly relevant to industries characterized by long-term contracts, such as shipping, commodities, and pharmaceuticals. Furthermore, our analysis provides a framework for antitrust policymakers to assess the impact of cartels in these industries. In the case of shipping, our results suggest that higher freight rates resulting from cartels have significant consequences for trade and commerce. A recent finding extends this concept to loom spaces in general, revealing that every loom space is uniquely linked to a distinct triangulation of a surface and a specific coloring of the triangulation's vertices. This newfound understanding also establishes a biological connection between chord diagrams and the topological structures known as Milnor fillables. A key aspect of this work is the identification of a specific surface coloring, referred to as'standard', which is derived from the underlying surface's topology. It is shown that this standard coloring can be utilized to define a unique norm for the space of functions between two loom spaces. Furthermore, this norm is found to be equivalent to another norm, which is derived from the total variation of maps between loom spaces. Finally, some compactness properties are established for sets of maps between loom spaces, provided that the target loom space is fixed and its triangulation is of finite edge count. These properties are shown to yield a compact embedding of the space of maps onto a loom space, when the source loom space is varied. A related result is the compactness of the space of maps from a fixed surface to a loom space, when the loom space is varied. This finding is bolstered by homeomorphism equations, which provide theoretical foundations for developing minimum energy configurations of vortex filaments under an helical motion. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved notable success in tackling complex graph-related tasks, albeit their underlying mechanisms aren't yet fully comprehended. A prevailing hypothesis proposes that GNNs leverage both node features and graph structure to extract relevant information. While previous studies have analyzed the importance of graph structure and node features separately, they have not yet examined their interconnected effects on GNNs. This study investigates the interplay between graph structure and node features in GNNs by means of attribute reduction in formal concept analysis. Our objectives are two-fold: first to visualize the interaction between graph structure and node features; second to measure the impact of both factors on GNNs. Our results show that graph structure has a more significant influence than node features and that both factors have a combined effect which is greater than their individual effects. Furthermore, our results indicate that the influence of graph structure is more pronounced at higher semantic levels. This research provides a novel, attribute-specific understanding of GNNs and may inform the design of more efficient GNNs that prioritize structure at higher semantic levels. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zhengzhengwang/Understanding-GNNs. Our study is also accompanied by concrete recommendations for future work. Both have been shared on the repository mentioned above. Our study is the first to examine the effects of graph structure and node features in GNNs. It has the potential to influence the design of more effective graph neural networks by optimizing graph architecture at higher semantic levels. This study undertakes a theoretical and practical examination of how adaptive
data influences the security of traditional estimators in dimensionality reduction.
Initially, we analytically assess the impact of adaptive input on the security of
L1 and L2 estimators in high-dimensional settings. Subsequently, we conduct a
quantitative assessment of the adaptive input's effect on the security of four
popular estimators in finite-dimensional settings. Moreover, a simulation is
conducted to gauge the adaptive input's effect on the security of L1 and L2
estimators in moderate-dimensional settings. Notably, we develop a new secure
estimator tailored for adaptive input and apply it to a real-world dataset
analysis. Our research reveals that utilizing the new secure estimator yields more
accurate results than traditional methods when dealing with adaptive data in both
the simulation and real-world analysis. The implementation of the secure
estimator and an accompanying tutorial are available on our repository. We have
also introduced a standalone R function for the benefit of other researchers.

This paper investigates the geometries associated with singular compact area minimizers in a specific setting. In the context of smooth boundaries, we demonstrate that certain 3D submanifolds with a specific singular point, accumulating at a point in a plane, can be achieved through compact, stable area minimizers. This result extends a previous finding by Simons in the context of surfaces. The proof strategy involves comparing a given minimizer to one with modified geometry, employing a surgery-style argument to demonstrate the equivalence of their associated geometries. Additionally, the paper establishes a relationship between the conformal structure of compact, stable area minimizers in 4-dimensional space and the geometry of their associated 3D submanifolds. This relationship enables the construction of stable, area-minimizing 3D submanifolds from minimal surfaces with a specific property in 4-dimensional space. A final section discusses potential applications of these results to the study of harmonic maps and Willmore surfaces. This work is a collaboration between two authors, one of whom has passed away and continues to contribute through these results. His influence on the development of these ideas is acknowledged in the preface. This work was inspired by Simons' 1976 paper showing that certain 2D surfaces with a specific singular point can be achieved through compact, stable area minimizers. The study is extended to the 3-dimensional space by comparing a given minimizer to one with modified geometry, utilizing a surgery-style argument to demonstrate the equivalence of their associated geometries. This relationship enables the construction of stable, area-minimizing 3-dimensional submanifolds from minimal surfaces with a particular property in the 4-dimensional space. A final section discusses potential applications of these results to the studies of harmonic maps and Willmore surfaces. The Ginzburg-Landau theories for superconductors and superfluids allow us to compare the entropy within a vortex core to the entropy associated with a moving magnetic flux line or a moving quantized vortex. In type-I superconductors and abelian superfluids, the entropy in the vortex core is significantly lower than the entropy associated with a moving magnetic flux line or a moving quantized vortex. In type-II superconductors and non-abelian superfluids, a moving magnetic flux line or a moving quantized vortex contains less entropy than the vortex core. A moving magnetic flux line or a moving quantized vortex can be considered as a vortex core with local depletion of the order parameter. The results can also be understood by recognizing that a moving magnetic flux line or a moving quantized vortex is equivalent to a vortex core with an expeditiously moving boundary of the order parameter depletion region. The boundary moves so quickly that it cannot keep up with the average motion of the condensate and thus, it cannot maintain a significant entropy difference with the surrounding condensate. In type-II superconductors, the magnetic flux line can choose an extra path with local increases in the order parameter and thus, it can be considered as an extra vortex core with local increases in the order parameter. In type-I superconductors and abelian superfluids, such an extra path does not exist for the magnetic flux line or the quantized vortex and thus, it cannot be considered as an extra vortex core. The results have implications for the dynamics of these systems, particularly in type-II superconductors and non-abelian superfluids where the movement of a vortex core may not be the primary mechanism for the movement of the condensate and in type-II superconductors where the movement of a magnetic flux line may not be the primary mechanism for the movement of the magnetic flux line. The condensate can exhibit its own characteristics in these systems and the vortex core can represent a different phenomenon that may not be directly connected to the movement of the magnetic flux line or the quantized vortex. The distinction between these systems and the distinction within these systems awaits further experimental and theoretical studies in the context of the dynamics of vortex cores and the condensate in these systems. A key challenge in the smart grid lies in the communication between systems, particularly between an aggregator and a discrete set of operators. To tackle this issue, an innovative approach called maximum entropy feedback (MEF) has been developed to enable efficient two-way communication. Initially demonstrated with an example involving the flexible load of air conditioners, MEF has shown potential in simplifying the coordination process between an aggregator and an operator, ultimately facilitating automatic demand response programs. To further explore this concept, an MEF-based framework is now applied to a more complex scenario involving multiple loads and operators. The effectiveness of this framework is validated through a simulation involving up to 50 participants in the power market. Results indicate that MEF can lead to optimal outcomes, achieving the highest possible probability of correct responses, and is capable of producing robust policies resistant to manipulation. Moreover, this approach yields outcomes at least as good as, and in some cases better than, those obtained through reinforcement learning and other comparative methods. Notably, MEF outperforms these methods even when they have access to twice the amount of training data. The proposed framework also offers a beneficial coexistence between different loads and can handle varying market conditions, providing clear guidelines for the aggregator in making pricing decisions. Ultimately, this research showcases the potential of maximum entropy feedback to revolutionize the way loads and operators communicate and interact within the smart grid ecosystem. By successfully managing distributed loads and influencing the behavior of individual components, MEF is poised to become a foundational component of future grid communication systems, requiring only minimal information exchange and minimal training, making it particularly suited for the rapid deployment of decentralized applications. Notably, this comprehensive analysis includes a detailed examination of double Higgs production in association with top quarks and/or anti-top quarks, top quarks and/or anti-top quarks and photons, top quarks and/or anti-top quarks and gluons, top quarks and/or anti-top quarks and bottom quarks, as well as all purely leptonic final states. Moreover, our study covers various polarization states of the Higgs bosons, and we have carried out the computation up to order $\mathcal{O}(v^4/m_H^4)$ in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory parameter space. In addition, we have gained specific insights into the dependence of the leading coefficients on the Standard Model Effective Field Theory parameters in the case of on-shell Higgsscattering processes. Finally, our analysis provides a framework for interpreting Double Higgs Global Fit results within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. In this context, we have explored several scenarios for the Standard Model Higgs self-coupling at the LHC and future colliders. Lastly, we have begun to investigate the implications of our computation for Standard Model Effective Field Theory interpretations of Double Higgs production data at the LHC and future colliders. In doing so, we have gained a deeper understanding of how the leading coefficients in the Higgs Effective Field Theory correspond to those in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory across all considered scenarios. An extension of this approach has now been developed to account for general, non-compact conformal matter fields in three-dimensional anti-de Sitter spacetime. The separation procedure involves solving a set of defining equations for the conformal factors and the harmonic components of the metric, obtained from analyzing the conformal structure of the gravitational and matter fields. The relative strength of two opposing forces, friction and drag, determines the motion of a solid object through granular materials.  A cylindrical intruder was used to investigate its motion through different granular beds at various driving rates.  When the driving rate is low, the intruder moves slowly due to drag, but at higher rates it breaks through the granular surface and is slowed by friction.  The relationship between the two forces is controlled by the Reynolds number of the surrounding granular material.  The study found that the drag experienced by the intruder is significantly greater than predicted by existing models, especially at high driving rates.  The results also indicate that the flow of granular materials around the moving intruder is highly nonlinear, and that the drag and friction depend on the intruder's velocity in a way that is not immediately apparent.  The ratio of drag to friction was found to be greater than one, which means that the intruder's motion is governed by a singular perturbation problem.  The results of the study were verified by conducting experiments in different granular beds at various driving rates, and the findings were used to develop a new model that accurately predicts the motion of the intruder.  The new model performs better than existing models, especially at high driving rates, and it may be applied to a broad spectrum of granular materials.  The study also explored the effect of different granular material properties on the intruder's motion, and the results indicate that the strength of the granular material plays a crucial role in determining its flow characteristics.  The study found that the flow of granular materials around the moving intruder can be classified into two distinct regimes, dependent on the intruder's velocity relative to the speed of sound in the granular material.  The study provides new insights into the complex interaction between moving solids and granular materials, and it may have significant implications for a broad spectrum of granular flows in natural and industrial settings. Using high-resolution spectroscopy from VLT/MUSE, we analyzed a distant starburst galaxy, examining how starbursts affect the surrounding ionized gas within and beyond the active region. Our data show a significant outflow of gas from the starburst, but it's being replenished by infalling gas due to an ongoing merger. Despite this, gas depletion times in the starburst galaxy are remarkably short. Our analysis indicates that ionized gas outflows enhance starburst activity by spreading star-forming regions and supplying gas to molecular clouds. However, molecular cloud formation is impacted by outflows, with many clouds being disrupted before they can form stars. As a result, molecular cloud masses have become bimodal, with a gap forming when comparing fragments of clouds affected by outflows to those that remain intact. This is the first time such a phenomenon has been observed. These findings suggest that massive starburst galaxies with outflows are more stochastic in their behavior, leading to greater variability in their overall activity and mass production compared to more quiescent, merger-driven starbursts. In such quiescent starbursts, molecular cloud formation is more continuous, resulting in less variable, more consistent mass production. Therefore, we anticipate greater variability in the light curves of distant massive starburst galaxies due to the presence of outflows. This could provide an alternative explanation for the dipolar structure observed in the Lyman-alpha forest. Lastly, we propose that a higher ionizing mean escape fraction during mergers could be a key factor in explaining the variation in gamma-ray burst progenitor masses, particularly for the most massive stars. These stars are more common in the early stages of mergers, and such an environment could also contribute to the formation of massive low-metallicity neutron star binaries, which could eventually give rise to gravitational wave signals similar to GW190521. Lastly, we suggest that outflows from starbursts can eject binary compact objects, including black holes and neutron stars, contributing to the population of such objects in the general population. Large-scale distributed systems require efficient configuration settings to achieve optimal performance, but discovering these settings proves difficult due to an extremely large number of possible combinations, exceeding the capacity of human analysis. While some algorithms exist to find optimal configurations automatically, they are extremely slow, taking months to complete, thus making them impractical for real-world applications. We present BoAnon, an innovative approach that uses a hierarchical division strategy and machine learning to efficiently identify high-performing configuration settings within a manageable number of possibilities, achieving results in a relatively short period of time. Compared to a basic search algorithm, BoAnon reduces the number of required trials by over ten times and completes the process up to twenty times faster. Furthermore, BoAnon's performance is more consistent, with some tests being completed two to five times faster than itself after each iteration, indicating that BoAnon's performance continues to improve as it is re-run. We demonstrate BoAnon's effectiveness by applying it to Hadoop cluster configuration, and our results show that it can accurately pinpoint configuration settings leading to superior performance, achieving a score of over 90% in distinguishing high-performing configurations from poor ones, as determined by machine learning algorithms. We have made BoAnon available as an open-source tool. We believe that our approach can serve as a starting point for exploring efficient configuration finding strategies in complex distributed systems. We also hope that researchers will contribute to BoAnon by incorporating new techniques into the framework, ultimately leading to more advanced methods for configuring distributed systems efficiently. We have already applied BoAnon to develop efficient configuration settings for another system, Apache Spark, and have seen comparable results, indicating that the approach holds value across multiple platforms. However, we acknowledge that BoAnon has a limitation in its current form, where it is only capable of identifying configuration settings that excel in a particular dimension, without considering overall performance across multiple dimensions. We plan to address this shortcoming, along with other potential drawbacks, in future iterations of the approach. We have already utilized BoAnon to develop efficient configuration settings for another system, Apache Spark, and have achieved promising results, and we intend to explore its applicability to additional distributed systems in the future. Ultimately, we view BoAnon as an initial step towards finding feasible and high-performing configuration settings in complex distributed systems, and we are open to collaborations with other researchers that can help us advance the approach further. Our study examines how the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow from certain particles relates to the same dependence of elliptical flow from the same particles. Using ALICE, ATLAS, CMS, and ALICE's data for p-Pb and Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC, we observe a similar shape in the transverse momentum dependence of triangular and elliptical flow for charged pions, charged kaons, and protons. This similarity holds across different centralities in Pb-Pb collisions and across various centrality ranges in p-Pb collisions. We also find that the magnitude of triangular and elliptical flow from these particles follows the same trend as the charged particle density along the acoustic vector in both p-Pb and Pb-Pb collisions. Furthermore, we found that the ratio of triangular to elliptical flow from these particles is roughly the same in all the measured cases. These findings can be understood through initial state geometry and particle production mechanisms in the LHC. In particular, we suggest that the triangular flow of particles with different masses could be explained by the combined effects of the initial state geometry, particle production mechanisms, and the particle formation time. All in all, our study provides direct evidence for the coherent particle formation in the early stages of heavy-ion collisions at the LHC. Our research also implies that triangular flow from various particles can be a valuable probe of initial state geometry and particle production mechanisms in future experiments. Finally, we suggest that the ratio of triangular to elliptical flow could be an important observable to investigate specific aspects of heavy-ion physics, such as the role of initial state v_3 in heavy-ion collisions. Our study's findings have significant implications for future experiments, such as the possible initial state geometry and particle production mechanisms in heavy-ion collisions at higher energy scales. Our research's approach could also be applied to deeper analyses of existing and future data in heavy-ion physics at the LHC. Determining the quality of large complex datasets is a challenging problem, especially when those datasets are used to support semantic queries. A suitable quality assessment approach should consider both data intrinsic flaws and the impact of data evolution. Our newly introduced framework, called DistQualityAssessment, is an efficient, distributed, and query-based quality assessment system for large RDF datasets. It evaluates the accuracy of query results and identifies data defects causing inaccuracies. Furthermore, it determines the effectiveness of updating specific data triads. We have evaluated our approach by using a dataset with over 10 million triads and observed that it determines data quality effectively while minimizing assessment costs. Additionally, we found that updating specific data triads can lead to substantial improvements in query accuracy. Nonetheless, we also discovered that certain types of updates may not significantly enhance quality in certain instances. Our approach is adaptable to various storage systems and query languages, including SPARQL. The implementation of our approach, comprising over 7,000 lines of code, is openly accessible for replication and as a service on top of a distributed RDF database. Consequently, our quality assessment framework is suitable for large-scale RDF datasets and could benefit from further research on quality assessment algorithms. The features of our approach are: efficient distribution-aware assessment, semantic query-based evaluation, effective data quality improvement through targeted cleaning, and feasible adaptation to various RDF storage systems. Our approach is distinguishable from existing quality assessment approaches in several ways. It is the first comprehensive RFQ assessment system, the initial distributed RFQ assessment framework, and the first quality assessment system for large-scale RDF datasets. It is also the first to consider data evolution, determine update effectiveness, and be adaptable to various RDF databases. This study investigates the properties of minimum density power divergence (MDPD) estimators in relation to Markov and independent increment processes. By analyzing the behavior of MDPD estimators, we establish their convergence and consistency, and demonstrate that under specific conditions, they achieve the same efficiency as maximum likelihood (ML) estimators. A statistical theory exists that favors ML estimators when models are correctly specified, but these estimators are often difficult to compute due to the complexity of maximizing the likelihood function, especially for large datasets. In contrast, MDPD estimators are derived from a divergence measure that can be easily computed for various models, including those with continuous parameters. As a result, MDPD estimators provide a practical alternative to ML estimators for process estimation. We further investigate MDPD estimators in the context of two well-known processes: the Poisson process and the stochastic process representing a fractional diffusion, and compare their performance to ML estimators. Our findings indicate that MDPD estimators exhibit similar efficiency to ML estimators for these processes and can be an effective alternative for estimating processes when the model specification is correct. However, when the model specification is incorrect, MDPD estimators may produce biased results. To address this issue, we discuss an MDPD estimator modification that incorporates an additional regularization term to prevent overfitting. The proposed regularized MDPD estimator can be an efficient alternative to ML estimators, especially when the number of observations exceeds the number of parameters and the model specification is incorrect. We provide a statistical theory for the consistency of the proposed estimator and its asymptotic normality under appropriate conditions. Moreover, we investigate the properties of the proposed estimator in the context of the Poisson process and the stochastic process representing a fractional diffusion, and compare its performance to ML estimators. Our findings indicate that the proposed regularized MDPD estimator achieves similar efficiency to ML estimators for these processes. To facilitate the computation of MDPD estimators, we introduce an iterative algorithm that can handle various models, including those with continuous parameters, and investigate its convergence properties. Finally, we apply the proposed estimator to two real-world datasets: a financial dataset containing exchange rates and a biomedical dataset related to the expression levels of genes. Our findings indicate that the proposed regularized MDPD estimator can be an efficient alternative to ML estimators, and we compare its performance to ML estimators in these scenarios. Notably, the proposed estimator has several advantages over ML estimators due to its ease of computation and derivability

A new method is presented for calculating the partition function when the Cayley tree structure is defined. Additionally, an exact series expansion for the free energy is obtained using a novel two-color representation of the Pauli algebra. This novel representation enables a direct application of group theory to solve complex magnetic systems on Cayley trees. Systems with multiple interacting spins can be solved by applying this method, including a Z$_2$ symmetric Ising model with long-range interactions and a spin-1 Ising model. A general approach is outlined for extending these results to more general graph domains. Several examples are numerically solved to illustrate the method's applicability and precision. A central feature of the series expansion - its clustering behavior as the size of the Cayley tree increases - is also examined through a new lens of multifractal analysis. We're exploring how stellar processes like pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae affect the formation of massive stellar clusters within broad molecular cloud environments. These processes release significant amounts of compact objects, such as black holes and neutron stars, which influence the formation of superbubbles through gravitational interactions. Once a superbubble forms, it's shaped by gravitational potential and gravitational waves, taking on an irregular morphology. The interaction between high-velocity supernova explosions and molecular cloud turbulence further carves out intricate paths, affecting where dust is formed through shock compression. Our research reveals that pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae contribute substantially to the overall dust within molecular clouds, especially when combined with heavier elements from supernovae explosions. These dust grains play a crucial role in molecular cloud cooling, potentially influencing cluster formation within those clouds. Our analysis also shows that stellar processes like pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae increase the cooling rate of molecular gases surrounding superbubbles by as much as a factor of five, which could accelerate cluster formation through gravitational potential energy released from stellar motions converted to kinetic energy in molecular clouds. Our research suggests that pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae have an indirect effect on cluster formation, possibly influencing it by a factor of two to three. However, this depends on factors like the rate of cluster formation and the available energy for cooling in molecular clouds. Our findings also imply that pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae could enhance cluster formation by identifying and collapsing dense stellar over-densities within molecular clouds more effectively, which could lead to the creation of massive stellar clusters. Our analysis predicts that pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae will produce clusters with masses greater than 10^5 solar masses through this mechanism. These massive clusters have a formation rate of less than one per century, which is consistent with observed data. Our research provides a framework for further understanding the complex interactions between stellar processes, molecular clouds, and the formation of massive stellar clusters. It also highlights the importance of pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae in shaping the environment of massive stellar clusters and influencing cluster formation within molecular clouds. Our findings offer potential for comparing observational and theoretical predictions of cluster formation, which can be tested through additional simulations and validated by upcoming astronomical surveys like the Square Kilometre Array. To address the issue of objects being detected at great distances from the camera in far-field 3D object detection, a combined approach is proposed that simultaneously processes both RGB and lidar point clouds. While current detection methods can effectively handle either RGB or lidar data separately, they fall short when confronted with distant objects in RGB images alone. To overcome this limitation, this work proposes a novel multi-modal detection framework called Multi-Modal Centralized Network (MMCN). In MMCN, two centralized features are extracted from the RGB image and the lidar point cloud using a feature extractor at two different scale centers. To accommodate objects across all scale ranges, MMCN employs a hierarchical classification method combining both a one-stage classifier and a centralized matcher. By matching detected objects with actual bounding boxes based on both their 2D and 3D characteristics, MMCN is capable of recovering accurate 3D box coordinates even from poorly resolved RGB images. To prevent overfitting when training with a large number of categories, MMCN is designed to be scalable to multi-class scenarios. To evaluate the effectiveness of MMCN, it is tested on the Waymo Open Dataset, with results showing significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, especially in far-field detections. While self-supervised flow estimation has achieved notable progress, significant difficulties persist, notably in regions with occlusions. These challenges suggest that a method that learns from a single image is unlikely to succeed and may benefit from additional information. We propose a novel approach that leverages two related images to learn unsupervised flow and stereo correspondence. Our method extends the feasibility of learning from occlusions by introducing an alternative matching cost function. Experimenting with self-supervised flow and stereo tasks, our results demonstrate performance superiority over existing methods on the KITTI dataset. Moreover, our code has been made publicly available for flow estimation at https://github.com/zwang84/MMFlow_SelfSupFlow and for stereo estimation at https://github.com/zwang84/ StereoMMFlowNet. 

Our contribution can be summarized into two parts: 
1. We establish a connection between self-supervised flow and stereo estimation. 
2. We develop an innovative method for learning from a single image pair with occlusions by introducing a new matching cost function and alternative flow estimation loss. 

To enhance robustness in the presence of occlusions and model complexity, we introduce a bidirectional flow estimation approach with a novel cycle consistency loss. The proposed cycle consistency loss is designed to minimize potential errors in flow estimation by leveraging information from both input images. 

Our results show that our approach outperforms existing self-supervised flow estimation methods while achieving competitive performance with supervised flow estimation methods. Moreover, our results indicate that our cycle consistency loss loss further improves flow estimation accuracy, especially in regions with occlusions and low dispersion. 

To validate the generalization of our approach to stereo estimation, we adapted our cycle consistency loss and cycle consistency matching cost function for this task. Our results demonstrate superiority over state-of-the-art self-supervised and stereo algorithms on the Scene Flow dataset and the Middlebury dataset, respectively. 

In summary, our main findings include: 
- Our approach outperforms self-supervised flow estimation algorithms, matching unsupervised flow estimation performance with supervised flow estimation algorithms.
- Our adapted cycle consistency loss and new matching cost loss for stereo estimation outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised and stereo algorithms, respectively. 
- Our code for flow estimation and stereo estimation has been made publicly available at the mentioned links. 

Finally, incorporating our approach's cycle consistency loss into other flow estimation algorithms leads to improved performance, demonstrating its versatility. We present a novel, general-purpose neural network that matches ANNs' performance while requiring significantly fewer parameters and having even lower power consumption. Our model's performance is on par with state-of-the-art methods for MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10, and it outperforms alternative models. It achieves this through an advanced use of linear transformations and categorization methods, and we have made the source code for our model publicly available. We also explore the potential applications of this model in real-world settings and show that it can be trained with existing general-purpose neural network tools. Inspiral resonators with circular polarization respond uniquely to incoming waveforms, either reflecting them or transmitting them depending on the direction of propagation. A new design incorporates a chiral interresonator coupling in a compact, layered structure consisting of a spiral microresonator and an adjacent microslot. This two-stream network consists of a feature-extraction stream and an attention stream, working in unison to identify and close detected loops. The attention stream utilizes an encoder-in-pooler module to pinpoint potential loop locations by emphasizing local feature patterns while suppressing global patterns. We calculate the renormalized quasiparticle velocity and density of states in doped graphene using a screened interaction obtained from random phase approximation. The renormalized quasiparticle velocity is found to be proportional to the square root of the chemical potential, and the density of states displays a linear increase with chemical potential, opposite to the expected quadratic relationship in intact graphene. These modifications lead to a reduced specific heat in doped graphene, and the associated umklapp scattering is quantitatively assessed in relation to the scattering amplitude. Furthermore, our approach correlates the quasiparticle velocity and density of states through a universal expression, and this relationship is demonstrated through self-consistency in the presence of umklapp scattering. The impact of umklapp scattering is analyzed in detail, and the associated reduction in quasiparticle velocity and density of states is found to be governed by the amount of doping relative to the Brillouin zone area. The inherent temperature dependence in the system is captured, and the thermal effects are seen to be overshadowed by the chemical potential influence. A distinction is drawn between the chemical potential-driven and temperature-driven cases in the density of states, and the reduction in specific heat is found to originate from the linear increase in density of states with chemical potential rather than the density of states itself. The model is applicable to both honeycomb and square lattices, and the additional umklapp scattering in the square lattice is attributed to the increased overlap between neighboring sites. The proposed framework may be extended to other systems with multiple bands and interactions. The renormalized quasiparticle velocity and density of states are found to be insensitive to the specific interaction details but sensitive to the total number of electrons and the underlying lattice structure. The renormalized quasiparticle velocity is directly compared to inelastic scattering data in graphene, and the predicted relationship between the quasiparticle velocity and density of states is verified through self-consistency in the presence of umklapp scattering. The model is used to simulate the specific heat of graphene at low temperatures and chemical potentials, and the results are validated against experimental data. The renormalized quasiparticle velocity and density of states are found to be reduced in the presence of umklapp scattering, and this reduction leads to a lower specific heat in the chemical potential-driven case. The proposed framework may be employed to analyze the thermal and chemical potential-driven renormalizations in other systems with multiple Brillouin zones. The model is particularly relevant to the study of graphene and graphene-like systems

The goal of speech synthesis is to create a natural and engaging listening experience, but existing neural-based approaches have limitations. Conventional methods, such as probabilistic concatenation, hidden Markov models, and probabilistic neural networks, fall short of replicating the spontaneity and nuance of human speech. To circumvent these constraints, we've developed a novel system called MaskedSpeech, which employs a unique architecture that learns from a dataset of recorded silence. By leveraging this approach, we've achieved significant breakthroughs in speech synthesis and are making our system available to the community. We specifically investigate how anharmonic effects influence stability in a system where one component has an harmonic interaction with the other, which interacts through a nonlinear force. Our study reveals that anharmonic forces can influence both the stability and location of solitary waves, with this impact visible in their orbital stability properties. A key finding shows that anharmonic forces can stabilize a solitary wave in an otherwise unstable system, or destabilize a stable solitary wave, depending on its amplitude. Our research also identifies unique connections between the anharmonic forcing and systems consisting of Bose-Einstein condensates, where anharmonic effects may be minimal at low amplitudes, exhibiting similar behavior to harmonic systems. Understanding how the complex structure of a fully developed retina emerged during development remains a key challenge. Since retinal nuclei migrate to their final positions independently, simultaneously, and without direction, modeling their movement and resulting distribution is computationally intensive. As a result, previous models of retinal development have focused on individual aspects of the process. This study develops an open-source framework that uses a flexible, multi-nuclei simulation to investigate the development of the retina. By applying this framework, we found that a simple, cooperative movement model can produce retinal patterns resembling those found in zebrafish. Furthermore, our results show that the initial distribution of nuclei has a significant impact on their final positions, and that specific patterns may require tailored mechanisms of movement. Notably, our findings also indicate that the final distribution of nuclei is robust to minor variations in movement speed. This framework is now available for others to use in exploring the development of the retina across different species. Current hydrodynamics theories successfully explain various scaling behaviors in active systems from $2$ to $5$ dimensions. However, there are two specific cases where linearized hydrodynamics falls short in capturing complete scaling patterns. These instances occur in the asymptotic regimes of very large and very small time scales. Recent studies have shown that these missing pieces can be found in the full hydrodynamics equation when considering the effects of memory and inertia. In this work, we examine the impact of these factors on active systems in dimensions between $2$ and $5$, and our findings indicate that the full hydrodynamics indeed includes the required additional scaling behaviors. Moreover, we demonstrate the precision of this approach by numerically solving the full hydrodynamics equations in three-dimensional space and comparing our results to actual experimental data from vapor-deposited monolayers of PtCl$_6$ in the presence of Sb$_2$S$_3$ particles. Our numerical simulations using the memory and inertia terms from the linearized hydrodynamics equations successfully reproduce the observed scaling patterns. Notably, we found that the fitted parameter values obtained from our numerical simulations show excellent agreement with those obtained from linearized hydrodynamics in three-dimensional space. In addition, we discovered that the full hydrodynamics equation is capable of reproducing the recently identified 'plateau regime' of activity in the corresponding hydrodynamics theory. Our work provides concrete evidence to support the completeness of full hydrodynamics in active systems across all relevant dimensions. Moreover, our findings highlight the precision of linearized hydrodynamics in approximating full hydrodynamics in three-dimensional settings, which is widely applicable. In conclusion, our research unequivocally validates the completeness of full hydrodynamics in active systems across all dimensions. This work is particularly relevant to ongoing and future studies in this field. However, incorporating Gd also raises the threshold energy of the detector system. In our optimized Gd-LSC, we've balanced detection efficiency and cost by selecting optimal concentrations of Gd, PC, and $^{232}$Th content. Our study shows that with 0.05 M Gd, 1.78 M PC, and 3.15 ng/g $^{232}$Th, the detection efficiency of the Gd-LSC can reach 51.42%, while the bias of the spectrum below 10 MeV remains within 10%. Notably, this optimization reduces the neutron spectrum bias by about 20% compared to our previous optimization. Moreover, we've simulated the performance of the Gd-LSC at different depths of water and depths of mud, and found that the optimal concentration of Gd can further reduce the bias of the spectrum by about 30% at 10 mW water equivalent depth (w.e.e.), but increases the bias at deeper mud depths. In the case of large volume liquid scintillator detectors like SUM, adding Gd may help reduce the neutron spectrum bias, but a more substantial increase in $^{232}$Th content is likely needed to maximize the benefit. In such cases, we recommend starting with a smaller than optimal Gd concentration in order to minimize the threshold energy of the detector system. However, even at 10 m.w.e., the bias of the metal-containing water spectrum remains within 10%. The proposed work investigates how the minimax principle from calculus of variations can be applied to tackle time-dependent optimal control problems. Originally, the minimax principle from the author's previous research was developed for variational problems; however, this study extends its relevance to control problems. To achieve this, the author establishes an equivalence between the original control problem and a new variational problem featuring a minimax functional. This new variational problem then inherits the properties guaranteeing the existence of a minimum from the calculus of variations. Consequently, this guarantee enables the existence of an optimal control for the original problem within the space of admissible controls. This research also explores the case where the space of states is bounded and demonstrates the optimality of a control that minimizes the maximum state within the set of admissible controls. This research is an early step towards addressing more complex optimal control problems involving partial differential equations. To this end, an example involving a distributed control for the heat equation is examined to illustrate the theoretical findings. Notably, the proposed approach does not employ dynamic programming or viscosity solutions. Instead, it establishes the connection between the original control problem and the new variational problem featuring the minimax functional through an equilibrium formulation. This approach is then compared to the standard first-order optimality condition and recognized as an alternative to the Pontryagin maximum principle. New studies using the Duchamps model for star cluster formation reveal how star systems are structured, and how these structures influence the creation of planetary systems. Analyzing 10,000 stars in 36 open clusters as potential parents for exoplanet hosts, researchers found that star-mass stars tend to be found closer to the cluster center, while lower-mass stars are distributed more evenly across the cluster. Using computer simulations, researchers traced the path of planetary systems as they formed around stars of various masses within these clusters. The results show that star-mass stars, which are likely low-mass white dwarfs, are found closer to the cluster center and have planetary systems with small, compact orbits. In contrast, lower-mass stars, which are likely brown dwarfs or red dwarfs, are distributed more evenly across the cluster and have planetary systems with greater variability in orbit sizes. Interestingly, the location of white dwarf candidates does not correlate with the location of planetary systems showing gas and metal abundance similar to that of the white dwarfs. The location of brown dwarf candidates, on the other hand, does show a connection with the location of T Tauri-like stars within the cluster, suggesting that brown dwarfs are forming through the collapse of molecular clouds. The findings also indicate that brown dwarfs are more resistant to being ejected from star clusters during the dynamic formation process. The results further suggest that star-mass stars, which are likely low-mass white dwarfs, are found closer to the cluster center due to their structure within the cluster, rather than any special properties, as they follow the same distribution of radii as lower-mass stars within their respective mass range. We investigate users' tendencies to shift between communities on Twitter by analyzing their responses to President Trump's tweets during his final year in office. Our results show that users generally stick to following accounts from their own perceived political affiliation, but occasionally venture out to respond to inflammatory or positively received tweets. We demonstrate that users' community affiliations are not solely defined by their vote history, and instead, evolve based on their interactions with users from different backgrounds, online conversations about various topics, and responses to notable events, including presidential tweets. Our findings prioritize users' temporal evolution within the online community, over their offline behaviors, and suggest that users' community identities are dynamic, multi-faceted structures that can be characterized by their temporary clusters of interaction. We outline potential methods for infusing our temporal community framework with external data, including offline vote records and profile information. By doing so, we may refine our approach by incorporating both user and information diffusion factors that influence community evolution. Our time-aware community model may also offer practical applications in identifying and mitigating the spread of misinformation within online political communities. Lastly, we discuss potential developments of our model with inclusion of external data, and suggest it may be utilized in conjunction with other network approaches to analyze community structure and diffusion processes. We've created a precise mass-radius relation for low-mass stars, specifically in the M-dwarf range, by using a sample of 342 exoplanating M-dwarfs and treating the stellar mass as the independent variable. This new relation can help characterize low-mass stars even without detailed spectroscopic analysis of the host star. It leads to a more accurate determination of stellar masses, reducing uncertainties by approximately a factor of two compared to standard anti-correlation analysis. We've applied our new approach to mass calculations for seven host stars and found that five of these stars had their exoplanating bodies' masses revised upwards due to the better-determined stellar masses. Furthermore, four of these stars were initially classified as M-dwarfs but were found to be smaller in radius and more massive in our new calculations, placing them in the MV-MIII range. These new assignments have significant implications for studies related to the period-radius relationship of low-mass stars. Additionally, we've identified potential issues with the Tully-Fisher relation when using stellar masses derived from anti-correlation analysis. However, these problems disappear with our new mass-radius relation. Our findings also suggest that M-dwarfs with super-Earth exoplanating bodies, such as GJ-625b and J1750b, may be subject to different planetary formation processes. Lastly, we've discovered that M-dwarfs with exoplanating bodies in the habitable zones have distinct properties, including smaller radii and more massive stellar hosts, compared to those outside these zones. These results set the stage for a thorough examination of the M-dwarf sample used in this study, which is part of a larger investigation into the properties of low-mass stars and their exoplanating bodies. Ultimately, our work has significant implications for the field, enabling more accurate determinations of stellar masses, shedding light on the physics of star and planet formation, and potentially leading to a better understanding of life-hosting planets in the universe.

By analyzing different graphene designs, we demonstrate that the line wave mode can be created in the optical domain if the graphene is connected in a specific way that forms an infinite pathway. Two examples - a Koch curve and a fractal design - are examined to show that their infinite nature enables line wave propagation, while a circular design does not. Additionally, it is found that the line wave mode can be generated at any location on the graphene using various designs, which provides flexibility for line wave excitation through subwavelength modulation. These findings could lead to the development of subwavelength modulators for graphene-based mid-infrared technology. The question of whether a given database query can be efficiently evaluated via standard methods has been a long-standing issue in the study of database tractability. To address this question, researchers initially focused on limiting the power of updates that can be performed on a database. In contrast, this work investigates the impact of restricting the ability to perform updates that use previous versions of data as input. A key finding of this research is a formal characterization of the query languages that are capable of using all previous versions of data without leading to infinite complexity when limiting to standard closure properties. In addition, this work introduces an informal framework for analyzing database queries that involves updating previous results and applies this analysis to identify both necessary and sufficient criteria for determining whether a given query is tractable. As a key aspect of this research, an informal proof is provided for the condition that a self-join capable query is log-space equivalent to a variant of the union-with-self-join operation. Finally, this work concludes with an exploration of potential avenues for further investigation in the context of updating databases using previous versions of data as input. We analyzed the performance of two signal generalization approaches: one that used a functional representation with a local functional and another that used a non-local functional. Our analysis focused on low-dimensional signals and examined how different boundary conditions affected the results. In the case of the local functional, the generalization improved significantly, and we were able to establish upper and lower limits for this improvement. Our study also showed that the non-local functional's performance varied greatly, sometimes mirroring the case of low-dimensional signals. We further investigated these scenarios through specific examples and discussed the implications of our findings. Our work initially drew from previous studies that compared local and non-local functional methods, especially in the context of high-dimensional signals. Those results indicated that both methods performed similarly, which prompted our examination of the low-dimensional scenario. To evaluate the generalization of both methods, we conducted experiments using synthetic and real-world data and assessed the accuracy of signals after processing them according to the approaches in question. Our results supported the theories we had established and demonstrated the degree to which the local functional's performance could be viewed as a representative of the non-local functional's performance in the low-dimensional scenario. Our work ultimately contributed to a deeper understanding of how signals should be generalized and laid the groundwork for further exploration of the non-local functional method in the context of high-dimensional signals.
