We investigate the long-term behavior of operator growth in the SU(1,1) Witten model using a symmetry-based approach that yields simplified calculations and confirms previous findings. By analyzing two-sided and one-sided operator norms, we demonstrate the exponential growth of operator dimensions and the scaling of operator norms within a specific range of the conformal Hamiltonian. Notably, our approach also facilitates the computation of operator dimensions across multiple unitary representations of the SU(1,1) algebra. In the context of the deformed SU(1,1) Witten model, we further explore how a symmetry-breaking term affects the operator growth rate and display the resulting operator spectrum in a diagram. Moreover, we establish a precise relationship between our results and those obtained via the "large charge" expansion. In the process, we outline the general framework for applying this approach to other symmetric systems, providing a blueprint for exploring operator growth in related quantum systems. Finally, we discuss potential connections between the SU(1,1) Witten model and both holographic systems and systems described by the free fermion matrix model.

Recently, learning geospatial distances from WiFi signal data has gained interest, particularly in inverse problems like localizing devices from partial or missing WiFi data. A key challenge in this task is that traditional machine learning algorithms are not effective due to WiFi signals being non-differentiable and noisy. This work develops an end-to-end model that learns the geospatial distances between WiFi access points and locations by minimizing the distance between their corresponding feature maps, leveraging WiFi signal data and spatial information as inputs. The proposed model is then used to solve an inverse problem of inferring device locations from partial WiFi data in a campus environment. Experimental results show that the learned distance metrics are similar to those obtained from physical distance measurements with low error rates, and can be applied to solve inverse problems, demonstrating the model's generalization across different datasets. A further experiment indicates that the model's performance can be enhanced when combined with conventional least squares methods. This work is significant because it demonstrates that machine learning models can effectively learn the geospatial distances between WiFi access points and locations without relying on prior knowledge of the environment's topology, and such models have the potential to solve a range of other open problems in wireless networks. The code for this work is available online at https://github.com/chenxuefeng/public/End2EndWiFiLearnableModel. Large-scale, complex systems rely on Service Level Agreements (SLAs) to define operational and performance requirements. Ensuring that these agreements are being met is essential, and violations need to be detected promptly to minimize their impact. A collaborative approach, enabled by Peer-to-Peer (P2P) technology, can facilitate efficient detection of SLA breaches by sharing local observations and expertise. However, implementing this approach poses challenges in achieving consensus, maintaining data integrity, and balancing collaboration and autonomy. Our study examines the design of a P2P network for detecting SLA breaches in performance data and presents a framework that addresses these difficulties. A prototype of the proposed system was implemented and tested on a real-world cloud environment. The results show that the system can find breaches quickly, with low overhead, and outperforms a centralized approach. Furthermore, data sharing within the P2P network leads to more accurate breach detection, especially in cases with limited local data. Our findings indicate that the system's breac detection precision can be as high as 98%. Our research provides a foundation for exploring other applications of P2P networks in cloud computing, such as load balancing and resource allocation. The system's extensibility to support multiple performance metrics and detection algorithms was also demonstrated. A comprehensive framework with modular design facilitates extension and customization of the system's components. This is accompanied by a detailed framework documentation that serves as a blueprint for developers looking to modify and expand the system. This documentation is an integral part of the project's GitHub repository, where the source code and protocol buffer definitions are stored. This repository is openly accessible, allowing developers to browse the code and modify it as needed. To reproduce the results presented in this study, the GitHub repository includes a comprehensive test suite along with instructions for replication. This replication guide outlines the steps required to execute the experiments and conduct further development on the project. It is an ongoing effort with the source code continuously being refined to accommodate new features and breach detection algorithms. In this context, we invite cloud computing researchers to join this effort and contribute to the project on GitHub. In doing so, they can leverage the existing code as a foundation for their own research, as the project offers customizable components that can be easily extended. In a multi-pass energy recovery linac, where a single RF cavity is shared among various passing beams with different energies, the number of charge sharing events that occur each time the beam interacts with the RF field can be significant. In our study, we examined how the choice of filling pattern in such an energy recovery linac affects beam-RF interactions and threshold current. By solving the one-dimensional weak-bump equation and considering the effects of coherent synchro-bunching, we were able to determine the impact of filling pattern on threshold current. Our analysis showed that the optimal filling pattern depends on the RF cavity's phase advance and the distribution of passing energies. Notably, if the energy distribution spans more than half the range from the minimum to the maximum energy, the optimal filling pattern can reduce threshold current by a factor of two or more, compared to a random filling pattern. We also observed that in some cases, coherent synchro-bunching can increase threshold current by a factor of ten or more. Our analysis provides a framework for optimizing filling patterns in multi-pass energy recovery linacs and highlights the importance of considering beam-RF interactions when designing these facilities. Moreover, our study suggests that a careful approach to filling patterns may be a key strategy for mitigating threshold current in future multi-pass energy recovery linacs. Finally, our research implies that the optimal filling pattern could be achieved through a combination of detailed design and in-depth beam study, with an appropriate choice of beam fill pattern taking into account various design parameters and constraints. Our study's findings are particularly relevant to the Next Linear Collider, where a multi-pass energy recovery linac with up to 16 passing beams will be employed. In this context, our analysis suggests that careful design of filling patterns may be essential for minimizing threshold current and ensuring the effectiveness of the energy recovery process. Ultimately, our research provides a valuable foundation for exploring more sophisticated filling patterns that incorporate time-dependent beam currents and are adapted to the specific requirements of each energy recovery stage. Along these lines, we believe that future studies should investigate the potential for implementing optimized filling patterns through machine learning algorithms, enabling the rapid identification of optimal solutions in complex multi-dimensional spaces. In this way, we may unlock even greater performance gains in future energy recovery linacs and other complex particle accelerators. Our previous research suggested that a temperature range of approximately 20-40 Kelvin might be ideal for the formation of planetesimals, given that their growth through sticking forces would increase significantly in super-dry samples at these temperatures. This finding was based on a model that accounted for the competition between sticking and fragmentation in collisions between solid particles. Now we're exploring how this temperature range might be affected by the presence of a volatile-rich component in the growing planetesimals. To do this, we're considering how the composition of the gas surrounding the solid particles influences their collision rates and the energy released during mergers. Ultimately, this affects the balance between sticking and fragmentation, and therefore the optimal temperature range for planetesimal growth. Our analysis shows that even in low-density environments, a distinct optimal temperature range exists, and it remains relatively insensitive to the presence of a volatile-rich component in the solid particles themselves. However, if the volatile component is abundant enough to influence the gas's thermal and chemical conditions, the optimal temperature range can shift by as much as a factor of greater than five. In such cases, the optimal temperatures for planetesimal growth are either the coldest or the warmest possible, depending on whether the gas cools down efficiently or is heated by the condensing volatile components during the formation process. This leads to either the primordial volatile components being trapped within the formed planetesimals at low temperatures, or being ejected from the growing bodies at higher temperatures. This could provide an explanation for the observed distinction between volatile-poor and volatile-rich planetesimals. In our own solar system, this could offer a possible explanation for the origin of carbon-rich and water-rich material found in certain meteorites, and ultimately, for the diverse chemical composition of planetary bodies existing today. Lastly, we propose that a similar competition between sticking and fragmentation, influenced by volatile components, could be a crucial factor in the formation of dust rings in planetary systems. In these environments, a particular balance of volatile components in the surrounding gas may facilitate or inhibit the formation of small particles over narrow temperature ranges, thus affecting the appearance of dust rings. Consequently, future observations of exoplanetary systems, including those aimed at detecting biomarkers, may need to account for this physics of volatile components in order to accurately interpret their data. Lastly, we suggest that a similar competition between sticking and fragmentation, influenced by volatile components, could be a crucial factor in the formation of dust rings in planetary systems, and that a deeper exploration of this physics may provide new insights into the composition of ring systems,

Robot skills must frequently be developed in an environment where a linear control system meets complex nonlinear safety constraints. Conventional imitation learning techniques fall short due to their inability to enforce such non-linear hard constraints. This paper introduces a method for constrained imitation learning that allows the incorporation of sub-optimal demonstrations, considering both continuous hard constraints and safety-critical boundaries. By redefining the imitable distribution through inverse reinforcement learning, our approach successfully leverages an efficient policy optimization algorithm to produce a safe and optimal policy. This method is mathematically equivalent to solving a constrained inverse problem, and a reliable online implementation is offered to handle uncertain environments. The proposed technique is experimentally validated on two distinct scenarios: a robot navigating a complex environment and a surgical application, achieving up to 25 times faster convergence compared to alternative methods. Moreover, our approach successfully generalizes to new, unobserved environments, outperforming competitive methods by an order of magnitude. A publicly accessible code is available on an open-source repository.

We examine the topological characteristics of a specific iron-based superconducting state found in BaFe$_2$As$_2$ with an in-plane twisted spin-orbit coupling (SOC). By applying a group theoretical analysis from the $AB_{2}$ type crystal structure point of view, we determine the SOC's impact on the band structure and Fermi surface in this compound. When SOC is included, we find that it has a significant influence on the topological characteristics of the superconducting state, particularly by altering the Z$_2$ indices and winding numbers of the Floquet Hamiltonian. Notably, we find that SOC can cause the merger of some Abrikosov nodes, change the lattice scale without closing the gap, and result in the formation of non-trivial zeros on the real axis in the spectral weight maps. Furthermore, we investigate how SOC influences the $\frac{d}{d\mu}$ of topological gaps and how it varies with mu. Our analysis provides a clear understanding of the complex interplay between SOC and superconductivity in BaFe$_2$As$_2$. Additionally, we highlight the significance of considering SOC in theoretical models of this material, particularly when analyzing topological characteristics and experimental implications. As an extension, we also explore the general applicability of our findings to other iron-based superconductors. Moreover, we discuss the potential experimental validation of our results through topological zero detection using sound waves in these materials. Lastly, we conclude that our investigation offers an inclusive framework for examining the topological properties of iron-based superconductors, encompassing BaFe$_2$As$_2$ and related materials, and can be employed to study other superconducting systems with SOC.

Our combined theoretical and experimental investigation of a niobate-doped YBCO sample reveals that the transition in the vortex lattice occurs at a magnetic field where the vortex lattice jumps to a more symmetrical and closely packed arrangement, mirroring predictions made by Glatz and Manohannat for d-wave superconductors and van Hove singularities. Despite initial difficulties in recovering the full structure of this transition through pair-distribution function analysis due to experimental limitations, our team was able to successfully match our findings to theoretical models for the vortex lattice on a triangular lattice at high van Hove singularities. This discovery highlights the importance of experimental structure determination in understanding the vortex lattice in d-wave superconductors. Furthermore, our results indicate a more substantial influence of the d-wave symmetry on the vortex lattice than previously thought, and suggest that the balance between this effect and lattice disorder may be adjusted through chemical doping in YBCO. This could potentially guide the development of superconducting materials with improved upper critical fields and ultimately, more efficient and reliable superconducting devices. Our method of pair-distribution function analysis can also be applied to other complex systems where local structure needs to be understood. Ultimately, our study emphasizes the value of combining numerical simulation and experimental measurement of the pair-distribution function in high-temperature superconductor research.

The effect of surface curvature on free energy due to stretching in polymer brushes has been studied using simulations of weakly stretched brushes on curved spherical and rod-like surfaces, particularly focusing on surfaces with positive curvatures less than or equal to that of spherical viruses (around 0.1 nm^-1). It was found that on positively curved surfaces with small radii, strong stretching occurs, causing the free energy to increase rapidly. This behavior, however, becomes less pronounced on larger positively curved surfaces. On negatively curved surfaces with large negative curvatures (around -1 nm^-1), the free energy is repelled rather than attracted to the stretching state. This is an unexpected result that contradicts predictions based on simple scaling arguments. It is suggested that this contradiction arises because such brushes are already highly stretched on deeply curved surfaces, hindering further extension. It is also noted that brush stretching on negatively curved surfaces with smaller curvatures (-0.1 nm^-1) follows the behavior seen on small positive curvatures. It is proposed that a brush's stretching on any surface can be understood through a fractal perspective, with the stretching free energy being the sum of the stretching free energies of all individual monomer units that make up the brush. It is further suggested that a fractal surface can be thought of as composed of curved monomers that are stretched to various degrees. It is argued that the degree of stretching in these monomers plays the key role in determining the free energy of stretching on any given surface, with an example given of how this model can be used to interpret brush stretching on negatively curved surfaces with small curvatures (-0.1 nm^-1). It is noted that strong stretching on small positively curved surfaces and on deeply curved surfaces may be understood through a different approach that takes into account the formation of hairpin loops and the stretching of brush chains across these surfaces. It is proposed that these surfaces represent a 'crumbling' of the brush, with the free energy in these cases being the sum of the free energies of the hairpin loops and the stretched brush chains. It is suggested that this approach may provide a more accurate understanding of the free energy of stretching on strongly curved surfaces. It is finally proposed that the ability of a brush to adhere to deeply curved surfaces relies heavily on its ability to stretch and 'crumble', with implications for the use of polymer brushes in biology and medicine. The term "truncated" refers to the maximum geodesic distance in G. Let's denote the size of the smallest S as $\delta_T(G,s)$ for a specific truncated distance s. The complex nature of active galactic nuclei (AGN) variability makes analyzing their behavior over extended periods a significant challenge. While there is a robust database of AGN light curves, many important factors regarding the long-term variability of these objects remain poorly understood. To address this limitation, we developed a statistical framework to analyze the variability of a large sample of AGN based on their variable flux fractions. By applying this framework to a dataset of 86,017 optical flux measurements from 77,795 spectra of 2,598 AGN, we calculated the variable flux fractions for each individual source and binned them according to cosmic environment. Our results show that the variable flux fractions follow a distinct symmetry in their distribution, with a peak at approximately 0.5, and taper off significantly at both higher and lower values. When considering the distribution of variable flux fractions across the entire sample, we found no strong patterns based on luminosity, redshift, type, or orientation of the AGN. However, we did observe a difference in variable flux fractions when analyzing sources with repeated spectra, with an average variable fraction of 0.58, and a clear asymmetry in their distribution. No significant correlations were found between variable flux fractions and host galaxy mass or stellar mass within our sample. Overall, our analysis provides a new perspective on the variability of AGN and highlights the diversity of their behavior. Notably, our study shows that a substantial number of AGN exhibit minimal or no variability, and that variable flux fractions are not solely confined to the most luminous sources. Instead, they can be found across the full range of luminosities. By comparing our results to those from X-ray studies, we propose that the variable flux fractions observed in our optical dataset may be the result of a combination of processes that affect both energy bands, including changes in disk inclination, variations in mass accretion rates, and changes in central black hole mass. Finally, we discuss the potential for future studies to further illuminate the complex variability of AGN by combining results from different energy bands and observing the longest possible time baselines.

Approximating social welfare in a multi-agent setting involves determining the overall optimum outcome when agents have diverse, self-serving preferences. Evaluating outcomes through valuations or "costs" associated with each possible distribution of outcomes is a key concept in this context. Specifically, when evaluated using notions of "distance" based on a particular metric, multi-agent approximation problems often become more computationally complex or even NP-hard. This study explores ways to compute approximate outcomes by learning valuations or "costs" associated with each possible distribution of outcomes through learning algorithms. We examine two types of valuations: those derived from bipartite matchings and directed graphs, and develop new algorithms for computing approximate social welfare when valuations are learned from graph-based methods or explicit feedback. Our results demonstrate improved accuracy across various metrics, including Hamming distance, particularly when feedback is noisy and valuations are learned from bipartite matchings. We also establish theoretical limits on the proposed algorithm's performance and provide empirical evidence validating its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. This research is relevant to any decision-making scenario involving outcome selection, and the associated code can be found by visiting https://github.com/alexliao Approximate Social Welfare Learning. However, identifying peer effects on isolated groups proves challenging.
This issue can be addressed by extracting information from online platforms that connect individuals who may not directly interact in the physical world.
One such platform is Amazon, specifically its product review section, where buyers leave comments about their purchasing experiences.
By studying the purchasing decisions of Amazon customers, researchers discovered that certain product categories, such as electronics and home goods, exhibit reduced peer effects compared to others, like health and personal care products, with implications for marketing strategies and social behavior. 
Furthermore, the data shows that consumers tend to base their purchasing decisions more heavily on previous buyers' actions for products with limited reviews, indicating a potential increase in peer influence as the number of reviews grows exponentially. 
Additionally, the ranking of the drivers of peer effects across all categories includes product characteristics, price, brand, location, category, trust indicators, the number of reviews, review quality, diversity, recentness, and purchasing centrality, with variations depending on the specific product category. 
Lastly, a novel econometric approach was applied to analyze the data and account for the endogenous connections within the network. 
This research has significant ramifications for marketers seeking to influence consumers' buying habits and contributes to a deeper understanding of network effects in the Amazon customer base.

This article presents an investigation into the different formulations of the chain rule formula for the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional derivative and integral operators. Building on earlier work by several authors, we develop additional expressions for the chain rule formula, exploring their validity and utility in applying these operators to composite functions. Notably, we identify and demonstrate the equivalence of various formulae, ultimately clarifying the distinct contributions of earlier researchers. Our findings are presented in a comprehensive table for easy reference. Further, we illustrate the practical importance of these formulations through specific examples involving the composition of these operators with common functions. Lastly, we outline the potential benefits of further research into the chain rule formula for these variable-order operators. Our analysis is confined to the Riemann-Liouville definition of these operators. Nonetheless, our examples offer key insights into applying these formulas to variable-order fractional differential equations. Our primary goal is to provide a clear and concise overview of the current state of the chain rule formula for variable-order fractional derivatives and integrals, emphasizing the necessity of clear terminology in this context.

To establish a baseline for performance, we first examine an idealized, computationally-intractable detection method that represents the optimal Bayesian approach in MIMO systems. Although this method's error rate is not achievable in practice due to its complexity, analyzing its performance allows us to assess the efficacy of other detection methods. Our research shows that the error rate of the optimal Bayesian detector remains remarkably low, even in systems with a large number of antennas at the transmitter and receiver. This prompts us to investigate the sensitivity of this performance to various system parameters and different multi-access schemes, such as fast spatial reuse and near-far neutrality. Our findings indicate that even in systems with a large number of antennas, moderate growth in dimensionality can significantly impact the optimal Bayesian detector's error rate. Furthermore, we find that using complex rather than real-valued symbols improves the optimal Bayesian detector's error rate by approximately one order of magnitude, and that increasing the number of base station antennas has a more substantial impact on the optimal Bayesian detector's error rate than increasing the number of user antennas. Additionally, our results demonstrate that in systems with a large number of antennas, the optimal Bayesian detector's error rate is sensitive to the number of active users and the level of spatial reuse, with a moderate increase in user count leading to a substantial decline in performance. Finally, our research includes an exhaustive comparison of various detection algorithms, accounting for their complexity, performance, and potential for optimizing parameters such as the modulation scheme and pilot sequence length. Based on our findings, we advocate for over-designing the number of receiver antennas to achieve optimal performance in MIMO systems. Our work is timely given the rapidly-evolving nature of MIMO technology and the expanding role that wireless communication will play in the future. As such systems will soon be capable of supporting numerous high-bandwidth applications, it is crucial to understand the limitations and potential solutions to detection problems in MIMO systems. Our research provides a foundation for this understanding, offering a framework for studying the performance of detection algorithms and potential solutions to detection problems in MIMO systems. This paper presents the implementation of an automated tool for analyzing galaxy spectra using emission line ratios, specifically a BPT diagram checker. The BPA Tools, available on GitHub, enable users to import spectra, obtain line ratios via full spectral fitting using the PROFTON code, and categorize galaxies into active galactic nucleus, star-forming, or composite types based on these ratios. The program also enables users to import existing line ratios from sources like MPA-JIVE-AMPS reduction scripts and SED codes like PROFTON-CODE. It includes a command to create customized BPT diagrams with desired galaxy categories. The BPA Tools provide a simple command to convert complex galaxy spectra into spectra of individual emission lines, and it supports multiple emission lines. The code uses the python library IPython and includes Jupyter Notebook examples for user convenience. The BPA Tools are compatible with European Southern Observatory and Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Galaxy Telescope data. It is particularly useful for analyzing wide-field survey data sets like VIKING, XSHOOTER, and H-ATLAS. However, its limitations include the difficulty in handling highly resolved outflows or multiple nuclei due to its one-dimensional approach. The author demonstrates the functionality of the BPA Tools by applying it to four galaxy spectra with known outflows or multiple nuclei, and it is available on GitHub at https://github.com/fernandogallego/BPA-Tools. It can be used in any research project and is available for download at https://github.com/fernandogallego/BPA-Tools. The breakup of the Gondwana supercontinent during the Mesozoic Era involved various extensional margins that significantly influenced global sea levels and oceanic gateways. To understand the evolution of these margins, particularly in South America, Africa, India, Antarctica, and the surrounding oceans, a comprehensive study of passive margins is necessary. This study examines how changes in velocity and direction of extension, as well as early rifting processes, affected the development of distinct margin types. Initially, high-velocity rifting (>10-15 km/Myr) and oblique extension led to the formation of narrow, highly metamorphosed corridors in the Dornals and Parecis regions of Brazil and western Africa. In contrast, slower rifting rates (<5-10 km/Myr) in eastern Africa, India, and Antarctica resulted in wider, less transformed rifts. The Karoo Basin in southern Africa presents a unique case, characterized by initially slow rifting that accelerated to high velocities following the eruption of massive volcanic floods (large igneous provinces). This study demonstrates that early rifting played a crucial role in margin evolution and that fast rifting caused extensive metamorphism and resulted in the formation of marginal basins with unique characteristics, such as the Epecuen Basin in Argentina. The evolution of these margins also depended heavily on the location of faults, particularly in cases like western Africa and Dornals, where extensive transformation zones developed in response to repeated right-lateral strike-slip movements. In conclusion, the distinct history of each margin, shaped by extension, early rifting, and faulting, has led to varied outcomes, resulting in an incredible range of passive margin styles that developed during the Gondwana breakup. These findings contribute to a enhanced comprehension of the evolution of rifted margins and highlight the significance of early rifting processes in shaping the morphology and tectonic evolution of passive margins. The ultimate outcome of extension in Gondwana, characterized by highly metamorphosed and narrow rifts as well as vast, minimally transformed basins, has left an indelible mark on the geography of the Southern Hemisphere. A new unsupervised learning framework, based on the principles of minimum distortion and maximum segmental length, is introduced and applied to a Segmentation-Consistent Image Masking (SCIM) technique. This method is utilized to create and utilize unsupervised masks for the common problems of low-light image enhancement and super-resolution. The proposed framework is evaluated through numerous experiments on various datasets and demonstrates notable performance improvements compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the proposed framework is tested on an actual industrial application, showcasing its capability to enhance low-light images in real-world scenarios. Studies have shown that incorporating a theory-of-mind (TOM) approach into reinforcement learning promotes cooperation and helps achieve goals in collaborative settings. However, existing methods face difficulties when modeling multiple agents' mental states due to the exponential growth of possible agent configurations. This challenge is particularly pronounced in complex environments and situations requiring long-term planning. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new model that allows for efficient inference of agents' mental states in scenarios involving multiple agents, allowing us to incorporate their TOM into action selection. This is achieved through an iterative process of observing an agent's actions and updating their mental state model based on that observation. We evaluate our model in collaborative games involving multiple agents, both in a first-person scenario (agents observe their own minds) and a third-person scenario (agents do not observe their own minds), and compare it to a method that assumes agents do not have mental states. Our results show that our model performs better than the baseline method and is superior to existing TOM models in complex environments and situations requiring long-term planning. Additionally, our model's performance is on par with the baseline method when evaluating its ability to model a single agent's mind state. We also successfully applied our model to a more intricate scenario involving a multi-agent scenario from the GameShow dataset. Our model's source code is available at: https://github.com/ku2086/efficient-tom-learning. Our paper's formal abstract can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.06218. Our work offers an innovative solution to an enduring challenge in collaborative reinforcement learning and highlights the value of incorporating a TOM approach into action selection through external observation. Our team also acknowledges the contribution of I. Gil. Our work is continuing in an effort to expand the approach to additional scenarios and theories of mind. Our team is open to collaborations and invites interested researchers to join us. We are continually seeking ways to enhance our approach and welcome feedback and criticisms from the RL and TOM communities. We are particularly interested in hearing from researchers who have experience with multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly when agents do not observe their own minds. We are also interested in collaborating with researchers from the cognitive sciences who have expertise in the development of formal theory-of-mind models and are interested in applying our efficient inference framework to their work. We invite these researchers to join us in an effort to expand our approach to additional scenarios

The problem of monitoring lexical semantic change has long been acknowledged as a challenge, and one approach aims to identify newly emerging words with changed meanings. While previous research relied heavily on traditional methods such as corpus analysis, recent work utilizing deep learning models has shown significant progress. This study proposes a practical framework for detecting words with changed meanings by leveraging contextual word embeddings and machine learning classifiers. Firstly, we used a sequence-based model to create a set of context vectors for each word from a large dataset, and then selected words with significant changes in semantic representation from this distribution. Secondly, we fine-tuned a multi-task deep learning model using the collected data to develop a robust predictor of semantic changes. The proposed framework achieved impressive results when compared to existing methods employing probabilistic models and other baselines. This framework's effectiveness can be attributed to the capability of deep learning models to capture intricate patterns and relationships in language. Furthermore, we observed that simply using the pre-trained word embeddings without further processing would not yield satisfactory results. Additionally, we found that building the model with a large dataset containing newly emerging words proved more effective than training it with smaller datasets and allowing it to generalize more freely. The proposed framework's success indicates that large-scale pre-trained contextualized models possess valuable capabilities for detecting words with changed meanings, and such an ability could be a natural by-product of their ability to grasp the dynamics of language. All code and data used in this research are available for replication purposes at https://github.com/robertlopyan/word-change-detection. The framework's ability to discover new words with changed meanings also raises questions about its potential for learning language itself. In this context, we view this work as an initial exploration aimed at laying the groundwork for future research in this area. In this research, we discovered over 1,500 previously unknown words with changed meanings, and a significant portion of these words have already entered common usage, with some even gaining popularity on social media. Many of these words with changed meanings are closely related to existing dictionary entries, and often their changed meanings are indicated by shifts in the words' part-of-speech categories. Although the proposed framework demonstrates impressive performance in detecting words with changed meanings, it is not without its limitations and raises several open questions. For instance, how does it compare to alternative approaches focusing on supervised learning? What factors contribute to the emergence of newly created words with changed meanings in language? Investigating protein folding, particularly knotted proteins, is complicated due to the absence of a systematic framework for categorizing protein knots. We introduce a system where proteins are classified as shallowly or deeply knotted based on the location of their knots in their primary sequences. Then, we apply dynamic sampling and metadynamics to compare the initial structure sampling and folding pathways of 18 shallow knots and 11 deep knots. Our results show that shallowly knotted proteins fold through native-like pathways, whereas deeply knotted proteins require alternative routes. These findings suggest that dynamic sampling in isolation might overestimate the accuracy of native-like pathway predictions for deeply knotted proteins. We also observed that deeply knotted proteins tend to fold more quickly than their shallowly knotted counterparts, which we attribute to the distinct folding intermediates formed during deep knot formation. These results provide new insights into the folding mechanisms of knotted proteins. We highlight the importance of differentiating shallow and deep knots in experimental and computational studies of knotted proteins. Furthermore, our research emphasizes the value of comparing results to generalizations that might not apply to all protein types. Finally, we highlight the need for more computational studies on deeply knotted proteins to further understand their folding mechanisms. Our dataset, containing folding pathways for 29 knotted proteins, is available for further analysis and can aid in validating and correcting existing protein structure prediction methods. It can also be employed to study the folding mechanisms of proteins in different conditions and mutations. This study represents a crucial step in our quest to comprehend the intricate processes involved in protein folding and how they relate to protein function and disease. We have investigated the possibility of early dark energy (EDE) within several popular cosmological models, including $f(R)$ gravity, Brane-World cosmology, and Modified Newtonian dynamics. Our aim was to determine how these alternative theories of gravity affect the EDE's fraction and its impact on the primordial power spectrum of curvature. We discovered that the Brane-World cosmology model exhibits the most notable effect, with the EDE's fraction varying between 0.13 $\sigma_8$ at the present day to 0.38 $\sigma_8$ in the early universe, depending on the specific model parameters. In contrast, $f(R)$ gravity and Modified Newtonian dynamics have an EDE's fraction of less than 0.01 $\sigma_8$ across all stages of the universe. Furthermore, we found that the EDE's fraction in the Brane-World cosmology model is directly proportional to the gravitational strength in this model, and we were able to establish a minimum value for the EDE's fraction of $0.083 \sigma_8$ in any cosmological theory. Our research also indicates that the EDE's fraction is highly sensitive to the cosmological model's parameters, particularly $\Omega_k$, whereas in standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, the EDE's fraction is largely insensitive to these parameters. Our findings also reveal that the primordial power spectrum of curvature is significantly altered in the Brane-World cosmology model, featuring a greater amplitude at very small scales. We anticipate that upcoming surveys will be capable of distinguishing between the $\Lambda$CDM and Brane-World cosmology models by the mid-point of their data collection periods. However, distinguishing between these two models may only become feasible towards the end of these surveys. Conversely, given current forecast limitations, different $f(R)$ gravity models remain indistinguishable from $\Lambda$CDM until far beyond the planned duration of any upcoming surveys. Nonetheless, we do anticipate that even beyond the scope of these surveys, certain $f(R)$ gravity models may be distinguishable from one another. Ultimately, resolving whether the universe does, in fact, follow an EDE cosmology will ultimately rely on cross-validation between various approaches to fundamental physics, necessitating an integrated understanding of all relevant aspects. This extended condition yields an irrational torus T^2 subset M, leading to the conclusion that T^2 is topologically embedded in a three-dimensional space M with a specific volume and chromatic characteristics. Additionally, this embedding results in a non-minimal and non-fillable embedding of T^2 in M. We also establish that a symplectic form on the manifold T^*S^3, obtained by symplectic reduction from the product of the sphere S^3 and its dual, satisfies the modified irrationality condition for an infinitely large range of parameters. This outcome is comparable to, yet distinct from, Cieliewski's findings. We explore more to show that when this condition is further enlarged, it may no longer be unique. Consequently, we are able to derive an upper limit for the volume of M in relation to its injective period length and betti number two, which extends a preceding result by Gajewski and Zehnder. Finally, we establish that on an arbitrarily large interval, there exists a degree-n map from the manifold T^*S^3 to the manifold T^*S^3, where n is either 2 or 3. This latter outcome is an outcome achieved through the combination of symplectic packing theory and the condition's irrationality. 

Keywords: symplectic form, irrationality condition, homology group, kahler manifold, topological properties.

To explore the properties of a massive Nambu-Goldstone boson, we draw parallels between the kaon condensation and the $\eta'$ meson, proposing the $\eta'$-condensation model. In this model, the $\eta'$ meson's mass generation is explained by the interplay of the $\eta'$ condensation and the diquark condensation, which is influenced by the $U(1)_A$ anomaly. We then analyze the $\eta'$-condensation in the presence of a strong external magnetic field, leading to the calculation of the mass of the $\eta'$ meson. Our results demonstrate that the $\eta'$ meson's mass can be significantly affected by the external magnetic field, with an estimated mass of approximately 145 MeV when the $\eta'$ condensation is fully realized. However, this occurs only if the $\eta'$ meson's decay constant is around 1.8 times the vacuum value. We also examine the impact of an increased $\eta'$ meson mass on the critical magnetic field strength required for $\eta'$-condensation, finding that the critical field strength increases in proportion to the $\eta'$ meson mass. Finally, we suggest that the $\eta'$-condensation could provide a possible explanation for the observed mass of the $\eta'$ meson, albeit through a more indirect mechanism. Moreover, we propose that the $\eta'$-condensation may be verified through precise measurements of the $\eta'$ meson's decay constant in reactions involving a strong external magnetic field. Additionally, we expect that the $\eta'$-condensation will lead to the creation of a massive Nambu-Goldstone boson in systems with an odd number of flavors and colors, such as the $\eta$ meson in the fundamental representation. Lastly, we anticipate that the $\eta$ meson's mass generation through $\eta$-condensation will result in a more readily observable effect than the $\eta'$-condensation. Consequently, we suggest that the $\eta$ meson's mass generation through $\eta$-condensation could provide a more compelling explanation for its mass than the $\eta'$ meson's mass generation through the $\eta'$-condensation model. Ultimately, we believe that the $\eta$-condensation offers a promising avenue for exploring the properties of the $\eta$ meson and may be further investigated to shed light on the underlying physics governing the $\eta$ meson's mass generation. However, an in-depth investigation into the effects of training with DISCO-generated data on model robustness and generalization has not been extensively explored. Our research investigates how training with counterfactual data produced by DISCO affects the robustness and generalization of machine learning models, with a focus on supervised learning scenarios. We conducted an empirical analysis, comparing the performance of models trained with real data to those trained with counterfactual data generated by DISCO, using both synthetic and real datasets in the context of classification and continuous output tasks. Our findings demonstrate that while training with counterfactual data often leads to improved robustness and generalization, the outcomes depend on various factors, including the type of data and loss functions employed. Moreover, we observed instances where models trained with such data exhibited increased accuracy across multiple domains. We also examined the influence of model complexity, data quality, sampling temperatures, and specification temperatures on the effects of training with counterfactual data, uncovering both general insights and scenario-specific outcomes. Ultimately, our research underscores the significance of thoroughly evaluating the effects of training with counterfactual data in various contexts. We hope that our exploratory analysis will serve as a starting point for more in-depth investigations into the effects of training with generated data, encompassing additional scenarios and methodologies. For positive integers $d$ and $k$, a total $k$-distinguishing equitable coloring of a graph $G$ involves assigning $k$ different colors to the vertices of $G$, such that the sum of the colors assigned to each vertex equals a unique integer from the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$. We denote the minimum number of colors required for this type of coloring as $e_{tsd}(G)$ and investigate its properties for circulant graphs. Similarly, a $k$-distinguishing coloring of a graph $G$ where the sum of the colors assigned to each vertex equals a distinct integer from the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$ is referred to as a neighborhood sum $k$-distinguishing total coloring. We denote the minimum number of colors required for this type of coloring as $nsd_t(G)$ and investigate its properties for circulant graphs as well. Our main goal is to determine the values or closed expressions for $e_{tsd}(G)$ and $nsd_t(G)$ for various circulant graphs. We also explore the relationship between these two concepts and discuss the interplay between them. In some cases, we are able to establish equality between $e_{tsd}(G)$ and $nsd_t(G)$. In other instances, we are able to provide a lower bound for the ratio of these two parameters. Our findings represent a significant expansion of current knowledge in this area, addressing multiple open questions and presenting new problems to investigate further.

We investigated the influence of growth temperature and methodology on the surface morphology of molybdenum disulfide, deposited through a two-step method onto a graphene substrate. Our results indicate that varying growth temperature significantly alters the epitaxial domain sizes at the MoSe2/Graphene and MoSe2/MoTe2 interfaces. Notably, a specific domain size was achieved by changing growth temperature rather than epitaxial domain distribution. Our findings suggest that higher growth temperatures (>850°C) result in larger domain sizes of the order of several micrometers in size, ultimately leading to the formation of bilayer MoSe2 and mixed-phase MoSe2(x)Te(1-x) materials. Conversely, lower growth temperatures (<800°C) result in smaller domain sizes and a greater range of x values, resulting in a more uniform MoSe2(x)Te(1-x) composition with x values between 0.4 and 0.7. Our study highlights the significance of controlling growth temperature to achieve desired material properties, particularly uniformity in composition. Moreover, our results demonstrate that changing growth temperature rather than growth methodology has the most significant impact in this study. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the potential for precise composition control in MoSe2(x)Te(1-x) materials through accurate temperature management. Nevertheless, our findings also indicate that further investigation is necessary to fully comprehend the underlying growth mechanisms. Owing to Baker's substitution method for $ \Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes, having characterised codes of specific ranks, new lower rank bounds have been derived. Consequently, a substantial code construction threshold of $4 \cdot 3^k$ for a code of rank $k$ has been established, thereby demonstrating the feasibility of constructing such codes of desired rank in a given range. Furthermore, this achievement facilitates the generation of codes with minimum distance greater than three for ranks three and above. Notably, this development makes Baker's approach an efficient code construction method. In our work, we enhance the capability of Baker's method by introducing an additional technique involving the application of a matrix of a particular type, namely a Vandermonde matrix. Interestingly, our modified approach reveals that codes of a particular rank can be constructed from a subset of coordinates, thereby implying the existence of a $ \Z_3 \Z_9$-linear code of rank $2 \cdot 3^k$ for codes of any dimension up to $9^k - 1$. Our advancement thus establishes a code construction threshold of $2 \cdot 3^k$ for codes of rank $k$, which provides a code of optimal distance greater than three for ranks three and above. In particular, this achievement leads to the construction of an $[81, 27, 5]$-linear code over $\Z_3$, along with a binary code of optimal distance greater than four. Our work thereby contributes significantly to the field of coding theory. 

Keywords: $\Z_3\Z_9$-linear codes, code construction, rank of codes, distance of codes.

This research focuses on examining the effects of varying viscosity within polymer injection zones, characterized by a Bingham plastic model. By applying the method of regularized Bingham, our model reaps benefits from the convergence of various viscosity approximations. Our study specifically aims to analyze how different approximation methods influence polymer injection profiles, crossing boundaries of zero and non-zero viscosity. Our results show that near the boundary, the polymer injection profile is significantly impacted, with different approximation methods yielding distinct patterns. However, at greater distances from the boundary, these patterns converge to a similar behavior. Our analysis also establishes conditions under which polymer injection profiles can be classified as smooth or singular. Finally, our results include explicit bounds on the norms of polymer injection profiles, both with and without consideration of the Bingham stress as an additional force. These bounds facilitate the application of our main result, providing a key implication for our analysis. Currently, multi-label classification models typically operate in a scenario where each data point is associated with a single relevant label from a comprehensive list. In contrast, real-world applications often involve single-positive and multiple-negative labels. To achieve significant reductions in annotation expenses, it is necessary to introduce a process that efficiently samples a limited number of positive labels for a range of categories. We introduce S2M sampling, a method designed for cost-effective multi-label data generation, building on the principle that certain categories merit more positive labels than others. S2M sampling leverages an iterative algorithm to prioritize categories and fine-tune the number of positive labels for each one, ensuring that the best value is obtained for the least amount of annotation. Our experiments demonstrate that S2M sampling, used in conjunction with an annotation tool, results in a highly efficient and effective data collection process, allowing for the acquisition of a large dataset with just a single round of annotations. Furthermore, our findings show that supervised learning models trained on datasets generated through S2M sampling perform competitively to those trained on the full annotated multi-label dataset. Additionally, S2M sampling can be applied to any existing single-positive multi-label dataset with no additional annotations required, offering a valuable tool for the research community to explore new ideas and evaluate existing ones on large-scale multi-label datasets. All S2M sampling code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/S2M-sampling, along with the annotation tool and datasets generated through this approach.

This final paper is a combination of my earlier articles, titled "Dynamic Behavior of the Time-fractional Allen-Cahn Equation" and "Global Existence and Boundedness for the Time-fractional Allen-Cahn Equation in R3", which we had published respectively on October 10, 2021, and April 18, 2021. We initially explored the global existence and boundedness of solutions for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation under small initial conditions in R3. Subsequently, we investigated the asymptotic behavior of the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation as time approaches infinity, establishing that the equation's energy reaches equilibrium infinite times and with gaps of 2/k. Both studies have a direct connection to the fractional diffusion equation from which the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation derived. Therefore, our primary objective is to present the complete analysis with a unified proof. We began by establishing the global existence and boundedness of solutions under small initial conditions. Next, we defined the long-time behavior of the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation's energy with intervals of two kilometers. Lastly, we discussed our previous related studies and potential future directions in this field. Ultimately, our combined study aims to provide an in-depth examination of the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation. Lastly, we hope this comprehensive study will inspire further research in this area. The traditional notions of naturality and universality within categories have counterparts in the context of categories with structure, known as weak naturality and universality. These concepts at this higher level of structure are closely tied to an expanded concept of adjoint functors, which includes a distinctive form of transformation known as trace. Specifically, for a monoidal closed category with structure, weak naturality and universality at this higher level of structure are characterized by the existence of an adjoint functor that maps a morphism to its trace, provided that the functor and its components exhibit certain properties of universality and naturality within that category. An example of such a category with structure is the category of Chow motives, which enables the definition of weak naturality and universality in the context of Chow-MU-Gelfand-Nelson conditions. Furthermore, the proposed theorem establishes under these conditions the existence of an adjoint functor that maps an isomorphism to its trace, which is equivalent to the definition of an operable field. In the case of fields of characteristic zero, weak operability is equivalent to strong operability, which in turn is equivalent to the property of being strongly operable, which has distinct prerequisites. The recommended model from the first Fermi Gamma-Ray Burst Burst Catalog, the MAD model, fails to fit observed gamma-rays for many GRBs. It has been proposed that an electron heating rate in the wind zone can explain the missing energy for some GRBs, while also producing the desired spectral changes. However, this solution relies on an inaccurate assumption about the electron distribution, which no longer holds after the additional energy is used to boost the electron's energy. In this paper, we examine how the density of the wind zone impacts the effectiveness of the modified MAD model in fitting GRB spectra, especially in the energy range observed by the Fermi satellite. Our findings suggest that a specific density range can fit most of the GRBs, and that this density is directly linked to the electron heating rate required to explain the energy budget of some GRBs, like GRB 160410A and GRB 170319A. However, the success of this simplified model is limited, and it falls short of fitting the observed gamma-rays for many GRBs, including the highly energetic GRB 190819B. The modified MAD model also struggles to fit the spectral data when the density of the wind zone is allowed to vary freely. In these cases, a significant increase in the density of the wind zone can fit the observed gamma-rays, indicating that this model may require a more fundamental revision than a simple adjustment of parameters. Upgrading the relativistic jet to a pair-dominated one, where the pairs originate from the decay of massive neutron stars or black holes, offers such a possibility. In this scenario, the additional energy is no longer a crisis, and the pair absorption can produce the observed gamma-rays, along with fitting the GRB light curve. This new perspective on the GRB spectrum and the possible origin of the pairs provides a basis for a broader discussion on the possible mechanisms for converting magnetic energy into gamma-rays, and on the possible roles that GRBs can play in the enrichment of heavy elements in the universe. The possible connections between GRBs and Gamma-Ray Bursts with Excess Emission, like GRB 060807, GRB 080703, and GRB 180720B, are also explored. Finally, the requirements for future multi-messenger surveys to uncover more of these connections are outlined. The study presented in this paper is an initial step in the framework proposed in Armitage et al. This study classifies Norwegian stocks into three categories based on the characteristics of their cross-sectional return distributions, which are then analyzed to identify patterns in the central moments of these distributions. By applying a non-parametric method to identify patterns, the analysis reveals that the first four moments of the cross-sectional distributions of stock returns exhibit significant structure. Further, the study utilizes a parametric approach to fit standard distributions to these returns data on an individual stock basis, which enables the exploration of stock characteristics that influence the shape of these distributions. Ultimately, the research finds that low-risk, highly liquid stocks with established market connections tend to have normal or boldly alternative return distributions, whereas volatile, less liquid, and exogenous stocks are more likely to have boldly alternative distributions. These findings are robust across multiple distribution fitting methods. However, the study does not establish a clear link between distribution characteristics and expected returns, or between these distributions and the cross-sectional returns volatility. Nonetheless, the analysis provides a comprehensive overview of Norwegian stock returns distributions, which can serve as a benchmark for future research or portfolio management strategies. Moreover, the study's dataset and methods are readily available for replication purposes. Ultimately, the classification of stocks into normal and boldly alternative distribution categories can be utilized in the development of financial products that are tailored to specific investor risk preferences. Ultimately, the research offers a data-driven classification system that portfolio managers or financial product issuers can leverage to categorize stocks into normal or boldly alternative distribution types, which may eventually inform the design of risk-targeted products. However, this approach requires further refinement before being applicable in practice. Nonetheless, the study's methodology and resulting classification can be a valuable starting point for any cross-sectional analysis of stock returns or asset allocation strategies within the Norwegian market. A proposed new detection method is presented, which enhances the accuracy of identifying cardiac issues even in noisy echocardiography videos. The algorithm's performance is bolstered by its ability to learn from a diverse range of data, including images with low image quality, that cannot be replicated in real-world environments. The algorithm's ability to handle noise is also demonstrated through an experiment where it is trained on clean data and subsequently tested on noisy data with varying levels of noise. The proposed algorithm is then compared to two alternative methods, one that uses a noise-reducing filter and another that is trained and tested on the same data, resulting in better than twice the improvement in accuracy compared to these alternatives. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on a large dataset of real-world echocardiography videos, resulting in a significant reduction in the number of false positives and improvement in the detection of cardiac abnormalities. The proposed algorithm is also found to be robust to different training sizes, outperforming the alternative methods even when trained on a smaller dataset. The explosion of wearable devices generating activity data has created vast opportunities and challenges for healthcare systems. While existing methods effectively detect individual activities from raw sensor data, their limitations become apparent when processing numerous users and activities. This performance bottleneck is addressed by a novel deep learning framework called FedHealth, which leverages a combined use of transfer learning and federated learning to optimize data utilization and safeguard user privacy. FedHealth's ability to handle multiple activities and users is demonstrated through a comprehensive evaluation using four commonly recorded activities and data from over 300 participants. Compared to both traditional activity recognition methods and a baseline deep learning network, FedHealth exhibits exceptional performance with an overall accuracy rate of 92.2% across all tested scenarios. This represents a significant improvement over the baseline and underscores the framework's potential to create more adaptive, secure, and reliable wearable-based activity recognition systems. Portfolio management, a critical activity in modern businesses, involves making strategic decisions about investments, funding, and resource allocation. Various optimization frameworks, including utility and multi-objective optimization, have been employed to develop computational methods to tackle this complex issue. However, the rapid changes in market conditions, investor preferences, and technological advancements demand a more dynamic and adaptive approach to portfolio management. This study introduces an artificial intelligence-based framework called DYNAMO, which integrates elements of utility, multi-objective, and constraint optimization within a genetic algorithm to provide a comprehensive solution for contemporary portfolio management problems. DYNAMO's unique feature allows it to respond effectively to shifting environmental circumstances due to its hierarchical structure, where the central controller makes strategic decisions while multiple agents oversee mid-to-short-term adjustments. This framework is evaluated through a simulation study involving various scenarios and compares DYNAMO to traditional portfolio management strategies like Markowitz's Mean-Variance and a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm. The results show DYNAMO to be an exceptionally robust and adaptable solution for modern portfolio management, exceling in both stable and volatile market conditions. Furthermore, DYNAMO's performance in response to sudden changes surpasses all other strategies, and it is capable of recovering from temporary setbacks. Ultimately, this study offers a groundbreaking artificial intelligence-based framework for dynamic portfolio management and provides valuable insights into the most critical components of optimization, which can be applied to other complex adaptive systems. However, DYNAMO's potential limitations due to its computational demands and potential for over-exploitation require further investigation. Additionally, incorporating external management interventions and adapting the framework to real-world scenarios will necessitate future research. In conclusion, DYNAMO signifies a significant step towards an evolutionary finance approach, addressing modern portfolio management challenges, and its source code is available upon request.

Recruitment panel interviews present unique challenges in scheduling and panel creation, particularly with large applicant pools and limited panel member availability. Existing manual methods for solving these problems are inefficient and often produce suboptimal results. In this research, we introduce an automated algorithm that combines a greedy approach with a 2-approximation method to create recruitment panels while adhering to schedule constraints and minimizing the number of required interviews. Our approach can handle large-scale scenarios and outperforms the current optimal solution while maintaining practical efficiency, as demonstrated by our experimental results on real-world datasets. Furthermore, we showcase the implementation of our algorithm through an interactive frontend, making it easily accessible and integratable with existing recruitment software systems. This innovative solution has the potential to be adopted by various institutions and can be found at our website listed in our appendix. We also invite other researchers to collaborate and contribute to this project. Our code is openly available on our GitHub repository.

This study involves examining the impact of a persistent underlying diffusion on an agent's optimal payoff, particularly in a scenario where the agent has the capability to adjust variables that affect the diffusion process. By applying backward stochastic differential equations, our research aims to model this problem and provide an explicit formula for the optimal payoff, ultimately leading to an investigation of the presence of a dominant underlying diffusion in the optimal payoff. In addition, our results include conditions for the convergence of optimal payoffs in relation to increasing diffusion coefficients, as well as an examination of the presence of an underlying diffusion with zero drift in the optimal payoff. Furthermore, our results can be applied to derive the optimal investment strategy for a European put option on a stock modelled as a stochastic differential equation with a dominant diffusion component. By scaling the diffusion coefficient, we are able to demonstrate the limiting behavior of the optimal payoff and the associated value process as the scaling parameter tends to zero or infinity. Our results can be compared with those presented in the existing literature. All necessary proofs are provided in the accompanying paper. Our research is an extension of the studies presented in Chen and Peng (2007) and the references listed within, which addressed the presence of an underlying diffusion with zero drift in the optimal payoff for a similar BSE model. In high-dimensional, time-dependent data scenarios, correlation and traditional feature selection methods are not sufficient, leading to the need for more advanced techniques that prioritize importance. Although artificial neural networks have achieved success in various tasks, their size and training time have been a limitation.

We present a novel, efficient method called BRAN-DNE that uses a part of the network to prioritize key variables in complex, time-dependent scenarios. By limiting the network to only consider past observations, it achieves significant performance gains without sacrificing accuracy. By further refining the technique with relevance learning, it becomes even more precise. The method works well across different datasets and scenarios and outperforms existing methods, making it a reliable option for scientists to use in conjunction with experimental and computational analyses. The code for BRAN-DNE is now available on an open-source platform. By providing a solution to the key variable identification problem, BRAN-DNE can serve as a substitute for dynamic graphical Gaussian models and facilitate the understanding of underlying mechanisms in biological systems. We analyzed ultraviolet spectroscopy from the Hubble Space Telescope, specifically looking at ionized gas around an extremely bright galaxy, ULIRG PGC 43289. This galaxy is undergoing incredibly rapid star formation and has an active galactic nucleus. To study the surrounding gas, we examined high-energy emission lines created by the collision of gas clouds, which indicated the presence of low-density molecular wind or circumgalactic gas reservoirs. These features are common in extremely bright galaxies and starburst galaxies, and they play a crucial role in suppressing the formation of stars and preventing the galaxy's feedback from returning to its center. Analyzing the ratios of these emission lines helped us understand the conditions within the gas clouds and their impact on the galaxy's development. Our analysis showed that the ionized gas around PGC 43289 has similar characteristics to that found in the Milky Way, but we did detect larger gas clouds extending further out from the galaxy, which could indicate a greater mass loss due to the galaxy's rapid star formation. These larger gas clouds may also be contributing to the surrounding gas reservoir, which is a crucial component of extreme starburst galaxies like PGC 43289. Similar wind patterns and gas reservoirs have been observed in galaxies like Arp 220 and Mrk 331, and they are critical for understanding how galaxies with rapid star formation can regulate their own growth. If large gas reservoirs are a hallmark of extreme starburst galaxies, they could also provide a mechanism for replenishing the gas consumed by galaxies like the Milky Way in the future. However, if these galaxies persist in their rapid star formation, their gas reservoirs will be used up, and the galaxies will enter a quieter phase of development. Based on our analysis of PGC 43289, we propose that galaxies like it will enter this quieter phase when their massive star bursts finish forming stars and the galaxies' feedback is returned to their centers, likely after 10-20 million years. During this phase, we expect to see lower rates of massive star formation and a more subdued view of these galaxies in the infrared spectrum. However, if the galaxies' gas reservoirs are gradually replenished with gas from surrounding wind patterns, and if their massive star bursts are interrupted, these galaxies may return to their rapid star formation cycles, and we may capture them in their most bright and active phases only when their massive star bursts are occurring. If so, it will be even more challenging to study the ionized gas around these galaxies and study the role it plays in shaping their development.

The connection between the persistent anomalies observed in bottomless meson decays, specifically $K$ and $B$ meson systems, and lepton-flavor universality has been thoroughly examined. Uncommon $K$ and $B$ meson decays have been documenting deviations from expected behavior in recent years. On the other hand, LFU has exhibited discrepancies in various processes, including rare $B$ meson decays and nuclear transitions. By incorporating experimental constraints and theoretical suppression factors, we have analyzed possible links between the mentioned flavor anomalies and U1 symmetry breaking in the electroweak sector. It has been found that COMMA-c crossings between the mentioned flavor anomalies and COMMA-compliance with LFU can occur only if the U1 symmetry breaking occurs at a scale greater than around 1 TeV. Moreover, we have examined how new physics contributions affecting the mentioned flavor anomalies and U1 symmetry breaking could be discovered at existing or upcoming experiments, such as top-quark decays, Higgs boson interactions, and radiative corrections to leptonic meson decays. In order to explain the mentioned flavor anomalies and U1 symmetry breaking, we have also developed a concrete new physics scenario featuring a dark sector containing an $SU(2)_L$ doublet and additional flavor non-universal vector-like generations. This model has a plausible parameter space that is in line with all given constraints and is capable of being discovered in the next generation of experiments. Consequently, we are advocating for continued thorough examination of existing and upcoming data in search of potential U1 symmetry breaking signs, as well as for the inclusion of nuclear transitions in new physics analyses. Ultimately, we believe that the persistence of flavor anomalies in the $K$ and $B$ meson systems will induce the high-energy physics community to thoroughly examine all possible new physics interpretations in the coming years.

We investigate the size of the largest overlap between two circular regions in a Cayley graph, particularly in the Hamming cube which is extensively used in coding theory and combinatorial design. By formulating the problem in a general framework, we derive an expression for the biggest common area between two metric balls of limited size in the Cayley graph. Specifically, in the Hamming cube $n$-dimensional space with binary edges, we focus on finding the exact size of the biggest common area between two metric balls of error rates $\epsilon$ and $\delta$. Notably, when either $\epsilon$ or $\delta$ exceeds half the distance between adjacent points, the common area shrinks to a single point. Moreover, when both $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ are less than half the distance between adjacent points, the common area remains a metric ball with the same center. By applying this framework, we are able to derive an explicit formula for the size of the common area in the Hamming cube $n$-dimensional space. Consequently, this enables us to establish a connection between the common area and a hypergraph formed by successive layers of binary vectors. Finally, this connection leads to a solution to a problem related to the minimum number of edges required in a certain type of graph. This solution, in turn, results in an improvement to the previously known upper limit for the size of the common area in the Hamming cube $n$-dimensional space when either $\epsilon$ or $\delta$ is less than half the distance between adjacent points. This new upper limit is $\min\{1,\frac{\epsilon}{\delta}\}2^{n-\delta}$. Consequently, this implies that in the case of error rates $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ that are both less than half the distance between adjacent points, the size of the common area is at most $2^{n-\delta}$. Additionally, this upper limit is achievable when the center of the two metric balls is an interior point of the Hamming cube $n$-dimensional space. Furthermore, this achievement is also valid for larger values of $\delta$ up to but not including half the distance between adjacent points.
