This study conducts an in-depth examination of prototypical networks in recognizing musical instruments from audio, with a focus on improving their performance. A novel hierarchical loss function is introduced, with results showing significant enhancements when combining it with data augmentation. Our findings reveal that the primary contributions of the hierarchical loss and augmentation methods are reducing the distance between distinct prototypes and achieving a more compact distribution of prototypes, respectively. To gain deeper insight, we conduct an in-depth analysis of our hierarchical loss function, which involves demystifying its underlying properties through mathematical proof and validating its effectiveness across multiple configuration combinations. Our approach offers several key benefits, including (1) enhanced network robustness, with reduced overfitting caused by the compact prototype distribution, (2) improved generalization, enabling the network to efficiently handle unseen instruments, and (3) streamlined codebook construction, where new prototypes are generated with minimal distance to existing ones, leading to overall computational efficiency. To support replication, the code and dataset used in this research are now available for public access at the links provided.

The quality of answers in product reviews on e-commerce platforms is crucial for consumers making informed purchasing decisions and businesses improving their products. To automate answer-quality assessment, we introduce the first comprehensive dataset with relevant contexts, product specifications, and category labels for 500 product-review questions. The developed dataset, called QASPER, enhances current question-answering models and facilitates progress in the following areas: (1) context-aware models can utilize product-specification information to achieve better performance; (2) product-knowledge-based models are capable of extracting accurate product features from text; (3) category-aware models can predict relevant product categories from product descriptions; (4) evaluation protocols that consider product specifications and categories for assessing answer quality. Notably, our work introduces the first dataset with review-contexts, specifications, and category labels for product-based questions, which poses significant challenges compared to existing question-answering datasets. To further complicate the assessment, we introduce two critical factors: (a) spurious correlations among product features and answers, along with (b) the need for domain-specific domain knowledge. To facilitate future benchmarking and progress in answer-quality assessment, we introduce evaluation metrics that consider product specifications and categories. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our models in assessing answer quality and predicting product specifications and categories. The complete code and dataset are available at https://github.com/ameerkhan0/QASPER. With ongoing advancements in product-based question-answering models, we believe it is essential to continually evaluate and improve the quality of answers by referencing product specifications and category labels. Ultimately, this research has the potential to contribute to various applications, including answer-generation systems, product-recommendation platforms, and customer-support services. It can also facilitate progress in other domain-independent question-answering tasks, such as improving fact-checking protocols and evaluating the quality of generated answers. Overall, QASPER offers an opportunity to push the boundaries of current question-answering models and assess answer quality in the presence of product specifications and category labels. It provides an ideal platform to develop context-aware models capable of extracting accurate product features from text and predicting relevant product categories from product descriptions. Additionally, it enables the assessment of answer quality considering product specifications and category labels, along with addressing the challenges posed by spurious correlations among product features and answers and the necessity of domain-specific domain knowledge. With ongoing progress in product-based question-answering models, continually evaluating and improving the quality of answers by referencing product specifications and category labels is becoming increasingly important

We derive an all-encompassing approximate analytic formula for the noise floor of signal-to-noise ratio in pulsar timing array experiments, considering the effects of direction, spatial separation, and orbital period on gravitational wave source positions. This formula can predict the noise floor at a given data span and $f_{\text{max}}$ for any PTA or proposed timing array, allowing for an initial assessment of a host institution's contribution to a particular gravitational wave source search without running full simulations. We demonstrate the accuracy of our analytic expression by comparing it to various other methods and across different PTA and proposed timing array scenarios. Ultimately, we apply our noise floor prediction to evaluate the potential sensitivity of various PTA and proposed timing array experiments in the coming decades. Unless accompanied by a significant increase in data span or $f_{\text{max}}$, we find that the sensitivity of these experiments will be dominated by their current or near-future data spans. Therefore, researchers are encouraged to prioritize the collection of longer-span data with existing and future telescopes and to conduct further investigations into how to optimize the sensitivity of these experiments. Nonetheless, even with no additional increase in data span or $f_{\text{max}}$, we find that various PTA and proposed timing array experiments will be capable of detecting significant sources in the coming decades, including the prominent sinusoidal modulation caused by the Galactic supermassive black hole in the center of the Milky Way, once high-frequency data becomes available. Furthermore, we find that a sufficiently sensitive dataset with a suitable data span and $f_{\text{max}}$ could potentially allow the identification of distinct pulsar partners in a binary system, such as the case with the pulsar pair PSR B1913+16. Ultimately, we believe that approximately knowing an institution's or a particular search's sensitivity could be beneficial in prioritizing contributions to specific gravitational wave source searches. Additionally, we suggest that future gravitational wave research initiatives incorporate evaluation of the potential sensitivity of participating institutions or searches in their review processes. We investigate how a specific particle travels in ASEP with two types of particles, monitoring its velocity distribution as time passes. Additionally, we examine the long-term behavior of this distribution and how it is affected by the bias in the system. Mathematical models of disease dynamics are frequently developed using systems of differential equations, which are then fitted to available data. While such models can provide significant insights when fitted accurately, there's a risk that poor fits can generate misleading results and hinder the development of viable epidemic control strategies. In response, we've developed a method for fitting these differential models to data while adhering to biological feasibility, which takes into account the initial conditions and variable boundaries that characterise real-world disease scenarios. This approach, based on a Tikhonov regularization framework, minimizes the difference between the model and observed data while restricting solutions to the feasible region defined by the model's equilibrium points and the presence of infection carriers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through two applicable examples: a classic SIR model and a more recent SIRS model, which has seen increased scrutiny in recent years. Notably, our results indicate that incorporating biological feasibility into the fitting process is essential, as it prevents the emergence of illogical large-scale outbreaks in the model. This new method for fitting differential models to data while considering their biological feasibility is the foundation for our proposed framework, which we believe offers a vital tool for validating and refining models of disease dynamics. This method is now available as the R function 'feaspopt' within our brmcs R package. This package can be accessed on CRAN. Our approach is an early adaptation of the feasible parameter optimization technique, which is also the basis for our optimal control method, which we will openly contribute to GitHub in the near future. In our accompanying manuscript, we outline the methodology and benefits of this new method, which we initially developed in response to our analysis of disease dynamics data from Western Australia. In this analysis, we identified significant discrepancies between predicted and observed epidemic patterns, which prompted us to re-evaluate our modeling approach and develop a more feasible solution. This new method for feasible parameter optimization has now been applied to our previous studies of disease dynamics in Victoria, New South Wales, and the Northern Territory, which are part of our broader epidemiology research efforts. However, these additional results are not included in this manuscript. Full implementation details, including all necessary functions and input parameters, can be found within our brmcs R package, which is readily available on CRAN. A exact statistical analysis reveals how the entropy, when the fermion number is fixed, is affected by a uniform linear potential and displays a bimodal distribution. This effect is further confirmed through a harmonic oscillator approximation and demonstrates that the potential's influence-co either repulsive or attractive-interacts with the pairing interaction's impact on the entropy's mean and standard deviation. Notably, for sufficiently strong linear potential, the fermions' behavior is analogous to that of bosonic Coherent State Majoranas in one-dimensional space, where the entropy's mean value follows a Gaussian-like distribution. Conversely, in the presence of pairing interactions, the linear potential's effect is modulated by its own one-dimensional quantization, resulting in an emergence of non-Gaussian entropy patterns. These findings are also verified through numerical simulations using the Wick decomposition method. The proposed framework is applicable to any one-dimensional topological superconducting chain with paired interactions and may be employed to analyze the entropy of Majorana fermions in those systems. Our study uncovers a novel category of solids with nodal lines in momentum space, characterized by isolated curves or sheets that pass through without crossing, unlike the points and lines that typically form nodal pairs. We demonstrate that in the orthorhombic crystal of Sr$_2$ZrO$_4$, a material previously considered a topological insulator, these nodal lines dominate, separating the hole-like and electron-like bands and generating unique directional transport phenomena along the nodal lines. Using ab initio simulations, we confirm that Sr$_2$ZrO$_4$ exhibits a robust non-trivial gap around the nodal lines, fulfilling the criteria for a topological semimetal. Our analysis distinguishes the electronic structure of Sr$_2$ZrO$_4$ from other nodal line materials like Sr$_3$Ir$_2$Te$_6$ and MnBi$_2$Te$_4$, further contributing to the understanding and classification of nodal line semimetals. Additionally, we propose that Sr$_2$ZrO$_4$ may be useful in the experimental study of topological transport along fixed directions. 

Our research is also extended to other doped and substituted compounds of Sr$_2$ZrO$_4$, such as Sr$_2$ZrO$_4$Sn$$_x$, Sr$_2$ZrO$_4$Nb$$_x$, Sr$_2$IrO$_4$, and Sr$_2$HfO$_4$, which offer opportunities to combine nodal lines with other topological states like point nodes and wheels. These materials provide a platform for exploring unique topological phenomena and potential applications in electronic devices. 

We validate the stability of Sr$_2$ZrO$_4$ using ab initio simulations and confirm that its nodal lines remain intact under the doping and substitution replacedments, with some compounds exhibiting additional topological features. A multi-task deep learning model has been devised and tested for both segmenting and classifying three different brain tumor types - Medulloblastoma, Meningioma, and Glioma. The proposed network overcomes previous limitations of single-input two-dimensional images by utilizing three input types: two-dimensional MRI scans and a three-dimensional MRI scan, along with their respective difference maps. The network's multi-task capability is achieved through shared convolutions and parallel dense layers. Experimental results show the proposed model's superiority over comparable methods on the BraTS dataset, while only using a relatively basic network architecture. Furthermore, the model successfully segmentated and classified real-world brain tumors with 85% accuracy at 0.05 confidence level. The best approach was determined through a comprehensive analysis involving five different network configurations and three input scenarios. The technique has the potential to be applied to other medical imaging diagnosis scenarios. The issue of the complex dataset being difficult to annotate was also addressed, and the study was conducted in accordance with strict ethical guidelines due to the involvement of sensitive medical data. The model's performance was evaluated using precision, recall, mean average precision, dice similarity coefficient, sensitivity, and specificity metrics. This paper introduces an innovative approach to shadow mapping, a crucial aspect of realistic computer graphics. Inspired by the success of neural volumetric lights fields in virtual lighting design, we investigate the potential of using implicit neural lights fields for shadow computation. However, existing INLF models are not suitable for this task due to their large size and computational demands. To overcome this limitation, we suggest using a compact neural renderer that leverages two separate models to achieve both shadow and lighting effects. However, training this system is challenging because only a single image is captured during shadow computation, leading to difficulties in recovering both shadow and light information. To address this issue, we propose refining the light field using the captured shadow image and estimate the shadow map through an optimization process. Moreover, we suggest using an alternative illumination model with adjustable parameters to facilitate extraction of light field details. To further improve results, we explore two alternative approaches one using multi-view optimization and the other a cycle-consistency loss. Our results demonstrate that our shadow computation approach outperforms traditional ray tracing methods, offering more realistic and detailed shadows. Moreover, this method enables efficient shadow mapping even in complex scenes with numerous light sources. Notably, our approach enables dynamic objects to produce accurate shadows without needing explicit reconstruction of those objects. Consequently, our compact neural renderer for shadow computation proves an invaluable tool for real-time graphics applications, offering a degree of realism previously unachievable. Moreover, this technique may also contribute to improvements in other computer graphics areas such as rendering. Recent advancements in Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have led to significant breakthroughs in image processing tasks with limited training data, particularly in the domain of video processing. Non-sequence-based methods, although requiring the fewest components for production, suffer from over-smoothing and loss of detail. In contrast, sequence-based approaches have shown the most promise for producing high-quality results but necessitate frame sequences during both training and testing phases. This study proposes a novel, efficient sequence-based method, predicated on a deep neural network, that utilizes two distinct sequences for both training and processing. Notably, this method achieves remarkable results even with a single training image and no additional data. When employed for real-world applications, it delivers outstanding results with minimal memory requirements. The developed framework boasts exceptional performance in various video processing tasks including video super-resolution, video denoising, video deblurring, deinterlacing, and video frame rate up sampling. Moreover, our research introduces an innovative iterative refiner that boosts quality without compromising efficiency. Comprehensive experiments validate our approach, demonstrating superior performance when compared to cutting-edge methods and existing techniques, while requiring substantially fewer parameters. The proposed framework is also highly versatile, enabling the incorporation of external information for improved performance during real-world applications. All code and models are freely accessible on GitHub.

A novel method called Principal Component Geostatistical Analysis (PCGA) is introduced to accurately estimate riverbed bathymetry using flow velocity measurements obtained from Eulerian-UltraSkin-Mounted Acoustic Doppler Current Profilers. This method effectively leverages the spatial correlations among flow velocities to enhance resolution of bottom reflectivity data and ultimately determine the riverbed topography. A key benefit of PCGA is its ability to tackle the ill-posed problem of inversely solving the Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler equations by utilizing a combination of the Empirical Orthogonal Function and Maximum Likelihood Estimation techniques. To demonstrate the efficacy of PCGA, it was applied to data collected during an UltraSkin field test conducted on the Delaware River. Results show that PCGA can successfully integrate flow velocity and bottom reflectivity data at multiple stations to obtain a continuous map of the riverbed topography and corresponding bathymetry in the study area. Furthermore, compared to conventional methods, PCGA yields more precise estimates of riverbed elevations with lower RMSE values of 0.078m and 0.084m for respectively two and three dimensional cases. Notably, these results do not rely on initial bathymetry data, instead using flow velocity and bottom reflectivity measurements only. Ultimately, PCGA is an efficient and effective method for accurately estimating riverbed bathymetry using flow velocity measurements from Eulerian-UltraSkin-Mounted Acoustic Doppler Current Profilers. This approach has the potential to play a key role in the development of autonomous riverbed mapping systems. We establish a higher-rank generalization of the Madsen-Weiss theorem by linking the stable rationality of del Pezzo surfaces in complex projective space to the simple connectedness of their moduli spaces. Additionally, this higher-rank extension connects the b-principle to stability theorems in topology, revealing that the Madsen-Weiss theorem serves as a prototype for the principle. Furthermore, our result enables the construction of explicitly described, higher-rank Madsen-Weiss type structures that exhibit the product property of the b-principle. Our proof of the surface del Pezzo case builds upon Il'yanugov's findings and incorporates the application of MUMSD by A. Kazda and V. Koytigev. Our higher-rank generalization also takes into consideration the properties of abelian varieties and their compactifications. Our research also establishes a relationship between the rationality of del Pezzo surfaces and the simple connectedness of their geometric fundamental groups, extending a similar connection between the rationality of surfaces and their geometric fundamental groups as shown by J. Harris, P. Shaferevich, and Y. Iyanugov. This research investigates how the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) method's performance is influenced by the selection of coarse space dimension and weight parameters when applied to a nonlinear algebraic problem resulting from a piecewise linear approximation of an elliptic partial differential equation. A new algorithm is developed to compute an optimal coarse space dimension and weight parameter that minimizes the BDDC preconditioner's complexity, and this algorithm is demonstrated to be effective in both two and three-dimensional scenarios. However, it's also shown that the optimal parameters obtained may not always lead to the smallest possible BDDC complexity, and this depends on the specific implementation and programming model being used. In particular, very large optimal coarse space dimensions can be obtained with some algorithms, which may not be desirable in certain computational environments. As a result, researchers should consider the trade-offs involved and balance the optimal performance with factors like memory usage and computational efficiency. This is illustrated by applying the BDDC method to a large-scale benchmark problem known as the Kandell-Meier problem. The implementation of this algorithm has been done using both PETSc's DDSCS module and a custom in-house solver, and the obtained results are then compared against each other and against other solvers like the Direct LCM and an in-house LCM solver. The results of this comparison are particularly interesting when large optimal coarse space dimensions are considered, and this could have implications for how LCM is studied in the future. The Python scripts used to generate these results and compute the optimal parameters can be found on an open-source repository on GitHub. The research presented here is part of a broader study on the BDDC method's performance, particularly when applied to LCM, and it paves the way for more in-depth analysis and more general theories to be developed. This paper investigates the conditions under which the limiting spectral distribution of an asymmetric random matrix, with entries drawn from a symmetric, uniformly distributed sub-group, converges in probability or almost surely. We establish that, provided the matrix dimensions satisfy $p=n^{\alpha}$, where $\alpha$ falls within a specific range, the spectral distribution settles into a stable form. Furthermore, we develop a method to accurately quantify the spectral distribution via a continued fraction-like structure. Interestingly, this framework offers insight into the spectral properties of various real-world networks, including those represented by matrices with specific symmetry properties. In particular, we apply our method to analyze the spectral characteristics of matrix embeddings, and we also establish a connection with the conditions required for the existence of a non-trivial stable point in the cubic Jensen mapping. This relationship gives us the ability to determine the required matrix dimensions ($p=n^{\alpha}$) for a stable spectral distribution, and we find that the particular value of $\alpha$ depends on whether we are concerned with spectral distribution convergence in probability or almost surely. Finally, we support our theoretical findings with numerical analyses and empirical studies from real-world networks. Notably, we find that our results can be applied to matrices with "almost-symmetric" properties, and we propose an applicable threshold for this condition. Additionally, we explore the relationship between our findings and the characteristics of the matrix's off-diagonal elements. Lastly, we identify and discuss potential directions for further research within this field of study. Persuasive videos are increasingly relied upon in marketing campaigns and political initiatives, particularly on social media platforms. These videos often include background music to engage viewers emotionally, but typically lack transparency into their underlying content and sentiment. In this study, we propose a method to automatically generate music for persuasive videos while making their emotional influence visible, essentially "auditing" their emotional impact. We have designed a system that creates music in a way that separates the emotional influence from the primary viewing experience, and incorporates a visibility parameter to control the degree to which the music conveys the video's underlying content and sentiment. Our system enables the simultaneous creation of visible and invisible versions of music for persuasive videos. We have conducted user studies to show that viewers' opinions about the videos are aligned with the music's visibility, and have analyzed the music generated by our approach to show that it accurately reflects the underlying content and sentiment of the associated video. Moreover, the music generated by our approach is preferred over music generated by a baseline method in user studies. Notably, the music generated for videos with hidden underlying content or biased intent can be surprisingly pleasant to listen to, highlighting the challenges of designing music that is both aesthetically pleasing and aligned with good moral principles. We have further investigated the musical preferences of different cultures, demonstrating that our approach generalizes across musical cultures. Finally, we have explored the application of our approach to music auditing in real-world promotional and advertising videos, demonstrating its potential to raise public awareness about the emotional influence of such content. Our approach and associated data are available online at https://music-auditing.github.io/. Our code is also available at https://github.com/strml/music-auditing-code. Our findings have significant implications for the design of music in persuasive technologies, and we propose a framework for music design that balances emotional influence, visibility, and aesthetic appeal. Notably, our approach to music auditing is the first of its kind, and we hope that it will inspire further research in this area. Evaluating a neural network's susceptibility to adversarial attacks involves assessing its ability to conceal its internal decision-making processes. While previous analyses compared the reliability of hidden layers across various neural networks using straightforward metrics, this study introduces a statistical approach to compare their gradient-masking effectiveness. Our results show that conventional neural networks are significantly better at protecting their hidden layers from unauthorized access than their simplified model counterparts, and this achievement is not solely attributed to overfitting. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the complexity of hidden layers has a limited impact on gradient-masking effectiveness and that other factors, including model compactness and data redundancy, play a more significant role. Our research offers a fresh perspective on the development of neural networks with enhanced security against unauthorized access and provides a framework for conducting related studies. All code and data used in this analysis are available for public access.  Our analysis leads to a new benchmark for comparing neural networks in high-stakes applications and informs the design of future secure models, one that prioritizes minimal exposure of hidden layer information. Research into acoustic meta-materials at the micro-level has been relatively limited due to heat transfer's significant influence, which complicates design. By incorporating thermoviscous theory into hydrodynamic equations, we've derived a new set of Brinkman equations that account for both heat transfer and fluid viscosity. Using these equations, we developed a multiple-scale asymptotic analysis to describe the acoustic flow in a micro-channel and identified the primary factors affecting it. Our model shows that thermoviscous effects can be viewed as combining the impacts of fluid viscosity and heat transfer on acoustic boundary layers. A numerical model based on the Brinkman equations was also confirmed by comparing it to simulations using the full hydrodynamic equations. Our results also demonstrate that the acousto-thermoviscous layer's viscosity-dominated sub-layer dominates the flow's resistance. Our study provides a foundation for a more comprehensive numerical model, which would consider the micro-device's geometry and potentially allow for the optimization of such systems. However, our current sub-layer model may be useful for a simplified analysis, especially when the thermal diffusion length is much shorter than the device's dimensions. This would imply that the sub-layer's resistance could be localized and represented by an equivalent boundary resistance, which could be determined through matching flows on either side of the acousto-thermoviscous layer. Notably, our findings might also be applicable to other acoustic channels, such as those in membranes and thin films, involving the acousto-thermoviscous layer's viscosity-dominated sub-layer. To validate our new model, we compared it to existing data for flow resistance in a micro-channel, revealing that it accurately captures the impact of fluid viscosity but may require an additional correction to fully align with the available data. A widely accepted theory posits that diffusion across a lattice over time complies with Gaussian statistics when the diffusion time is sufficiently long. However, recent analyses have revealed that mean squared differences can become distorted due to correlations and diverse starting points. In this study, we examine how these factors influence the distribution of diffusion times. We show that simply averaging the time it takes for particles to travel between two locations can lead to biased results. Instead, we determine the proper average time by considering the unique paths that particles take and how long it takes to get from one point to another along those paths. We develop two methods to calculate this time and show that they yield the same results. We also establish that the spread of particles after a given time is equal to the time it takes for all diverse starting points to be evenly distributed across the lattice. This occurs when the correlation between the particles' positions and their velocities is eliminated and the particles start from a uniformly random configuration. We provide two approaches to determine how long it takes for all diverse starting points to be evenly distributed across the lattice. One approach is based on the principle of detailed balance, which is commonly used in the Monte Carlo method. The other approach involves examining the spread of particles as they move through the lattice and is related to the central limit theorem. We conclude that the standard assumptions of Gaussian statistics can be affected by correlations and heterogeneity, which can result in biased results if not properly accounted for. To illustrate this, we present two simulations: one with correlated movements and one with diverse starting points. In both cases, the distribution of diffusion times does not comply with Gaussian statistics. We also discuss how our findings can be applied to the study of biological systems that exhibit complex movements. In particular, we believe that our analysis of correlated movements has implications for the understanding of the spread of diseases and the movement of prey and predators in ecological systems. Furthermore, we suggest that our analysis of diverse starting points can be applied to the study of the dissemination of genetic mutations in populations of living organisms. Finally, we propose that our methods for calculating the proper average time it takes for particles to travel between two locations can be used to improve the accuracy of simulations in biological and ecological systems. A loop resonator, capable of producing identical cross-phase and self-phase modulation in counterpropagating light beams, was developed.  A continuous wave laser was used to test the $\chi^{(2)}$ nonlinear process, and a cw laser with varying frequency and power was employed to examine the xpm and spm differences first theoretically, then confirmed through experiment. Two methods were devised to measure xpm and spm in this resonator - one involving a cw laser in each direction, and the other employing a cw laser in one direction and a modulated laser in the other.  Both approaches yielded comparable results as predicted by theory.  Furthermore, it was found that xpm was 10 times stronger than spm, and this occurred due to differences in conversion efficiency between xpm and spm.  A figure illustrating the xpm and spm variation with laser frequency also showed that xpm exhibited a larger frequency shift than spm.  In addition, xpm was found to be sufficient to generate a nonlinear optical buffer that can store information in the form of optical solitons.  Therefore, this loop resonator-based xpm setup may provide a feasible means to achieve this storage capability.  A potential application of this work could lead to the development of an optical memory system capable of retaining information for an extended period.  This could be especially useful in the context of optical communication systems.  In such systems, information is transmitted over long distances in the form of optical signals. Finally, although this particular design may have limitations in terms of the maximum power it can handle, future variations of this setup with improved damage threshold may indeed become a crucial component in advanced optical communication systems.  In the meantime, this study provides valuable insights into the fundamental characteristics of cross-phase and self-phase modulation, which could also inform the development of novel optical communication technologies. A particular challenge is capturing the correct behavior of flows at different Reynolds numbers, particularly the transition from laminar to turbulent at Reynolds numbers less than 500. By incorporating a precursor network into the generator, we successfully demonstrate the benefits of this approach in both synthetic flow evaluation and direct numerical simulation turbulent flow scenarios. For example, our model exhibits significant improvement in predicting the correct transition behavior from laminar to turbulent at Reynolds numbers less than 500 when trained with data up to $Re=1800$. Additionally, using an appropriately designed training loss is found to be crucial for accurate transition prediction. By incorporating the total kinetic energy as an additional penalty term in the loss function, we can force the transition to a specific Reynolds number, thus enabling control over the transition process. Using a formula for energy quantization, we derive an equation for the behavior of an atom in a monochromatic electromagnetic field. As the field's amplitude increases, energy levels around the original value split and repel each other. For strong fields, these levels are analogous to the energy differences seen in the Balmer series of hydrogen. A quantum treatment of this issue leads to an electric field threshold at approximately 10^(-5) V/m, which corresponds to the 4d orbital in a hydrogen atom. This threshold is also present in other atoms, yet its significance depends on the orbital's electric susceptibility. In the classical limit, this threshold disappears. Our theoretical model yields results comparable to those obtained through other Equations, such as the Heisenberg-Weyl picture. Our analysis offers a novel, simplified explanation of how energy levels around an atom's ground state can exhibit the spectra seen in the Balmer series. This phenomenon requires an atom to be placed within a strong electromagnetic field that can alter its energy levels significantly. In such an environment, an atom can transition from any energy level to the ground state by releasing the quantized amount of energy. If the field remains constant, the energy differences around the ground state will replicate the patterns seen in the Balmer series, and we can identify the thresholds for exciting specific orbitals in various atoms. These results could contribute to an understanding of how atoms in strong electromagnetic fields may behave in environments like those surrounding black holes or neutron stars. Moreover, this phenomenon might provide a way to identify atoms that have been exposed to such environments, even if the atoms have moved distant from the source of the electromagnetic field. In such a scenario, the atoms' energy levels would reflect their origin, offering a clue about their environmental history. This could be particularly useful if we can develop a method to measure the thresholds for exciting specific orbitals in atoms that have been removed from strong fields and are now located in laboratory settings. Despite significant advancements in deep neural network technology for image classification, their vulnerability to adversarial attacks remains a significant concern. Unfortunatly, conventional deep neural network models are prone to producing unreliable results, especially when their classification output has a very high confidence level. This issue motivates the search for a reliable deep neural network model that not only minimizes misclassification risk but also provides more realistic prediction confidence levels. In this paper, we propose a method to enhance the robustness and calibration of deep neural network classifiers through an iterative process of training with adversarial data, collected based on uncertainty in prediction confidence. This approach involves first identifying the confidence threshold $\tau$ for which the untrusted network performs best. Then, an iterative process is used to collect adversarial data from samples that the untrusted network correctly classified with confidence greater than $\tau$, but incorrectly classified by the trusted network. This process is repeated until the trusted network is at least as accurate as the untrusted network on n-domain samples. Moreover, an efficient method is devised to collect adversarial data by obtaining the uncertainty-based sampling probability from a continuous approximation of the confidence function. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over alternative approaches to enhancing the calibration of deep neural network classifiers. Additionally, the performance of the trusted network on robustness tasks is on par with that of the untrusted network. The source code for this project is available on GitHub at the address provided in the acknowledgments section. Keywords: deep neural networks, image classification, robustness, calibration.

To fairly assess reinforcement learning algorithms, it's essential to modify the curriculum in a controlled manner. Our study proposes a new task called Biased Reachability Curriculum Generation (BRCG), which involves creating a series of sub-environments with varying levels of bias that guide an agent toward specific states. We argue that this task represents a comprehensive framework for evaluating the ability of algorithms to adapt to changing curricula over time. To provide a concrete evaluation method, we introduce a metric called Average Minimum Path Length (AMPL), which quantifies an agent's performance as the mean of the fewest steps required to reach a target state in each stage of the curriculum. Our research trains agents using evolutionary algorithms and compares their results to those obtained through direct training within each sub-environment. We discover that while direct training yields the best AMPL score under a linear curriculum, agents perform equally well when faced with BRCG. Conversely, EVOL RL outperforms direct training in all other cases examined. Our findings suggest that reinforcement learning algorithms should be evaluated in dynamic, complex scenarios to better reflect the challenges of real-world problems. Moreover, our study finds AMPL to be a valuable performance metric that captures an agent's ability to adapt to varied curricula over time. To facilitate further research, we make all data and implementations freely accessible for others to utilize and expand upon. Our most recent developments are also incorporated into the Multi-Adversarial Shape World toolkit to provide a comprehensive framework for conducting a wide range of challenging experiments. Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for a critical area of study centered on the design of adaptive curricula within complex, dynamic scenarios. As such, we hope that others will join us in exploring this research path and contributing their own findings to the field. Our study includes a comprehensive set of experiments conducted with both state-based and image-based agents, includes a plethora of distinct evaluation setups, and successfully integrates multiple existing methods within a unified framework. Consequently, we believe that our work will not only advance the study of adaptive curricula but also facilitate breakthroughs in numerous other relevant research areas. Temporal process matching aims to compare and analyze different processes that operate over the same variables and have a common domain, by determining which process data points correspond to each other. This comparison is represented as a connected component in a directed graph, where two process data points with a corresponding temporal difference of Delta exist between two process data points. We have developed an efficient algorithm to join process data points based on their similarities and temporal differences, by utilizing a high-performance data structure called Hash Table. This allows us to detect potential correspondences on a large scale, and refine them by considering only nearby process data points in the temporal dimension. We evaluated our comprehensive approach by conducting experiments on real-world datasets, and observed a notable increase in performance and accuracy compared to existing methods. Our innovative technique of combining data analysis with temporal filtering yields an accurate and efficient result, indicating that process data learning can be applied to real-world applications. Furthermore, our approach to modeling process changes through Dynamic Conditional Random Fields graphs provides a more comprehensive understanding of how processes evolve over time. This is accompanied by a new dataset of financial processes, which serves as a challenging benchmark for future research in temporal process matching. Ultimately, our goal is to leverage temporal process matching to support decision-making by providing an understandable and accurate learning method for process data. This will ultimately enable decision-makers to focus on what truly matters, by refining the learning process and addressing key issues such as process classification and forecasting. In this research, we are presenting our innovative temporal process matching approach, which includes a new dataset, efficient algorithm, and comprehensive evaluation, all of which offers many opportunities for further exploration in the field of process data learning. This new framework is now available online at https://github.com/AhmadHayajneh/TPMF. A detailed demonstration of our approach, including source code, can be found at https://ahmadhayajneh.github.io/TPMF-Demo/. A comprehensive evaluation of our approach is presented in the accompanying technical report [1]. The new dataset introduced in this research is further analyzed in the accompanying additional file [2]. In quasiperiodic lattices, certain systems exhibit a phenomenon where light localization switches back to delocalization as the coupling between sites strengthens. This reentrant transition can be understood through a simple qualitative analysis, and in this study, we examine the optical properties of the higher-order Fibonacci lattice by employing a diagonalization method for both dielectric and conducting sites. Our findings indicate that in isotropic three-dimensional lattices, the reentrant transition occurs when photons with long wavelengths transition from delocalized to localized states as the energy increases. A more in-depth exploration of the optical properties is also conducted to gain insight into the parameters influencing this reentrant behavior. Additionally, we investigate the impact of anisotropy on the optical properties by comparing the results for two-dimensional Fibonacci lattices with those of the 3D equivalents, and our results demonstrate that anisotropy can counteract the reentrant transition occurring in two-dimensional lattices. Notably, the anisotropy present in the higher-order Fibonacci lattice can give rise to an additional peak in the localization length vs. energy plots. A theoretical explanation for these observations is also provided. Our study offers a comprehensive understanding of the optical properties in the higher-order Fibonacci lattice and sheds light on the influence of anisotropy and dimensionality on light localization and delocalization. Liger is an upcoming Facility for Anti-Particle and Ion Research (FAIR) experiment at the Gesellmann Institute, which will be based on the SAGA spectrometer and enable Liger to fully exploit its potential. A key component for Liger's functionality is the Data Reduction System (DRS), responsible for reducing raw data from the spectrometer's 25,000 twelve-bit ADC channels. The DRS system consists of four identical reduction units, with each unit capable of processing up to 1.6 GHz of data at a rate of 1.6 Tbps. The system's performance is critical as it affects the Liger detector's overall response time. We have successfully built and tested the first full-scale DRS prototype, which showed promising results with data rates exceeding 1.4 Tbps and a total data reduction capacity of around 1.2 Tbps for real-world FAIR data. Furthermore, we were able to achieve substantial improvements in power consumption by upgrading the FPGAs, reducing power consumption from 192 W to as low as 56 W per board while maintaining high performance. Notably, our findings imply that a subset comprising 'k' elements frequently contains an arithmetic progression of length 'h', with 'h' being a key factor that influences this property. Notably, our results also demonstrate that a subset's ability to contain an arithmetic progression of length 'h' is equivalent to the ability of its square having elements that form an arithmetic progression of length 'h'. This equivalence holds as long as 'h' is less than or equal to 'k'. We also examine subsets with elements that form an arithmetic progression of length 'h' and establish a lower bound for the density of these subsets. This lower bound is directly proportional to 'h' and inversely proportional to 'k'. We also establish a more general lower bound that takes into account additional properties of the subset's square. Finally, we present a counterexample to show that allowing a bounded number of summands can significantly alter the properties of subsets in relation to arithmetic progressions. This counterexample comprises 'k' elements and contains an arithmetic progression of length 'h', but its square does not have an arithmetic progression of the same length when 'h' is greater than 'k'. We conclude that the relationship between 'h' and 'k' can be flexible and is dependent on the subset's structure, particularly its square, and that allowing a bounded number of summands can significantly alter the properties of subsets in relation to arithmetic progressions. We apply our results to a related problem concerning polynomials with non-negative coefficients and investigate the properties of these polynomials in relation to arithmetic progressions. We establish a lower bound for the density of such polynomials and provide a counterexample to show that this lower bound is optimal. We also examine the possibility of generalizing our results to a broader context, including sums of recursive sequences and sums of powers of integers

Finally, we explore the relationship between this condition and the global uniqueness of the solution.

A well-performing neural program generator also requires accurate program validation.
However, this validation should be free from the limitations of a static program analyzer
which is used for training the neural network. To overcome this constraint, we propose
using a weakly supervising program analyzer to correct the neural network's mistakes
and guide its program generation. This approach allows the neural network to succeed
in complex program synthesis tasks that a standalone program analyzer cannot solve.
Our method leverages the analyzer's output to classify program validation errors
into three categories: no-issue, warning, and error. To achieve this, we used a
text-classification model and trained it with data labeled as no-issue, warning,
and error. We evaluated our method on the finding bugs task of the Minimanipulator
domain from the Coarse-to-fine program synthesis dataset. The results show that
this approach allows the neural network to succeed in 57.2% of cases where it failed
without the analyzer, resulting in an overall success rate of 85.3%. Moreover,
when the analyzer is highly inaccurate, a simplified version of our method still
achieves similar performance. Notably, this method also improves the quality of programs
generated for successful examples by 11.2% in terms of precision. In summary, our work
establishes that a weakly supervising program analyzer can be an effective tool for
training neural program generators and suggests that this method has considerable
potential for addressing one of the most challenging issues in program synthesis,
i.e., generating programs that are valid according to their specifications. System code
and data used in this research are available at https://github.com/parbeval/parbeval-smt.

Anomaly detection in large-scale datasets is often facilitated by deep neural network-based methods, yet creating and training these models is costly when starting from scratch. To address this limitation, we developed an incremental anomaly detection approach, allowing for detection capabilities to be refined as new data becomes available. Our method leverages the benefits of progressive neural networks and prototyping techniques to create an efficient and effective solution. It can be used with diverse data types and is particularly useful for monitoring large-scale datasets with continuously incoming data, as it only requires minor updates per batch. Our results demonstrate substantial processing efficiencies and precise detection capabilities, outperforming standard approaches in some cases and matching them in others. The incremental approach we present serves as a valuable reference for the community in evaluating anomaly detection methods. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/kuhnha/incremental-anomaly-detection. Our paper is openly published on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00648.

A compelling issue in the study of cryptography is the interplay between privacy and power dynamics. Researchers investigate whether a strong encryption method exists that allows an all-powerful adversary to induce a user to decrypt specific encrypted data, given that the encryption process has a deniable origin. It has been previously established that such an encryption method exists if the user has a limited number of attempts to correctly decrypt the data. However, the existing proof fails to provide a clear upper limit on the number of allowed attempts. In this study, we demonstrate that an encryption method with deniable origin exists, even if the user has an unlimited number of attempts, and this encryption method is equivalent to the one derived from homomorphic encryption. Furthermore, it was discovered that previous proofs relied on unbounded decision-making capabilities in common applications such as email clients and web browsers. This research offers an improved approach to inducing decryption, which is more feasible in practice. Finally, a theoretical connection is established between this problem and the theory of computationally complex games. This research was supported by the Israel Science Foundation, the European Union, the Technion Computer Science and Engineering faculties, and Google. This work was also influenced by the Cryptography and Technology for Cybersecurity (CTC) project at the Technion, in collaboration with the Israeli industry. This work was presented at Eurocrypt 2022. A video presentation and corresponding code can be found at https://crypto.iu.edu.edu/projects/2022/eurocrypt22_deniable_inducible_encryption/. A paper on this research is published in the Journal of Cryptology, Volume 35, Issue 3, 2022, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10589-022-00445-5. A related paper on this research was presented at TCC 2021, https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/1035. A common industry scenario that this research addresses is an unencrypted email being read by a mail server, and the goal is to encourage the user to re-encrypt specific email content. This problem is relevant to various Inducible Encryption Schemes (IES) applications, and this research presents an first-ever construction of Public-Key Inducible Encryption with a special property - it is deniable - if the encryption method is used in a specific way. This research also establishes an unprecedented connection between this problem and Computational Complexity Theory, and it was supported by the Israel Science Foundation, the European Union, the Technion Computer Science and Engineering faculties, and Google. This assessment metric calculates the achieved final key rate after undergoing coding, sifting, and fault-tolerant decoding processes. We utilized this metric to analyze the performance of eight recently proposed MDI-QKD protocols, collecting their underlying gain and error characteristics from the respective source documents. We then simulated the full implementation process for each protocol under ideal and realistic channel conditions. The results showed that although some protocols maintain high effectiveness even in challenging scenarios, others may perform poorly (with key rates less than 10^(-30) when gain is below 10^(-6), for instance). Notably, the behavior of some protocols cannot be understood through single-parameter analysis alone. We also identified several protocols that exhibit poor performance, despite initial promises, and offer alternative, more efficient implementations of the same concepts. This study contributes to the existing dataset of stellar surface measurements with an examination of the stellar rotation profile of the A-type star KIC 9267654. Initially detected as the outlier in a field of four identical stars from the Kepler mission, its unusual rotation pattern suggested targeting for surface characterization. Revealing a notable latitudinal variation in spectral line widths, we mapped the stellar surface using the Cochran-Taylor technique and found significant variations in line width, temperature, and chemical composition across different latitudes. Our findings show an equatorial region with reduced line widths, higher temperatures, and enhanced chemical abundance of iron, chromium, and magnesium. Conversely, the polar regions exhibit wider line widths, lower temperatures, and decreased chemical abundance of these elements. One possible explanation for this distribution is a tidal heating process caused by a massive planetary companion orbiting the star. Alternatively, the morphology could result from a stellar secular chaos pattern generated by the gravitational influence of a small planetary companion and the stellar spin. Previous studies on average age of information (AoI) for discrete time systems have been limited to examining the AoI distribution at a specific time point or its overall average value. This work is an initial step in investigating the AoI distribution for a wide range of time points. A discrete time system with update periods of $t$ is considered, and a general approach to calculating the stationary AoI distribution is developed. Calculations for geometric, binary and refresh AoI are also derived. Notably, our results demonstrate that the AoI distribution at any given time $t$ is less than the update period $t$. This finding contradicts the common perception that the AoI is greater than or equal to the update period. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the AoI for continuous and discrete time systems with same update periods have distinct distributions. As an example, the AoI distribution for a discrete time system with update periods of 1 time unit is shown to be uniform at $[0,1]$ instead of being concentrated at $1$, as observed in continuous time systems. This work is relevant to systems with same update periods but different time bases, such as wireless sensor networks with time-varying sampling rates or those that adapt their update periods to minimize AoI. Finally, our results provide bounds and properties of the AoI distribution, and offer approaches to calculate the AoI distribution in specific systems. As an added benefit, a new algorithm was developed to verify the stationarity of the AoI distribution numerically. This method can also be applied to other discrete distributions. As shown in the results obtained for geometric, binary and refresh AoI, our approach provides an alternative to existing analytical results. This study explores the existence of quaternary Golay complementary array pairs in various dimensions. We examine the requirements for a quaternary GCA in four dimensions and provide a method for constructing a ternary GCA in four dimensions. However, our analysis indicates that a quaternary GCA pair in four dimensions is only possible if all array sizes are even, specifically divisible by four. A construction for a quaternary GCA of size $2^{m}$ in three dimensions is also described, demonstrating its applicability. Notably, a quaternary GCA pair in two dimensions has already been demonstrated by Singer in 1970, and a higher dimension quaternary GCA can be derived from its lower counterpart, though this would result in duplicate arrays. Consequently, our findings are mainly focused on the non-duplicate arrays in four dimensions. Two necessary criteria have been identified to feasibility in four dimensions: first, the array size must be an even number, specifically divisible by four, and second, a particular ternary GCA can be converted to a quaternary GCA in four dimensions. Constructing a feasible quaternary GCA pair in higher dimensions would necessitate finding suitable lower-dimensional quaternary GCPs that could be extended upwards. Notably, our method of converting a ternary GCA to a quary GCA in four dimensions offers an innovative approach that may offer a new strategy for tackling other complementary array constructions. In the final section, open problems are presented for further research and consideration. Specifically, constructing a quaternary GCA pair in five or six dimensions, or a octonary GCA pair in any dimension remains an unresolved challenge. Moreover, the feasibility of a quaternary GCA pair in dimensions three or above, other than 4 and converting a octonary GCA to a non-duplicate quaternary GCA in any dimension also await a definitive answer. Consequently, this study hopes to stimulate fresh ideas and motivate researchers to participate in this thought-provoking field of science. Researchers explored the influence of substitutional dopants on the spin exchange interaction with interstitial hydrogen in a silicon crystal lattice.  By examining the high symmetry sites around interstitial hydrogen and calculating the energy differences of the spin triplet and doublet states with and without the presence of the dopants, they found a significant exchange interaction when the dopants are placed nearby.  The largest exchange interaction occurred when the dopants are positioned at the nearest neighbor site to interstitial hydrogen, and it depended on the dopant's spin orientation.  A notable increase in the exchange interaction was seen with group IV and XIII dopants, whereas group XV and XVI dopants led to a reduced exchange interaction due to the localization of electrons on the dopants.  The study suggests that exchange interaction mediated by a silicon host could be an effective means of controlling the behavior of hydrogen in silicon.  Furthermore, it highlighted the possibility of achieving a deliberate placement of hydrogen in the silicon lattice by utilizing exchange interaction with dopants as a guiding force.  This concept may have implications for the development of silicon-based quantum devices.  In addition, the study found that exchange interaction with dopants could be an efficient means of detecting the presence of interstitial hydrogen in silicon.  This detection method may provide valuable insights for the understanding of hydrogen-related phenomena in silicon.  The research also delved into the comparison of theoretical calculations with experimental data obtained through NMR of hydrogen in silicon, and it highlighted the complexity associated with accurately positioning hydrogen atoms within the silicon lattice.  Finally, the study concluded that a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental techniques such as NMR, combined with the development of new placement techniques, will be crucial for achieving a deliberate placement of hydrogen in the silicon lattice.  This outcome may pave the way for innovative quantum technologies based on hydrogen in silicon.  More broadly, this study highlighted the necessity of developing computational tools that can efficiently handle large systems consisting of multiple hundreds of atoms and various types of defects within them.  Until such methods are devised, researchers will continue to rely heavily on empirical modeling techniques such as the one used in this study.  It is worth noting that the development of new first-principles Monte Carlo methods, which can simulate complex systems consisting of multiple hundreds of atoms, may require the integration of multiple theoretical approaches including the one presented in this study.  These new methods will not only enable the accurate placement of hydrogen in silicon but also expand our understanding of various other systems in the materials science of semiconductors. In domains like process discovery and system identification, where data evolves over time and is often partial and noisy, learning about an unfamiliar system can be approached through probabilistic inference. A key aspect of this domain involves establishing the underlying structure of a new system instance using time series data, a problem previously addressed by assuming access to all system variables. A recent study demonstrated an alternative method without this assumption, but it came with significant computational costs. In this work, we build upon this achievement by developing a more efficient algorithm and demonstrating its effectiveness with synthetic and real-world data across various system scenarios. Additionally, the proposed method is applicable to a broader range of systems characterized by slow variable dynamics. A notable feature of our algorithm allows for real-time adaptation in systems with changing structures. A publicly accessible implementation is available online. Overall, our findings represent a crucial advancement in flexible process discovery, enabling learning about changing systems and opening up new possibilities for real-time applications. Moreover, this progress is making process discovery a more suitable framework for understanding complex natural systems that evolve gradually.

This paper investigates the interplay between graded polynomial rings and the configuration spaces of a manifold, providing a combinatorial framework for understanding partitions in stable homotopy theory. By examining the properties of these graded polynomial rings, we establish connections to the symplectic and orthogonal groups, particularly focusing on the configuration spaces of these manifolds. Our analysis reveals that the graded polynomial rings $R(\lambda)$, derived from the symplectic group, have combinatorial interpretations linked to partitions $\lambda$. Our method prioritizes astrobot movements that minimize travel time while maximizing the number of observed targets. We tested this approach using a simulation-based framework and found that it produces high-quality solutions that outperform traditional single-objective methods. Furthermore, our method successfully prevented collisions with astrobots and celestial bodies, and we were able to scale it to large target populations. Our code is now openly available for astrobot trajectory optimization through planetary field spectroscopy. Additionally, modifications were made to the graph and function data structures as well as the array operator to fully take advantage of BigArray's features. As a result, existing array-based graph programs required revision, however, new features such as increased scalability and support for in-memory graph sizes over 1TB were introduced. Furthermore, GP 2 now includes a variable-size BigArray-based node representation, enabling it to process extremely large graphs with over 1 billion nodes and with memory usage below 100GB, with dependent jobs also fully supported. Various applications were developed utilizing the new framework, including two stream processing applications, a recursive query application, and an extrinsic asteroid orbit analysis application. All of these applications along with their data sets are publicly accessible on the GP 2 cloud for testing and development purposes. The GP 2 cloud can be accessed via the NASA's HPCC cloud portal. A unified deep learning framework is introduced by combining regularized deep canonical correlation analysis (DCCA) for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction.  The proposed method, S2N-UDAF, introduces a regularized canonical correlation analysis for supervised learning by linking two cross-domain tasks. Recent studies have shown that utilizing pre-trained models on knowledge graph triples allows for significant advancements in question-answering tasks, with some models even achieving comparable performance to those pre-trained on vast amounts of text. However, knowledge graphs are often incomplete and unreliable, which raises concerns about the effectiveness of this approach. It is unclear whether models pre-trained on factual knowledge graph triples can excel in comparison to those trained on extensive text-based data for question-answering tasks. This study contrasts the performance of models pre-trained on knowledge graph triples with those trained on vast amounts of text across three question-answering tasks, with both single-sentence and paragraph-based contexts being evaluated. Our results demonstrate that models pre-trained on knowledge graph triples perform variably, sometimes outperforming and sometimes being outperformed by their text-trained counterparts, with performance being particularly sensitive to the quality of the knowledge graphs used. Additionally, we found that using high-quality knowledge graph triples can lead to models that perform well above the baseline, but may still struggle with entities that have limited or no coverage in these graphs. This suggests that while models pre-trained on knowledge graph triples hold promise, they require more reliable and comprehensive knowledge graphs to maximize their effectiveness, with potential remedies including the incorporation of unsupervised methods for correcting and completing these graphs. As a byproduct of this research, we found that utilizing pre-trained models on knowledge graph triples allows for significant reductions in required training data, with some models achieving comparable performance to their text-trained counterparts after being trained on as little as 128 examples per entity. This has significant implications for data-efficient training on question-answering tasks. Recent advancements in computer vision have enabled efficient image capture and processing for panoramic scene reconstruction. Unlike traditional methods relying on optical cameras, IMUs offer a more compact and lighter alternative for real-time image capture. However, existing research primarily focuses on accurate IMU-based image capture without considering the inherent benefits of using this technology. In our work, we explore using IMUs to capture images that are more suitable for panoramic stitching. Specifically, we utilize the orientation information from on-board IMUs to guide the capture process in real-time. This allows us to selectively retain or discard images based on their perceived usefulness in the stitching process. Our approach leverages a graph-based algorithm to evaluate and rank the quality of each image for optimal selection. Our results show that our proposed method not only reduces the number of images required but also yields superior stitching outcomes compared to traditional capture techniques. Moreover, our approach offers greater flexibility and efficiency in real-time image capture. This has significant implications for various panoramic scene reconstruction applications, including remote surveillance, virtual tourism, and urban planning. Our code is openly available on the GitHub platform.

This paper investigates the relationship between Weyl group cosets and degenerate Eisenstein series for the general linear group $GL_2(F)$, where $F$ is a non-Archimedean local field. By establishing an explicit connection between the absolute values of Weyl group cosets and the magnitudes of degenerate Eisenstein series at their critical point, we derive new results on the distribution of these cosets and, as a consequence, gain insight into the behavior of certain L-functions. Specifically, we show that the normalized L-function $L(s,\chi)$ exhibits subconvexity for $s$ near $1/2$. This result extends a earlier finding by Diaconu and Kumaresan. Moreover, we examine the relationship between Weyl group cosets and certain Dirichlet L-series, and demonstrate nontrivial cancellations within these series. Finally, we outline a broader framework involving the interplay between Weyl group cosets, degenerate Eisenstein series, and Hecke algebras. This framework may be employed to investigate the geometry of Weyl group orbits and the distribution of geometric objects associated with representations of the general linear group. Multiple complex pathways are involved in Parkinson's Disease, making both its diagnosis and treatment extremely challenging. Researchers are using computational models to better comprehend the disease's mechanics and devise effective treatment strategies. One approach involves building multi-faceted models that capture the interactions between Parkinson's dopamine dynamics, motor function, and cognitive processes. These models enable researchers to simulate various Parkinson's Disease scenarios and assess the therapeutic outcomes of different treatments in a consistent and reproducible way. Unfortunately, these models are generally bespoke and not easily adaptable for other applications due to their complex nature. In our study, we introduce a general framework that represents Parkinson's Disease dynamics using a network of coupled oscillators and consider it an ideal candidate for implementing neurostimulation therapies such as deep brain stimulation. Our network includes a group of neurons with distinct frequency bands that interact with one another and an external influence. We have developed a numerical tool that quickly evaluates the impact of changing network parameters such as the number of neurons, frequency band widths, and stimulation frequencies on the disease's mechanics and response to treatment. This framework can be used in conjunction with optimisation algorithms to find the most effective treatment for particular Parkinson's Disease scenarios. We have demonstrated the capabilities of our approach by applying it to a hypothetical patient with delayed cortical dopamine release and varied brain anatomy. The results show that our network can produce different movement and cognitive disorders associated with distinct frequency patterns and that DBS can be an effective treatment by eliminating abnormal oscillations and restoring natural movement frequencies. Moreover, we have found that our network can be an efficient tool for evaluating various DBS delivery methods such as target location, stimulation intensity and frequency. Ultimately, this research offers a promising foundation for further development of computational models of Parkinson's Disease and could contribute to the discovery of innovative and targeted treatments. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ihmc-robotics/pd-network. The project also includes a user-friendly GUI that allows users to adjust and simulate their own Parkinson's Disease scenarios. In the future, we plan to expand our research by incorporating more of the more than 300 known Parkinson's Disease risk factors into our model. This will involve integrating additional biological processes and potentially incorporating additional data sources such as genetic and life history information. Despite its limitations, our simple Parkinson's Disease model has already shown that computational models can be an effective way to evaluate complex neurodegenerative disease dynamics and guide the development of innovative and targeted treatments. Analysts have explored ways to differentiate between the two dark sectors by analyzing the growth of perturbations and the expansion of the cosmos. They discovered that rare, exceptionally proportional turn-around radii in galaxy clusters could serve as a distinctive indicator. The success of data-driven dialogue systems heavily relies on their ability to generalize beyond training data. While pre-trained models like BERT have improved performance in various tasks, their ability to adapt to new roles or tasks from a single conversation has not been extensively explored. To evaluate the ability of a dialogue system to adapt to new roles and tasks from a single conversation, we propose a method that incorporates role specifications and task instructions. We also introduce a new framework called Adapting Dialogue Systems from Scratch (AD4S), which enables the system to adapt to new roles and tasks from a single conversation. AD4S is evaluated in a controlled setting where the system must simultaneously adapt to new roles and tasks during a single conversation. We found that admissible role and task specifications significantly improve performance and found the optimal way to provide these specifications for best results. Furthermore, we discovered that incorporating context from the first half of the conversation into the system's decision-making process leads to the best outcome. Immersive videos offer an engaging, first-person perspective but pose a challenge: predicting where the viewer's attention will focus. Recent research leverages additional information, such as video subtitles, to improve accuracy, but it assumes that subtitles are available for the entire video duration. However, in real-world scenarios, subtitles might be missing for certain segments, particularly difficult ones. In this study, we investigate a more practical scenario where subtitles are present for just a part of the video. Our approach involves training two separate models: one that can make predictions based on the available subtitles, and another that can leverage the remaining unannotated video segments. Our results show that our multi-model approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art models that rely on annotated segments only. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that our approach is robust in handling varying amounts of annotated video, and it provides valuable insights into the video segments that are most crucial for accurate viewport prediction. Our code and data are openly available for replication and future improvement. In the long term, our approach may contribute to more effective use of video subtitles for user attention purposes. This study specifically targets the task of viewport prediction in virtual reality, but its concepts are applicable to other attention-related tasks across different interaction modalities. The goal of black-box knowledge distillation is to facilitate knowledge transfer between a trained base model and a less accurate target model, with the target model potentially being the base model's counterpart in a real-world deployment setting. A novel framework, called decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, has been proposed, where the target model's class decisions are utilized to obtain the base model's posterior probabilities. This approach has been shown to effectively enhance the target model's performance, especially when the two models cannot be directly connected. Although DB33 has been applied successfully to various image classification tasks, the underlying relationship between the two models remains poorly understood. This study investigates the theoretical connection between DB33 and traditional knowledge distillation, with a focus on the case where the target model's decision function can be inverted. A key finding reveals that DB33 is equivalent to a form of label clean noise knowledge distillation, providing valuable insights that can inform the design of new DB33 methods. To further explore the case where the target model's decision function cannot be inverted, this study proposes a new framework, called pseudo-posterior knowledge distillation, where the target model's decision boundary is analyzed to estimate its posterior probabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed pseudo-posterior knowledge distillation outperforms existing DB33 methods on various image classification tasks. However, DB333 may not consistently outperform traditional knowledge distillation across all scenarios, highlighting the need for more robust and universal DB333 methods. 

One potential future direction for DB333 is to investigate other methods of utilizing the target model's decision data, such as decision confidence for knowledge distillation. Moreover, DB333 is an attractive technique for cross-domain knowledge distillation, facilitating the transfer of knowledge between models with different input domains.
