The Strong Geodetic Recognition problem has been proposed, which involves identifying in a graph G whether a specific vertex subset S contains a strong geodetic set. A strong geodetic set within a graph G is defined as a vertex subset S, for which there exists an associated family of geodesics, covering all graph vertices, with no geodesic intersecting more than one member of S. The Strong Geodetic Recognition problem is classified as NP-complete for general graph inputs and becomes NP-complete even for bipartite graphs or distance-2-cubic graphs. However, the problem exhibits tractability on specific graph types, including trees and planar graphs, with an algorithmic time complexity of O(n^2). An experimental study has been conducted using various natural graph instances to evaluate the effectiveness of two proposed algorithms against human-made strong geodetic sets. The results show one of the tested algorithms consistently outperforms the other across all tested datasets in terms of solution accuracy. No significant difference was observed in the performance of the two algorithms against increasing graph sizes. A notable feature of this research is the public dissemination of strong geodetic set instances for frequently used benchmark graphs. This data is available online to facilitate future comparisons and evaluations of strong geodetic set-related research. An initial analysis has been performed using extensively studied vertex cover and dominating set problems in comparison to strong geodetic sets. Additional investigation has been undertaken to establish a potential link between strong geodetic sets and recently introduced graph measures, specifically the minimum strong geodetic index. No significant correlation was found between the strong geodetic index and graph size or connectivity level. A new parameter-based problem, strong geodetic recognition, has been defined and its applicability to various parameterized complexity classes has been explored. Even with the advancement of cutting-edge algorithms in imitation learning, there remains a significant issue of high sample efficiency. The majority of existing algorithms suffer from poor sample efficiency due to their high data demands. To tackle this problem, we develop TRAIL, a new algorithm that learns from only a limited number of supporter samples. Unlike previous algorithms which rely on expected policy loss per step, we introduce a distinction between on-policy and off-policy learning based on the variance of the sample loss. Experimenting with TRAIL on complex games showed significant improvements in sample efficiency, achieving comparable performance with much fewer supporter samples. Furthermore, TRAIL successfully learned from only a limited number of trials in the complex game "cheeger house", and its sample efficiency allowed it to learn from humans with various policies. The source code for TRAIL is now available on the gym-imitation website.

Co-learning with peers from mixed groups is a common occurrence in life, where individuals can also learn from those who are less experienced. Expert guidance, on the other hand, is often confined to selective feedback from a smaller group of highly skilled professionals with profound knowledge. Our research, Co-Imitation Learning, focuses on leveraging peer learning to enhance expertise guidance, particularly in scenarios where only a limited number of high-quality demonstrations are available for complex tasks. It utilizes a dual network model to combine the benefits of peer and expert feedback, with separate optimization objectives to ensure consistency. It produces more plausible imitations from peers and more accurate imitations from experts, with robust loss functions that can be trained via simple alternative methods. Our experiments show significant improvements over baseline methods, proving that Co-Imitation Learning can effectively supplement limited expert guidance with peer learning for faster expertise acquisition. Moreover, our analysis of cross-task transfer reveals that pre-training on one task facilitates expert learning for similar tasks, along with a finding that high-quality peer imitations can aid in learning from few expert demonstrations for new tasks. Ultimately, Co-Imitation Learning has the potential to tackle the challenges posed by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations in real-world reinforcement learning scenarios. The code for this project can be found at https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/Co-Imitation-Learning.

A sequential decoder's error probability can be analyzed using the polarized cutoff rate and a specific bias value, which is the expected rate of a sequence under the polarized distribution. The impact of choosing a particular bias value, specifically one that reflects the rate at which polarized sequences tend towards the maximum or minimum rate, is examined in this research. Findings indicate that if the bias is set to the expected rate of a sequence under the polarized distribution formed by mixing two sequences with significantly different rates, the decoder's error probability remains relatively low, especially when the distance between the two rates is substantial. However, if the two sequences have similar rates, the decoder may struggle with errors even with an infinitely large code length. This phenomenon is demonstrated mathematically using the density evolution method and the relaxation technique. Despite the success of sequence-to-sequence frameworks in machine translation, reinforcement learning still faces difficulties. It has been discovered that conventional action spaces for word generation contain numerous suboptimal actions, hindering the training process. To address this issue, this study proposes a method to refine action spaces based on action values, which yields significant improvements in translation accuracy, particularly when combined with value models. Our experimental findings, supported by thorough analyses, demonstrate notable enhancements in performance on both small-scale and large-scale machine translation tasks, delivering the best results to date on the WMT'14 English-to-German translation task. Moreover, this action-space refinement technique leads to improved performance when applied to low-resource setting domain adaptation, showcasing its versatility and practical value. Accurate end-effector pose estimation is crucial in robot-assisted systems, particularly those involving minimally invasive surgery. A key factor that influences this process is the selection of sensing technologies, which can be optical, acoustical, or a combination of both, depending on the application. In this research, we investigate the use of a single-depth camera to enhance the robustness of end-effector pose estimation through the calibration process. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on two cameras for cross-validation, we propose a method that utilizes the depth camera's self-calibration capability to estimate end-effector poses. This approach leverages the relationship between projection matrices and the fundamental matrix formed during the calibration process. A robust estimation algorithm is implemented to handle any discrepancies or ambiguities that may arise. Experimental results show that our method's accuracy improves when using a single-depth camera for calibration and that it can determine the end-effector pose even when the camera is moved a certain distance away from the calibrated position. Notably, our method outperforms a method that uses correlation-based image matching when the camera is moved a short distance. However, further research is needed to extend this work to systems that involve moving the camera over longer distances. A potential application of this research is robot-assisted procedures that require minimal calibration, such as placing adhesives or sutures. Additionally, this method may be useful in cases where other sensing technologies are not feasible or would compromise the procedure's safety. Finally, this work suggests that a single-depth camera can enhance the robustness of end-effector pose estimation when the camera is moved a certain distance away from the calibrated position, which has implications for the design of end-effector systems that incorporate cameras for autonomous pose estimation. This research is relevant to any robot-assisted system that relies on end-effector pose estimation, including medical procedures, manufacturing, and consumer robotics. The corresponding code for this research can be found at https://github.com/eduardorcs/end-effector-robust-estimation. The benefits of using a single-depth camera in end-effector pose estimation lead to lower costs, increased portability, and more compact design. Despite the advantages of this research, further work is needed to address challenges that arise when the camera is moved over longer distances. Potential avenues for extension include developing more robust algorithms and exploring additional sensing technologies, such as acoustical sensors, for end-effector pose estimation. Ultimately, this research has the potential to enhance the safety and efficiency of robot-assisted procedures by minimizing the need for extensive calibration

The Web's impact on the rise of political polarization has led researchers to examine online platforms that facilitate browsing and how they influence people's ideological views. Uncovering the effects of Google's search results, social media feeds, and news websites requires access to users' browsing history and online account data. In contrast, studying offline elections provides valuable insights that are unaffected by online factors, offering a suitable alternative for exploring how browsing habits contribute to political polarization. To analyze voters' shifting affiliations, we propose a mathematical approach using optimal transportation and democracy theory. By applying this method to real-world data from multiple U.S. elections, we reveal how browsing habits influence political polarization beyond online factors and what effects party platform shifts have on voters' views. Furthermore, our approach enables us to identify how different groups are affected by changes in election dynamics. By doing so, we emphasize the importance of considering online factors in the study of political polarization and suggest that our methodological framework can be applied to various electoral systems. Additionally, we highlight that our research raises pressing questions about the influence of search engines, social media, and online platforms on democratic elections and urges further investigation into their effects. In doing so, we also introduce a new metric that measures extremaphoric distances to better capture extreme shifts in voters' views. Lastly, we demonstrate the applicability of our approach to other datasets that exhibit similar trends. In conclusion, our study offers a novel framework for examining political polarization and highlights the significance of considering online factors in democratic elections. Moreover, we anticipate that our research will spark further inquiry into the influence of online platforms on democratic elections, as well as the effects of these platforms on society as a whole. In the process, we also introduce a new metric for measuring extreme shifts in voter views, and we believe this has the potential to be useful in a broader context. Ultimately, this study is just the beginning of a larger exploration into the interplay between politics and technology, and we look forward to continuing this investigation in the future. In fact, we are already examining how online platforms contribute to the rise of political polarization in democratic elections, and we aim to publish additional findings as part of a broader study. In this paper, we are focusing specifically on offline elections, and we hope that our approach will be particularly useful in this context. However, we also believe that our methodological framework has the potential to be applied to online platforms, such as Google's search results, social media feeds, and online account data, and we plan to explore this further in the future. The Thompson group V was initially defined through its action on oriented graphs from a specific class, and researchers have previously shown that V's word problem is equivalent to a deterministic context-free language. In this work, we establish that V's word problem is also equivalent to a context-free language that is not regular. This result connects to a broader conjecture regarding the finite group syndrome of V's word problem, and it is interesting to note that both V's word problem and its group, when combined with the free group on two generators, result in a group with a finite group syndrome. This discovery about the word problem of V adds to the current understanding of this group and its properties. Additionally, this research is linked to recent studies of context-free languages and their connection to group theory.

An open quantum system can exchange information with its environment, contradicting the principle of causality. This phenomenon of bidirectional information flow can be understood through the concept of causal correlations. By applying a transformation based on the environment's state, we successfully achieved reverse information transfer between the system and environment. Furthermore, this process is demonstrated using a quantum system composed of two modes and an environment represented by a continuous variable system. We show that the mutual information between the system and environment initially increases from zero, indicating a successful transfer of information. Subsequently, we observe an increase in the entropy of the environment due to its interaction with the system. Notably, we found that the time-evolved state of the environment allows for the recovery of the system's state with high accuracy, thereby achieving reverse information transfer. Finally, we relate our findings to previous work involving a system composed of two modes and an environment represented by a discrete variable system. We compare the time-evolved state of the environment and system in this scenario, revealing an imperfect reverse information transfer. Moreover, we discuss how increasing the dimension of the system enhances the efficiency of reverse information transfer. Lastly, we propose that our approach can serve as a foundation for developing quantum heat engines and batteries. This could leverage the system's ability to store energy from the environment and utilize it to generate work during a disentanglement process. This concept is particularly relevant given the recent success of continuous-variable quantum information processing technologies. In fact, experiments have already demonstrated the feasibility of reversing information transfer between a system and environment in the context of non-equilibrium states. This has been achieved through the application of environmental correlations based on the system's state, thereby enabling the system to behave as an operator that modifies the environment's state. We've investigated an anomalous U(1)' extension of the standard model, a model where the Anomalous U(1)' Magnetic Screening Mass term breaks the Peccei-Quinn symmetry, to understand its capacity to solve the strong CP problem and stabilize the electroweak vacuum. Through a thorough scan of parameter space, constrained by the magnetic moment discrepancy and the absence of lepton flavor violation below the experimental detection limit, we found that model predicts an unusually small value for the theta angle, thus successfully addressing the strong CP problem. Moreover, we found that most of this model's parameter space is located in the weak scale stability region of the standard model, and that this occurs in a way that is correlated with the Anomalous U(1)' photon coupling. Consequently, we expect this model to predict a value for the Anomalous U(1)' photon coupling that is significantly smaller than the current bounds, and thus, this model provides a novel explanation for the stability of the electroweak vacuum without relying on an extremely light scalar particle. Lastly, we found that this model's capacity to solve the strong CP problem is largely independent of its capacity to stabilize the electroweak vacuum. A new way to structure Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) called Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs) has been proposed to improve their capability in image segmentation. This method creates an additional network that operates in parallel to the primary network and produces a complementary output, which is then combined with the original output to generate the final result. Studies have shown that EG-CNNs possess an equivalent number of parameters to standard CNNs, while providing superior performance. Nonetheless, one major limitation of EG-CNNs is their difficulty in learning from raw data images due to the absence of an explicit self-learned feature extraction step. To overcome this, we propose incorporating Self-Supervised Pre-training (SSP) for the egated and base components alike. Our experiments across five diverse image segmentation datasets demonstrate the substantial benefits of SSP, with overall improvements ranging from 5.6% to 14.8% in terms of Dice Score. Moreover, SSP is applicable across various EG-CNNs models and our results show consistent performance gains without utilizing any extra labels during the pre-training process. Our code has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. 

Keywords: Edge Gated CNNs, Self-Supervised Pre-training, Image Segmentation, Deep Neural Networks.

We investigate the applicability of the $e$-positivity conjecture of Stanley to a specific subset of CSF, namely those associated with Dyck paths of size $n$, and confirm the conjecture for this subset. Additionally, we establish a connection between the $e$-positivity of these chromatic symmetric functions and the Eulerian poset of Dyck paths of a given size, and a specific subposet of the Eulerian poset of Dyck paths, characterized by paths that do not pass above the diagonal. This subposet is shown to be isomorphic to a subset of the poset of Dyck paths of a given size, and this subposet's rank generating function is derived as $E(u,v) \cdot (1-E(u,v))^2$, where $E(u,v)$ is the generating function for the Eulerian poset of Dyck paths. Lastly, we determine that the $e$-positivity of a comprehensive set of monomials related to CSF, namely those derived from Dyck paths, follows directly from this connection. The idea of hindsight summarization can be used to reduce attended prediction error in learning systems. This concept involves condensing a sequence of predictions and their corresponding errors into a more manageable summary, allowing the system to refocus its attention and improve future performance. While research exists on predicting summarization targets and the structure of these summaries, there is currently a lack of models capable of generating accurate hindsight summaries. To address this, we propose a novel framework that combines neural memory networks with an order-agnostic attention mechanism, enabling our model to generate summaries that not only accurately reflect the underlying data distribution but also facilitate effective reFocus. This is achieved by exploring different evaluation metrics that prioritize semantic matching and a simplicity-based consistency constraint. Our results demonstrate substantial advancements in hindsight summarization performance, surpassing baseline models and showcasing superior robustness across various sequence lengths and prediction errors. Furthermore, our model's ability to generate precise summaries is confirmed by both internal and external assessments. The code for our work can be found at https://github.com/hjdwzh/hssum. Overall, our research provides both a comprehensive study on hindsight summarization and a comprehensive dataset, thereby paving the way for related tasks such as general summarization. Moreover, our findings and approaches may also contribute to mitigating attended prediction error in learning systems. The success of all-data performance by deep learning models in medical image analysis relies on them generalizing across varied patient populations, imaging modalities, and techniques. Despite being hidden, implicit biases in datasets can hinder generalization, posing a critical problem for the field. We investigated the presence of biases in six publicly available datasets for the analysis of abdominal imaging and developed a framework to measure them. Our experiments demonstrated that pre-trained models overfit to hidden biases, compromising their ability to accurately identify normal tissue classes on unseen images. Notably, we found that models performed worse when confronted with imaging modalities different from those used to train them, highlighting a notable example of an apparent generalization across datasets. We further discovered that models performed significantly better when confronted with modalities they had been exposed to during training. Our results suggest that models are not just vulnerable to explicit prejudices but also face challenges when confronting differences in data quality, patient physiology, and imaging protocols. We believe that our findings have important implications for the field and stress the need to develop more robust models that perform well in real-world settings. We also propose several potential strategies to mitigate biases in datasets, assess models' performance, and facilitate reproducibility in medical image analysis. Ultimately, achieving generalization across datasets and the diverse data they contain will necessitate a careful balance of theory, methodology, and applications. Our study is the first to systematically investigate biases in publicly available abdominal imaging datasets and provide actionable recommendations for enhancing model performance in this domain. It is our hope that this work will spark a field-wide discussion on the topic and motivate further research in the area. Our study is available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01704. By analyzing the full hysteresis loop for the first time, scientists have uncovered how interactions between spins at the vertices of these triangles affect the shape of the hysteresis loop, and found that it undergoes a discontinuous change as the temperature is raised, and also exhibits two distinct memory patterns depending on the strength of intratriangle interactions. The study reveals that the Ising model on triangle networks exhibits distinct behavior compared to other fundamental graph structures, and provides a framework for understanding hysteresis in these complex systems. Newly designed solar sails with advanced reflective materials like MFSA could achieve significantly higher $\Delta V$ at close ranges to the sun, potentially surpassing values seen at 1 AU. To assess their safety, we simulate $\Delta V$ distributions for these sails when visiting regions frequently accessed by spacecraft, such as inside Earth's orbit and among the asteroid belts. Our calculations account for both optimal and non-optimal flying orientations, along with the effects of solar wind and the gravity of solar system bodies. When orbiting Neptune at 20 AU, we find $\Delta V$ remains minimal at less than 1 m/s. In contrast, when the sail passes through Earth's orbit, $\Delta V$ may reach as high as 70 km/s. However, when visiting solar system bodies within 5 AU of the sun, $\Delta V$ ranges from 13.4 to 41.5 km/s, with distributions that show significant variability. For comparison, classic solar sails with optimal orientation reach $\Delta V$ up to 42.5 km/s at Earth's orbit. While frequently visited regions of the solar system may pose some risks to solar sails, particularly when passing near solar system bodies at the close ranges to the sun, the danger appears manageable with existing safety design features. Moreover, when operated in the solar wind, these sails are unlikely to collide with spacecraft over periods longer than a few weeks. To minimize potential dangers even further, we suggest establishing guidelines for solar sail operations, including design standards and protocols for avoiding debris accumulation. By taking these precautions, we believe solar sails can effectively contribute to deep space exploration. To this end, we propose a framework for conducting thorough analyses of potential dangers in various solar system environments. Ultimately, a collaborative effort between theorists and practitioners is necessary to fully assess and mitigate these risks. The complex nature of the human emotion spectrum renders constructing comprehensive and finely-grained emotion dictionaries a challenging task. While recent studies have achieved notable success in emotion recognition using neural models, the existing methods are largely confined to specific languages and have not achieved a level of adaptability. This limitation becomes even more pronounced when extending the scope to constructing emotion dictionaries from scratch. To overcome these constraints, we introduce a novel multi-lingual emotion recognition framework that leverages an emotion encoding matrix learned through an end-to-end self-supervised procedure. This learned encoding matrix enables the model to recognize emotions not only across multiple languages but also on diverse corpora. By combining the predicted emotion labels with the encoding matrix, a shared latent space is constructed for each word in the vocabulary. This model's capacity to adapt to new languages and data is demonstrated through thorough experiments on the EmoCommons dataset, comprising 10 languages and 5 datasets. The evaluations indicate that our proposed model achieves superior performance and greater adaptability when compared to the baseline models, which are confined to specific languages and corpora. Moreover, the our model's ability to construct an emotion dictionary from scratch is showcased on the recently introduced EmoDict dataset. The adaptability of our model is further validated through an analysis of the learned emotion encoding matrix in the multi-lingual setting. We studied the effects of high-pressure on the crystal structure and phase of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ using synchrotron radiation at high-pressure temperatures from 1.6 GPA and 300 K up to 6.5 GPA and room temperature. Our results indicate that this compound undergos a phase transition at high pressures, with the lattice parameters a, c and volume decreasing more significantly than b, and that the degree of anisotropy increases under high-pressure conditions. A phase transition was confirmed through the use of the P-CPMAS $^{35}$S NMR technique at room temperature and high pressures, showing a change in the chemical shift of Bi sites I and II. Our data suggest that the phase transition is related to a structural change from the $a$2$_{1}$a' structure to one with a $a$2$_{1}$a' structure similar to that of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15$$:x with x=0.08, which incorporates some Ti atoms into octahedral sites that surround Fe ions. A combination of experimental evidence allowed us to estimate that the phase transition occurs at approximately 4.5 GPa at room temperature. Our study provides the first direct evidence of a phase transition in Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15$ through the use of X-ray diffraction at high pressures and temperatures, and also confirms previous indications of a phase transition through the use of NMR at room temperature and high pressures. A comparison with other bismuth ferrite compounds is also included.}

The error bound comparison is a significant method for analyzing the performance of algorithms, especially those involved in finding shortest paths on high-dimensional manifolds. However, existing error bound analysis techniques are typically developed with global considerations in mind, which can result in overly conservative estimates when only localized performance is of interest. This paper addresses this limitation by introducing a method for localized error bound comparison in the context of smooth manifolds and Lipschitz-continuous metrics. We demonstrate the practical applications of this method by applying it to a specific problem of finding discrete paths in $\left( \mathbb{R}^d, \ell_2^d \right)$, and show that it yields more accurate error bounds than global comparison methods. Notably, this method can provide precise error bounds for local regions where the Hessian matrix has a non-zero determinant. We also establish a connection between our method and the second-order sufficient conditions for optimality, and discuss its implications on the design of algorithms that converge locally but may not guarantee global optimality. Finally, we demonstrate the benefits of this method using an example from the field of medicine, relating to the optimization of dose finding trials. This example highlights the value of our method in evaluating the performance of locally optimized discrete paths, even if those paths may not guarantee global optimality. This method is particularly relevant to the field of optimal transport and related problems, and can be an invaluable tool for analyzing the performance of algorithms in such contexts. We integrate the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed methods for estimating decay rates in heavy meson decays, developing a unified picture that allows for a broader exploration of various factors influencing decay rates. Within this integrated framework, we thoroughly examine and systematically organize previous research, shedding new light on the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert series and its relationships to the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed approach. Furthermore, we employ lattice QCD data to gain insight into the decay constant patterns characteristic of different mesons, and differentiate between heavy mesons that primarily follow a linear or quadratic series in the decay rate expansion. Our analysis particularly focuses on mesons composed of heavy and light quarks, with either the heavy quark being significantly heavier than the light quarks or their masses being relatively balanced. Ultimately, we use our findings to re-evaluate decay rate predictions made by the lattice QCD community. For instance, we discover that the over-predicted percentage for the $K^0_{\ell3}$ decay rate reaches as high as 100%, whereas the $D^0_{\ell3}$ decay rate is instead under-predicted by about 5%. Our study also highlights the importance of distinguishing between these meson series when interpreting lattice QCD data, and suggests that a more precise determination of first-order coefficient values is needed to provide accurate, reliable decay rate predictions. Consequently, we advocate for multiple independent determinations of these coefficients by the lattice community to ensure consistency and trustworthiness of the predictions. Moreover, we identify potential sources of systematic errors in the current lattice QCD approaches, specifically citing the need for improved methods of calculating decay constants and performing systematics evaluations. Ultimately, we anticipate that integrating the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed frameworks will stimulate fresh perspectives and new research within the lattice QCD community on heavy meson decays. Moreover, this integrated framework may also be applicable to other systems featuring a slow time scale, such as baryons or heavy quark systems in motion, and thus has the potential to contribute meaningfully to a deeper understanding of these systems. We are examining an asymmetric SQUID loop consisting of two Josephson junctions with distinct values for $E_J$ and $I_c$, as well as considering the impact of the loop being part of a longer circuit that may induce phase locking between the junctions. Our analysis focuses on the switching current of the loop when an externally applied voltage causes it to transition from a zero-voltage state. Our findings show that if the loop's behavior is governed by a single-emitter model with no phase locking, the switching current can be significantly higher than the critical current of either junction. However, if phase locking is present, it may greatly reduce the switching current, potentially below the value of either $I_c$ depending on the loop's asymmetry. Notably, if the loop is part of a circuit with multiple emitters and no isolated regions, we can determine the switching current without assuming a particular junction is responsible for switching the loop, thus offering a more general understanding of switching in these circuits. Our analysis also reveals that in such a case, the switching current can be greater than either $I_c$ despite the loop's asymmetry. These findings provide a more comprehensive insight into switching in SQUID loops, especially those involving multiple Josephson junctions and loops within complex circuits. These results may have implications for the operation of superconducting quantum circuits, particularly those involving macroscopic quantum loops and multi-junction SQUIDs in phase-qubit applications. To facilitate experimental verification, our theoretical predictions are accompanied by feasible and controllable experimental scenarios for various loop configurations involving two, three, and multi-junction SQUIDs. The flux fraction of tidal features in early-type galaxies rises with mass in a manner that depends on the galaxy's location within the cluster. A previous study discovered that tidal features in the cluster environments of the Virgo and Coma have similar trends of mass dependence, but the result was based on data for which signal-to-noise ratio was less than 5 in more massive galaxies. We performed an analysis of the stellar flux fraction within three degrees centering on the cores of the Coma cluster and the Virgo cluster, using a sample of 695 candidate galaxies with signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10. We distinguished tidal features from the host galaxies by creating reference images for each line of sight, considering factors such as orientation, shape, and brightness. We found that tidal features are more prevalent among more massive galaxies in the core of the Coma cluster, and that their flux fraction follows a similar pattern of mass dependence found in the Virgo cluster, with a notable increase at log(M_*) > 10.7. No significant differences were found when comparing the two clusters, or when considering various galaxy populations within each cluster. However, we did find an increase in tidal features at intermediate masses (9.0 < log(M_*) < 9.5) when looking at the core of the Coma cluster, and a decline in tidal features above log(M_*) = 10.2 in the core of the Virgo cluster. We also discovered a higher incidence of tidal features within three degrees of the core of the Coma cluster when comparing galaxy samples for the core and the surrounding regions of the Coma cluster, and when comparing galaxy samples for the core of the Virgo and Coma clusters. We believe that the increased tidal features in intermediate-mass galaxies in the core of the Coma cluster, and in the core of the Virgo cluster above log(M_*) = 10.2, may be a result of the stripping of satellite galaxies that have merged with more massive galaxies in these regions. We also found evidence of recent galaxy mergers contributing to tidal features in the core of the Virgo cluster, particularly in the mass range 9.0 < log(M_*) < 9.5. We did not find significant differences in the orientation or shape of tidal features when considering various galaxy populations within each cluster, or when comparing galaxy samples for the core and the surrounding regions of the Coma cluster. However, we did find a higher incidence of tidal features with an aspect ratio greater than 0.5

A society's distribution of opportunities essentially determines the chances of success for its members, and this in turn affects the prospects of future generations. While this concept may seem intuitive, measuring opportunity across different populations is a complex task. A potential measure, the Opportunity Index, could provide a more tangible framework for assessment. This index would capture various aspects of opportunity of of upcomng generations through their parents' success rates. Focusing on educational attainment as a key indicator, our research finds that an Opportunity Index indeed reflects the chances of children entering young adulthood with a higher level of education, and that it varies significantly across different demographic groups in the US. Notably, the index appears to be a more direct measure of the socioeconomic status of an individual's birth place, and it also correlates with intergenerational mobility. Furthermore, our research finds that the opportunity of upcomng generations is influenced by the socioeconomic status of their parents in the US. This finding holds true even after controlling for various factors such as parental education, income, and whether or not the parents own their home. This discovery suggests that there are non-tangible aspects of family wealth at play. Our research also finds significant regional variations in opportunity levels, with children born in the South and West having higher chances of success compared to those born in the Northeast and Midwest. Additionally, there are notable demographic variations in opportunity levels, with African-Americans, Hispanics, and Native Americans experiencing lower opportunity levels compared to Whites and Asians. These findings highlight the significance of considering opportunity in discussions of socioeconomic status and highlight the need for more targeted data to better understand the varied experiences of different demographic groups across different locations in the US. This research can also serve as a foundation for further exploration of opportunity levels across different populations in other contexts. In our research, we also introduce a novel concept of intergenerational mobility through opportunity, and we explore the relationship between opportunity levels and individual and family socioeconomic status over time. This work is particularly relevant in the current social discourse where there is growing interest in understanding opportunity levels and their impact on future generations' socioeconomic status. In our research, we are also inspired by recent works that have highlighted significant variations in intergenerational mobility and mobility through opportunity across different demographic groups in the US. In our research, we are agnostic about the underlying mechanisms that drive opportunity levels and we do not attempt to provide a comprehensive explanation for our findings. However, our research does offer potential directions for policymakers who are interested in mitigating adverse opportunity levels and improving the socioeconomic status of certain demographic groups. This research focuses on resolving a critical issue in distributed optimization, where some non-cooperating nodes may convey false information, compromising the efficiency of the algorithm. To address this problem, we propose an adaptable strategy for communication that takes into account the reliability of nodes. This approach involves assigning different levels of trust to nodes based on their past behavior and utilises a robust consensus algorithm to update parameters. We demonstrate that our proposed method converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{k})$, where $k$ represents the number of iterations. This result establishes that our robust framework offers comparable performance to standard methods under benign conditions and outperforms existing solutions in scenarios with malicious activity. Moreover, our approach minimises the level of node cooperation required to achieve optimal results. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our approach through numerical experiments conducted on various instances. Moreover, our approach can be applied to a variety of distributed optimization applications, including spam control on social networks, advertising budget allocation, and signal processing. Our results have been integrated into the CoRaDA knowledge repository at https://www.corada.org/i/Bingol20. Lastly, we outline possible research extensions in the field of robust distributed optimization. The creation and dissemination of deepfakes have outpaced their detection efforts, leading to significant concerns about their harmful potential. Deepfake detection models that excel in specific domains often struggle with others. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a multi-domain deepfake detection network called MDNet, which incorporates cross-stitch connections to facilitate useful feature sharing across domains. By leveraging cross-stitch connections, our network can exchange relevant features between domains without the need for explicit fusion methods. Our experiments demonstrate that MDNet achieves remarkable performance on several public datasets, particularly in scenarios with limited training data. Notably, our evaluation shows that a single-domain baseline model performs worse than many of the recent competing methods on the Celeb-DF dataset when evaluated on the Celeb-DF test set. In contrast, our proposed MDNet model surpasses these results while being trained on just a single dataset. Moreover, we find that MDNet exhibits a notable ability to adapt to new domains with only a limited number of samples from 45 to 450. Ultimately, our results validate the effectiveness of our domain sharing mechanism and suggest that MDNet represents a premier foundation for future deepfake detection research to build upon. Current high-performance LDPC codes exhibit a high degree-degree correlation, which poses challenges for reliable channel estimation. Research into non-trivial degree-degree correlations, or those differing from the Poisson distribution, has been limited by the lack of suitable LDPC ensembles generating easy-to-solve graphs. This study introduces a new class of binary LDPC ensembles with negative degree-degree correlations that can be efficiently constructed using regular graphs and an interleaving technique. Our findings indicate that LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlations lead to an increased erasure probability threshold, which suggests an improved performance in reliable channel estimation. Furthermore, numerical results demonstrate the superior performance of these new codes in both reliable channel estimation and conventional communication scenarios. An increased signal-to-noise ratio threshold of almost 4 dB is achieved for LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlations in reliable channel estimation, which represents a significant improvement over standard LDPC codes. This advancement is attributed to the code's ability to accommodate more erasures, allowing for successful decoding in situations where the received signal contains significant noise. Unlike standard LDPC codes, those with non-trivial degree-degree correlations do not solely rely on the Poisson distribution at sufficiently high density, which implies that these codes possess inherent advantages in reliable channel estimation scenarios. As a result of their negative degree-degree correlations, these codes exhibit an alternative correlation pattern that facilitates successful channel estimation in scenarios where standard codes would fail. This newfound understanding of LDPC codes with non-trivial degree-degree correlations may lead to the development of faster channel estimation techniques that leverage their distinct correlation structure. As a byproduct of this research, an extremely high-density code with a negative degree-degree correlation was constructed, which demonstrates a surprisingly low erasure probability in comparison to standard high-density codes. This code's exceptional performance in reliable channel estimation scenarios, coupled with its ability to successfully decode messages even when subjected to high noise levels, has significant implications for the fundamental limits of reliable channel estimation. As a result of this research, new open questions have arisen in the field of coding theory, particularly regarding the coding gap in reliable channel estimation and the optimal code ensemble with negative degree-degree correlations. This research also raises the possibility of applying the constructed code ensembles in practical communication scenarios, which could leverage the advantages of these codes through techniques such as coding order and channel selection. As a numerical example, we demonstrate the coding gap of a specific code ensemble with negative degree-degree correlations, which achieves a 2.5 dB gain over standard LDPC codes in reliable channel estimation scenarios. In 2007, a proposed quantum key distribution (QKD) system using vacuum and weak decoy states was found to be insecure if an eavesdropper could perform a specific attack undetected - one that involves adding phase noise to the weak decoy state. Surprisingly, this attack has an remarkably high success rate yet leaves the system's performance appear normal. Notably, if the generator uses a low-quality source for the weak decoy state, an eavesdropper can launch this attack without being detected, as it falls within the system's expected error rate for the weak decoy state. This attack results in the eavesdropper acquiring user's baseline key data efficiency of approximately $10^{-11}$, which is remarkably high. To mitigate this attack, we propose two practical improvements for the QKD system: (1) calculating the phase error rate of the weak decoy state, which allows for a more precise bound on the key generation rate, or (2) using a pseudo-random number generator with high quality to generate the weak decoy state, which effectively prevents the attack by increasing the eavesdropper's detection probability. Both improvements are highly effective in preventing the attack, resulting in highly secure key generation with minimal efficiency loss. In experiments using a source with low and high quality, we successfully demonstrate these attack prevention methods. In the case where the source has high quality, we found the system's performance to be optimal. When the source has low quality, we found that the proposed attack prevention methods result in very small efficiency loss of less than 10% when compared to the optimal performance. Notably, both improved methods can be implemented with existing QKD systems using a vacuum and weak decoy state without the need for new equipment, as the change involves a software update alone. In addition to preventing this specific attack, our proposed methods can be viewed as an important first step in designing robust countermeasures against other potential attacks on QKD systems. Ultimately, our study underlines the significance of taking into consideration the properties of the source used in QKD systems and highlights the value of ongoing research aimed at developing a wide range of robust and versatile QKD systems. In particular, systems that can effectively handle various source characteristics, including different phases and pulsed modes, are particularly desirable. The current study employs pressure gradient measurements from a previous investigation by Hjertaas (2005) to examine the effect of pressure on the development of the nitrogen jet and the resulting shear layer interaction with the surface. The initial and fully developed phases of the jet were compared to understand how pressure influences the rate of transition. The results show that increasing pressure slows down the transition process, causing the jet to retain its initial characteristics for a longer period. The relationship between pressure and the dimensionless time it takes for the jet to reach its fully developed state was found to be directly proportional. Additionally, the location of maximum shear stress and the corresponding Reynolds number were found to remain relatively constant across different pressure conditions, both in the initial and fully developed phases. However, it was observed that with increased pressure, the maximum shear stress occurs earlier, both in the initial and fully developed states, and that the Reynolds number at which the maximum shear stress is located remains unchanged at approximately 1000. The findings of this study provide new data for validation of numerical models used in the space industry. The results from a turbulent nitrogen jet at a high pressure point (barobaric to the main fuel) are missing from the current literature, making this study the first of its kind to examine a high-pressure jet with conditions similar to those found in rocket engines during ground testing. The data analyzed in this study can be used to validate one-dimensional and full-domain numerical models used to simulate the performance of full-scale engines during ground firing tests. Ultimately, ongoing and upcoming infrared surveys, along with improved analysis techniques, may ultimately shed light on the planetesimal formation process and help identify the presence of planetesimals in our galaxy. In the decentralized learning setting, the convergence rate of decentralized stochastic gradient descent (DR-DSGD) is influenced by the number of devices and iterations. We derive an explicit convergence analysis for DR-DSGD with a varying number of devices, and find that the method achieves a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{NT})$ after $T$ iterations for a strong convex and smooth objective function. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the convergence rate is affected by the number of devices, and that adding more devices can accelerate convergence until a certain point. Building upon this analysis, we develop a new algorithm called DR-DSGD with adaptive communication, which dynamically adjusts the communication frequency among devices based on the magnitude of the local gradients. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms standard DR-DSGD in terms of convergence rate, particularly with an increasing number of devices. Additionally, the adaptive communication method results in significant reductions in communication cost, achieving a return on investment of $2-4$ in scenarios with a large number of devices. Moreover, the new algorithm exhibits robustness in scenarios with slow devices and large data sets. The code for the proposed algorithm and associated experiments is available open-source.

Researchers have long been intrigued by the sudden shift in the behavior of close-packed disks under increasing pressure, with many attempting to observe and study this transition since the 1950s. Despite initial skepticism that such a significant change could occur, experts now consider the event so remarkable that it must be a critical phenomenon, with the exact mechanism still to be determined. To better understand it, scientists believe it may be a key to revealing new principles governing the behavior of continuous systems at their limits. To further explore this idea, researchers have been experimenting with simplified systems consisting of disks that can be adjusted to mimic various pressures, with the goal of identifying any underlying patterns or relationships that could provide clues to the nature of the phase transition. In this work, we focus specifically on a method involving the direct observation of individual disk collisions, with the aim of identifying any recurring patterns of motion that could be indicative of the transition. By using a specialized high-speed camera to record the collisions in slow motion and analyzing the data in detail, we have discovered a notable feature - a remarkable consistency in the duration of collisions. Interestingly, this level of precision has only been achieved in recent years, with the advancement of high-speed imaging allowing for the capture of sequences of collisions with unprecedented detail. Notably, our study reveals that even when the pressure is increased to the point where the transition occurs, there is virtually no difference in the distribution of collision times - a finding that initially seemed counterintuitive. However, upon closer examination, we found that the reason for this lack of distinction lies not in the duration of collisions themselves, but rather in the time it takes for the disks to travel from one collision to the next. When we removed this "travel time" from our analysis, we found that the distribution of collision times does indeed change significantly - a discovery that provides valuable new insights into the dynamics of the system and may have important implications for our understanding of the transition. Finally, we also discovered a fascinating relationship between the velocity of the disks and the energy released during collisions, with the effect becoming more pronounced as the transition approaches. This observation opens up a range of questions for further exploration, with potential connections to ideas such as temperature and friction. While our study offers only a initial foray into this complex and intriguing topic, we believe it presents a valuable new perspective that is sure to spark further research and debate. Through our work, we hope to contribute to a deeper understanding of the shift in behavior among close-packed disks and pave the way for a more comprehensive study of this remarkable phenomenon. Up

Nuclear parton distribution functions influence jet characteristics, which can be studied using perturbative jet functions in EFT. Our research focuses on explaining jet formation within EFT, specifically addressing how nuclear PDFs impact jet structure in nuclei through in-medium parton jet functions. We represent in-medium parton jet functions with lattice-derived correlations of parton and jet operators, and demonstrate how nuclear PDFs are extracted from data using evolution equations for parton distribution functions, incorporating the impact of in-medium parton jet functions at a temperature transition in QCD. The transition from in-medium parton jet functions to in-medium parton distributions is facilitated by an evolution equation for in-medium parton distributions from nuclei at a temperature to those at a temperature below the deconfinement one. The research is extended to unmixed jet functions using factorization properties of in-medium parton jet functions. The influence of nuclear interactions on jet formation is probed using an auxiliary problem of unmixed jet functions in vacuum at a finite temperature, represented by an evolution equation for in-medium parton jet functions from quarks and gluons at a temperature below the deconfinement one. The properties of nuclear parton distributions are expected to influence jet evolution in nuclear collisions at various energy scales. The research is relevant to the study of jet formation in relativistic nuclear collisions at the LHC, especially in experiments involving precision jet studies. The theoretical framework can also be applied to investigate observable jet properties, such as differential jet spectra, jet shape, and differential differential distributions of heavy-flavor hadrons, which could provide further understanding of nuclear parton distribution functions and the internal nucleon structure through comparison with corresponding calculations in vacuum. The research can also be extended to studies of jet-medium interactions in less complex systems, such as proton and neutron targets, which offers new opportunities for extracting nuclear PDF information through precise jet studies in existing and future deep-inelastic scattering and Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator experiments. The framework can also be used to investigate jet formation in nuclear collisions at lower energies, such as SIS300 and EIC, which can provide insights into nuclear parton distribution functions at higher scales. A pervasive issue in cryptocurrency projects is the prevalence of pyramid schemes, which are often disguised as legitimate investments. Forsage, presented as a multi-level marketing platform, has been identified as a pyramid scheme and has damaged over $1 billion in user funds. In an effort to understand the impact of Forsage on its users, we analyzed over 300,000 unsolicited emails sent to addresses on the Forsage referral list. Our study discovered that a substantial number of users, 94.5%, suffered financial losses in Forsage, with an average decline of 71% in available funds. Notably, nearly one in five users (22.5%) invested their entire cryptocurrency balance in Forsage, resulting in complete loss of those funds. Our research uncovered additional insights into Forsage user behavior and how the scheme's design accommodates user investment, along with suggested counter-measures to prevent similar schemes from exploiting users through email. To facilitate this research, we created a publicly accessible dataset that includes over 300,000 emails from Forsage referral lists, along with associated metadata. This dataset provides a rich source of data for analyzing email-based multi-level marketing schemes and other pyramid schemes that engage with users through email. It is available under a permissive license that allows free use, sharing, and adaptation. Our study offers valuable insights for cryptocurrency users on how to make informed investment decisions and avoid falling prey to pyramid schemes. In addition, our research is accompanied by a publicly accessible dataset that includes over 300,000 emails from Forsage referral lists, along with associated metadata, which is freely available under a permissive license that allows free use, sharing, and adaptation. This dataset is particularly suited for analyzing email-based multi-level marketing schemes and other pyramid schemes that interact with users through email. Our study's findings can serve as a benchmark for evaluating future counter-measures against such schemes. Our research is now openly accessible in the hope that it will contribute to the ongoing discussion on cryptocurrency, cryptocurrency investment, and email-based multi-level marketing schemes. However, in the standard implementation of these models, the velocity gauge suffers from significant deficiencies near atomic sites, causing inaccurate results.  This issue can be addressed by refining the models with an accurate kinetic energy operator derived from tight-binding parameters, ensuring that they match the second-order Schr\"{o}dinger equation.  The proposed method also provides a way to assess the adequacy of the tight-binding models by comparing their electromagnetic responses to all-order quantum mechanics, offering a more reliable method to adjust the models and optimize their performance.  This approach is particularly useful when the models are limited to a range of 10-20 \angstrom, giving 1-5 {\angstrom} improvement in the accuracy of electromagnetic responses.  To make this method more accessible, a Python module called 'emva' has been created to automate the conversion process, so that even basic users can convert the models with the proposed refinement by running a single command.  The 'emva' module can be used from the command line or integrated into Python scripts, and it supports a variety of tight-binding formats, including those employed by the real-space Kubo formula calculators, 'kubpar' and'matpara'. Furthermore, the development of electromagnetic responses in tight-binding models is compared to their ab initio counterparts.  The 'emva' module is available at https://github.com/atsasaki/emva, and it can be used to improve the accuracy of electromagnetic responses in tight-binding models.  The code has been tested on Linux and macOS systems. The proposed method can be applied not only to electromagnetic responses but also to other quantities, such as the electron density, by combining the tight-binding models with quantum mechanics. To tackle dynamic business processes, many organizations rely on advanced prediction models that can forecast future events and enable proactive decision-making. Yet, in practice, these models often vary in their accuracy across different process stages. This study introduces a novel approach called FUTURE-DRIP, an explanatory model for high-dimensional data, that can handle scenarios with only a limited number of samples at each process stage. This is achieved by incorporating a novel component that models the variance of data samples at each stage and helps to mitigate the challenges of varying data sizes. To evaluate FUTURE-DRIP, the study includes multiple experiments involving real-world data from an e-commerce platform and a manufacturing system, demonstrating its superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art approach, CURE-DRIP. Furthermore, an important aspect analyzed through user studies is the practical applicability of FUTURE-DRIP models to domain experts in their respective fields. Lastly, an empirical exploration is conducted to illustrate how FUTURE-DRIP can be employed in a real-world setting with an infinite number of data samples. This study leads to an important finding that process stages with predicted outcomes tend to have fewer actual outcomes, likely due to the natural tendency for processes to converge back to their estimated trajectories. This research paves the way for future studies on FUTURE-DRIP, such as developing new techniques to enhance its performance and exploring its potential connections to other scholarly works. The study concludes by highlighting potential directions for improving FUTURE-DRIP as well as potential connections to other research areas. The study's findings and methodologies are already contributing to new research questions and potential applications, and the implementation of FUTURE-DRIP is now available as an open-source tool. This paper investigates the behavior of functions within Gelfand-Shilov spaces in relation to their Fourier transforms, extending classical results to a broader context that includes the Beurling's stable translation group. Key findings include growth estimates for functions whose Fourier transforms exhibit subexponential growth and explicit characterization of functions whose growth rates are tempered by a Bessel function. Furthermore, a distinction is made between rapidly decreasing functions within Gelfand-Shilov spaces and their Fourier transforms, demonstrating that a function with a rapidly decreasing Fourier transform does not necessarily belong to the Gelfand-Shilov space of rapid decay. Additionally, the paper analyzes the relationship between the growth of a function and its Fourier transform in the context of Gevrey spaces, establishing the equivalence of temperedness conditions for functions and their Fourier transforms in these spaces. A regularity criterion for functions within these spaces is also obtained, linking microlocal and global regularity properties. A key technique employed is the use of microlocalization and the Helmer-Oberhofer theorem. A notable outcome derived from this research is a generalization of the Fejér-Helson theorem to its full extent. A photonic unit cell based on a meta-structure from the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model is designed and fabricated to exhibit parity-time (PT) symmetry. The design allows for the transmission of light through the unit cell via two different paths, $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$, that correspond to the PT symmetric and broken phases, respectively. It is observed that light travels in group-like and skippable manners along $\mathcal{C}_1$, whereas it travels in coherent and coherent-missing manners along $\mathcal{C}_2$. This distinction highlights the distinct characteristics of wave behavior in the PT symmetric and broken phases. Researchers propose a new method to enhance the symmetry restoration in heavy nuclear systems, drawing from quantum mechanics' principles, particularly the Overlap Correlation Method. This approach has shown success in accurately determining root mean square radii in nuclei, offering a viable alternative to statistical methods like RPA+Sky. Additionally, the new scheme can be more efficiently implemented using realistic interactions directly from Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov+QRPA calculations. Recent predictions for the neutron drip line and magic numbers in the tin and strontium isotopes have validated the method's accuracy. Comparing RPA+Sky and HFB+OCM methods for these cases found that while both yield similar results, HFB+OCM generally prefers smaller configuration interaction spaces. Notably, the preferred sizes in the two methods differ by several orders of magnitude. Despite some discrepancies, both methods consistently predict the same neutron number of 126 as crucial for the next-isospin major neutron shell closure in $^{132}$Sn, a finding supported by the QRPA oscillation energies. Furthermore, both methods also identify $^{31}$Mg and $^{40}$S as the next-isospin magic nuclei, reinforcing previous studies and suggesting a broader applicability of the methods to various isotopes along the drip lines. In conclusion, the new overlap correlation approach demonstrates its value as a viable tool for accurately determining ground state properties in exotic nuclei. This method may be particularly useful in situations where statistical approaches face difficulties, such as in calculations involving high-Hamiltonian perturbations or unusual configuration predictions. Notably, both methods employed realistic interactions throughout the studies presented here. Ultimately, further exploration of the new scheme's potential is warranted to fully assess its utility in exotic nuclear research.

This paper explores the application of the Koopman operator theory in analyzing nonlinear systems from a linear algebra perspective. By examining the spectral properties of the extended operator, we aim to identify a low-dimensional invariant subspace that captures the dynamics of a high-dimensional system. Utilizing matrix-valued functions, we define the Koopman operator and establish its relationship with the original system dynamics. A low-rank approximation of the Koopman operator is then obtained through a linear approximation of the operator's action on an invariant manifold, enabling efficient computation using neural operators. Leveraging this low-rank approximation, we devise a method for an optimal invariant subspace reconstruction and demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying the dominant dynamics of chaotic systems via a spectral analysis of the operator. Full-state time-series data from the Lorenz '96 model and a neural operator-trained system showcase our method's applicability. Moreover, our approach facilitates an innovative spectral analysis that reveals an invariant subspace corresponding to a 3-dimensional dynamic structure within the original system's high-dimensional space. By combining this subspace with an invariant manifold tool, we are able to construct a 3D plot illustrating the system's dynamics. Additionally, our method allows for an optimal low-dimensional dynamic structure discovery, which caters to the limited observational capacity in many real-world systems. Building meaningful sentence representations from generative neural networks is extremely difficult, as these networks inherently produce semantic noise. To overcome this challenge, the SparseGAN algorithm was developed to learn a sparse embedding from a generative neural network. This embedding represents a concise and semantically pure summary of the sentence. By utilizing the sparse embedding in a discriminative neural network via an attention mechanism, the SparseGANModel was trained to generate accurate and semantically rich sentence representations. Our experiments showed that this approach significantly outperformed alternative methods for generating sentence representations, as evaluated by semantic similarity and diversity metrics. Moreover, the sparse attention weights of the model provided new insights into the compositionality of sentences. Our findings also demonstrated that the generated representations exhibit a high level of similarity to actual sentence contexts, as measured by contextualized language models. Ultimately, the SparseGANModel's generated sentences ranked higher in quality and diversity when assessed by human evaluators. Open star clusters and stellar associations with low stellar densities and wide spatial configurations pose a compelling possibility for the interstellar dispersal of life. Evaluating panspermia in these ecological hotspots is crucial, but we lack observations of these regions in the microwave range. To address this, we conducted thorough continuum observations at 1.5 GHz with the FAST radio telescope, as well as follow-up measurements with the YSZT-20 radio telescope at 2.7 GHz, 4.8 GHz, and 7.1 GHz for 13 such targets. These targets include well-studied clusters like the Pleiades, the Double Cluster, and the Omega Centauri star cluster, in addition to various less-explored associations in the Galaxy's fourth quadrant. Our sensitivity levels allowed us to detect bright radio sources with powers exceeding 10^23 Hz/Hz, and we were able to measure upper limits for radio flux at each frequency for each target. Among the targets studied, we did not detect any radio flux above background noise levels, which indicates that the detected targets do not contain extant radio-emitting life. However, this does not preclude possible microbial existence in these regions, as we were unable to access the desired frequency range that could provide clearer evidence. Furthermore, our study also sets a precedent for observing celestial environments that harbor extraterrestrial life during upcoming high-energy particle events, such as the approaching GLE119, which may offer further insight into the connection between high-energy radiation and potential life in these regions. Researchers propose that dark matter is composed of a single substance with varying energy levels, specifically a scalar field that transitions between a cold dark matter state at low energies and a warm dark matter state at higher energies. This theory is tested using a pair of entropy equations that relate the different levels of this single-field dark matter model. A previously established connection between the warm and cold dark matter sectors is confirmed, with an indicated mass scale that this model assumes must be greater than the grand unified theory scale to effectively distinguish between the two sectors. Furthermore, this model predicts specific parameter values that can be validated through future experiments, particularly in particle physics and cosmological structure formation with high-resolution simulations. Additionally, this model raises the possibility that warm dark matter could be linked to the matter-antimatter asymmetry, with implications for beyond-Standard Model scenarios. Ultimately, this model may provide a unified framework for understanding both dark matter and dark energy. Several high-resolution structure formation simulations within this model are also presented, revealing that its fundamental characteristics can be replicated within the Standard Model of particle physics. However, when the mass scale of this model is lowered to the inverse of a mega-electron-volt, these structures fail to form in accordance with recent structure formation versus collapse observations. The implications of this single-field dark matter model on other research areas are also considered, including primordial black hole formation, the stability of the Standard Model, and the effectiveness of the gravitational stability phase space fillings. Ultimately, this model highlights the possibility that a single, multifaceted dark matter field holds the key to understanding both the cold and warm dark matter phenomena. This research provides a foundation for further exploration of this single-field dark matter paradigm through various other theoretical frameworks and experimental searches. The associated code for the structure formation simulations is available online for the community to use in future studies. The findings presented in this research offer a starting point for the ongoing discussion of this single-field dark matter model and its potential to clarify our understanding of the cosmos. The authors are open to feedback and look forward to contributing to the development of this research through community engagement. In an analysis of network resilience, we are given a graph G and multiple source-destination pairs, and the objective is to identify k edge disjoint paths between these pairs. This task is particularly challenging when the number of required paths (k) exceeds the number of source nodes (st). In this case, the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem seeks to find the fewest possible power levels needed to establish at least k edge disjoint st-paths in the network. We investigate this problem for both undirected and directed graphs, and our research focuses on a specific parameter - the number of source nodes (st) - as it significantly impacts the problem's tractability. When st is greater than or equal to 3, the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem becomes NP-complete even with k=1. However, interestingly, when st is 2 or k is 1, the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem can be solved efficiently for both undirected and directed graphs. Our research also explores the relationship between Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths and the Multi-Commodity Minimum Spanning Tree problem. We establish an exponential relationship between these problems and various power levels. Finally, our research investigates polynomial-time solvable special cases of the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, including a specific instance where the graph has a particular hierarchical structure. This finding is significant as it provides a non-trivial k=2 instance that can be solved efficiently, in contrast to an NP-complete status when k is 1. Our research involves an analysis of both general graphs and specific grid topologies. We establish an upper bound for the number of required power levels when k is 2 in a hierarchical graph structure and investigate the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem in a grid graph where st and k both equal 2. In this case, we establish a tight upper bound of log(r+1) for the number of required power levels, where r represents the maximum degree of the graph. Our research involves a comparison with an existing approach that focuses on maximizing the minimum edge weight in a k edge disjoint st-paths configuration. We demonstrate that our proposed approach has a polynomial conversion time from the earlier method and establish an exponential lower bound for a specific instance of this problem. In swarm operations, predicting the behavior of individual entities from their observed interactions is crucial for inferring the global configuration. We demonstrate how the Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli (GLMB) method can be applied for target tracking in a swarm from proximal sensor data alone, leveraging the low-cost and dissemination-based communication method of many swarm systems. By modeling target identities as components of a multi-variate probability distribution, and updating this distribution as new data becomes available, we show how to efficiently manage a large number of potential targets, even when only a small number of entities communicate with the commander. Our approach results in a practical and reliable method for estimating the global configuration of a swarm, and can be applied to a variety of scenarios, including Cloosterman's "target swarm" scenario. Furthermore, our approach outperforms alternative methods, such as the Probability Hit Association (PHA), in scenarios with large numbers of targets and limited communication. A thorough evaluation of our method is performed through a series of simulations, and the associated code is freely available for download. By extending the capabilities of target tracking to a broader context, we believe this research opens up new avenues for the study of swarm behavior. The associated code is freely available for download at https://github.com/TueUAS/SWAT. The GLMB method is now also part of the PDA3++ tracking library at https://github.com/TueUAS/PDA3PlusPlus. Researchers studying the spread of diseases within complex networks often focus on reviewing the underlying structure of these networks rather than analyzing dynamic processes. A notable exception occurs when networks exhibit a non-trivial or "rich club" structure. Here, individuals who share common characteristics also tend to have similar epidemic prevalence levels. Investigating a mean-field model on a non-homogeneous network, researchers found that when networks contain a delocalized component near a critical transition phase, the prevalence of the epidemic there tends to be uniformly high. This prevalence then corresponds to the average prevalence seen across the network, effectively making it a key driver of the epidemic's spread. In contrast, closer examination of the network's structure around the critical transition reveals that the high prevalence areas are not necessarily located at the network's core. This finding contradicts the long-held assumption that the central nodes are the primary targets for intervention to slow the epidemic's spread. As an example, on a Colombian university network that exhibits a rich club structure, targeting the top 10% of the nodes for vaccination is shown to be no more effective than randomly selecting nodes. These results underscore the importance of considering the specific characteristics of each node, as well as the network's overall structure, when developing strategies to combat the spread of diseases. Furthermore, this study highlights the value of analytically modeling the dynamic processes that occur within complex networks, particularly when these networks exhibit non-trivial topologies, and stresses that such models can provide actionable insights to inform public health policy. In this regard, it is notable that a comprehensive review of the epidemic model applications considered here is included in the Supplemental Material. In addition, the tools employed to analyze the mean-field model are general enough to be applied to any non-homogeneous network. Consequently, this study is confident that its findings will prove relevant to the analysis of other complex systems and networks that exhibit similar non-trivial structures. In such environments, the coexistence of highly connected components and robust syndical structures may give rise to widespread delocalized patterns of behavior, with significant implications for our understanding of the underlying dynamics. In the case of Colombian university networks, this study's findings also have meaningful policy implications for the distribution of resources and targeted interventions in large, complex networks. Ultimately, this study's results are expected to resonate with researchers studying other topical issues, such as the spread of ideas, cultural norms, or technological adoption, on similarly structured networks. In these contexts, as well as in future research, this study hopes to contribute to the development of a deeper theoretical understanding
