Automatically interpreting handwritten documents contains various challenges, particularly when dealing with documents that contain pre-printed components and free-form input. This difficulty is compounded in the case of documents scanned from physical sources, which can introduce significant noise. While previous research offered effective solutions for validating document contents, the relationships between these contents were left unexplored. In response, we develop a novel approach called Relationship Detection in Noisy Documents (RDenNoDoc), which identifies connections between pre-printed text and user-generated text within documents. To facilitate training for this task, we also created a new dataset called Relationship Detection in Noisy Documents (RDenNoDoc) and implemented a specially designed evaluation metric called Matching Accuracy at k (MA$k$). Our experiments confirmed that our approach not only outperformed alternative methods but also demonstrated the utility of the RDenNoDoc dataset and MA$k$ metric in supporting further research. The code for our approach and the dataset is now available on GitHub. Alongside the code, we included a sample implementation of the self-correction technique mentioned in our paper. In addition, the dataset and evaluation metric have the potential to contribute to advancements in other related document analysis tasks. A Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Model (HiP-RSSM) is a model that enables the learning of complex, underlying dynamics from partially observed data and variable sampling rates. HiP-RSSMs achieve this by representing system variables and observation functions as distinct functions, allowing them to be structured and efficient to update during inference. Unlike standard RSSMs, HiP-RSSMs do not require the learning of separate functions for system and observation variables. Our analysis shows that HiP-RSSMs can learn and infer systems with non-linear underlying dynamics and missing data, and can handle variable sampling rates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HiP-RSSMs through experiments in forecasting and filling in missing data for complex time series datasets, and show that they can efficiently learn and infer systems from data with high missing rates and variable sampling schedules. HiP-RSSMs outperform traditional RSSMs in these tasks, and can also be used in an unsupervised setting to discover underlying structures and variables from data with missing values. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/hidden_parameter_recurrent_state_space_models. HiP-RSSMs have the potential to enable the efficient learning and inference of complex systems from partial and variable sampling rate data, a common issue in many real world dynamic measurement problems. HiP-RSSMs can be used for the partial data regime by filling in missing values, and this could have applications in completed data regimes as well. HiP-RSSMs can also be used in an unsupervised setting to discover underlying structures and variables from data with missing values, and this could have applications in systems with complete data as well. HiP-RSSMs can be used to model a variety of dynamic systems, such as economic trends, population dynamics, and medical measurement patterns, and can be combined with other models such as HiP-GRNNs. This breakthrough involves proving that given certain independent motivations, the standardized additive projections of Biggie and Shyamperumenee's "big" matrices will exhibit similar eigenvalue characteristics. These "big" matrices are constructed from extensive use of circular unitaries and Wang's "small" matrices, which themselves possess unique characteristics which stem from an independent and free process. Furthermore, some methods are susceptible to manipulation through artificial manipulation of degree distributions. In order to better understand the phenomena of polarization, it is essential to utilize measurement methods that are robust and unbiased. Originally, applying this approach would have required nearly 10 times the number of equations present in the new model. Our simplified method equates the dynamics of each individual oscillator to a single first-order differential equation, while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. Notably, this method successfully replicates the exact stability standards as the original multi-layer model. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that our approach can provide valuable insights into the complex phenomena observed in multilayer networks without the need for extensive numerical analysis. As an example, we analyze a collective synchronization phenomenon in a network consisting of two interconnected populations using our simplified method. Our results reveal that our approach can not only match the level of accuracy of more comprehensive models but also offer a level of detail previously only accessible through highly simplified models. Roudeault recently proposed a categorification of differential modules in terms of twisted differential operators, which he calls differential modules in the classical sense. Here, we show that this construction is equivalent to categorifying a specific family of twisted differential operators, which we define as operators with separated poles in $x^{-1}$. Here, $x$ represents the leading polynomial in a Weyl algebra. Two operators belong to the same family if their coefficients have the same analytic classification in $x$. Building on work by Birkner, Chaudhuri, and Katz, we also demonstrate that vanishing $a$-analytic invariants of a family of operators imply the existence of an operator in that family over fields of positive characteristic. Finally, we utilize this result to prove that an irreducible representation of a complex reductive group has a highest weight vector if and only if its non-Borel part has vanishing $a$-analytic invariants. This result in algebraic geometry is validated by an example using the non-commutative resolution of singularities developed by Bondarkyn and Korashvili. This example enables us to demonstrate that an operator of a specific family over a field of positive characteristic can be lifted to a field of higher characteristic. Not all software bugs are human-error based; some originate from flaws in programming languages or environments.  Current strategies for detecting software bugs are unhelpful when dealing with errors caused by language or environmental flaws.  A novel algorithm for anomaly detection is introduced in this study, and it demonstrates exceptional results in identifying previously unknown software bugs in popular programming languages like C, Java and Python, and database management systems like MySQL.  The algorithm works its way backwards from faulty program output to the faulty program source, bypassing the need to analyze low-level operating system and compiler processes.  The study also presents data showing the effectiveness of the algorithm in detecting new software bugs on popular open-source programs.  For example, it identified 139 software bugs in the Linux kernel, and 35 bugs in MySQL, and all of these bugs were confirmed by human developers as actual software bugs.  The amount of time the algorithm takes to detect these bugs is significantly less than the time it takes human developers.  The algorithm was optimized to work with a team of human developers in a collaborative environment, and it was found that when it pinpointed the location of errors, human developers could correct them in half the time it would have taken otherwise.  The method the algorithm uses to find these errors can be applied to other complex systems that rely on program output, such as video games, and it can be used to create more effective testing tools that can learn from user feedback.  The algorithm is available online for download and can be used with popular integrated development environments (IDEs) like Eclipse.  Future work is being considered to enhance the algorithm's ability to identify software bugs in programs that use graphical user interfaces, and to investigate new applications for the algorithm in fields like security and data analysis. Our work aims to enhance the flexibility and computational speed of HyperNetworks in PBM by utilizing a method that combines Cardinality Restriction and Federated Learning. This approach allows for the reduction of unnecessary computation and model fine-tuning. Our proposal utilizes CR-FL in a Decentralized manner, which enables Cardinality Restriction and Federated Learning to work together seamlessly. This cooperative framework facilitates efficient learning among sub-networks, making it possible for the overall HyperNetwork to achieve optimal results with minimal computational expense. Our method also enables the creation of diverse sub-networks without requiring significant memory allocation. In evaluations using both MixMatch and FederatedSearch for pre-trained BERT, our method shows a notable increase in task efficiency with improved performance. Furthermore, our method successfully generates a wide range of generalizable sub-networks without incurring additional memory costs when compared to the baseline model. In this work, we investigate a special root in the root systems of types A and D - the maximal root. We demonstrate that, in both systems, the remaining roots can be constructed from the maximal root through a specific, orderly process of reflecting roots across hypersplanes defined by certain coefficients. This method of construction allows us to establish a specific sequence or order among the roots in both systems of type A and systems of type D. A deeper analysis into this ordering leads to our discovery that this ordered list of roots shares the same sequence as the integers from 1 to l in the case of type A, and from 1 to (l-1) in the case of type D, in a non-decreasing order. Finally, our research also examines the relationship between the number of positive roots, the dimension of the root system, and the Coxeter number, which is the sum of the shortest path between the maximal and minimal roots in the graph of the root system. We have found that the number of positive roots is equal to the dimension of the root system times a fraction whose denominator is the Coxeter number, providing an expression for the Coxeter number in terms of the number of positive roots and the dimension of the root system. We have also discovered that this fraction equals 1/(Coxeter number) times the sum of the shortest path between all pairs of positive roots in the graph of the root system. We have further found that the Coxeter number in the system of type A is equal to l, and system of type D is equal to (l-1)/2, and that 1 plus the Coxeter number in type D is equal to 2 times the Coxeter number in type A. We have also proved that this relationship between the Coxeter numbers of type A and D holds for all l greater than or equal to 3. In a set of coupled cavities, the interaction between light and matter can generate correlated photon emissions, offering a foundation for quantum communication systems. Notably, entangled photons are produced in a specific pattern, dependent on whether the correlation is even (additive) or odd (subtractive). By incorporating a controllable phase-shift in one cavity, via the placement of a SQUID loop, the generated correlated photons' emission pattern can be manipulated and switched between entangled and anti-entangled states. This is achieved when the SQUID is operated in a flux regime lacking clear transitions, thereby smoothly controlling the correlation type through modulation of the phase-shift. This technique may also enable the development of quantum communication systems capable of distinguishing between additive and subtractive correlations, thus providing a means to securely encode and transmit information over long distances. Furthermore, this approach offers a possibility to implement a quantum protocol known as entanglement amplification. A system based on superconducting cavities and SQUID loops has been simulated and analyzed, showing that its performance can be optimized by adjusting the phase-shift and SQUID flux, respectively. This simulation also illustrates the advantage of utilizing a controllable phase-shift, offered by the SQUID loop, in managing the emitted correlated photons' properties. This technique may also find applications in other multi-cavity cavity QED systems, involving various types of matter systems and interactions. Ultimately, this could lead to secure long-distance quantum communication and the development of novel quantum protocols. A simulation of a trimer cavity system, consisting of two isolated cavities and one coupled cavity, is also provided, revealing that the controllable phase-shift has a significant impact on the emitted correlated photons' properties when the system is driven by a coherent light source. This study compares the accuracy of nonparametric and parametric methods in estimating queue lengths. While nonparametric techniques offer flexible modeling, parametric approaches can provide intuitive insights and facilitate further analysis, although they require specifying a probability distribution. To determine the effectiveness of these methods in a real-world setting, we analyzed traffic data from Google Maps and evaluated their performance under different simulation conditions. The results show that nonparametric methods generally yield more accurate estimates than parametric methods, with a median absolute error of less than 10 seconds for nonparametric and 15 seconds for parametric. However, our findings also indicate that some parametric models can achieve high accuracy in specific scenarios, with an example being the exponential distribution which closely resembles the nonparametric estimate at a busy urban intersection. Interestingly, we observed that heavy-tailed distributions like the power law and generalized Pareto, which are commonly associated with congested lanes, are less accurate than the normal distribution in our dataset. This suggests that drivers' arrival patterns may be more consistently aligned with the normal distribution than the tail behavior, which may be influenced by factors such as lane changes and vehicles merging onto the road. Our results also highlight that the choice of parametric model is less critical than the queue length estimation method itself, with over 50% of all estimates falling within 5 seconds of the true value regardless of the specific model used. Notably, our analysis indicates that the majority of lanes are not truly busy, with the majority of the data falling into the light traffic category rather than the heavy traffic expected. To facilitate replication and further research, we have made the traffic data and associated Python code available on GitHub. In our experiments, we employed popular nonparametric and parametric methods, including the Gaussian mixture model, which demonstrated a notable ability to capture complex arrival patterns, with a median error of around 15 seconds. Our study provides a foundation for ongoing research into queue length estimation and may contribute to the development of more accurate and practical algorithms. Despite extensive research, the exact mechanisms underlying anomalous Nernst effects (ANE) in materials without long-range magnetic order remain poorly understood. Studies have shown that ANE can occur in both magnetic and non-magnetic materials, however, there have been limited investigations on materials that transition between these states. Antiferromagnetic antiperovskites, which can be both magnetic and non-magnetic, offer a rich environment in which to study ANE. In the study presented here, we investigated the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN by combining experimental and theoretical analyses. Our experimental approach involved measuring the transverse Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN single crystals as a function of temperature, magnetic field, and direction. Our results showed that the anomalous Nernst effect is strongest at the magnetic transition temperature and follows a similar temperature dependence as the magnetic scattering. Additionally, our theoretical model revealed that exchange interactions between distant neighboring spins play a crucial role in inducing the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials. Furthermore, our results suggest that the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN is dominated by the motion of magnetic domains during temperature changes, and that this effect could potentially be utilized to develop sensitive temperature sensors. Our study provides valuable insights into the mechanisms governing the anomalous Nernst effect in materials that transition between magnetic and non-magnetic states, and highlights the unique opportunities offered by antiferromagnetic antiperovskites for exploring and exploiting the anomalous Nernst effect. Our research offers a starting point for further investigations aimed at comprehensively understanding the anomalous Nernst effect in materials without long-range magnetic order.

Currently, deep neural networks for image classification primarily rely on an ensemble of models that incorporate an ensemble of neural network components, each producing a probability distribution in the form of logits over possible labels. While this approach has yielded notable achievements in the field, the assumption that each component model produces a reliable probability distribution over labels is often unrealistic, especially when the model is not adequately trained. This paper challenges this common practice by proposing a method called PILE, which utilizes label information through an iterative process. By leveraging the implied relationships among labels, PILE aims to enhance the performance of deep neural networks in image classification tasks, specifically those with prototypical datasets, such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. The paper evaluates the proposed approach by comparing it to three baseline methods and finds that PILE outperforms these approaches consistently across all evaluated datasets. Furthermore, an analysis of Demixing Analysis is conducted to provide insight into how PILE operates. Despite its effectiveness, the paper discovers that PILE is vulnerable to label noise and advises future research to enhance its robustness. Despite its current limitations, PILE offers an innovative perspective on how to utilize neural network components and is now publicly available at https://github.com/leiming1992/PILE. The code for the baseline methods used in the paper can also be found at https://github.com/leiming1992/PILE_baselines. The dataset and model files for the experiments conducted in the paper have been uploaded to Dropbox at https://www.dropbox.com/s/6yqy6y6y6y6y6y6y.zip?raw=1. The paper's results can be replicated by executing the command python main.py --data cifar-10 --num-classes 10 --num-components 128 --num-iterations 5 --batch-size 256 --num-experiments 128. Additionally, the paper includes an examination of the component models learned by PILE and finds that they exhibit a level of diversity comparable to that of standalone neural network components. Lastly, the paper finds that PILE is capable of generalizing across different datasets and is not dataset-specific. This finding suggests that the improved performance of PILE is attributable to its ability to exploit implied relationships among labels rather than a better fit to the specific dataset at hand. The paper also conducts an analysis of the iterative process itself and finds that the logit values produced by PILE through this process are consistent with the latent variables extracted from a mixture model comprising the component logit matrices.

Quantum annealing is an optimization technique that relies on gradual changes to reach a ground state and solve complex problems. This method's potential is hindered by decoherence, which causes the loss of phase-symmetry and hinders state-finding. We investigate how decoherence affects quantum annealing on the Edwards-Selby model, a freely rotating spin glass system. We demonstrate that certain decoherence rates can prevent the successful targeting of the ground state and investigate the impact of decoherence on quantum annealing through the application of Z2-symmetry. Our analysis reveals that certain decoherence rates disrupt the system's symmetry during quantum annealing, hindering state-targeting. We also establish the connection between these decoherence rates and Z2-symmetry breaking in the corresponding Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we propose a quantum annealing protocol that accounts for decoherence and Z2-symmetry to improve the target-state success rate. This protocol involves introducing a symmetry-conserving phase in the annealing schedule. We show that this protocol raises the target-state success rate in the presence of decoherence and Z2-symmetry, and that it may lead to better outcomes even in the absence of Z2-symmetry. We also examine the influence of various decoherence rates on the target-state success rate and the associated Z2-symmetry breaking in the corresponding Hamiltonians. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the execution of quantum annealing on physical platforms prone to decoherence. These include the use of bi-directional annealing and the integration of symmetry-conserving phases into mainstream quantum annealing protocols. This may enhance the target-state success rate, particularly in scenarios with low decoherence rates. Ultimately, our study highlights the importance of considering the effects of decoherence in quantum annealing applications and provides a framework for evaluating the influence of environment interactions with physical systems. This understanding is crucial for the development and execution of reliable quantum annealing algorithms in real-world settings.

Our study offers a theoretical basis for exploring more complex biological systems and can provide valuable insights when applied to real-world environments. This distinction arises due to the high-energy scattering driving the near-extremal black hole to an extremal state, and the extremal black hole remaining unchanged. In an effort to simplify the proof of complexity theorems for lattice-based systems, the anti-classicality axiom can be employed as a key lemma. This study utilizes ECoG recordings from patients who are awake and performing walking tasks to investigate the feasibility of predicting their future walking abilities following a corpus callosum lesion. We explored the effectiveness of ECoG-based predictions in relation to conventional EEG-based predictions and found that both methods successfully forecasted walking outcomes with a high degree of accuracy. Notably, ECoG-based predictions exhibited greater than 90% accuracy across all outcome measures, which is remarkably consistent with our earlier EEG-based study. Interestingly, ECoG-based predictions showed excellent performance even when data from a single parietal electrode site was analyzed in isolation. This was particularly evident in predicting residual gait performance and overall walking functionality. We also found that both ECoG and EEG-based predictions shared common neural substrates, targeting areas of the brain responsible for sensation integration, spatial awareness, and movement control. These shared areas survived a comprehensive set of controls, suggesting that the observed overlap is unlikely to be attributed to confounding variables. In contrast to EEG, ECoG recordings offered the additional benefit of more precise neural source localizations, with several key areas of interest exhibiting greater than 10mm of difference in Brodmann area locations. Notably, our results demonstrated a strong correlation between the accuracy of ECoG predictions and the extent of damage to these areas, particularly the posterior parietal cortex, which has been previously implicated in post-surgical walking recovery. These findings provide new evidence supporting the use of ECoG-based predictions in identifying at-risk patients who may benefit from intensive walking rehabilitation programs following corpus callosum lesions. Moreover, our study sets the stage for exploring additional sensory motor functions in awake patients with brain tumors, offering a valuable tool for clinicians to guide pre-surgical counseling and post-surgical rehabilitation planning. In doing so, it may ultimately improve walking outcomes for patients with tumors in critical motor areas. In conclusion, our findings establish the feasibility of using ECoG recordings to forecast post-surgical walking abilities in awake patients with corpus callosum tumors, providing a strong foundation for future studies into this promising approach. Ultimately, this research may contribute to a greater understanding of the neural basis of walking functions in humans. In the long term, this knowledge could lead to more effective clinical applications, such as using ECoG-based predictions to guide tumor resections and enhance walking outcomes in patients with brain tumors in critical motor areas. Computing the mean entropy of a probability distribution is a fundamental task, yet this becomes increasingly difficult when the distribution can't be directly assessed, which is common in dynamic systems with only observable functions and a partial description. Entropies as a result have been largely theoretical, whereas our algorithm expands their applicability to such scenarios. By utilizing the observable variables to construct a manifold, our method calculates their corresponding entropies and weights them according to their local dimensions. This approach is efficient, user-friendly, and adaptable to any type of probability distribution. We demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to two complex systems - a synthetic dataset and the human brain - and show how it helps identify the role of different regions in the temporal loopy grid world and the gradual development of Alzheimer's disease. The source code for this method is now available online.

Dynamic graph classification is a complex task due to the ever-changing nature of graphs, which requires existing approaches to often be reconfigured or updated in real-time. To address this, we propose DECENNT, a novel decentralized graph neural network model that leverages unique node features and spatial correlations to enhance the representation of graphs. In contrast to standard GNNs, DECENNT exhibits improved robustness and reduces the difference in representation for changing graphs. Our experiments demonstrate that DECENNT outperforms centralizeable baselines and rivals centralized methods in dynamic graph classification, while its decentralized version matches the performance of its centralized counterpart in static graph classification tasks. The code for DECENNT is openly available on GitHub at the specified URL.

The movement of living organisms, especially microswimmers, is distinct from the motion of inanimate objects due to its self-correlated and directed nature. This distinction makes it possible to track and study individual living cells within complex mixtures using experimental techniques that lose effectiveness for heavier particles. In the field of dipolar active matter, simulations can be run to observe the behavior of self-propelled dipolar particles under various conditions. However, these simulations often assume that the movement of these particles is free from constraints and does not account for the influence of confined spaces on the particles' behavior. In the mentioned study, the motion of discrete steps was substituted with a continuous motion model that took into consideration the forces exerted by particles moving in a limited space. This approach was applied to evaluate the impact of confinement on the phase behavior of active dipolar particles across various activity levels and spatial restrictions. It was found that highly active particles exhibit strong directional control, causing them to swim towards the center of the confinement and eventually accumulate, while lower activity levels result in the formation of polar domains. Moreover, the effect of increasing activity above a specific threshold can be seen as an expansion of the high-density core into the surrounding areas. This research provides a foundation for exploring the influence of constrained motion on active dipolar particles and lays the groundwork for comparing its outcomes with experimental data obtained from living cells within confined environments. We investigate how the Neumann algorithm's performance is impacted by its inception depth, a measure that reflects the number of layers skipped before the algorithm's first application. By developing a new implementation of the Nested Neumann algorithm that iteratively increases its inception depth, we demonstrate its ability to achieve optimal model accuracy. However, we also observe that the algorithm's convergence rate is affected by its inception depth, with larger values resulting in decreased convergence speeds. As a result, we suggest limiting the inception depth to the model's deepest hidden layer to minimize computational efficiency losses. Through our method's application to Berntsen-Chaouchi-type models, we demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately estimating optimal model parameters, with a notable reduction in estimation error compared to existing methods. Furthermore, our approach allows for the derivation of upper and lower bounds on optimal model parameters, with a level of precision influenced by the algorithm's inception depth. We validate our method using empirical data from inflationary and growth models. Additionally, we explore alternative algorithms, including one that leverages the model's parameter space for improved performance, but with increased computational costs. Our code is openly accessible and can be utilized to estimate optimal model parameters, as well as implement the algorithms discussed in our study. We also include the source code for our paper's figures and tables. We hope this contributes to the advancement of the econometric modeling community. In a non-uniform transmission system, the characteristics of waves can become complicated, consisting of multiple, varying intensity patterns as they propagate and interact with each other. These intensity patterns, or over-laps, at specific points within the system are directly linked to the eigenchannels of a system - its unique pathways for transmission. This paper investigates the problem of constructing valid inference methods for network autoregressive models with incomplete or inaccurate information, due to a lack of identifiability. We develop a new statistical test, based on the residual autocorrelation of observed variables, which does not rely on the exact parameters of the model. The test has the ability to accommodate non-identifiable parameters and we demonstrate that it achieves the desired significance level correctly. Additionally, we find that the test is powerful enough to detect the presence of a specific network structure. Our method can be applied to time series data from a multi-layer network by performing separate tests for each layer. Through simulations and an empirical analysis, we show that our proposed test outperforms a competing alternative. The software for the new test is freely available online.

This paper addresses this crucial issue by introducing a novel approach to test the network autoregressive model using temporal network data.

The test has several advantages, including the ability to handle non-identifiable parameters, achieving the desired significance level, detecting specific network structures, and outperforming competing alternatives. 

Our method can be applied to multi-layer networks by conducting separate tests for each layer. We evaluate our method through simulations and an empirical analysis, and the corresponding software is freely available online. 

Furthermore, we illustrate the challenge of validating network autoregressive models using a famous empirical example, and provide a method for selecting the best network autoregressive model. 

Finally, we discuss several potential research avenues related to this topic.

The backward pass, crucial for resolving issues like Lipschitz constant calculation and penalty parameter tuning, can sometimes be computationally intensive due to the large size of the Jacobian matrix. Despite this, the forward pass is generally much faster and already computed during the solution of the original problem using a solver. Therefore, we investigate ways to utilize problem structure by leveraging the forward pass results to improve computational performance. Specifically, our study focuses on two approaches: utilizing the Sherman-Morrison rank one update for efficient Jacobian matrix inversion, and applying the Cramer rule for approximate solution recovery. We also examine the impact of these methods on the accuracy of the approximate solution and discuss related pricing strategies within a dynamic framework. Finally, our findings are validated through numerical experiments conducted across various applications. Moreover, our experiments include an interesting extension where the subproblem is defined as an optimal control problem with differential equations being the constraint structure. Interestingly, this subproblem instance exhibits a distinct challenge where the Jacobian matrix cannot be computed directly in a feasible manner, further highlighting the computational benefits derived from our proposed strategies. The mechanics of cells is largely influenced by stress fibers, with the actin cytoskeleton playing a key role. Research has been focused on understanding how individual stress fibers generate mechanical force and contribute to cell behavior. Studies have shown that contractility within stress fibers is the result of actin assembly dynamics, with the underlying mechanism attributed to molecular interactions between actin-binding proteins such as filamin and vinculin. However, the exact mechanism by which these proteins affect actin assembly and influence cell mechanics is not yet fully resolved. In this study, we used combined force and fluorescence measurements to investigate the mechanical properties of single stress fibers in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs). We found significant variability in the mechanical properties of stress fibers, with some exhibiting rigid behavior and others displaying greater deformability. Notably, we found that increasing contractility within stress fibers led to a rise in rigidity, with this effect being influenced by the activity of the Arf6 pathway. Furthermore, we showed that stress fibers with rigid behavior were resistant to disruption by Arf6, with this resistance also seen in stress fibers from MEF cells expressing a constitutively active form of Arf6. Our results highlight the importance of contractility in determining the mechanical properties of single stress fibers and suggest that stress fiber rigidity is influenced by actin assembly dynamics, contractility, and the activity of the Arf6 pathway. Additionally, we propose a multi-scale framework that integrates contractility with the mechanics of stress fiber assembly to better understand cell mechanics. In this framework, stress fibers with rigid behavior are viewed as first-order structures, with further analysis required to fully elucidate the underlying mechanisms. Despite the complexity of cell mechanics, our study provides initial insights, with future research needed to comprehensively explore and validate this new framework. In this work, we have focused on stress fibers; however, we anticipate that this multi-scale approach will also be applicable to other cellular structures and that it may shed light on the mechanical properties of cells in different states of contraction. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the mechanics of stress fibers will lead to greater insight into cell mechanics and contractility, with this knowledge also having the potential to inform and guide the development of bioengineered stress fibers that mimic their natural counterparts. Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin have gained popularity in recent years, yet they are prone to illicit transactions, representing a significant challenge for law enforcement agencies. These agencies can gather valuable information from cryptocurrency transaction graphs, particularly those containing temporal data, but existing research primarily focuses on static graph analysis. In this paper, a novel approach is proposed to study the evolution of cryptocurrency transaction graphs over time by dividing them into equal periods and applying the method of cyclic behavior analysis. This approach identifies patterns of repetition or change within the graphs at an intra-cycle level and also considers longer-term trends up to three cycles. A new metric called the cyclic community similarity (CCS) is introduced to measure the similarity between communities within a graph cycle and is demonstrated to effectively pinpoint suspicious nodes that have evolved over time. The evaluation of the proposed method on real-world data sets shows its capability to detect previously missed illicit transactions and nodes with high accuracy. We propose using reinforcement learning to enhance the performance of quantum error correction by improving decoding algorithms. By leveraging a QAOA-based decoder, we demonstrate how to train a classical policy to optimize the parameter values for each repeat step in the VQE decoder via classical simulations. Our results show that this approach yields significantly lower average error probabilities compared to the standard VQE decoder. Furthermore, we observe that the optimal policy values correlate with the faulty channel's noise level, offering potential guidance for selecting decoding algorithms in various quantum error correction scenarios. While the optimal policy cannot be directly applied to actual quantum experiments due to the need for classical simulation of the encoder's operations, we still see an overall advantage in using the reinforced decoder over the VQE decoder, despite this limitation. Moreover, we find that training the policy is computationally efficient and scales well with growing qubit numbers, offering the potential for tackling more complex codes in the future. However, we also find that the VQE decoder's performance can vary greatly depending on the specific faulty channel, raising questions about the decoder's overall effectiveness in real-world applications. In conclusion, our study showcases the capability of reinforcement learning to enhance the performance of quantum error correction, particularly when combined with variational decoding approaches, and paves the way for exploring additional training environments that could further improve the outcome. Ultimately, this could provide a valuable framework for addressing the fundamental challenge posed by the poor fault-tolerant threshold of most current variational algorithms. As such, this research could play a crucial role in enabling the development of scalable quantum algorithms capable of fully leveraging the capabilities of near-term quantum devices. This could be critical to achieving meaningful outcomes from quantum algorithms in the future. This approach we're investigating could also have implications for controlling the performance of other types of quantum algorithms that rely on similar variational decoding processes. In addition, this study raises interesting questions about the potential applications of reinforcement learning within quantum computing itself, presenting an area worthy of further exploration. This research could also have additional outcomes, and we encourage the broader scientific community to build upon and contribute to this work. Cloud-based high-performance computing (HPC) systems offer cost-effective access to computing resources and address global accessibility concerns. However, these clouds often suffer from high latency and limited bandwidth due to their distance from the end users. Furthermore, other clouds, including federated HPC clouds, integrate systems with varying latency and bandwidth characteristics, complicating application performance prediction. Existing methods fail to accurately forecast application performance and execution times in such environments. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach, APEx, which uses machine learning algorithms to dynamically model application performance based on execution data across different cloud environments. By incorporating online prediction into the model, APEx provides executive decision support for application refactoring, workload management, and future application development. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments involving up to 512 nodes in four different cloud environments. The results show that APEx achieves an average performance prediction error of less than 20% across various environments and applications. Additionally, APEx can incorporate application performance data from as little as one hour to as much as several days. Our approach also exhibits scalability, with all predictions made within the execution time of the application itself. In contextual linear bandits, an agent makes decisions in a varying context and learns the impact on rewards. A recent method, CORRAL, addresses this challenge by minimizing the number of bits needed to understand the context distribution for optimal action selection. However, CORRAL is limited to contexts with low dimensionality. An alternative approach, ContextLCB, focuses on linear combinations of contexts but only considers settings with infinite context space and no confounding variables. In contrast, we introduce an adaptive procedure, AdapLCB, for contextual linear bandits with finite high-dimensional context space and no confounding variables. AdapLBC utilizes a general linear mixture model and a variant of the least squares estimator to estimate the underlying parameters and determines a context subspace with a reduced dimension that allows for efficient context representation, requiring a linear number of bits. Notably, AdapLBC's context representation size is the minimum required to achieve an $\sqrt{d^*/\mathfrak{N}}$ regret bound, where $d^*$ represents the underlying context subspace dimension and $\mathfrak{N}$ is the number of context samples. AdapLBC's context representation size is comparable to or outperforms existing adaptive procedures in various scenarios. In particular, AdapLBC's context representation size is $\mathfrak{N}^{2d^*/(2d^*+1)}$ which is an improvement over ContextLCB's $\mathfrak{N}^{2d^*/(2d^*+2)}$ and nearly optimal when comparing the two. Additionally, AdapLBC's context representation size is $\sqrt{\mathfrak{N}}$ which is an order of magnitude better than CORRAL's $\mathfrak{N}^{1/4}$. AdapLBC's performance is verified through simulations on various context distributions and data structures, including hash tables and k-d trees. An application of AdapLBC is presented in a contextual linear bandit scenario with medical intervention, based on real-world healthcare data. While Scrum methodology is widely used to enhance project success, adopting it in a home-based environment poses unique challenges. Our research explores the connection between working from home and Scrum's effectiveness on project outcomes. By combining a systematic literature review with original survey data from 252 home-based software developers, we found that collaborating from different locations decreases the success of Scrum implementation and project success in general. Nevertheless, we discovered that, contrary to popular belief, working from home does not raise the difficulty of adopting Scrum. Instead, our study indicates that home-based development introduces new challenges which can be addressed by increasing the complexity of Scrum usage. Based on these findings, we propose an adjusted theory of Scrum usage in a home-based environment and identify several factors that influence the success of home-based software development projects. Our study provides a foundation for further research and offers home-based development teams practical guidelines derived from the Scrum best practices. However, it does not provide answers to questions regarding home-based development outside of the software industry context. To validate our research hypotheses, we plan to conduct additional experiments with more diverse participants in the future. By doing so, we aim to refine our model and explore new research directions. Our study is available on arXiv, and we look forward to receiving feedback from the scientific community. Our results can be improved with more data and other methods, and we invite researchers to explore our findings critically. Moreover, we are open to collaborating with researchers from other fields to validate our findings with diverse participants. Until then, our study remains a starting point for further investigation into the Scrum best practices in a home-based environment. Our study is currently available on arXiv, and we invite the scientific community to review our research and provide feedback before we plan to share the results with the broader industry audience.

In policy learning, using efficient value function estimates has proven beneficial, especially when combined with a model, by enabling the learning of policies from a limited number of samples. However, the impact of batch size in testing has not been extensively explored. Our research delves into this aspect, investigating how batch size affects the performance of various sampling methods in an actor-critic policy learning setting using a learned model. We discovered that, surprisingly, smaller batch sizes can lead to more accurate and efficient value function estimates, which in turn, result in improved policy performance. To further understand this phenomenon, we analyzed the performance of different sampling methods across various batch sizes, identifying that a method previously thought suboptimal actually achieves comparable results with an efficient sampling method when given a specific batch size. This study presents charged hadron, pion, kaon, and proton transverse momentum distributions in Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 2.76 TeV and 5.02 TeV. Initially, we observed that the distributions of positive and negative charged hadrons exhibit similar patterns in both examined energy levels. Furthermore, investigations into the transverse momentum distributions of pions, kaons, and protons uncovered distinct trends, with heavier mesons displaying higher normalized yields than expected at low transverse momenta. Additionally, our data analysis revealed variations in the elliptic flow coefficient for various particles in different transverse momentum ranges, which can be used to inform theoretical models. By comparing our data from 2.76 TeV and 5.02 TeV, we found relatively small dependencies on center-of-mass energy in mid-central Pb-Pb collisions at these energy levels. Our findings also enable comparisons with existing theoretical models, such as perturbative QCD, and offer new insights into the behavior of hadrons in high-energy heavy ion collisions. Notably, our results on charged hadron and pion elliptic flow at 5.02 TeV contribute to validations of event shape engineering techniques and help inform the interpretation of existing and future experiments in heavy ion and quark-gluon plasma research. Lastly, our study sets the stage for more in-depth analysis of particle spectra and elliptic flow in heavy ion collisions at the LHC.

This advancement effectively diminishes the possible range for the values of x and y by one, according to Yang's classification, thus necessitating the supplementary proof of existence for a new pair of values within the narrowed parameters. The resulting pair $(x_0,y_0)$, obtained through our method, holds the characteristic that $x_0$ is equal to $y_0$ for the first time in the sequence. A further mathematical manipulation allows us to derive the relationship between $x_0$ and $y_0$, with $x_0$ equating to three and $y_0$ equating to two. A subsequent examination is carried out to establish that our novel solution ($x_0, y_0$) represents the solitary instance within the broader domain of natural numbers, as evidenced by the application of a recent breakthrough by Kyoudo and Tominaga in 2021. Consequently, this novel solution ($x_0, y_0$) effectively equals the only existing pair of values within the specified range, as confirmed by Yang's prior study. A further extension of this existing knowledge enables us to broaden the scope from base seven to any randomly selected base 'a' for a specific polynomial equation, with the constraint that the base 'a' is greater than or equal to $\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$. Using lattice QCD, our research calculates the charge radii of mesons made of heavy quarks, specifically the $\eta_c$, $\Jpsi$, $\eta_b$, and $\Upsilon$ mesons. By analyzing the correlation between twisted momentum states in the spatial plane, we determine the magnetic susceptibility of each meson, which is directly related to its charge radius. Lattice enzymes are used to calculate the correlation functions. Two distinct ensembles of lattices are utilized: one generated by the $2$ geometric method and the other by the fermion action known as "IFR". Our results for the square of charge radii are expressed in units of the lattice spacing and the energy of each meson's mass. We have also derived the mass of each meson from its energy, allowing for a comparison of our results with existing data. Our study employs three distinct methods to analyze the correlation functions. The first method employs the "2$-point function" method, the second method uses the "twisted-mass" chirality and the third method uses the "IFR" action. All three methods yield comparable results for the square of the charge radius, which range from $0.189$ to $0.194 \rm{fm}^2$ for the $\eta_c$ meson and $0.0378$ to $0.0394 \rm{fm}^2$ for the $\Upsilon$ meson. Notably, our calculations for the $\eta_c$ and $\Jpsi$ mesons indicate a charge radius that is roughly $5$ times smaller than the charged meson $K^*$. Additionally, our study finds the charge radius of the $\eta_b$ meson to be comparable to that of the $\Upsilon$ meson. In contrast, the charge radius of the $\Jpsi$ meson is substantially smaller than that of the $\eta_b$ meson, which can be attributed to the differing spin structures of these mesons. Our study provides a initial assessment of the charge radii of these heavy quark mesons, which is crucial for further research aimed at understanding the hadron structure through deep inelastic scattering processes. Ultimately, our study sets the stage for more precise calculations that can directly compare with experimental data as accuracy improves with the advancement of computational power and lattice resolution.

This paper examines how a droplet's movement affects the transfer of heat and mass, as it oscillates through a surrounding gas. By using the Levy method, even large deformations can be accounted for in the droplet's shape. The influence of these deformations on mass and heat transfer is then studied in various fluid dynamics regimes. In the limiting case of small deformations, an analytical solution is compared with the Levy approach to reveal their equivalence. Conversely, when considering moderate to significant droplet movements, computational fluid dynamics becomes the most suitable method for analyzing the resulting complex fluid dynamics. A parameter-based analysis, encompassing both incompressible and compressible gases, is consequently employed to identify the premier approach for factoring in the droplet's shape and movement. Ultimately, this study positions the Levy method as the ideal framework for integrating droplet shape and movement into multi-dimensional code implementations. A key advancement of this work is an explicit algorithm for calculating droplet temperature and composition from level-set data. A key application of this research is high-fuel-loading gas generators for Small Modular Reactors. Notably, this study has implications for enhancing heat transfer in droplet-based fuel systems. By understanding how droplet movements influence mass and heat transfer, potential efficiency gains can be identified and investigated. One such potential gain is the ability to operate at higher fuel loads by managing droplet movements. Another potential gain is the ability to utilize lower volatility fuels. One such fuel is acetylene (C2H2), which has been challenging to handle in gas turbines due to its low volatility. A parametric analysis of mass transfer from stationary and moving acetylene droplets in air at 20 bar and 200 K shows that, despite its lower volatility, acetylene can be handled efficiently if droplet movements are managed. The "not" marker serves numerous purposes in language, making it challenging to pinpoint a single, unified definition for negation. Despite this complexity, research has focused mainly on one aspect - negating - and has left other functions of "not" unexplored. In contrast, our study delves into an often-overlooked aspect of negation, specifically in the context of expressing doubt or uncertainty, particularly in relation to medical text. To investigate this, we created a dataset of negative sentences without a clear negation component and applied it to evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art models that have previously demonstrated success in more straightforward negation-based tasks, such as identifying negation spans and determining negation scope. Notably, our findings reveal a significant performance gap between these models and human judgment on this new task, with an F-score of 0.40 compared to the medical community's actual performance of 0.90. To further examine this discrepancy, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the errors made by these models and found issues like misclassifying doubt as confirmation and vice versa, largely due to their failure to incorporate contextual elements that human interpreters take for granted. To enhance the accuracy, we experimented with augmenting the training data with contextual features, such as the negation span itself, but surprisingly, this had a negative impact and instead propose a simpler yet more effective approach - using a character-level encoder. Our results show a notable improvement with this change, closing the performance gap between humans and machines by half, with an F-score of 0.60, and highlight the potential for similar techniques to be successful in other complex NLP tasks. Additionally, our work raises important questions about the current state of medical language understanding, highlights the challenges posed by the "not" marker, and calls for a more comprehensive study of this aspect of language. HDTM excels in tackling these complexities by establishing relationships between topics across different documents in the network. Through comparative evaluations using well-known datasets from research domains, HDTM consistently outperformed both Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Correlated Topic Model in terms of topic coherence. A case analysis of the model revealed that topics derived from HDTM tend to be more coherent and less diverse than those from non-hierarchical models. Additionally, topic hierarchies generated by HDTM facilitate the identification of key topics at the network level that can be absent in single-document models. To provide network-level topic insights, we introduced a method to summarize topic hierarchies in an intuitive and visual way. Quantum annealing is a method for solving combinatorial optimization problems, though its effectiveness can vary due to the annealing gap. To improve this process, it's essential to understand the origins of the annealing gap. One major obstacle in quantum annealing is quantum noise, which disrupts the coherent application of perturbation theory and results in an enlarged annealing gap. This study investigates how noise level and annealing schedule influence the annealing gap in quantum annealing. We examine multiple types of noise with diverse correlation properties and find that the annealing gap is heavily influenced by these correlations. As a result, the shape of the energy spectrum and the relevant diagonal and non-diagonal perturbation orders play critical roles in the annealing gap in the presence of noise. This leads to the possibility of closing the annealing gap through careful scheduling and noise management, even in the presence of strong noise. This could potentially be achieved by identifying and targeting specific quantum states that facilitate efficient combinatorial optimization. This research was conducted using quantum annealing on a finite Ising chain with a semi-Pauli X interaction and two commonly used noise sources: amplitude damping and Pauli X noise. The findings provide valuable insights into optimizing quantum annealing, particularly in relation to scheduling and noise management. This could be particularly relevant in broader applications of quantum computing, such as the development of better simulation methods and more effective quantum algorithms. In this case, understanding the annealing gap requires a deep comprehension of quantum systems and the effects of noise, best realized through the use of full quantum trajectories. This approach goes beyond conventional chemistry-based approaches, such as Monte Carlo simulations, by incorporating the coherent evolution of quantum systems and the impacts of noise on annealing schedules. Ultimately, this research offers a framework for investigating the annealing gap in complex systems and could be adapted for the development of new quantum algorithms and the identification of critical quantum states in combinatorial optimization problems. This could ultimately lead to the creation of more effective scheduling and noise management protocols in quantum annealing. This research was conducted using the D-Wave Q 2000 quantum annealer and the D-Wave Cancer simulator, in collaboration with D-Wave Systems. In process execution analysis, a technique called alignment is utilized to compare two usage scenarios. However, standard alignments may not effectively capture the relationships between method calls in modern, object-oriented programs. Infix and postfix notations offer alternative visualizations of execution paths, which can provide more accurate representations of method call sequences. However, implementing these notations for comparing usage scenarios involves determining the structure of the control flow graph for each method call. A set of rules is then applied to ensure the correctness of these implementations in a programming language based on ML-like specifications. Our results demonstrate that these implementations enable effective comparison of usage scenarios, enabling the identification of bottlenecks in process execution. A demonstration of the proposed techniques is also accessible online. Our implementation of infix and postfix alignments is part of the PaPER tool, which is publicly available at https://paper.informatik.uni-rostock.de/. In addition, a demonstration of our approach can be found at https://paper.informatik.uni-rostock.de/demo-sca-2022/.

Recently, a series of experiments have been conducted on well-characterized, epitaxial layers of nickelates, specifically study the unusual band structures in these materials despite extensive theoretical analysis. The findings from band structure measurements have been incorporated into a comprehensive framework that suggests that strong correlations, mixed valence, and orbital selection are central features of nickelate band structures. A systematic examination across various nickelates has been performed to identify key elements of the band structure that contribute to magnetic and superconducting behavior. Notably, a commonality between the nickelates that exhibit superconductivity is the presence of an anticrossed band featuring in-gap states at the Fermi level, and we demonstrate that this feature is also present in the band structure of hole-doped nickelates, despite initial misinterpretation. Furthermore, our study shows that the band structure of electron-doped nickelates can be adjusted through layer thickness, with thinner layers displaying the desired in-gap state within the Fermi level. Ultimately, our framework positions the research community to explore and understand the intricate relationships between material properties, electronic structure, and phase behavior in the diverse class of nickelates.

This paper investigates decay rates for solutions to the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak singularities in the collision kernel, specifically when the singularity is greater than or equal to two. By leveraging Fourier multi-resolution techniques and prior estimates, we obtain upper and lower bounds for time-scales of decay, which exhibit sensitivity to the spectrum of the linearized operator and the singularity of the collision kernel. Notably, when the singularity is two, we find that decay rates are comparable to those of the grassmannian Boltzmann equation, which features an $N^2$ time-scale. In contrast, when the singularity is greater than two, we observe an $N^\delta$ time-scale, with $\delta$ varying continuously between one and two as the singularity crosses the critical point of two. Finally, we validate our analytical findings with numerical simulations, further illustrating the phenomenon of decaying solutions exhibiting wild behavior at higher wavenumbers. Ultimately, this research suggests that the wild behavior observed in solutions to the full non-cutoff Boltzmann equation may stem from its linearized counterpart. In this regard, we identify potential avenues for exploring additional mathematical issues surrounding the wild behavior phenomenon. The spread of infectious diseases such as COVID-19, along with their psychological impacts, poses a significant threat to individuals and the economy.  Social media platforms like Twitter play a crucial role in disseminating opinions and health-related information, making their proper management even more crucial.  Maintaining public confidence through positive social media discussions can be instrumental in reducing the pandemic's adverse effects.  Consequently, accurate Twitter data analysis is necessary to inform strategic public health interventions.  In this study, a multi-step approach utilizing machine learning techniques is employed to effectively classify and predict the content of Twitter posts.  Initially, the data is labeled based on designated health-related topics and sentiment categories.  Next, ensembles of decision trees were trained to accurately classify and predict user engagement metrics such as retweets and likes.  Our comprehensive experiments using real-world COVID-19 related Twitter data demonstrated the efficacy of these methods in a relatively dynamic environment.  Notably, the incorporation of topic modeling techniques like Latent Dirichlet Analysis allowed us to develop sophisticated machine learning models that consider semantic aspects of Twitter posts, thereby enhancing their performance.  Our analysis also revealed valuable actionable insights that can be utilized by social media platforms, online communities, and marketing organizations to enhance user engagement.  All source code necessary to replicate our experiments is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/abhishek9306/COVID19_Twitter_Analytics.  In conclusion, the methods presented in this paper can serve as a foundation for the comprehensive analysis of Twitter data in various applications, particularly those involving public health issues.  Future research directions are also outlined, including the incorporation of sequential machine learning techniques and better handling of missing data to further improve the methods' performance.  As one of the many consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic is the increased reliance on social media for information, it is more crucial than ever to develop these analytical methods.  Ultimately, the code developed from this research can be utilized in conjunction with other machine learning techniques to promote the safe usage of Twitter during public health crises.  As the pandemic continues to evolve and pose significant challenges to the healthcare system, more extensive studies are necessary to equip healthcare systems with actionable data that can inform strategic interventions.  Furthermore, the methods presented in this paper have implications for the analysis of Twitter data in other applications, such as community management, online marketing, and crisis management. A unified theory has yet to explain the diverse behavior of cuprate superconductors, which depends significantly on the average intralayer and interlayer couplings. Notably, the interlayer coupling in these compounds is relatively weak, with a characteristic energy of around 0.1 eV, compared to the strong intralayer coupling with a characteristic energy of about 5 eV. A crucial observation in cuprates is that the superconducting transition typically occurs when the interlayer coupling is strong enough to bridge a gap of around 4k_B T_c, which lies in the range of 20-40 K. A key finding of our study is that when the interlayer coupling is adjusted to this optimal level in a microscopic model, the resulting phase diagram exhibits a notable similarity to that of an actual cuprate, with an s-wave symmetry and a critical temperature that scales with the interlayer coupling strength. However, increasing the intralayer coupling beyond its already high base level in these systems makes the superconductivity more stable, but at the cost of destroying the s-wave symmetry. In contrast, the s-wave symmetry can be restored through additional symmetry-breaking intralayer couplings, which do not affect the interlayer coupling. A major implication of our study is that the interlayer coupling, long considered a minor force in cuprates, plays a crucial role in the superconducting transition, and that the intralayer coupling, though very strong, can be adjusted to some extent in experimental systems through the application of varying external pressures, strains, and chemical doping. Our research suggests that the long-standing problem of the varying phase diagrams of cuprates may ultimately be an issue of "tuning liability" induced by the strong intralayer coupling in these systems, which could have significant consequences for our understanding of the physics and the development of new, more effective strategies for discovering and stabilizing high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates and other systems. Our study also highlights the significance of interlayer coupling in layered materials and highlights the need for a more comprehensive reevaluation of its influence in these systems. Our research offers a fresh perspective on the physics of cuprates and provides a foundation for further theoretical and experimental investigation into the fundamental role of interlayer coupling in these systems. In addition, our study presents a new general framework for analyzing and comparing the behavior of systems with multiple coupling layers in systems with strong intralayer coupling, such as transition metal dichalcogenides, organic superconductors, and heavy-fermion superconductors

However, many applications require associating weight values with the nodes of these trees, leading to the need to identify the highest-weight structure that meets a particular criterion. In the case of unordered trees, computing the maximum-weight Tai mapping or anti-Tai mapping represents a critical step towards achieving this goal, although this process involves a computationally expensive iteration of $O(n^4)$ for trees containing n nodes. Our research aims to enhance the efficiency of this process by a factor of $n^2$, enabling the computation of exact maximum-weight Tai or anti-Tai mapping values for trees with over one thousand nodes. Additionally, our approach allows for the derivation of closed-form expressions that capture the computational complexity of this process. To assess the accuracy of damping parameters in optomechanical metrology using a compass state, a detailed analysis of the state's number variance is crucial. In this study, we examine how increasing the photon variance in the compass state affects its ability to determine unknown damping parameters. Specifically, we investigate the relationship between the variance of the compass state and its metrological performance. Our findings indicate that while increasing the variance up to a certain point improves the compass state's ability to estimate certain damping parameters, its ability to determine other parameters is impaired. This behavior is demonstrated through a full end-to-end simulation, involving an optomechanical system and a coherent laser source. The results show that the compass state's ability to estimate certain damping parameters is limited by its non-classical characteristics, and that this limitation can be an advantage in certain applications. However, the compass state may not always provide the most accurate measurements in all scenarios, and other states with higher variance may offer better performance in certain cases. In addition, the results indicate that the optimal optomechanical gain should be adjusted in proportion to the variance of the state used, in order to achieve the highest possible accuracy in damping parameter estimation. The study also explores the impact of laser amplitude noise on the compass state's ability to estimate damping parameters, and finds that while this noise has a limited effect on the system's performance, it does influence the optimal optomechanical gain required. The findings provide valuable insights into the design of optomechanical metrology systems, particularly when using non-classical states such as the compass state. The study's results are highly relevant to a wide range of applications involving the measurement of damping parameters in optomechanical systems, including the detection of Dampener malfunctions in parameter estimation problems related to feedback control systems. The research may also contribute to the development of new, sensitive methods for detecting tiny changes in the morphology of materials at microscopic scales. In this context, the study's results may pave the way for the exploration of new, high-variance states such as 'compass states' in optomechanical systems, offering better accuracy in detecting minor alterations in a system's morphology. The study's findings are achieved through a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, and the associated code is publicly available for replication of the results presented. Our research demonstrates that, under certain standardized growth constraints, the set of harmonic functions on a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton forms a closed subspace. Furthermore, this harmonic subspace is concave and its dimension is at most half the dimension of the underlying space. Our findings also establish that, when the growth of harmonic functions exceeds a certain threshold, they must be constant. Alongside these results, we establish a connection between the dimension of harmonic functions and their growth rates, which may be of interest in their own right. Lastly, our study implies that, within the context of a complete, non-compact gradient shrinking Ricci soliton with harmonic function growth exceeding a specific threshold, a compact subset must be isolated by a constant harmonic function. While they have achieved notable success, constructing and testing trigger-based backdoors on complex tasks like the MNIST handwritten recognition has proven difficult. Existing approaches to creating backdoors on such tasks typically rely on training from scratch or employ sophisticated neural networks with high memory requirements. In contrast, our research aims to develop and test a stealthy, adaptable backdoor on various classification tasks using pre-trained models. To accomplish this, we've modified existing methods for creating hidden agendas to use a method called Label Masking, which allows us to build and test a hidden agenda on the CIFAR-10, MNIST, and German Traffic Signs datasets using pre-trained models with good accuracy. Notably, our research shows that both neural network triggers and label-based triggers can fail in certain situations, resulting in clean triggering and incorrect classification. An intriguing phenomenon in precision astrometry is the apparent variation of proper motion with ecliptic latitude. Researchers attribute this to a distortion of astrometric measurements caused by nearby giant stars in the Galactic bar. A key prediction of this theory is that the parallax of stars with high ecliptic latitudes should increase beyond a certain point. Although this effect has been seen in data from the Spitzer and Gaia missions, it remains relatively subtle. In the search for larger examples, we examined a sample of 1769 T-Tauri candidates from the Gaia archive, focusing particularly on objects at extremely high ecliptic latitudes ($\gtrsim 60^{\circ}$). Using Gaia's position, we identified nearby stars that could cause the observed effects and eliminated candidates with nearby stars that could induce the predicted parallax shift ($\Delta\pi \sim 5$ mas). A larger population with enhanced parallax is then expected in the remaining candidates. We found that our selection process yields a population with a bar-like parallax distribution, likely due to the presence of the Galactic bar. A linear fit to these distributions shows a notable increase in parallax with ecliptic latitude, consistent with predictions ($\Delta\pi = 5.45\pm 0.76$ mas per $10^{\circ}$ of ecliptic latitude). Notably, this effect is observed in close-by and distant T-Tauri stars alike. The increased parallax in these objects exacerbates the scattering of proper motion with ecliptic latitude. We estimate the mass of the bar causing this effect to be in the range of $3.2\times 10^{5}$ to $6.4\times 10^{5} M_{\odot}$, and suggest that the completion of a full barry rotation will allow for more precise measurements of the bar's mass and shape. Ultimately, we expect that the upcoming generation of astrometric missions will be capable of resolving individual stars within the Galactic bar. As a result, we expect that a more detailed analysis of the observed parallax shift will provide even greater insight into the mass distribution and structural characteristics of the Galactic bar.

This paper introduces cutting-edge algorithms for approximating small-scale nonlinear models under specific input conditions, specifically the Reduced Order Model (ROM) method. Although the Galerkin method has been the traditional choice for nonlinear model reduction, it becomes computationally expensive when the number of degrees of freedom is large. In contrast, the new methods enhance the ROM's efficiency by narrowing down the dominant modes for a given input, and can be applied directly to systems without a separation of variables. We demonstrate two novel approaches, both derived from linear subspace methods, that offer faster computations and simpler implementations compared to the standard methods. The methods also provide mode approximations that can be utilized in a linear operator-based integration framework, resulting in highly effective model reduction. We evaluate and compare the methods with each other and the Galerkin method on a linear example and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, a nonlinear benchmark case. Notably, the new methods outperform the Galerkin method in terms of accuracy and computational speed. Additionally, we showcase that one of the new methods yields an exceptionally simple and highly efficient approximation method, achieving a notable improvement of over two orders of magnitude in computational speed while maintaining comparable accuracy. In conclusion, we believe these novel methods will significantly contribute to the nonlinear model reduction field, offering faster, more accurate, and more feasible alternatives to existing methods, particularly for complex systems and in real-time applications. Furthermore, this study lays the groundwork for utilizing these methods in data-driven reduction frameworks. In such an environment, we would like to employ these methods to identify compact expressions for nonlinear functions represented by sparse data sets, a crucial aspect that deserves separate investigation. Ultimately, we hope this study will pave the way for a more efficient, general-purpose data-driven nonlinear model reduction framework. In a Bose-Einstein condensate composed of two interacting components, we find that opposite interactions can produce solitons with contrary effective masses at zero resonance. These solitons can either be stable or prone to instability. A theoretical model is employed to analyze the solitons' behavior in a cavity bounded by highly reflective mirrors. We explore how interactions affecting solitons with positive and negative effective masses differ. Additionally, we investigate how these differences are impacted by photon loss and phase shifts that occur when the solitons move between the condensate and the cavity fields. Our research reveals that the solitons' motion is governed by an effective classical mechanics equation, modified by an extra term that takes into account the Berry phase effect, when the two-component condensate is subjected to an oscillating magnetic field. This results in the precession of solitons with positive effective mass and a different response from those with negative effective mass. We also identify an appropriate loss regime where solitons with opposite effective masses behave distinctively and can exist side by side. Our research provides a foundation for understanding the dynamics of the 'dual' solitons in two-component Bose-Einstein condensates.
