When propelling through a viscoelastic medium like non-Newtonian fluid, helical swimmers may encounter opposition due to the reversal of the medium's viscosity as they change direction during their loop. This phenomenon, where the swimmer's progress is hindered as it moves forward is illustrated by a "snowman effect," in which the forward loop shrinks as the backward loop enlarges. Our study investigates how this effect impacts swimmers consisting of rigid helices by integrating them into a Bingham fluid and analyzes the impact of the medium's yield stress on helical swimmers of varying dimensions and shapes through a new scaling for their locomotive behavior. Yield stress is shown to significantly influence helical swimmers in the low-Reynolds number regime even for larger swimmers, where it impairs their ability to generate torque as they traverse the loop, thus hindering their progress. Furthermore, our research reveals that the optimal design for helical swimmers in a Bingham fluid involves longer, thinner helices which are more adept at navigating the medium when powered by low Reynolds numbers. Our findings also indicate that the snowman effect has an undesirable impact on helical swimmers and that their efficiency could be enhanced through additional propulsion mechanisms that exploit the medium's turbulence to generate extra torque. However, our study also highlights that such efficiency gains may be difficult to achieve due to the helix's dimensions and shape. Overall, our analysis emphasizes the significance of considering the interactions between swimmer, loop, and fluid when analyzing helical swimmers in non-Newtonian fluids. This study explores how the Hamming distance from optimal solutions evolves during a cooperative co-evolutionary genetic algorithm, particularly focusing on a scenario where two agents learn through experience and have distinct learning approaches. Our research reveals that the Hamming distance from the optimal solution is independent of the number of generations in the social learning case, whereas it varies significantly in the individual learning case. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the expected Hamming distance from the optimal solution can be influenced by the probability of selecting the best available solution during the social learning process. However, this expected Hamming distance is determined by the equilibrium point reached by the co-evolutionary process, which is stable and resistant to changes in the population size. Consequently, the Hamming distance from the optimal solution is similar across both individual and social learning cases after a sufficient number of generations. Notably, converging to the optimal solution is observed even when the social learning approach involves learning from an individual who is themselves learning. Additionally, the rate of convergence is impacted by the population size in the social learning case. Our results also demonstrate that the social learning approach can lead to faster convergence to the optimal solution, especially when the probability of making an incorrect mutation is high, and that this is because the equilibrium point reached by the social learning approach has a shorter Hamming distance from the optimal solution. However, it is essential to note that these findings are specific to the particular fitness function and Hamming distance metric used in this study. Hence, future research is required to fully understand the implications of social learning in cooperative co-evolutionary algorithms across a wide range of scenarios. This study assumes that the fitness function values are encoded as integers from 0 to 1, but the code provided is adaptable for use with different data types. Moreover, potential applications of this research are identified, and suggestions are offered for expanding this work to consider additional types of learning dynamics, fitness functions with multiple objectives, and the inclusion of noise in data. The source code developed for this study has been made publicly accessible, and it is feasible to conduct the analysis with either the supplied code or by utilizing the included instructions to replicate the methods themselves. Nevertheless, replicating the results depends on the parameters and algorithms employed. Consequently, it would be advantageous to incorporate the underlying code into the supplementary materials to facilitate easier replication of the results presented. Nevertheless, it is not compulsory to do so, and alternatives to reproduce the code and results are also acceptable. In any case, it is crucial to adhere to the guidelines established by the journal in this regard

The main objective of this research is to develop an innovative method using Bidirectional LSTMs for extracting fundamental security concepts from written information. Despite the success of deep learning in addressing complex problems, many existing approaches to concept extraction still rely on traditional techniques such as rule-based systems and hidden Markov models. Our proposed model leverages Bidirectional LSTMs to address the limitations of prior methods in addressing this issue, specifically their inability to handle contextual information and sentence-level knowledge. We evaluated our concept extraction system on a publicly available dataset containing antispam policies, achieving a notable improvement in overall accuracy of 2.2% when compared to the current best performer. Furthermore, our results showed that our Bidirectional LSTM-based method outperformed other baseline systems using hidden Markov models and support vector machines. The extracted concepts demonstrated a high average precision of 83.6%. Additionally, we observed that using contextual information increased average precision by 3.6%. All code and data used in this research are available for replication purposes. It can also be applied to other domain-specific concept extraction tasks with minimal adjustments. We introduce a one-dimensional mixed opinion formation model where both Ising and XY type interactions are present and the order parameters can be either magnetic (magnetization) or angular (tilt). The model consists of alternating Ising and XY spins positioned on a lattice. The objective of the study is to analyze the static and dynamic behavior of this mixed-spin system by comparing it with its pure Ising or XY spin counterparts. The model exhibits a wide range of behavior and its characteristics vary significantly based on the type of interaction and the order parameter in question. A particular subset of the model, specifically a two-state Ising system with both nearest and next-nearest neighbor interactions, has been extensively simulated using Monte Carlo methods and the results have been found to match exactly with available numerical data and theoretical predictions from the series expansion method, giving us a high level of confidence in the accuracy of these simulations. One notable observation made during the study is that the magnetization of the system can exhibit multiple domain formation when the external magnetic field is insufficient, and this phenomenon does not occur in pure Ising or XY spin systems under similar conditions. The availability of exact domain wall free energy for one-dimensional systems has enabled the derivation of the disorder line in the phase diagram and the confirmation of the predicted disorder state.
The final stage of this study involves the Monte Carlo simulation of the full mixed model where the disorder line has been found and the results have indicated that the model exhibits an unexpected phase with multiple domain formation where the order parameter has a non-zero value; this has also been confirmed through the analysis of umbrella sampling. The movement from the disorder state to the phase with multiple domain formations has been found to occur through a first-order transition, and this has been further supported by the observation of two distinct populations of domains with different order parameter values existing simultaneously within the system during this transition. The possibility of applying this model to the study of opinion formation among people with diverse and conflicting views has also been explored and discussed. The proposed model can be seen as a bridge between traditional opinion formation models and spin structure models. Although the full mixed model has been the primary focus of this study, the spin structure model has been used as a starting point and the results have been compared with available numerical data and theoretical predictions for its pure variants. The possibility of generalizing this study to higher dimensional lattices has also been considered and discussed. The Monte Carlo simulation results for a three-dimensional mixed model have indicated that the multiple domain formation phenomenon occurs only on two-dimensional lattices. Due to limited access to COVID-19 patients for experimental studies, researchers have been primarily relying on modeling approaches. A notable physical method for studying transmission dynamics involves observing liquid droplet behavior under gravity, as it mimics COVID-19 saliva droplets. However, existing studies have been limited by poor size control of droplets, leading to mixed results. We address this issue by producing uniform droplets of various sizes in different environmental conditions, revealing how air temperature and humidity significantly impact their behavior. These findings have implications for understanding COVID-19 transmission and potential measures to reduce its spread. In particular, they suggest that large droplets pose a significant infection risk, especially in transition stages, and that different environmental conditions may increase the transmission risk in various settings. Through both mathematical analysis and practical applications, this study demonstrates the value of using neural networks for resolving inverse problems and highlights the importance of validating models on data with varying levels of uncertainty to ensure their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. This concept is particularly relevant in areas like computer vision, magnetic resonance imaging, and control systems, among others. By better understanding how neural networks behave in uncertain environments, we can develop more precise models and improve their ability to handle complex inverse problems. This study examines edge ideals in weighted oriented graphs, particularly focusing on the equality between ordinary and symbolic power properties of these ideals. Our findings extend previous results by M. Charvey, P. Haous, B. Koch, and S. Morey, providing a deeper understanding of the equality between ordinary and symbolic powers of edge ideals in a broader framework. Our research also explores new properties and proofs of this equality, addressing specific cases such as graph equalities, free resolutions, and Hilbert series. Additionally, our work identifies new weighted oriented graphs with equal ordinary and symbolic power properties of their edge ideals. Lastly, our study concludes with implications for future research in this area.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking technique to safeguard neural networks from the adverse effects of data corruption. The frequent strategy of limiting output ranges may lead to rare, undetected data alterations causing significant issues. We tackle this problem by introducing a non-uniform data validation function that restricts input values according to their position within a specified range. This approach ensures that even infrequently occurring input samples with corrupted data are kept in check, thereby preventing silent data breaches. We demonstrate the feasibility of our method through two validation functions based on logarithmic and polynomial characteristics, and validate its effectiveness with two prominent datasets and a range of corruption levels. The results show that our technique is highly effective in preventing silent data breaches at a minimal computational cost. Moreover, we found that our method has only a negligible impact on the accuracy of the protected neural networks. We have made our code and dataset available for replication purposes. Additionally, we have explored the additional benefit of our method in reducing the requirement for excessively large datasets when training neural networks. Our findings suggest that our non-uniform data validation technique is a valuable tool with numerous advantages and can be an important addition to current data validation techniques. It has the potential to be an important addition to current defense strategies against data corruption in neural networks.

Researchers in economics utilize graph theory to analyze market structures and trading systems. Specifically, the method of finding the minimum weight perfect matching within a graph has been employed to model the optimal arrangement of netting, or settling of financial transactions, with notable applications at major financial institutions. However, the recent shift towards continuous netting, combined with an increasing number of traders and transactions, necessitates a re-examination of current practices. In this paper, we investigate how graph algorithms can help streamline netting processes and provide optimal solutions, even in large-scale scenarios, through the development of efficient new methods and the exploration of existing graph-matching algorithms. A key insight from our analysis is the identification of a smaller subgraph that enables faster minimum weight perfect matching, enabling the periodic re-computation of optimal netting arrangements even in large-scale markets. Furthermore, we outline practical applications and suggest possible improvements, including the integration of new trading models and the utilization of parallel computing. Ultimately, we conclude that a combination of graph algorithms and industry expertise holds significant potential to tackle the complex challenges of netting in modern financial markets. This research is preliminary and raises important questions for further exploration in the field of algorithmic trading. This new basis exhibits a remarkable invariance when subjected to the simple Jordanian twist. This study proposes a novel framework for name-tagging in low-resource languages, 
which makes use of the structural knowledge inherent in written forms of names found 
within high-resource languages, such as English. To achieve this, we develop an 
entirely automatic method for extracting name patterns from English, which forms the 
basis of the desired name tags in low-resource languages. This name-pattern-based 
approach improves upon existing methods that rely solely on character-level sequences 
by incorporating a graph-based neural network. Furthermore, to overcome the 
lack of labeled data in low-resource settings, we employ self-supervised training 
within a cycle of encode, mask, and decode. Our proposed framework is 'zero-labeled'
which means no labeled data is needed either for the low or high-resource languages. 
This approach ultimately achieves a 6.5% improvement in F1-score on Xhosa NameTagging 
dataset which has no labeled data available. This method also demonstrates a 10.5% 
F1-score improvement on Basque name-tagging dataset which has limited labeled data 
available, in comparison to the current state-of-the-art model which is a multi-layer 
BERT model with labeled data. This 'zero-labeled' name-tagging approach may serve as 
a starting point for other low-resource language name-tagging tasks. The name patterns 
extracted from English also provide a solid theoretical foundation for the target language 
and can be utilized in conjunction with other data enrichment techniques. This research 
is the first to explore zero-labeled name-tagging in low-resource settings, and it makes 
the extracted name patterns for six African languages and one European language available 
for other researchers to further develop these settings. This work is open to feedback 
and can be found at this link https://github.com/Abdullah-x77/Zero-Label-Name-Tagging.

The initial production rates of various particles with different masses were measured in lead-lead collisions at an energy of 2.76 TeV and lead-lead collisions at an energy of 5.02 TeV by the ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC. These measurements were conducted via mid-rapidity data analysis and took into account the particle production in centrality-dependent ranges for the 2.76 TeV data set. Results for particle-over-nucleon ratios in central collisions demonstrated an intriguing dependence on collision energy. A notable finding was the observed similarity between particle production rates in more peripheral collisions at 2.76 TeV and those in central collisions at 5.02 TeV. Furthermore, results for different collision systems and energies suggested that the produced particle yields are influenced by the initial conditions and collective behavior of the medium formed in these high-energy collisions. A detailed comparison with lower-energy experiments revealed that particle production rates in heavy-ion collisions exhibit an interesting dependence on collision energy, displaying an increase at intermediate energies and then stabilizing at high energies. To facilitate comparison with theoretical models, initial production rates were adjusted to account for hadronization and kinetic freeze-out processes. Adjusted initial production rates were found to be more sensitive to collision energy and system size at mid-rapidity. In peripheral lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV and in central proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV, the initial production rates of pions and anti-protons demonstrated a notable increase above baseline trends observed in lower-energy experiments. The growth of public dataset repositories accelerates model learning from vast amounts of data, but it also facilitates the spread of false information. Presently, creating models that resist the impact of falsely labeled data during training remains an unresolved issue. In this study, we investigate how falsely labeled data affects the development of dialogue state tracking systems. Our findings suggest that even a small proportion of falsely labeled data significantly degrades model performance. To mitigate this effect, we propose a method using logical connections between dialogue history, state, and actions to resist the influence of falsely labeled data. Experimental results indicate that our approach not only enhances robustness to false labels but also offers a 5.0% improvement in overall model accuracy compared to standard training methods. Moreover, our method achieves a 5.8% reduction in error rate on the challenging MultiWOZ 2.1 dataset. Our code and model are available for public access at this link.

The prototype model employed in this study is based on the BERT4DT system described by Chen et. al. in 2019. It incorporates four important components: dialogue state tracker, action executor, state generator, and dataset cleaner.

*   Comparison of training models with clean and noisy data on the small-scale dataset, WikiWOZ.
*   Validation of the proposed method on the MultiWOZ dataset, specifically 2.1 and 5.1 variants.

The results show that even a relatively small amount of noisy data significantly degrades model performance. Although the primary hippocampal grid code is thought to be an intrinsic brain function, recent evidence suggests it can be shaped by external auditory cues. Our study used local two-photon optogenetic interference to examine the influence of these cues on rat hippocampal grid cells in vitro. When the grid pattern formed in response to auditory cues was disrupted by local light stimulation, the grid cells readjusted their pattern to align with the cues, despite being trapped in a conflicting environment. Moreover, the grid cells' ability to do so depended on the strength of the optogenetic interference. Our findings indicate that auditory cues can modulate rodent hippocampal grid cells in vitro and suggest a novel framework for understanding grid code dynamics. According to this framework, grid cells exist on a multidimensional continuum, with their specific module, angle, and spacing being determined by the interplay of internal forces and external inputs. We contend that this continuum model applies not just to hippocampal grid cells but also to other spatially periodic neural patterns found in the brain. Moreover, it provides a useful framework for exploring broader questions about the nature of neural codes and their underlying mechanisms.

When the grid patterns formed in response to auditory cues were disrupted by local light stimulation, the grid cells responded differently. Some cells with tight modules stayed relatively unaffected, whereas others with larger modules were more affected. Moreover, the grid cells' ability to do so depended on the strength of the optogenetic interference, with stronger interference leading to more pronounced effects. Interestingly, when we altered the frequency of auditory cues, the grid cells' responses changed accordingly. 

Our data also revealed a possible correlation between the size of grid modules and the distance animals can travel before needing to reorient themselves according to magnetic navigation cues. We analyzed a specific family of degree 4 extensions of the rational numbers, defined by S4 symmetries, to determine when a particular family of elliptic curves gained rank. Initially, we set parameters $a, b, c$ to establish an S4 action on the projective line, then defined a family of degree 4 extensions through this action, using a base field $K = \mathbb{Q}(j)$ with Galois group $S4$. We constructed a family of elliptic curves $E_{\alpha}$ over $K$, such that their minimal models are defined over some degree 4 extension $K_{\alpha}$. By examining the action of Galois automorphisms on the Néron models of $E_{\alpha}$, we determined conditions for isomorphism classes of $E_{\alpha}$. This allowed us to apply Diamond's and Kraizer's results on Galois realizations, under assumptions that $E_{\alpha}$ has rational 2-torsion and certain conditions on its L-function. By analyzing the structure of $S4$, we found that there are exactly 80 isomorphism classes of $E_{\alpha}$. For an infinite number of cases, with specific conditions on $a, b, c$, we showed that $E_{\alpha}$ has no additional rank over its defining field $K_{\alpha}$. This result holds under constraints that either $E_{\alpha}$ has a rational point defined over an imaginary quadratic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, or its analytic rank is 1. Consequently, this implies that there are infinitely many $E_{\alpha}$ with no additional rank over $\mathbb{Q}$. Moreover, we established that at least $39 \cdot 20 = 780$ distinct $E_{\alpha}$ exist, such that their quadratic twists gain rank over $\mathbb{Q}$. This number represents a substantial portion of the total $84 \cdot 20 = 1680$ isomorphism classes of $E_{\alpha}$. Our work also involves advancing Iminishi's result on Galois generalizations of modular polynomials. Finally, we outline various applications and potential research directions related to this family of curves and their quadratic twists.

We examine the time-dependent behavior of an isolated many-body system after a sudden change in its Hamiltonian, known as quantum quench. This process causes a sudden shift in the system's microscopic parameters, such as its hopping amplitude or magnetic field. Observing that quantum quenches result in a lasting, irreversible entropy increase within the system, we focus on studying this entropy growth as it relates to changes in entropy and temperature following the quench. Our analysis reveals a direct connection between the initial and final states during a quench, allowing us to accurately measure the total entropy produced and understand its underlying physical mechanisms. Furthermore, our study shows that quantum quenches always result in an irreversible entropy gain due to the spreading of correlations within the system. Additionally, we found that this entropy growth can be described using a heat capacity-like function associated with the temperature change following the quench, with contributions from both equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium components. The onset and duration of these processes are governed by the Malamud-Lawson theorem's classification of Lie algebra semi-simple types. Through numerical simulations of a specific quench scenario involving a one-dimensional XXZ spin chain, we demonstrate the universal entropy growth patterns observed across all non-integrable systems, influencing systems with long-range interactions and those in higher-dimensional spaces. Our findings provide a foundational framework for understanding the irreversible entropy production in quantum systems undergoing quenching, a ubiquitous phenomenon occurring in experiments involving quantum quenching, offering a pathway for extracting physical insights from experimental data. Non-unitary quantum dynamics arises in various applications such as quantum measurement, decay processes, and quantum many-body systems in contact with environments. In this study, we examine the time-twirling of an initial state that includes both the quantum system and its surrounding environment, and relate it to the time it takes to distinguish between different states during non-unitary evolution. Our approach is grounded in the theory of quantum entanglement and information loss, and involves using unitary twirling to separate the unitary and non-unitary components of the dynamics. We demonstrate that time-twirling has an irreversible effect on the initial state, and results in a more pronounced time-scale for entanglement formation with the environment. The time it takes to distinguish between two time-twilled states is determined by the smallest of two timescales: one associated with unitary evolution and another with non-unitary decay. The unitary time-scale serves as an upper bound for the time it takes to distinguish between two time-twilled states, and is applicable even in the absence of non-unitary decay. We further examine the conditions under which unitary unitwilling can recover entanglement between two separated systems, and discuss the role of time-twilling in non-unitary dynamics. Finally, we demonstrate that time-twilling can exhibit a more significant delay in forming entanglement between a system and its environment, and that this delay can result in a greater time to distinguish between two time-twilled states. The latter is particularly evident in the absence of non-unitary decay, and is characterized by the unitary unitwilling time-scale. By analyzing this model, we've identified two possible cycle periods and how they depend on the interior processes' timescales. When the core-insulating effect is strong, a longer cycle emerges, influenced by the rate at which the core tries to lose mass. Recent advancements in quantum circuit learning have shown potential in extracting physical insights from small-scale quantum experiments. However, these methods generally assume two-dimensional circuit structures, neglecting the value of deeper, fractal-like tensor network architectures in describing complex systems. In this work, we illustrate how to adapt the variational tensor network evolution method to transform compact, higher-dimensional tensor networks into detailed quantum circuits, leveraging the quanta library for tensor network operations and the pyqcircuit library for circuit manipulation. This approach enables us to efficiently convert the ground states of the one-dimensional Heisenberg model and the two-dimensional square lattice XXZ model into precise quantum circuits, consisting of up to 50 qubits and displaying improved simulation efficiency in comparison to traditional methods. Full-scale simulations are around 100 times faster when using the circuit representation, particularly for systems with larger bond dimensions and higher accuracy thresholds. Notably, our approach also facilitates the direct translation of tensor networks to stochastic circuits, paving the way for applying quantum circuit learning to large-scale shell-like systems by targeting individual tensor module learning. This innovative framework is broadly applicable across all tensor network simulations and may have a transformative impact on the field of quantum circuit learning and related fields. High-resolution tissue section analysis holds significant potential for cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and research, but its exploration is hindered by the large amount of data associated with histology images. Recent advancements in graph neural networks have indicated their capacity to comprehend complex structures and relationships within data, but training models on such datasets is computationally intensive and necessitates substantial datasets. Specialists in the field spend months to several years labeling tissues, but their expertise can be utilized to create more precise and relevant annotations through interactive methods. By combining the power of graph neural networks with interactive annotation collection, we demonstrate the capability to enhance the precision of classification across various tissue representations, surpassing previous benchmarks in certain cases and showing comparable performance in others. Moreover, our approach allows the generation of artifacts similar to those found in actual tissues, enabling the creation of synthetic datasets with greater diversity and relevance for cancer research applications. Our code and datasets are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Informatics-Cell-Analysis/Interactive-Tissue-Classification. Our findings show that graph neural networks and interactive annotation collection play a crucial role in precise and efficient tissue classification, and we look forward to further developing this approach with more advanced models and additional challenges.

Approximating long-range interactions in complex systems is a crucial challenge, particularly when it comes to highly detailed simulations. The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) offers a computationally effective solution for this problem, allowing for the rapid calculation of far-reaching gravitational interactions in astrophysical scenarios. Although FMM is integral to various Gadget-2 simulations, the underlying principles of this algorithm have not been extensively explored in the context of astrophysics. This study delves into the fundamental aspects of FMM and investigates its implementation in Gadget-2, analyzing factors that influence its performance and potential avenues for further optimization. A comparative analysis is also conducted across multiple simulation configurations, demonstrating that the inclusion of FMM leads to a significant reduction in the overall computational time and energy consumption, with minimal impact on accuracy. Furthermore, we identify key variables that FMM affects, including force calculation, potential field determination, and overall performance, and discuss how these findings can inform strategies for future simulations. Ultimately, this study provides a foundation for ongoing research aimed at fully leveraging FMM's capabilities within the Gadget-2 framework and across the broader field of computational astrophysics. This work is part of the researchers' code contribution policy, seeking to enlighten the community, facilitate replication, and stimulate discussion among experts in computational astrophysics. This project's code and findings are now available for public review and utilization at the specified URL.

This study examines the unique properties of rank metric codes in error correction ability, particularly near the maximum achievable rate of $1/2$. Our analysis focuses on the design of rank metric codes with high error correction thresholds and reasonable complexity in decoding, with an initial investigation into the code rate above $1/2$. We establish that certain low-density parity check codes have an error correction threshold of nearly $1$, with further exploration into the codes' properties and construction methods. Our analysis reveals that while some rank metric codes can correct errors up to half the message length, their construction involves the Reed-Solomon code, limiting the code rate to $1/2$. To overcome this constraint, we develop a new code with a rate greater than $1/2$ and tight error correction threshold of $0.499$, indicating that codes with rate greater than $1/2$ and optimal error correction threshold do not exist. Our research offers various code constructions, along with performance simulations, demonstrating the efficacy of our proposed codes in error correction scenarios. Notably, our results demonstrate that near-capacity performance can be achieved using rank metric codes in error correction scenarios. Our code constructions and related theories have implications for the application of rank metric codes in channel codes, enabling reliable communication over noisy channels with high data efficiency. This has significant potential for adapting rank metric codes in computational tasks, such as error-correcting machine learning codes, with research into their integration with neural networks just beginning. Our code constructions and research code are publicly available at https://github.com/yingzhihao/LMC, with further modifications and improvements to rank metric codes welcomed. This article presents an original idea proposed by D. Gelfand and D. MacPherson on combinatorial differential manifolds. A key concept in their work is the definition of a preface, serving as a translation of differential manifolds into a graphical representation. Gelfand and MacPherson's work also established a connection between combinatorial differential manifolds and their corresponding prefaces. Furthermore, they utilized this connection to develop an algorithm to generate all possible combinatorial differential manifolds from a given preface. This implementation of their method is an essential component of a software tool designed to visualize and interact with combinatorial differential manifolds. In addition, the software can be employed to explore various scientific data plots, including parametric curves, surfaces, volume rendering, and scatter plots. Moreover, the software enables user-input for importing various types of data and plotting specific graphs. However, its primary purpose is to serve as a foundation for future applications tailored to the principles of Gelfand and MacPherson's work. As such, the software remains a basic prototype in need of further refinement and optimization for practical use. Despite this, it can still be employed to exhibit conceptual ideas and demonstrate the underlying mathematics behind combinatorial differential manifolds. As an open-source project, the software is freely accessible and distributable under the terms of the GNU Public License Version 3.0. As such, users are permitted to utilize, modify, and contribute to this software with proper attribution. As an example of the software's capabilities, it has been utilized to visualize certain scientific data, namely the plot of a Kleinian group's limit set. This article also includes a brief discussion on the underlying mathematics behind this plot, particularly the intersection of the Kleinian group's limit set with a combinatorial differential manifold representing a torus. This article examines how level set techniques can be employed to analyze second-order fully nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) by reinterpreting such equations as methods for evolving levels sets. We particularly focus on an equation of the form $F(x,u,p,\\|D^2u\\|_2)=0$, where the function $F$ is an arbitrary given function, and consider two specific subcases: when it is quadratic in the second variable's second derivatives, and when it depends only on $x$ and $p$. We derive an alternative formulation for the first subcase by converting it into a first-order fully nonlinear PDE, and can thus apply previous knowledge about level set methods for such equations. We then discuss how this approach relates to other existing methods for solving these equations. Moreover, we introduce an iterative numerical technique for approximating solutions to the original equation by combining the method of successive substitution with an extension of the Clarke-Jost variational level set algorithm. We also provide an example of applying this method to a specific equation. Finally, we consider an equation with non-uniform diffusion when the coefficient varies significantly, and propose an alternative formulation by transforming it into an equation with uniform diffusion. We then analyze the properties of this new equation, and establish its relationship with the original equation. Additionally, we consider an equation with non-monotone dependence on $u$, and propose an iterative algorithm for approximating solutions. We also discuss an example of applying this method to a specific equation. Lastly, we conclude by discussing potential directions for improving the proposed algorithm.

Researchers have discovered a long-standing issue with cosmological simulations: once formed, halos maintain a nearly constant mass over time, contradicting theoretical predictions. This challenge affects the accuracy of halo mass forecasts, particularly when considering a range of amplitudes for initial scalar perturbations. Utilizing highly resolved initial conditions and a highly detailed simulation, we discovered that using a density-only model instead of a potential-only one results in an excessive halo formation and leads to over-predicted halo masses by approximately one order of magnitude. This finding applies not only to late-time observations but also to the early universe. When using an appropriate level of smoothing, however, we found that using a density-only model reduces halo masses by less than factors of five. Furthermore, we found that using an excessive level of smoothing leads to an improvement in halo mass accuracy by roughly two factors of five. This improvement is attributed to the reduction in excessive halo formation caused by artificial amplification of an over-smeared initial spectrum. When using an appropriate level of smoothing, we found that using an artificial viscosity in an N-body code results in artificially slowed down halo formation and increased halo masses by roughly a factor of four. This finding applies not only to our current simulation but also to similar simulations with $10^{12}h^{-1}\mathcal{M}_\odot$ halo masses at $z=4$. When considering artificial viscosity, we found that using an excessive level of smoothing leads to an improvement in halo mass accuracy by roughly two factors of five. This challenge affects the accuracy of halo mass forecasts, particularly when considering artificial viscosity, where an appropriate level of artificial viscosity is required to achieve a level of accuracy within a factor of five. This effect holds true for our current high-resolution simulation as well as our previous lower-resolution studies. When using an appropriate level of artificial viscosity and smoothing, however, we found that forecast accuracy improves by less than factors of four. Lastly, we found that using both an appropriate level of artificial viscosity and smoothing results in artificial slowing down of halo formation and leads to over-predicted halo masses by approximately one order of magnitude, until $z \approx 4$. Therefore, our findings suggest that both artificial viscosity and smoothing play a significant role in cosmological simulations of halo formation, and that their effects are prominent until $z \approx 4$. We introduce a semi-supervised version of the Convolutional Matrix Factorization (CNMF) method, tailored for piano transcription. This adapted technique competes with leading low-rank factorization methods and surpasses supervised deep learning methods in the Michigan State University Piano Dataset. Additionally, the proposed semi-supervised approach achieves accurate results on the LMD piano dataset with limited annotated data, outperforming its supervised version and other low-rank factorization techniques. The process of obtaining labeled data for machine learning models is made more efficient through selective labeling by allocating annotation effort based on predicted model uncertainties. Although this method effectively directs experts towards the most crucial annotations, doing so is often done subjectively, without clear guidance for decisions that impact the quality of the labeled data. We investigate quantitative approaches to guide the selective labeling process objectively and evaluate the benefits of such methods in terms of an expert's productivity and data quality. Additionally, we examine the influence of different objective functions in a simulation-focused study and analyze the limitations of applying these methods in real-world scenarios. Our findings suggest that guided selective labeling can result in more efficient expert time and better data quality compared to conventional methods, but with some drawbacks in real-world scenarios. To further improve the process, we propose augmenting uncertainty-based selection with an additional heuristic that considers the relationship between annotation costs and model performance. Through experimentation, we show that incorporating this heuristic into uncertainty-based selection yields additional benefits in terms of expert productivity and data quality, especially in high-cost scenarios. Our approach is universally applicable across any machine learning model and dataset. We publicly disclose our code and findings at this link: https://github.com/ghulghoul/guided-selective-labeling. We hope this research will contribute to the development of objective strategies for efficiently acquiring high-quality labeled data for machine learning models.

Understanding the social determinants of health relies heavily on available data, which is often inaccessible due to being embedded in clinical notes without proper extraction.  To address this challenge, our proposed framework combines natural language processing techniques with spatial analysis to effectively extract relevant information from clinical notes and associate it with neighborhood-level data.  By linking extracted information to community characteristics, our framework enables quantitative assessment of the influence of social determinants on health outcomes.  We applied this approach to analyze mortality rates following cardiac arrests, utilizing data from MIMIC-III and Medicare claims, and incorporated neighborhood data from ZIP code levels.  Our method demonstrated strong performance in extracting useful data from clinical notes, with an F-score of 0.79 for initial outcomes and 0.83 for in-hospital outcomes, according to a human evaluation of 500 samples.  By integrating this framework with natural language processing models that learn from large datasets, we anticipate even better results in the future.  Our analysis revealed that individuals living in disadvantaged neighborhoods had higher mortality rates following cardiac arrests, with delays in care contributing to these outcomes.  By harnessing the power of clinical data and community information, our framework offers a versatile tool for comprehensive health outcome assessments that can inform healthcare improvements and social determinant interventions. Previous 5G exposures have been compared to pre-5G exposures, and significant differences were found, including lower downlink power, reduced max EIRP, and limited use of the 26 GHz band. Furthermore, new restrictions on in-building max EIRP have been implemented, resulting in reduced max EIRP compared to pre-5G exposures within buildings. A quantitative analysis of the changes in exposures from 5G to pre-5G is being conducted and initial findings are presented, showcasing the modification in exposure patterns from 5G to pre-5G in various locations, including indoors, and highlighting potential implications for research and policy decisions. In some cases, further research is considered necessary to fully understand the consequences of the changes in exposure patterns. In order to facilitate the comparison of exposure data from different time periods and locations, a standardized format for numerical exposure data has been proposed. As of March 2022, preliminary findings on the changes in exposures from 5G to pre-5G in various locations were shared with research collaborators, and it is now time to share these initial observations with a broader audience. In addition, an update on the quantitative analysis of the changes in exposures from 5G to pre-5G is also being presented. In indoor settings, in-depth analysis has been conducted in over 1,500 locations across the US, Europe, Asia, and Australia, comparing max EIRP exposures from 5G to pre-5G, and examining potential factors contributing to the differences. The analysis indicates that in approximately 55% of locations, the 5G max EIRP is comparable to or lower than the pre-5G max EIRP, with around 45% of locations exhibiting higher max EIRP with 5G. No clear correlations with location categories, frequency bands, or other factors were identified. Nevertheless, further research is considered necessary to comprehensively understand the implications of these differences in exposure patterns. In-depth analysis has also revealed an interesting phenomenon where the 5G max EIRP appears to be influenced by the specific antenna model being used, with some antennas showing significantly lower max EIRP in 5G mode, often by as much as 20-30 W. It is worth noting that these variations in max EIRP could have a considerable effect on the exposure levels, with potential factors such as beamforming, antenna gain, and cell size also contributing to the differences in max EIRP from 5G to pre-5G.

The surface layer theorem is a significant tool that enables the extension of differential forms from a subspace within a locally convex space. By utilizing this theorem, our research delivers an extension of differential forms to the closure of a subspace within a locally convex space, thereby contributing to the advancement of previous results. This extension is particularly useful in facilitating the application of Michor's theorem to closed subspaces. Furthermore, our research introduces an operation that facilitates the restriction of differential forms from the closure of a subspace to the subspace itself. This operation exhibits desirable properties and is seen to be connected to the surface layer operator through the application of Michor's theorem. Finally, our research investigates the topological characteristics of the vector space of differential forms on the closure of a subspace, with focus on the properties of its restriction to the subspace itself. This investigation is conducted in the context of Frechet spaces and is accompanied by an examination of the related topological characteristics of the space of vector fields. Our research delivers an extension of the surface layer operator to Frechet spaces and is consequently able to provide an exact description of the vector space structure of the space of differential forms on the closure of a closed subrelative subanalytic subset within a real vector space of finite dimension greater than or equal to two. This is achieved through the application of Michor's theorem and results in the demonstration of the homological properties of the surface layer operator itself. Interestingly, even though the suboptimal policy appears inefficient in some cases, its average performance is close to optimal. As an example, when switching from a uniform to a bipodal distribution, the average computational complexity decreases dramatically. Additionally, we find that the suboptimal policy's performance can be understood through the lens of its interaction with the underlying channel conditions and the resulting ordering of user messages. As a result, we are able to provide insights into the suboptimal policy's performance by examining its components in isolation. In large-scale datasets with extensive annotation, ensuring the consistency of individual annotations is a pressing issue.  One strategy to achieve this goal is by leveraging paraphrasing techniques in the data creation stage.  Based on the assumption that semantically equivalent texts should have identical annotations, we propose a method to validate annotation consistency by generating paraphrases of parts of a dataset and checking for labeling alignment.  Specifically, we investigate the ability of two generation models to produce valid samples that are similar to existing data in a dataset.  Our approach focuses on finding parts of the dataset where the generated samples differ significantly from existing data, as these likely indicate annotation errors or inconsistencies.  We also analyze the relationship between data quality and the performance of generation models, as well as the impact of paraphrasing techniques on annotation validation.  Our results demonstrate that our proposed method is effective in identifying annotated texts with inconsistent labels by comparing them with newly generated samples.  We compare our approach using two generation models and find that one of them is more effective in our experiments.  We also find that our proposed method is capable of identifying nearly 50% of the annotated texts with inconsistent labels, as validated by human annotators, in the big legal dataset.  Our approach can be viewed as a data quality validation technique rather than a method for generating new annotations.  Therefore, we do not quantify the quality of the newly generated samples, but instead focus on their similarity to existing data in order to validate annotation consistency.  Our code and datasets are available for download at this link:  https://github.com/ghrua/validating-annotations.  One of the datasets used in our experiments is also being contributed to the Paraphrase Selection InContext repository as additional data.  We plan to expand our method to other data validation tasks in the future.  We hope that our work will contribute to the development of more effective data validation techniques using generation models. We introduce a new concept called half-positional winning condition for game theories on finite graphs, in addition to examining combinations of specific winning conditions, including mean-payoff, discounted-sum, half-positional, and dependent positional conditions. Our investigation focuses on understanding the interconnections between these different winning conditions. Notably, we show that while the union of all prefix-independent half-positional conditions does not capture any additional complexity beyond half-positional conditions, the same is not true for the union of dependent half-positional conditions, which does indeed result in a condition more intricate than half-positional but less comprehensive than total dependence. Furthermore, we explore multi-objective variants of these conditions and examine conditions with an infinite graph domain. Our findings also extend to symmetric and bi-linear variants of these conditions. Our analysis is grounded in computationally efficient and backwards-induction style algorithms for determining winning conditions, as well as Pareto optimality in multi-objective scenarios. Notably, implementing these algorithms requires the ability to determine whether a given state is winning for a specific player in a particular game. This underlying ability is considered an integral component of the underlying game and therefore its computational efficiency is inherently understood. Consequently, our primary focus is on developing the algorithms for determining winning conditions in various dependent positional conditions, rather than the underlying games themselves. Our study is an initial exploration aimed at laying the groundwork for future research in game theories with multiple objectives, where games are defined by multi-objective winning conditions. These conditions define desirable outcomes as those exceeding specific threshold values for multiple independent payoff functions. Our research specifically delimits payoffs to integer values, making the computation of winning conditions more complex than if payoffs were continuous. Notably, our analysis opens up new research directions, such as investigating the complexity of calculating winning conditions in games with continuous payoffs or when payoffs are partially observable. Another potential direction for investigation could involve extending the concepts of dependent positional conditions to more intricate game theories. Asynchronous polars are a rare subclass of cataclysmic variables, having a white dwarf primary star in orbit with a late-type main sequence companion in a eccentric orbit. What sets these systems apart is the white dwarf primary star experiencing a synchronized spin and orbital period. 

Upon examining the X-ray spectra of these three systems using the multi-dimensional chi-squared minimization method with temperatures, abundances of elements including iron, neon, oxygen, and nitrogen, and line broadening, significant variability in spectral characteristics were found. 

The X-ray spectra of BY Canum Venacis show a temperature range of 15-40 million Kelvin, with an iron abundance in the range of 0.5 to 2 times the solar value, and a highly absorbed spectrum in all but one of the Chandra observations. In contrast, the X-ray spectra of PG 1415$+$61 and PG 1603$+$319 have temperatures over 40 million Kelvin, with the former having temperatures as high as 70 million Kelvin, and the latter displaying temperatures ranging from 40 to 160 million Kelvin.

To overcome the difficulties of integrating these distinct systems, a partitioned approach is employed, where a different solver is used for each domain. Within this methodology, an explicit fluid solver and an implicit solid solver are employed, resulting in a direct method for solving the fluid-structure interaction system. Due to the explicit nature of the fluid solver, only a single step from the implicit solid solver is required, and the fluid-structure interface can be determined through a snapshot of the fluid solver at this single time step. As a result, the fluid-structure interface can be represented by a single surface defined by the endpoint of the time integration method employed by the explicit fluid solver. Based on this representation, the interface accuracy relies on the choice of time step size for the explicit fluid solver, and high-order accuracy requires a very small time step size, resulting in significantly increased computational costs. To achieve better precision at a lower cost, a higher-order implicit integrator can be employed by the explicit fluid solver, and this paper explores just such an approach. Based on this new understanding of the fluid-structure interface, studies have shown that it can be represented with comparable precision to the original method using approximately half the number of time steps, resulting in a substantial decrease in computational costs without compromising accuracy. To validate these findings, both a simple one-dimensional rod coupled with a potential Navier-Stokes equation and a more complex three-dimensional cylinder subjected to fully developed turbulent flow were simulated using this implicit surface representation, and the results showed that it is equivalent to the original method while offering up to a 50% reduction in computational costs. We examine the performance of an alternative method, the effective gap width model, in calculating the light speed and wavefront propagation across ionization gaps compared to the established equivalent overlap model and local functionals. This assessment is part of a broader study that aims to guide the development of efficient and accurate approximate methods for calculating molecular electron densities within nonuniform boundaries in real-space grids. Ionization gaps in three molecules, consisting of He$_2$, BeH$^+$, and BH$_2$, are investigated using three different approaches: one where the gap is adjusted to match a specific width, and two approximate methods, effective gap width and equivalent overlap models. The results for the electron density at isodensity contours in molecular systems demonstrate that whereas local approximations are sufficiently accurate in the vicinity of ions, the effective gap width approach yields a more precise light speed and wavefront propagation compared to the traditional local models. Nevertheless, both approximate methods exhibit comparable performance when considering the overall electron density within the gap. A crucial finding indicating that, for sufficiently large gaps, both approximate methods converge to similar results also emerges. A key insight derived from this study could potentially be applied to the development of more accurate approximate methods for calculating molecular electron densities within nonuniform boundaries in real-space grids. The calculus of constructions, introduced by Girard, has significantly impacted
the development of modern programming languages and type theory. Its innovative
approach to integrating constructive logic and functional programming as a unified
whole has inspired numerous other calculi, such as Twelf's extension of higher-order
logic through dependent types. This project specifically explores an unexplored
variation of the calculus of constructions, where dependent types are derived
from operational semantics, using the example of a dependent type theory for array
operations. The resulting system is then applied to prove the correctness of an
array-based implementation of map and filter functions within the Agda proof
assistant. This work's underlying goal is to investigate whether dependent types
could be viewed as emerging from operational semantics, thus deviating from the
traditional definition found in the calculus of constructions. This research is
ultimately aimed at enabling the expression of dependent types within Twelf's
extension of higher-order logic with dependent types. Although the explored
variant remains unorthodox, it shows that dependent types can be represented in a
way consistent with the calculus of constructions, paving the way for further

A recent model introduced by Christian et al. (2017) divides high-latitude stratospheric clouds into three sections: a core, a veiled core, and a surrounding layer. Utilizing high-resolution images from the DLR's MIPAS instrument, this study seeks to refine the classification by incorporating mathematical probability and spatial analysis methods. Initially, the core is identified through probabilistic thresholding of the cloud's density. A veiled core is proposed as an intermediate layer, defined as the area between the core's boundary and the edge of the cloud. Cloud thickness is then determined by projecting a plane onto the core and veiled core boundaries, and calculating the distance between these two shapes. The results show that cloud thickness can range from 1 to over 10 km, and that incorporating the veiled core into the analysis increases the average cloud thickness by nearly a factor of two, from 5.1 km to 9.4 km. In some cases, clouds are found to consist of up to 90% veiled core. These findings suggest that the veiled core plays a significant role in the structure and geometry of these clouds.

In stars, the magnetic field typically follows a mix of toroidal and poloidal patterns, with a clear equilibrium formed when these components balance each other. We show that, in the absence of magnetic diffusion, a small fraction of toroidal magnetic field within a vacuum star can significantly enhance the stability of the poloidal field, thereby stabilizing the magnetic field as a whole. Conversely, in magnetized plasmas, magnetic tension can counterbalance the destabilizing effect of magnetic diffusion on toroidal field, thus potentially maintaining stable toroidal components even in large-scale stars. These findings apply specifically to axisymmetric modes of instability in stars like solar-type G-type main-sequence stars. We also demonstrate that in stars like Antares, binary companion to the black hole V616 Mon, our results hold true, yet with a notable limitation - when the stars' rotational period exceeds about 10 days. Notably, our study indicates that toroidal magnetic field can be both chemically enriched and stable in massive stars. Finally, our theory may provide insight into the formation of toroidal fields in young, rapidly rotating T Tauri stars. We also propose that magnetic multiplets observed in some T Tauri stars could be attributed to stable toroidal fields generated through the concentration of magnetic wind streams. Ultimately, our research underscores the significance of considering the interplay between toroidal and poloidal fields in the dynamics of stellar magnetic fields. It also emphasizes the necessity of refining numerical models of stellar magnetic field evolution, especially in cases of massive stars, where toroidal fields dominate, and in scenarios of magnetic accretion in T Tauri stars, where magnetic multiplets emerge in regions of intense accretion. We further suggest that Zeeman splitting in spectral lines can offer a direct means of detecting stable toroidal fields in stars. Lastly, our theory may provide a framework for better understanding magnetic field behavior in stars undergoing magnetic convective turbulence and for making more accurate predictions in scenarios of magnetic field evolution in stars. It is essential to test our findings numerically through high-resolution simulations, especially in cases of magnetic accretion in T Tauri stars, and then verify our results with actual data from stellar observations. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for a comprehensive theory of stellar magnetic fields, one that acknowledges the coexistence and interplay of toroidal and poloidal components in stars. It is our hope that this study will contribute meaningfully to this endeavor, one that will, in turn, yield greater insight into the fundamental processes governing stellar interiors and evolution.

This framework also introduces an equivariant perspective, leading to a description of gerbes on X when considering actions of X's automorphism group on gerbes. A recent discovery established a profound connection between finite Godel algebras and forest combinatorics. This groundbreaking relationship reveals that every finite Godel algebra can be viewed as an extension of a Boolean algebra, closely tied to a specific forest that is invariant under the algebra's operation. Building upon this groundbreaking insight, we embark on an expedition to explore the intricate realm of finite Godel algebras through the captivating world of forest duality. Our ambitious mission encompasses two objectives: first, identifying the precise forest configuration that underlies finite Godel algebras; second, categorizing all finite Godel algebras using forest properties, with a focus on algebras associated with binary trees. By successfully achieving this mission, we derive key insights into the fundamental structure of finite Godel algebras and reveal various instances of these algebras. Furthermore, our work lays the groundwork for investigating more comprehensive classes of algebras within the finite Godel domain. Lastly, our research introduces an innovative approach to applying forest duality, a methodological framework that can be applied to an even broader range of algebras and forests. This framework is subsequently applied to a specific class of algebras, the median algebras. All necessary computations have been performed using the ROSA system. Our study is a pioneering effort to explore the intricate world of finite Godel algebras within the context of forest duality and we hope it will inspire further research in this captivating field. Some of the algebras previously unknown to the scientific community have been added to the Godel metatheory section of the database. This work has been presented at the 2019 conference of the International Society for the History of Mathematics.

Recent advances in LiDAR-based 3D object detection have primarily focused on techniques using rich context from nearby points, but our research suggests that the context provided by nearest neighbors is often insufficient and may even negatively impact performance. Instead, we propose that a more suitable approach would involve combining a simple, efficient method that directly processes isolated point clouds for shallow features and utilizing additional context only when necessary. To support this idea, we conducted experiments using three common scenarios from the KITTI dataset and found that classification performance is highly sensitive to context in complex scenes but relatively insensitive in simpler scenes. Based on these findings, we developed an approach called Context-Aware 3D Detection (CA3D), which first classifies detected boxes into two categories: those that require (hard) and do not require (easy) additional context. Context-Aware training and sorting of neighbor points by distance were employed to improve performance on hard samples. Our results indicate that CA3D outperforms existing top-performing methods on KITTI dataset v7.3 with an average precision of 82.35%. Moreover, CA3D achieves superior performance on easy boxes and modifies the detection pipeline for hard boxes, resulting in improved overall performance. The long-term persistence of liquid foams is attributed to two key factors: the high surface tension that prevents bubbles from merging and the unique flow characteristics of fluids within the foam's interstitial spaces. The latter's influence is particularly notable at low Reynolds numbers. Research has identified a crucial parameter, the roughness factor, which measures the fraction of area contributed by plateaus in the foam structure. Studies have demonstrated that this parameter's impact is most evident in fluids with low viscosity. However, the relationship between the roughness factor and the flow of liquid foams has not been extensively explored, especially in situations where the flow rate exceeds the rate of diffusion. Therefore, we have conducted a series of experiments utilizing a parallel plate rheometer to investigate the flow characteristics of liquid foams in close-range shear and extensional flows, focusing on foams with low to moderate viscosity and different plateau spacings. The results showed that the flow of these foams is non-Newtonian, with viscosity dependent on the type of flow and the roughness factor. In particular, we observed that the shear flow's viscosity is directly proportional to the roughness factor, whereas extensional flow's viscosity exhibits an inverse relationship. Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have achieved notable success in image classification tasks. Nevertheless, their potential is often hindered by overreliance on accurately labeled training data. Ensemble-based approaches offer a solution to this limitation by training multiple networks with different parameters and minor labeling for each. While this method is commonly utilized for dataset aggregation, less consideration is given to ensemble-based decisions at the individual data level. In this study, we propose Decision-based Ensemble for Convolutional Neural Networks (DICNN) to resolve this issue. DICNN comprises multiple component networks that are trained with minimal labeling and different transfer learning approaches. Each component network makes an independent prediction for an input image, and their outputs are collected to determine the final ensemble decision through a novel data-efficient voting strategy. Experiments on the Cityscapes dataset demonstrate that DICNN outperforms the standard ensemble-based approach, with enhanced accuracy and reduction of labeling requirements. Moreover, DICNN achieves higher precision and accuracy compared to the current SOTA methods, while needing less than half of the required labeled data. The source code of DICNN is openly accessible on the GitHub platform.

A non-buoyant fluid suspended between two parallel plates that are rotating at the same speed and distance from the center forms a Hele-Shaw cell. When the rotation is strong enough, the membrane breaks into distinct patterns of instability, which can take the form of stars, stripes, or quads. These patterns are influenced by the membrane's tension and the viscosity of the surrounding fluid. In contrast, a rotating surface covered with a single layer of Hele-Shaw cells exhibits capillary waves and chaotic patterns when the membrane is highly viscous. However, when the membrane tension is strong enough, these patterns become more stable. Notably, both the rotating Hele-Shaw cell and the single-layer membrane exhibit similar pattern stability transitions at the same dimensionless speeds, which correspond to the Froude number and the Squitieri number. However, the underlying physics governing these stability transitions differs. Additionally, we demonstrate that these stability transitions mark the onset of nonlinear patterns within the membrane, which can be understood through a simple laboratory test involving a rotating plate covered with a single layer of Hele-Shaw cells, revealed through X-ray imaging and subsequent analysis using nonlinear elasticity theory. This discovery opens up avenues for exploring other complex membranes in fluids at high Reynolds numbers. We examine the idea that work done on a system by external forces can also be understood as the sum of an average work increase for all possible microstates, each weighted by its probability in the thermodynamic equilibrium. To support this concept, we use a simple harmonic oscillator to demonstrate that its average energy can be expressed as a sum of work values for individual microstates, and that these work values are evenly spaced. A classification of microstates by their energy and corresponding motion also enables us to define forward and backward trajectories between any two microstates, allowing us to calculate the dissipated work from the average change in internal microwork. This calculation is then generalized to any thermodynamic system with a discrete energy spectrum, confirming that the total dissipated work for a transition between any two microstates is the difference between their work values. A simple example using a two-level system shows that this result is unaffected by external factors such as temperature or lighting levels. A more comprehensive analysis involving an N-level system reveals that the work values for the ground state and the highest energy state are zero and largest, respectively. The space between these two extreme work values can be divided into any number of segments, depending on the energy spectrum of the system. The average work increase during a transition from the ground state to the highest energy state is equal to the average energy increase, which is entirely absorbed by the system's internal degrees of freedom, now at their highest possible energy. This result is valid for any discrete energy spectrum, and applies not only to a two-level system but also to any system with a degenerate ground state, such as one involving spin degrees of freedom. The discussion is then expanded to include forward and backward trajectories between any two microstates, even when the energy spectrum is continuous, using the tools of equilibrium statistics. The relationship between work values, or internal microwork, and the total work or energy is therefore independent of how these quantities are defined, and involves a total ordering of all work values, whether the energy spectrum is discrete or continuous. The resulting ordering of work values, or internal microwork, is therefore fundamental to the thermodynamics of all systems, and provides a basis for further analysis of forward and backward trajectories between any two microstates. A theoretical analysis using a discrete variable representation approach was conducted to examine the vibrational coupling in cyclopentadiene and benzene when probed by ultraviolet light. This investigation focused on these molecules' CCH and CN vibrational coupling frequencies and intensities as the cyclopentadiene and benzene rings twist. A comparative study between the two molecules was performed to identify similarities and differences in their vibrational spectra under rotational motion. This comparative study found a greater than five times abundance ratio of CCH over CN in cyclopentadiene, along with a significant increase in the CCH combination band intensity in benzene. Notably, when the light angle is optimized, the abundance ratio of the CCH combination band over the CN fundamental band increases by more than two times in cyclopentene compared to benzene. This greater CCH abundance in cyclopentene is attributed to the higher degree of bond alternation in this molecule. In contrast, benzene exhibits little bond alternation, and when excited, it readily undergoes a ring twist transformation, leading to a increase in the CN fundamental band intensity at the expense of the CCH combination band. In contrast, cyclopentene prefers a bond-alternated structure and exhibits little increase in the CN fundamental band intensity when excited. Instead, it shows a significant increase in the CCH combination band intensity in this state. These findings provide a theoretical framework for interpreting recent experimental data obtained using UV-IR pump-probe spectroscopy in these molecules. These results may also contribute to a better understanding of the molecular dynamics and vibrational predissociation in these systems. Lastly, this study suggests that benzene's ability to easily twist its ring when excited may be a key factor in its ability to undergo large amplitude vibrational motion and ultimately dissociate from a ring-twisted state. In contrast, cyclopentene, with its higher degree of bond alternation, may prefer a different reaction path to undergo vibrational predissociation. In this case, a ring-twisted state may not be an intermediate state in the vibrational predissociation of cyclopentene. In summary, this investigation indicates that benzene and cyclopentene exhibit distinct vibrational coupling behaviors under rotational motion, and these differences may significantly influence their vibrational predissociation pathways. Therefore, further experimental and theoretical studies of these systems, particularly when probed by ultraviolet light, are warranted. A key challenge in neural machine translation (NMT) lies in the difficulty of properly modeling long-term dependencies and sentence-level relationships. To address this issue, a look-ahead attention model was previously proposed, allowing the model to concentrate on parts of the sentence that are relevant for the target word. However, incorporating this attention into the standard decoder consists of costly computations and inefficient memory access. In this paper, a more efficient look-ahead attention model is proposed by re-examining the attention mechanism within the decoder. Instead of incorporating the look-ahead attention as a standard attention, it was discovered that simply adding the look-ahead attention over the standard attention can achieve comparable performance with minimal computational and memory requirements. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves a 1.1% improvement in sentence-level BLEU score on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task with significantly reduced additional computation and memory access. Moreover, the proposed model achieves a 0.6% improvement in BLEU score on the WMT 2019 English-to-Robertsonian paragraph-level translation task. Code is available at: https://github.com/ghrua/laa-nmt.git. The proposed model also demonstrates a clear superiority in difficult-to-translate sentences with an improvement of 5.1% BLEU score.

The GridGain enterprise distributed database platform utilizes a translational approach to provide query and transaction processing capabilities. By supporting SQL, Hadoop MapReduce, and other interfaces, the self-contained, in-memory data storage solution accelerates existing database systems and enables seamless data integration across dispersed datasets. Initially developed through a translational approach and subsequently refined with a self-contained in-memory store, the GridGain team discovered that its technology could also translate data across diverse storage systems, turning each storage unit into a small, self-contained grid unit. In response to user demand for broader data coverage, the team considered alternative approaches to enlarge data scope, but instead, they refined their translational approach and applied it to different storage systems, leading to successful projects including a QlikView application and a Hadoop-based data archiving solution. Notably, the company's translational approach enabled it to maintain full ACID compliance across distributed datasets, achieving this through periodic data unifications that ensure data coherence. In scenarios where datasets change infrequently, GridGain's approach ensures full consistency across dispersed data. In practice, this is demonstrated through a large-scale e-commerce case study, in which GridGain's translational approach and data unification strategy are shown to maintain full consistency across millions of items in a dynamic environment, in collaboration with the Apache Hadoop ecosystem. In this paper, the underlying technology of GridGain's translational approach is also made available to the research community through an open-source implementation of a self-contained, in-memory grid unit in Java.
