Recent research emphasizes the significance of peer influence on curiosity, suggesting that friends and acquaintances spark curiosity through their diverse experiences. This study explores a theoretical framework that incorporates peer impact within an individual's curiosity system, adapting Clayton's control system model to include a desire for distinct experiences. A computational model is developed using this framework and is further modified to include a novelty-driven decision-making component, where an agent chooses between repeating a familiar state or seeking a novel one. This model is utilized to investigate how peer influence affects curiosity in a social setting, revealing that peers encourage the exploration of novel states and the consolidation of new memories in the hippocampus. A novelty detection algorithm is implemented to demonstrate how the proposed framework can generate unexpected observations that arise from exploring novel environments and states. Notably, this framework provides a theoretical basis for understanding recent empirical evidence indicating that social relationships can lead to improved performance in novel state recognition tasks. A key feature of this model is its ability to preemptively initiate novel state explorations, capitalizing on its temporary advantage before performance improves in those states. A corresponding algorithm is developed to identify novel states in real-time, and its effectiveness is confirmed through state-of-the-art results on the Minerva dataset, a renowned dataset for novel state recognition. The proposed framework is also applicable to contemporary datasets such as Meta AI's TaLoQA. Furthermore, a simple implementation of a memory-augmented neural network using this framework achieves superior performance compared to baseline models, outperforming them in novel state recognition tasks even when trained in a supervised manner. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/curiosity-framework. The associated dataset is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/taloga. The pre-trained models and additional resources can be found on PaterNet at https://patern.net/ghulam-eissa/curiosity-framework. The research is further accompanied by a theoretical analysis of the proposed framework in Chapter 2. The code for the computational models developed in Chapter 3 is also included in the appendix. The proposed framework's novel state recognition algorithms have been successfully integrated into a publicly available implementation of the LAMO model at https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/lamo. Current applications of Gaussian processes (GPs) are restricted by traditional limitations of exact inference and conjugacy requirements. We devise a method of GP representation on relational data structures by introducing graph Matérn GPs, which enables efficient mini-batch and non-conjugate learning configurations. Furthermore, this formulation incorporates a data augmentation technique, allowing for precise inference while adhering to a widely used inference framework. The proposed graph Matérn GP model outperforms GP models in multiple real-world dataset settings. Additionally, our method achieves comparable performance to graph neural networks while maintaining interpretability, and we make the implementation publicly accessible. Resource code can be found at https://github.com/ghulamali/graph-matern-gp. We also provide source code for the experimental protocols at https://github.com/ghulamali/graph-matern-gp-experiments.

In monitoring and managing urban road networks, a network of static sensors can provide comprehensive coverage, but their reliability may decline over time due to calibration issues. In contrast, mobile ridesourcing vehicles, which are increasingly common and nearly always equipped with sensing technology, can offer a more consistent and widespread surveillance system. We propose an algorithm that learns the movement patterns of these vehicles and predicts future coverage to optimize sensing reliability across the network. Our goal is to allocate resources between maintaining coverage in areas with high reliability and those with low reliability, and we develop a framework that leverages multi-objective optimization to achieve a balance between these competing interests. Through simulations, we show that our approach outperforms static sensor configurations and can handle large networks of ridesourcing vehicles. Furthermore, our algorithm responds quickly enough to accommodate dynamic changes in the network. We also explore different strategies for predicting vehicle movements and find that incorporating contextual information about the vehicles' behavior improves the accuracy of our predictions. Finally, we examine the limitations of our algorithm in relation to real-world ridesourcing networks and suggest areas for further research. Our algorithm is efficient, versatile, and robust, and it could potentially be applied to other mobile sensor networks that operate in similar environments. We publicly disclose our code and dataset to facilitate ongoing research in this field. Overall, our study demonstrates the potential of ridesourcing vehicles to enhance sensing coverage and reliability in urban settings. However, our findings also indicate that the effectiveness of this approach depends heavily on the underlying traffic dynamics that influence the movement of these vehicles. We therefore conclude that future research in this area should prioritize both the technological aspects of mobile sensor networks and the social implications of deploying such systems within existing transportation networks. We hope that our study paves the way for further exploration of the opportunities and challenges presented by the rise of ridesourcing vehicles. A persistent anomaly in dark matter direct detection experiments, specifically the $J/\psi$ invisible decay discrepancy, may indicate the existence of a dark matter particle weighing around 140 MeV. Constraints on the interaction between this dark matter and nucleons are still somewhat undefined, mainly due to a lack of theoretical understanding about the underlying physics behind the $J/\psi$ invisible decay process. However, it's possible that a dark matter nucleon interaction could explain the observed magnitude of the $J/\psi$ invisible decay rate. In this study, we examine the implications of a dark matter nucleon interaction within the context of the unitarity of the flavour gauge group $SU(3)_{L\times U}$, which could result in a hidden sector messenger model. Considering this unitarity constraint, we place limits on the cross-section of a 140 MeV dark matter particle interacting with nucleons, which fall below the current experimental limits set by the PNDGamma and DMTPC experiments, specifically at the level of $10^{-29}$ [cm^2]. Nevertheless, even without this unitarity constraint, we find that the unitarity of $SU(3)_{L\times U}$ still imposes a cross-section limit of $10^{-28}$ [cm^2] on a 140 MeV dark matter particle. This study also explores the possibility of dark matter being a component of the $J/\psi$ decay process that goes undetected, which we estimate could account for around 1-10% of the total decay rate. This research is further expanded upon in the accompanying paper [2].

This study develops variable stepsize Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-weighted Linear Models (SGLMs) for approximating smooth functions on both uniform and nonuniform grids. By adapting the stepsize based on local function smoothness, variables stepsize SGLMs are shown to provide comparable or better approximation accuracy than their fixed-step counterparts. A new variable stepsize formulation is introduced for nonuniform grids, offering a distinct approach different from standard fixed-step and uniform-variable stepsize methods. We examine both uniform and nonuniform grid scenarios, establishing convergence and smoothness preservation of the updated models. No a priori error bounds exist for variable stepsize methods; however, we discuss how recent work applies to this study. We demonstrate the efficacy of our variable stepsize methods with SNR weights across both grid scenarios, highlighting performance relative to fixed-step and adaptive methods. Additionally, we explore how our approach works with limited or no noise data, addressing critical problems in computer vision and robotics. All necessary code can be accessed via https://github.com/ashish1729/VarStepSGLM.

A recent algorithm called MFSSA combines K-Means and SPCA to group similar data sets together, and enables the reconstruction of each individual data set's unique component. This method can be applied in real-world scenarios, including tracking internal temperatures, remote sensing, or signal processing. However, assigning the number of clusters (K) correctly is a challenge. A new variation of MFSSA, called Auto-MFSSA, addresses this issue by naturally determining the optimal K value directly within its framework, without the need for preliminary cluster specification or iterative updating. Compared to the original MFSSA, Auto-MFSSA exhibits worse performance, but is more straightforward and consistent. The algorithm's ability to self-organize is both beneficial and its limitations clear. While it can naturally identify K, it also increases computational demands and may become overly aggressive in grouping data sets together. Two main variations of Auto-MFSSA, Auto-MFSSA-I and Auto-MFSSA-II, address these challenges, resulting in more efficient algorithms that balance cluster size variability and processing power. When applied to temperature curve analysis and synthetic data, these algorithms outperformed the original MFSSA, and their source code is available for public use. Overall, Auto-MFSSA, its derivatives, and its code contribute to a reliable self-organizing algorithm that easily adapts to diverse data sets and settings. This algorithm's ability to efficiently group similar data sets together makes it an invaluable tool for various applications, including temperature curve analysis, and facilitates further research into its applications and underlying principles. Additionally, Auto-MFSSA's consistency and straightforward implementation make it an ideal starting point for other self-organizing algorithm studies, allowing researchers to focus on modifying rather than tackling its fundamental aspects. Consequently, the algorithm's code and results it achieves will benefit the scientific community, promote discussion, and spark interest in its extensions and related algorithms. This research is part of the author's PhD studies.

This final version responds to queries posed in versions 1 and 2 and provides a fully detailed analysis of the paper titled "On the asymptotic behavior of a random walk with independent increments" by A. David and A. Zebera. The main argument is now presented with the alternative approach suggested in version 2 included in the appendix for completeness. The key argument revolves around the concept of a 'critical' point that determines the asymptotic behavior of a random walk with i.i.d. increments, and it is contended that this point is incorrect. A key observation is that the original proof is flawed due to an incorrect application of an established result. A critical component of the argument involves the characterization of the walk's asymptotic behavior being influenced by the presence of an $\mathcal{L}_2$-integrable component with zero mean. A crucial insight is derived from a specific conditioning strategy that essentially strips away this $\mathcal{L}_2$-integrable component, and it is demonstrated that the walk's asymptotic behavior is then solely determined by a subwalk that is independent of the initial condition. The relationship between this subwalk and the original walk is explored, and it is shown that its asymptotic distribution is a scaled version of the distribution of a random variable whose characteristics depend on the parameter $b$. A key finding is that for $b<2$, the walk's asymptotic distribution is the same as that of the subwalk, and thus is zero. Conversely, for $b>2$, the walk's asymptotic distribution is the same as that of a scaled version of a standard normal distribution. Identifying external factors affecting dynamic systems is crucial, and researchers have developed effective methods discovering these variables has significant implications for reinforcement learning outside of a black box setting. However, existing approaches assume easy access to system data and fail to account for a critical aspect: many external influences cannot be directly observed because they occur rapidly and no intermediate data is available to capture these events. To address this limitation, we aim to discover exogenous variables that impact continuous dynamic systems from just input and output measurements, without relying on system data. Our research involves framing the discovery of these variables as a model selection problem among an exponential number of possible models, and we develop an algorithm using a narrow search strategy to identify the best model by minimizing its error. This algorithm is efficient and has a polynomial time complexity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to discovery tasks in multiple areas, including chemistry, medicine, and astronomy. Notably, our method successfully identified subatomic particles contributing to scattering patterns and found an overlooked astronomical event with characteristics that match a newly discovered astronomical event. Our algorithm discovered an influential variable in a medical scanner and a critical factor in a chemical reaction that was previously difficult to replicate. Additionally, we highlight the vast model space that exists even in simple cases, and we highlight potential future directions for our research. All code and datasets are available online.

Recent breakthroughs in graph learning have been fueled by adaptations of conventional neural network architectures. We investigate the underlying patterns that allow these models to effectively utilize input information. Through modification and simplification of CNNs, fully connected Neural Networks, and other basic architectures, we observe that they inherently apply graph filtering or neighbor aggregation. We validate our framework by training multiple of these models on various datasets and experimenting with artificial datasets. We demonstrate that in theories described by Chern-Simons gravity in $3d$, the wormhole defects serve as a non-invertible symmetry, and their fusion rules are related to those of graviton states in $4d$. This connection allows us to compute the wormhole fusion rules using the irreducible representations of the conformal algebra in four dimensions. Notably, our analysis reveals that the conservation of angular momentum in fusion processes gives rise to specific crossings when plotting the fusion rules for the graviton state with a particular spin against the charge of the wormhole in a specific range. We interpret this phenomenon as the shadow graph of the graviton scattering amplitude in $4d$. This derivation is free from any ambiguities and relies solely on the Chern-Simons gravity in $3d$. In the context of automated program verification, logical pseudocodes serve as intermediate representations for specifying programs. These pseudocodes deviate from conventional pseudocodes in their emphasis on ensuring programs conform to desired specifications. Despite this difference, researchers and practitioners often use logical pseudocodes as if they were typical pseudocodes, which can lead to safety issues and inaccuracies in understanding their purpose. To address this misconception, we propose a method for automatically identifying areas within these pseudocodes that require human intervention to clarify their connection to actual program implementations. Our approach relies on parsing and analyzing both implementation codes and their corresponding logical pseudocodes from various programming languages. To facilitate human review, our system provides a set of guidelines that incorporate both theoretical and practical considerations. These guidelines encompass rules for expressing programs as pseudocodes, template-based best practices for rewriting pseudocodes, and a set of questions to guide human reviewers in validating the pseudocodes against actual implementations. To accommodate diverse programming languages, our approach is designed as a plug-in framework compatible with existing program analysis tools. To demonstrate the feasibility of our approach, we applied it to two specific programming environments, one centered on the Z3 theorem prover and another focused on the Spark/Ada language for reliable software development. Ultimately, our goal is to integrate our method with existing program development tools to create a more effective and collaborative workflow between humans and automated reasoning systems, promoting greater understanding and safer use of program specifications expressed as logical pseudocodes. To achieve this, we plan to continue improving our approach by addressing scalability issues and exploring ways to automate the review process itself. Nonetheless, we believe that clarifying the intent behind program specifications in the form of pseudocodes represents an important step towards greater safety and understanding in program development. Consequently, we invite feedback and contributions to our work in this area. Our approach is currently available online at https://github.com/jcbaps/pecs. Using a diverse range of combinatorial techniques and arguments, we have made significant discoveries regarding the Boolean rainbow Ramsey number in 3-dimensional space. Additionally, we have established a connection between these numbers and the rainbow sum of a pair in a Boolean lattice, and have found the values for $brn_s(\hat{1},\hat{1})$ and $brn_s(\hat{1},\hat{2})$. Our research also explores new ideas and methods for analyzing the Boolean rainbow Ramsey number. Notably, we demonstrate a 2-dimensional value that surpasses any previously reported number. A one-pass algorithm was introduced by Franks and Har-Peled for creating small representations of data points for the $k$-means clustering problem. Although the algorithm works quickly, its output may not lead to an optimal $k$-means clustering. However, we demonstrate that using the one-pass algorithm results in a 'coreset' with only $O(k)$ times the number of data points, while maintaining nearly optimal $k$-means clustering and doing so in linear time. Furthermore, the algorithm allows for finding the optimal $k$-means clustering from the reduced set in linear time. Unlike previous methods which required a large number of data points to be stored, this algorithm uses the one-pass method to create a smaller representation of the data, leading to significant memory savings. We also discuss an adaptation of the algorithm for creating a small set of representative points for the farthest point clustering problem. Our work offers an efficient solution for large-scale $k$-means clustering problems where adding or removing clusters is frequent, such as in collaborative filtering applications. Our algorithm results in a 5-10 times faster computation for large datasets and is 5-10 times more accurate than the traditional farthest point clustering algorithm when applied to image feature detection. We also showcase the algorithm's effectiveness in image processing by utilizing the K-means coreset to improve the accuracy of object detection in satellite images. Consequently, our work offers an efficient and accurate solution for large-scale $k$-means clustering problems and can be applied to various real-world applications. In large environments, high-dimensional action spaces can impede the performance of algorithms in pursuit-evasion tasks. To mitigate this, we propose using a grid-based partitioning method called superstates, which breaks down the space into more manageable sectors. By doing so, we achieve two goals: we derive a compact representation of the state space that facilitates motion planning and enables the efficient storage of past encounters, effectively addressing the memory issue commonly faced in recurrent policies. Our approach, (1) simplifies action selection through local decisions, (2) offers a degree of robustness to mapping errors, and (3) showcases an exemplary way to design grid-based algorithms that are adaptable to complex environments. We evaluate our method on a notable example, the "multi-agent gridworld escape room," which involves evading multiple pursuers in a large, partially observable environment. Our results demonstrate that using superstates yields significant reductions in computation and memory usage without a notable decrease in evasion success, and they also provide valuable insights into the effective design of grid-based policies in pursuit-evasion tasks. Our code is openly accessible at https://github.com/ultralytics/superstates. Our paper is also hosted on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.06218. An n-tuple of positive integers is considered nonstandard if it meets certain unique criteria. The concept of nonstandard n-tuples has significant implications for the study of nonavertable inequalities, which would be voided as a result of their existence. This paper explores the condition for an n-tuple to be classified as nonstandard and provides a closer examination of the relationship between nonstandard n-tuples and nonavertable inequalities. A key finding reveals that an n-tuple is nonstandard if and only if its dual inequality is strongly active at a particular point, effectively linking the two concepts and implying that a nonstandard n-tuple would make the dual inequality highly active. This finding can be utilized to develop an efficient method for identifying nonstandard n-tuples, which in turn enables the construction of specific instances of nonavertable inequalities. A key theoretical result derived from this investigation expands upon a previous generalization involving n-tuples and provides a more precise condition for which sums of n-tuples would result in nonstandard n-tuples. Furthermore, this analysis facilitates the construction of explicit examples of nonstandard n-tuples in both the finite and infinite contexts. As an offshoot of this investigation, new conditions for the nonavertability of inequalities have emerged, which place additional constraints on the coefficients within these inequalities. It is also demonstrated that there exists a fundamental limitation to which all nonstandard n-tuples must conform, effectively limiting their diversity. Ultimately, this paper presents an open question regarding the existence of nonstandard n-tuples with specific characteristics and proposes a related conjecture for infinite n-tuples. It is also shown that a particular well-known sequence, which shares similarities with the well-known Dirichlet series, exhibits behavior akin to nonstandard n-tuples and may be of interest in this context. This paper also introduces an novel induction framework, which enables the efficient demonstration of the existence of certain sums of n-tuples under specific conditions. It is additionally proved that this new framework is equivalent to an earlier method for constructing specific instances of nonavertable inequalities. It is also shown that both this new framework and the earlier method are also applicable to constructing new inequalities within the context of complex n-tuples. It is worth noting that while this paper provides a comprehensive examination of the relationship between nonstandard n-tuples and nonavertable inequalities, further research is still necessary to fully characterize the behavior of nonstandard n-tuples. This study offers a new understanding and a revised method for the cycleGAN model in transferring the style of makeup images. We first point out the limitations of the original cycleGAN model, which primarily focuses on re-establishing a one-way connection between the real and synthetic images. Subsequently, we propose that the cycleGAN model should maintain bidirectional connections with both real and synthetic images. Our analysis also reveals that the adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layer plays a key role in the cycleGAN model, with two alternative implementations – the attribute vector and the input patch – that directly contribute to the cycleGAN loss. Building upon these findings, we introduce a revised cycleGAN model that incorporates a additional layer, namely the AdaIN layer, with the attribute vector and the input patch. Our experimental results on the WPU dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, with an overall improvement of 4.8% in Inception score compared to the original cycleGAN model. Moreover, our results on the large-scale WVU dataset show that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art methods with only a single-scale approach. The concept of deformed halo rotors is an intriguing topic that has not been thoroughly explored in nuclear physics. To better comprehend the structure of these unique rotational states, we developed a new class of deformed halo models using the non-local density distribution approach. By introducing an asymmetry parameter in the deformed potential, our model successfully replicates the irregular shape of rotational states within halos. Our analysis of alpha-emitting nuclei such as $^{19}$C and $^{26}$Al demonstrates that the density distribution of high-spin states in these halo nuclei assumes a prolate deformed shape, whereas lower-spin states or those with more extended distributions tend towards oblate deformation. Notably, our results also indicate that the shape of these rotating halos is significantly influenced by the extrusion of matter from the equatorial region, causing particles to occupy higher orbital levels and strengthening the prolate deformation. Our predictions also highlight the significance of considering multiple rotational states when inferring the ground-state shape of exotic nuclei. Finally, our study emphasizes the value of conducting alpha decay systematics in relation to rotational states to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the low-lying structure of these enigmatic nuclei.

This study presents an extension to existing parton distribution functions for electroweak bosons, W and Z, based on an interpretation of universal corrections in high-energy collisions. Relying on an effective treatment, the proposed PDFs effectively capture the impact of electroweak evolution beyond QCD alone, even if the underlying mechanism driving this evolution remains unclear. Our model places the electroweak boson PDFs in a broader context of leading-twist contributions, complementing other fundamental PDFs, such as those of the Higgs boson, top-quark, and bottom-quark. The added insight from top-quark PDF evolution contradicts a previous hypothesis, and our electroweak boson PDF analysis employed a robust set of LHC data at up to 13 TeV, encompassing not only vector boson scattering but also top-antitop associated production and top-quark PDF constraints. Our findings are expected to inform future precision studies at the LHC and future colliders. Additionally, this research introduces a publicly available code, {\tt NNPDF4EW}, encompassing the fitted PDFs and facilitating the computation of unpolarized electroweak splitting functions in the context of the DGLAP evolution equations.

This leads to the learning of an ill-conditioned world model, which can result in inaccurate predictions and guide the policy toward suboptimal solutions. To address this problem, we propose using multiple dynamics models with different focuses on action and observation spaces to improve the robustness of world models and enhance the quality of value function estimates. Our method involves developing an adversarial training technique for these models to enhance their diversity and utility. We evaluated our approach on a variety of multi-task episodes and found that it led to the generation of more accurate and robust value functions when interacting with real-world environments. Additionally, our method succeeded in enhancing the diversity of policies without incurring additional computational costs. Our results also revealed that our approach generates multiple viable solutions when confronted with complex problems, indicating that it has potential as a problem-solving framework. We present the analysis of radio observations taken in the K-band of the binary pulsar PSR B1133+16, conducted by the Five-Hundred Meter Aperture Radio Synthesis Telescope (FAST). The observations were carried out over 7.5 years, allowing for the detection of 24,576 on-plane phases and 1,536 off-plane phases. Within the on-plane phases, we pinpointed 31 distinct scattering patterns, featuring varied times of dispersion and swing periods. Notably, all screens were located at a cosmic distance of approximately 5 kiloparsecs from Earth. Our analysis of the data revealed the presence of an Earth-approaching screen during the initial stages of the orbit, as well as an Earth-receding screen towards the end of the orbit, both at a distance of around 0.06 AU from the pulsar. We estimate that these screens will take approximately 2-3 years to pass from the Earth-receding to the Earth-approaching position. Our research offers an opportunity to study the behavior of the pulsar's scintillation pattern over an extended period and from varying perspectives. Furthermore, our findings may contribute to a deeper understanding of the structure and dynamics of the interstellar medium in the direction of the pulsar. Additionally, we examined the properties of the screens in relation to those of the binary system and found no substantial evidence for an alignment between the screens and the orbital plane of the pulsar. However, we did detect a relationship between the times of swing and times of dispersion, which we attribute to the presence of an additional medium, likely associated with the binary system, affecting the propagation of the pulsar's signal. Lastly, we calculated the screen velocities relative to the pulsar and found them to be consistent with velocities observed in high-velocity clouds, suggesting that the screens may originate from the pulsar interacting with the interstellar medium but do not necessarily require a significant amount of time for it. Creating high-quality annotations for large datasets of text is a complicated task, especially when done manually. Annotators must follow numerous guidelines to effectively prepare their work for subsequent machine learning tasks. For applications such as sentence classification, label annotation involves not only identifying the class but also providing a reason for that classification. We investigated ways to simplify the annotation process by leveraging contextual language models such as BERT by asking two related but distinct questions: Can technology help reduce the time and effort required to annotate large amounts of text by facilitating easier interface use and by enabling the integration of contextual pre-training models to produce more accurate annotations? Our findings from testing different interface designs and model applications yielded promising results, showing both reduced annotation time and higher accuracy levels when using the more advanced models with better integrated interfaces. Specifically, we found significant decreases in annotation time (up to 25%) and overall improved accuracy (above 5%) when using the contextual LMs with better designed interfaces, even after accounting for additional annotation time in better designed interfaces. We also found that some annotation guidelines are more suited to the use of machine learning models and that these models can produce more accurate annotations even when compared to highly trained model performers in some cases. Finally, our results indicated that while the contextual LMs can produce higher quality annotations, there is still a significant discrepancy between model and human performance, with much room for improvement in using these models for annotation purposes. We believe our findings can guide future work aimed at enhancing the annotation process with machine learning models and also make available the code and data used in our experiments for other researchers to build upon. At high temperatures, the zero-energy peaks are significantly diminished, but at lower temperatures, they regain prominence, influenced by the spin-orbit coupling and fusion of zero-energy peaks due to time-reversal symmetry breaking. Experimentally, this distinction may only be observable through full-counting-field measurements; our results also demonstrate how temperature and fusion of zero-energy peaks affect the end-state signature in parity-inverted devices. Furthermore, we find that temperature can be used to distinguish between zero-energy peaks caused by vortices in superconducting loops and those resulting from the fusion of zero-energy peaks in nanowire devices. This distinction may only be achievable through comparison with finite-temperature Ginzburg-Landau theory and experimental manipulation of the loop geometry. Mobile data collection platforms can be an efficient tool for conducting road inspections, but their full potential is often hindered by slow data processing times and limited road network coverage. To overcome these limitations, we've developed RoadAtlas, an innovative open-source platform that utilizes spatial query optimization techniques and leverages in-memory database technology to significantly boost inspection performance. By minimizing data retrieval times and enabling users to take full advantage of their mobile device's capabilities, RoadAtlas can deliver up to 2.5 times faster data collection speeds. Furthermore, our solution includes a set of high-performance mobile apps designed to tackle various road inspection tasks, and we've observed a notable increase in data collection efficiency in real-world applications. Despite its speed benefits, RoadAtlas consumes minimal power, yielding little to no decrease in device battery life. To facilitate even greater performance improvements, we're actively contributing to the BetterFormatter project, which aims to refine the format of mobile data collection applications and promote the adoption of best practices across the industry. By providing both a high-speed platform and accompanying mobile apps, we're offering a comprehensive solution that can help other organizations optimize their own road inspection processes. Organizations interested in trying out RoadAtlas can download our source code from the GitHub repository listed in our project credits section. To learn more about our platform, including its features, design, and mobile app components, we invite readers to explore the remaining sections of this document. Finally, we're excited to share both our performance improvements and the associated data with the broader community, and we look forward to continuing the conversation through future development iterations. To achieve these results, we conducted a series of benchmark tests using both real-world and synthetic data sets to compare the inspection performance of RoadAtlas against other mobile data collection platforms. Our results have significant implications for the field of mobile data collection and provide a foundation for ongoing research and optimization efforts. We're actively seeking input and feedback from other developers and researchers who can help us refine RoadAtlas and explore new opportunities for performance improvement. To initiate this dialogue, we outline several key research questions and possibilities for collaboration in our conclusion section. Ultimately, we believe that our speed-enhanced RoadAtlas platform offers a valuable contribution to the mobile data collection community, and we're confident that its source code will inspire other innovators to create their own high-performance applications. As we continue to evolve RoadAtlas, we're committed to maintaining an open development approach that prioritizes community engagement, fosters collaboration, and promotes the rapid dissemination of new ideas. This study extends topological Hochschild homology (THH) to a bicategorical version, referred to as $\mathrm{THH}^{\mathrm{bic}}$, by incorporating the fundamental properties of bicategories through the language of shadows. By examining $\mathrm{THH}^{\mathrm{bic}}$ on the bicategory $\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{Comm})$ of perfect complexes in the category of abelian groups, we derive an unexpected connection to topological Hochschild cohomology (THHC). Additionally, we show that $\mathrm{THH}^{\mathrm{bic}}$ can distinguish between different bicategorical approaches, such as shadow conjugacy and strict conjugacy, by examining a family of bicategories generated by the sphere spectrum through stabilization. Finally, we establish a comparison map from $\mathrm{THH}^{\mathrm{bic}}$ to absolute homotopy groups, leading to a computation of $\mathrm{THH}^{\mathrm{bic}}(\mathrm{S}^2)$ as the absolute homotopy group $\pi^{\mathrm{abs}}_2$. Notably, this computation bypasses the need for an absolute homotopy group functor. By examining $\mathrm{THH}^{\mathrm{bic}}$ on the bicategory of fractals, we also obtain an expression for $\mathrm{THH}^{\mathrm{bic}}(\mathrm{S}^2)$ as the absolute homotopy group $\pi^{\mathrm{abs}}_2$, now including an action of the absolute Galois group of the rational numbers. This research is a preliminary step towards a bicategorical approach to homotopy group theories within the context of stable homotopy theory. It integrates the concepts of shadows and fractals to determine how homotopy groups are encoded in the structure of bicategories and functors between them. By generalizing THH in this manner, we aim to establish a connection between the algebraic structure of Hochschild homology and the geometric properties of homotopy groups, enabling the computation of $\mathrm{THH}^{\mathrm{bic}}(\mathrm{S}^2)$ as a nonabelian absolute homotopy group $\pi^{\mathrm{ab}}_2$, whose definition encompasses both abelian and nonabelian perspectives on homotopy groups. Lastly, this study paves the way for a broader investigation of the relationship between fractals, shadows, and homotopy

Sound source separation (SS) has flourished in recent years, primarily fueled by the success of deep neural network models, yet a significant obstacle in the field remains the limited availability of high-quality, labeled datasets. To address this issue, we introduce VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS), the first comprehensive dataset that incorporates source separation labels for 10 object categories, along with a broad range of 125 objects, and trains them on a fine-grained ImageNet dataset. VGG-SS surpasses existing datasets in terms of diversity, size, and precision of annotations, with an accurate classification rate of 0.85% on the Labeled Source Separation Dataset (LSS) scale. We also establish a publicly accessible dataset along with a separate evaluation setup and a simple baseline model for each category to facilitate and accelerate the development of advanced source separation algorithms. You can download VGG-SS at this link: https://drive.google.

This paper introduces the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), an innovative model that builds upon existing hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (H-GCNs). Our analysis reveals that H-GCNs' node encoding dimensions are arbitrarily selected, which can result in suboptimal representations. We rectify this limitation by incorporating a regularization term that minimizes dimensionality loss during hyperbolic graph learning. Our method enables tractable computation on the full hyperbolic space while ensuring that learned representations are compact and efficient. Moreover, we establish a connection between our approach and standard graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to demonstrate that our method extracts comparable performance from significantly fewer node dimensions. Experimental findings validate our method's efficacy when compared to contemporary H-GCNs and reveal that compact representations facilitate seamless adaptation to new nodes. Additionally, we observe that our approach yields engaging visualizations of embedded nodes in the hyperbolic plane. The code for Lorentzian graph convolutional networks is openly accessible on GitHub.

This study focuses on the stability of the inverse problem of identifying an initial condition in an acoustic equation governed by a boundary control system. A new approach involves establishing an observability inequality for the solution of the equation in question, which provides a measure of the visibility of the observation points. This inequality serves as a crucial element in forming a priori bound for an approximation of the initial condition. Utilizing the observability inequality and the a priori bound, we demonstrate stability of an approximation method based on a boundary control system. Specifically, we show that this approximation converges to the exact initial condition at a rate of $O(h^2)$ in the $L^2$ norm, where $h$ represents the step size of the discretization. This result is an enhancement to earlier stability estimates obtained through other methods. Consequently, this enhanced stability of the approximation leads to improved convergence rates in iterative methods such as the Tikhonov regularization and the Landweber iteration. Notably, this setting yields the optimal convergence rate of $O(h^{-2})$ in the $L^2$ norm for the Tikhonov method, which is the limiting case of a previous suboptimal estimate. Similarly, the optimized method achieves a better convergence rate than the previous known estimate in the case of the Landweber iteration. Finally, this increased stability of the approximation method translates to improved convergence rates for iterative methods even when the data is noisy. This is illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the paper. Notably, the paper introduces a new approach to establishing observability inequalities via the observability inequality of a related system with distinct modes. This new approach is applicable to a broader range of equations and systems than earlier methods. As an example, it facilitates derivation of an explicit $L^2$-based observability inequality for the acoustic equation in a rectangular domain. Additionally, the paper explores alternative methods of regularizing the inverse problem under uncertainty, especially when using observation data that is noisy. This is demonstrated through additional numerical experiments. The study employs a variety of techniques including Carleman estimates, observability inequalities, and theorems on stability estimates, as well as iterative methods such as the Tikhonov and Landweber iterations. The paper also introduces novel stability estimates for the approximation method based on the boundary control system and the observability inequality. Building the ideal optomechanical interface requires understanding how light and mechanical parameters interrelate at the single-photon level. A useful tool for this goal is the optomechanical scattering matrix, which describes how it converts optical modes into mechanical modes and vice versa. However, observing the optomechanical scattering matrix in action has been challenging until now. In our study, we use a hybrid optomechanical system consisting of an optical microresonator surrounded by an optomechanical nanowire to visualize the optomechanical scattering matrix at low-photon levels. This is achieved by observing the optomechanical parametric amplification process and back-converting a mechanical mode to an optical mode, which allows us to map out the optomechanical scattering matrix. Notably, we demonstrate that the optomechanical scattering matrix retains its diagonalized structure even in the presence of mechanical-mechanical correlations. Moreover, our findings show that the TSS effect can be an efficient means of optomechanical mode conversion, particularly when interacting with nearby optomechanical surfaces. Our work offers a new approach for studying and visualizing optomechanical phenomena in hybrid systems. This approach has the potential to advance our understanding of light-matter and matter-matter interactions in hybrid systems, which could lead to new applications in optomechanical communication and sensing. This technique may also enable the detection of tiny changes in optomechanical parameters, which could be useful in sensing mechanical properties or environmental changes in hybrid systems. Our study focuses on microwave-optical optomechanical systems, but the concept can be extended to other systems, such as sound-optical or far-field optomechanical systems, by modifying the optomechanical scattering matrix to accommodate different parameters. This work has the potential to contribute to the development of optimal interfaces between light and mechanical waves in optomechanical systems. This could be crucial for improving the efficiency of optomechanical communication and sensing, particularly in far-field optomechanical systems. Our study demonstrates that the TSS effect can occur even in the presence of nonlinear interactions within the mechanical resonator, which could lead to the creation of mechanical soliton waves. However, this requires a highly nonlinear regime involving large-amplitude mechanical waves. Our findings show that the TSS effect can also result from linear optomechanical interactions in hybrid systems, which makes it an efficient means of optomechanical mode conversion. This could have implications for the generation of mechanical soliton waves

In our study, we combine $u$-calculus with atoms from Boolean algebra, set theory, and relational algebra, examining how the addition of these atoms influences the computational properties of $u$-calculus. Our investigation shows that the presence of any individual type of atom within $u$-calculus results in either no enhancement or a significant increase in satisfiability, alongside an upgrade in Medved's reduced $u$-calculus to full $u$-calculus. Furthermore, we establish that the interplay between different atomic structures can lead to additional complexity in satisfiability and Medved's reduced $u$-calculus. These findings demonstrate the value of atomic components in the study of logic-based formalisms and facilitate discussions on future areas of research. Our theoretical advancements are complemented by concrete examples and proofs. Moreover, we contribute a publicly accessible tool for verifying our results and exploring additional scenarios. This resource is currently only accessible through our custom-built engine in a non-interactive mode. However, future developments aim to integrate this into a more versatile and user-friendly framework. The Tsallis distribution has been extensively utilized in various disciplines such as physics and social dynamics. However, many people remain unaware of the connection between the Tsallis distribution and a specific social system - online social rankings. In this study, we demonstrate that followers' voting behavior in platforms like Reddit, Twitter, and China's Weibo can be analyzed using a single parameter, the Tsallis distribution, which reveals valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of these systems. By examining the Tsallis distribution in online rankings, we identify key factors that influence them, including the quality of the ranked product and the pricing of the ranked service. Our research further shows that followers' voting behavior adheres to the Tsallis distribution when they choose between two options: optimizing the best result or averaging all results. In conclusion, we believe that analyzing online social rankings using the Tsallis distribution offers a valuable framework for understanding social dynamics in these systems. This study could also be applied to other rating systems, such as those employed in economic systems. Investigating the impact of a mass term in gravitational perturbations, our study finds that adding a certain mass term leads to a pure ghost-like degree of freedom instead of the expected two additional degrees of freedom. This phenomenon occurs when a mass term is added to specific scalar modes in a linearized gravity theory. Consequently, we demonstrate that an effective Lagrangian can be formulated using a higher derivative term for a specific ghost-like degree of freedom. Utilizing this new Lagrangian, we calculate the gravitational perturbation's one-loop correction to the Higgs decay width into two gravitons. Notably, this correction opposes the enhancement caused by the top-quark loop in the decay width. Additionally, we consider the influence of this new term on gravitational wave spectra generated during inflation and cosmic dissipation. Our analysis indicates that the mass generation in gravitational waves offers an alternative explanation for the amplitude of certain tensor modes observed in certain multi-field inflationary scenarios. Furthermore, we find that the mass-driven decay of gravitational waves can resolve the phase transition enigma by stabilizing the SM vacuum during the early universe. However, this outcome hinges on the universe's temperature during the first phase transition falling below 140 TeV. We also explore the possibility of detecting this new ghost-like degree of freedom through future decay width measurements of Higgs bosons at the LHC with upgraded luminosity or through indirect detection via fifth-force searches at low-energy particle colliders. We find that certain mass ranges can be probed up to 10 TeV, depending on the experiment's sensitivity. If not confirmed, our findings predict that Higgs decay to gravitons will significantly underpredict the observed decay rate at future LHC with upgraded luminosity. We also identify that future LHC with upgraded luminosity has the potential to investigate mass ranges that could explain the amplitude of certain tensor modes generated during multi-field inflation, provided that initial conditions are minimal. Nevertheless, if the universe's initial conditions were substantial, this scenario would fall outside the LHC's detection capacity. A new hypothesis is introduced, suggesting that extended double covers of signed graphs are completely planarizable only if the original graph is a planar embedding. To support this idea, a previously known result is restated - that the EDC of a signed planar graph is topologically equivalent to the original graph. A new feature is established - if a signed planar graph's EDC is topologically equivalent to a planar embedding of another graph, then that graph is also topologically equivalent to a planar embedding. Finally, a method is shown to derive a complete EDC of a signed planar graph from any planar embedding of the graph, indicating that such an EDC is always topologically equivalent to the original graph. Consequently, it's concluded that the concept of finding an extended double cover that is topologically equivalent to a given planar embedding is equivalent to the halting problem for a Turing machine that can decide any computable problem, implying that there is no efficient algorithm to determine whether an extended double cover of a signed graph exists that is topologically equivalent to a specific planar embedding. Additionally, it's proposed that the ability to determine if an extended double cover of a signed graph exists that is planar and topologically equivalent to the original graph, is equivalent to the ability to decide any computable problem, although further research is required to validate this conjecture. Several open questions are also posed regarding the relationship between extended double covers and the ability to decide any computable problem. Lastly, three theorems are proved that demonstrate the computational completeness of certain graph cover operations, including extended double covers, for any context-free languages that have linear context-free representations. These theorems provide sufficient evidence to support the broader conjecture that any graph cover operation is planar-completeness equivalent to deciding any computable problem for graph classes that have an extended double cover that is topologically equivalent to any planar embedding. Notably, this is already confirmed for single-source out-trees, multi-source out-trees, and context-free graphs. Furthermore, it's shown that for any graph class that has an extended double cover that is topologically equivalent to any planar embedding, there is an algorithm that can decide any computable problem when restricted to that class, provided that the graph class can be recognized in polynomial time. This paper delves into the comparison of four types of Hamiltonian dynamics found within quantum equilibrium states: microcanonical, canonical at finite temperatures, grand canonical with temperature and chemical potential as parameters, and classical dynamics as described by Liouville equations. The investigation focuses on evaluating thermal time-scales $\tau_\text{th}$ for different systems and dynamics using a simple harmonic oscillator model from these four dynamics. The thermal time-scales are found to correlate with energy decay rates $\Gamma$ in the presence of small perturbations, with values ranging from $2\Gamma$ for microcanonical states to $\Gamma$ for canonical and grand canonical states. The distinction in $\tau_\text{th}$ among these three dynamics originates from distinct scaling of thermal correlations with temperature, influenced by overcounting in the canonical ensemble. The comparison also reveals that quantum effects reduce $\tau_\text{th}$ by roughly an order of magnitude compared to their classical counterparts, with additional variations arising within different quantum states due to coherent oscillations and dephasing dynamics. The definitions of thermal time-scales are applicable across multiple systems and could provide a common framework for comparing timescales within different quantum equilibrium states and their corresponding classical counterparts. The proposed framework of thermal time-scales may offer a way to reconcile timescales across various systems and help answer fundamental questions about the coherence of systems at different temperatures. The potential of this approach is illustrated through the example of one component of a coupled harmonic oscillator system, where coherent oscillations in $\tau_\text{th}$ could potentially be exploited for constructive aims. The concepts introduced in the paper have implications for a broader range of systems, including those involving multiple modes and those described through Liouville equations. The comparison of thermal time-scales could also raise questions about the underlying dynamics of systems and their equilibrium states, giving rise to possibilities for further research and the application of the framework to existing theoretical and experimental data. The concepts of thermal time-scales can be probed through experimental techniques such as spectroscopy, offering avenues for validating theoretical predictions. The comparison of thermal time-scales could also highlight the necessity for a reevaluation of theoretical descriptions in favor of those that do not overcount, such as the microcanonical ensemble, particularly for systems requiring strong restrictions. The distinction of thermal time-scales also has implications for our understanding of thermal correlations and how they evolve over time, influencing our perception of thermal equilibrium within isolated systems. The comparison of thermal time-scales may ultimately lead to a deeper comprehension of the dynamics of systems in various equilibrium states

This phenomenon is confirmed through numerical simulations for different system and bath parameters. Moreover, we've established that system-bath coupling strength affects the rate of negentropy transfer, and this rate is minimized at a specific coupling strength that corresponds to an anti-Newtonian dynamics condition. These findings contribute to a better understanding of the thermodynamic arrow of time in open systems. In turn, this could facilitate the visualization of negative temperature in these systems. A cutting-edge method has been introduced for the automatic classification and severity assessment of colorectal polyps through a combination of deep learning networks. This innovative approach utilizes a convolutional neural network to analyze endoscopic images and accurately identify and grade polyps by analyzing the entire image, rather than relying on semi-supervised data from the Optima platform. Remarkably, the team achieved outstanding results even without utilizing specialized medical knowledge, achieving high accuracy levels in both classification and grading tasks. Furthermore, the method demonstrated remarkable robustness in handling images from diverse sources, or in cases where the training and testing datasets significantly differ. The study's findings were exceptionally high, with an overall accuracy rate of 96.14% in classification and a mean absolute error of 0.22 in grading, according to the SMI scale. Notably, the team's method outperformed other comparison models with deeper structures, demonstrating that complex networks are not always necessary for optimal performance. Additionally, the study examined various loss functions and optimization techniques, determining that the Adam optimizer and categorical cross-entropy loss yielded the best results. The team also implemented an easy-to-use command-line tool called ColonClassifier, making it simple for healthcare professionals to utilize the model with minimal technical expertise required. This practical solution allows users to classify and grade polyps through a straightforward command-line interface, making it an extremely useful resource in clinical settings. In conclusion, the study presents an exceptionally effective deep learning-based method for detecting and grading colorectal polyps, producing remarkably accurate results even in the absence of specialized medical knowledge. The accompanying software, ColonClassifier, also provides a highly convenient solution for healthcare professionals to utilize the model easily in clinical environments. The NLSWACF method was initially developed to address computational challenges in frequency-domain methods for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering problems, particularly those featuring high frequencies and irregular surface mappings. To provide a more feasible and stable implementation, the algorithm has been modified to use an interior penalty approach within a nested multigrid framework. This modification maintains the original's spirit of complexity while improving its practicality. To facilitate solution of the linear system, the implementation includes an iterative Krylov solver and a multigrid solver for the coarse problem. A crucial aspect is the introduction of interface degrees of freedom, which are determined through a weak enforcement of boundary conditions. The algorithm has been evaluated on several scenarios, including scattering off an implicitly defined obstacle and simulations of seismic wave propagation in complex geological environments. Results comparing the NLSWACF method to an explicit FEM implementation are presented, highlighting its performance in terms of computational efficiency, accuracy, and feasibility for large-scale applications. Furthermore, results from the algorithm are verified against industrial standards and published data. All implementations are available open-source as part of the Alfewac project. We've analyzed the water content in three Antarctic finds from common asteroids (Qubera West, Qubera East and Sherdog) and compared it with two recent asteroid falls from the same category (Benenitra and Chelyabinsk). Using laser-based techniques to measure water content, we found similar H2O levels in the Antarctic finds and the Benenitra and Chelyabinsk meteorites, indicating little change in water content over time for these specific asteroid types. Building upon the existing framework for spin-lattice tensor products, we've derived expressions for the scalar products and form factors of the XXZ chain with an arbitrary number of descending sites. These expressions are valid for both ferromagnetic and anti-ferromagnetic ground states and lay the groundwork for in-depth investigations of the model's corner behavior, edge singularities, and string hulls that influence the model's dynamics. Our study specifically explores the two-lattice version of the XXZ chain, often referred to as the "dynamical corner transfer-matrix model." By relating the model to its semi-infinite counterpart, we've obtained precise expressions for the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenoperators of the model. These expressions offer a detailed understanding of the model's edge behavior and provide a robust framework for analyzing the associated operator-algebraic representation. Notably, our study reveals a direct, bilinear mapping between the operator-algebraic charge and magnetization operators in both the finite and semi-infinite systems. This mapping significantly simplifies the analysis of edge singularities and string excitations in the two-lattice XXZ chain. As a central aspect of our study, we've developed a comprehensive framework for accurately calculating form factors and edge correlations in the two-lattice XXZ chain. This framework is an essential precursor to a more in-depth examination of the model's corner behavior, edge singularities, string excitations, and descent properties. As such, our study offers a foundational contribution to a broader, more in-depth analysis of the two-lattice XXZ chain. As an ancillary investigation, our study also derives a new algebraic realization of the $gl_2({\mathcal C})$ Lie algebra using the quantum channel operator ${\mathfrak E}$, which is defined through the matrix product form ${\mathfrak E}(x) = f(x) {\mathfrak T} x$, where $f(x)$ is a scalar function dependent on $x$. Notably, this new algebraic representation precisely replicates the scalar product formulas we've previously obtained. As such, our study offers a direct proof of these formulas via the use of quantum channels. As an added benefit, our study also presents a novel proof of the $Q$-matrix orthogonality and determinant calculation for the XXZ chain, both of which are well-established results. This paper introduces a suite of innovative methods to achieve zero-shot speech translation, focusing on applying pre-trained speech and translation models to tackle language barriers in audio data domains. Unlike conventional approaches to speech translation that rely on fine-tuning models within the target domain, our proposed frameworks leverage the strengths of pre-trained models to overcome linguistic obstacles in audio data domains with no need for domain-specific training. Notably, our methods excel in few-shot settings, demonstrating substantial gains in performance when only a limited amount of target domain data is available. We evaluate our approaches through extensive experiments in zero-shot speech translation for English-to-English and multilingual zero-shot speech translation, covering seven languages. Our findings show that our proposed methods surpass baseline techniques by achieving average sentence-level isolation scores of 75.3% and 68.9% in zero-shot speech translation and 78.8% and 71.4% in zero-shot multilingual speech translation for the 5-shot and all-shot settings, respectively. Unlike previous studies, our methods successfully generalize well to new speakers and domains. We also observe notable performance gains in low-data settings, with some methods showing significant improvements over strong baselines even with as few as 5 target domain examples per speech translation pair. All models, data, and code are openly accessible for replication and further research. In particular, our frameworks represent viable solutions to address the data isolation problems commonly encountered in speech translation. Overall, our work represents a significant step towards achieving true zero-shot speech translation, i.e., speech translation without the need for labeled target domain data or domain-specific training, an essential milestone given the massive data requirements of current speech translation models. As such, it offers valuable insights to the community for developing zero-shot speech translation models capable of generalizing effectively to any audio data domain. We introduce Generalized Spherical Multipoles (GSMs), a novel general form of multipoles that can accurately account for the interaction between light and complex systems. By applying an unitary transformation to the standard Cartesian multipoles, GSMs offer an intuitive and efficient way to analyze and assess light scattering properties. Utilizing GSMs, we demonstrate that the end result of light scattering, the far-field density matrix, can be fully understood and computed using only a few key multipoles. Specifically, we find that only quadrupoles and octupoles are essential for complex structures lacking spherical symmetry. We further show that structures composed of multiple disconnected parts can be analyzed on a case-by-case basis by considering only the multipoles associated with each individual component. Our approach is validated through numerical simulations and comparisons with existing data. Moreover, we derive an analytical expression to extract optical scattering coefficients from standard multipoles and offer a simple algorithm to determine the optical scattering properties of any complex system. Our method is highly versatile and can be applied to charged particles as well as dielectric systems, providing a comprehensive framework for studying light scattering off complex systems. Our findings are highly relevant to the development of metasurfaces and electromagnetically interacting systems, and we anticipate that our approach will pave the way for innovative designs and a deeper understanding of light-matter interaction in complex environments. By publicly sharing the associated software, we strive to facilitate the utilization of our method by the scientific community. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the growth of multipoles as a full-fledged paradigm for the analysis and engineering of light-matter interaction in complex systems.

We utilize exact diagonalization to analyze the behavior of interacting electrons in a two-dimensional square lattice, specifically for d-orbitals in transition metal oxides such as cuprates and nickelates. By adjusting the on-site interaction strength and a classical spin-orbit coupling within this framework, we investigate the impact of these parameters on the emergence of topological phases in transition metal oxides. Our study reveals that large spin-orbit coupling in these materials is hindered by strong interactions and opposing effects from neighboring orbitals, and that a minimal effective spin-orbit coupling is required for topological phase formation, influencing the entire phase diagram of interacting electrons in this context. Furthermore, interaction strength and crystal field splitting are found to compete with a minimal effective spin-orbit coupling to drive the system towards a topological phase, with this minimal effective spin-orbit coupling being a critical factor in determining the overall phase diagram. Additionally, we identify that interaction-strength- and crystal-field-induced variations in orbital occupancy are key to understanding the behavior of the system, and that the smallest orbital components contributing to these effects hold the most significant importance. This research is relevant to ongoing experimental studies aimed at uncovering the fundamental physics governing transition metal oxides, particularly in narrow d-orbitals. Given a smooth subvariety defined by intersecting a toric variety with complete intersections, its relative $I$-function can be computationally determined using the Aoki-Hattori formula. For certain types of smooth subvarieties, their relative $I$-functions exhibit a meaningful relationship with each other. In this study, we establish that this relationship holds not just for certain types of smooth subvarieties, but for all smooth subvarieties in toric complete intersections. Additionally, this relationship can be expressed through a graph that implies the rational connectivity of the subvariety. This graph also contains the information to compute the relative $L$-function of the subvariety. In the case where the subvariety is defined over integers, its relative $L$-function also reflects the rational connectivity of the subvariety. This study expands upon known results for smooth hypersurfaces and rational normal curves, and it provides the foundation for a more comprehensive investigation into the properties of relative $I$- and $L$-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. This investigation will shed light on the diverse and unique properties of these functions. This study's goal is to examine how generative models' underlying representations of medical conditions and patient identities contribute to the creation of biased images. We argue that code-space manipulation offers a clear and effective pathway for analyzing and addressing bias issues. To facilitate this analysis, we introduce a simple yet practical approach to identifying and extracting relevant latent codes from generative models like GANs. Applying this approach to a synthetic dataset that mimics real-world clinical data, we investigate how different models' underlying representations of medical conditions and patient characteristics influence the generation of biased images. Our findings highlight the advantages of using generative models that incorporate disentangled latent codes and demonstrate methods for codifying medical conditions and patient identities into latent space. Furthermore, we showcase a user-friendly visualization of our findings on a real-world dataset of chest X-rays from the MS-Coco dataset. Exploring high-dimensional data is a complex task that requires both technical and visual expertise. To make data analysis more accessible, we've developed ViDaExpert, an intuitive web-based application that enables easy, interactive visualization of multiple-dimensional spaces. By simplifying the process of data reduction and clustering, ViDaExpert allows users to quickly gain insights into their data sets, regardless of their technical background. The application is now available as an open-source platform on GitHub, along with a set of pre-built tools that include Mozilla Alchemy for text data and ELK for numerical data. ViDaExpert is particularly useful in promoting computational thinking and data literacy among students and young professionals. Additionally, it can be a valuable teaching tool for demonstrating key data analysis concepts, such as data dimensionality and clustering, and is suitable for use in both academic and industrial settings. ViDaExpert is compatible with big data sets, given its underlying technology is based on Elasticsearch, a robust database capable of handling large amounts of data. For more information, please visit the project website at http://vidaexpert.com. The application is available for download at https://github.com/vidaexpert/vidaexpert. ViDaExpert is the result of a project initiated by the European School of Data Science, and we'd like to express our gratitude to the project sponsors for their support. This research focuses on developing a second-order two-dimensional monomial approximation using a mesh-based approach and applying it to approximate functions and their derivatives. Unlike one-dimensional monomial extrapolation, two-dimensional monomial approximations have multiple equivalents, leading to different choices in order of accuracy. Our studies reveal that a carefully selected, high-order approximation can yield precise results, even when compared to higher-order methods, given a sufficiently fine mesh. Our strategy allows for efficient function and derivative approximation across existing mesh structures, offering a useful technique for various applications, such as multigrid methods, where function and derivative information can be leveraged to accelerate convergence. Our results demonstrate that using this approximation, we can achieve similar accuracy to that of a second-order ODE solver using the method of lines, without requiring internal time-stepping, and that it can be an effective way to improve the accuracy of the multigrid method, especially for difficult problems. Moreover, our approach can be an alternative to the recently introduced spatially compact difference operators, providing similar accuracy with less storage requirements. We demonstrate the efficiency of this approximation by applying it to a range-dependent Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, a model reduction problem, and a control system, an ODE system, and an elliptic PDE system. The implementation of the monomial approximation is made available as part of the PyGS library. Future work is planned to expand this work to higher-order approximations and multiple dimensions.
